plications when a significant degree of sparing is
not possible. For nasal tumors, this is likely to cor-
respond to increased risks of bone necrosis (poten-
tially leading to fistula development) due to the
alpha/beta ratio of bone.
A related concept to the above topic is that of
tumor control probability (TCP) and normal tissue
complication probability (NTCP). For a given dose
or course of radiation, there is some probability of
tumor control and a corresponding probability of a
severe normal tissue complication (Hall and
Giaccia, 2011). At low doses, the probability of
either is minimal and at high doses, both become
increasingly likely. Ideally, we would select a radia-
tion dose that maximizes TCP while maintaining a
low and acceptable NTCP, thus maximizing the
therapeutic index of radiation. Advanced radiation
techniques may allow the radiation oncologist to
escalate the effective dose to a tumor target
(increasing TCP) while still sparing or minimizing
dose to neighboring normal structures (thus
decreasing or maintaining low NTCP). As dis-
cussed later in this chapter, the goal of using drugs
that could act as radiation sensitizers or radiation
protectors is to similarly widen the therapeutic
index by improving TCP without a corresponding
increase in NTCP (radiation sensitizer) or to
decrease NTCP without a corresponding decrease
in TCP (radiation protector).
Factors Infuencing Radiation Response
(The Rs of Radiation)
How any tumor responds to radiation is impacted by
a variety of factors. There are factors associated with
the tumor itself including its intrinsic radiosensitivity,
the total tumor burden/volume, and the rate of cell
proliferation and cell loss. There are also factors
associated with the radiation course itself including
total radiation dose, radiation dose per fraction,
and the period of time the radiation course extends
over, collectively referred to as time, dose, and frac-
tionation. Finally, there are factors related to the
patient that may include the patient’s normal tissue
radiosensitivity, immune response to the tumor, and
perfusion to the tumor.
Radiation courses are typically fractionated or
divided into multiple doses in order to improve the
rate of tumor control for a given level of toxicity.
Classically, the “four Rs” of radiobiology were
described by Withers and have been used to describe
the factors or biologic events that occur between
fractions of a radiation course that impact tumor
response (Lett and Adler, 1975). These are Repair,
Repopulation, Redistribution, and Reoxygenation.
An expansion of this concept to include a fifth factor
known as intrinsic Radiosensitivity was introduced
by Steel (Steel et al., 1989). More recently, additional
“Rs” describing tumor and host factors that influ-
ence the response to a course of radiation have been
proposed including Remodeling of the tumor micro-
environment, Rejection by the immune system, and
Remote bystander effects (Brown et al., 2014; Golden
and Formenti, 2014; Kim et al., 2015; Arnold et al.,
2018).
Repair
Many experiments have demonstrated the impor-
tance of cellular repair and recovery in the response
to fractionated doses of radiation. Specifically,
repair of DNA that is damaged by radiation plays
the largest role. Based on experiments looking at
split doses of radiation or continuous irradiation at
varying dose rates, radiation damage can be char-
acterized as lethal damage or repairable/sublethal
damage (Frankenberg-Schwager et al., 1985;
Bedford, 1991). Sublethal damage can be repaired
unless it compounded by additional damage that
can accumulate to become lethal to the cell.
Different types of cells have varying capacity to
recover from sublethal damage. This is often dis-
played by how much the initial portion of a cell
survival curve bends as dose increases. This is
described quantitatively by the linear–quadratic
model of radiation survival and the alpha/beta
ratio (described in the previous section). This
alpha/beta ratio is typically low for most tumors

-- 29 of 258 --

and rapidly-dividing normal tissues and is high for
most late-responding tissues which have much
higher potential for repair of sublethal damage.
Since late-responding tissues and late effects are
classically the most dose-limiting, this phenomenon
is exploited by giving many smaller radiation frac-
tions as the sublethal damage from these smaller
individual doses can be repaired more readily by
the late-responding tissues compared to tumor
cells. A meta-analysis of hyperfractionated radia-
tion trials in human head and neck cancer reported
significant benefit from hyperfractionation com-
pared to conventional fractionation on survival
and locoregional control (Budach et al., 2006;
Anonymous, 2017).
Repopulation
The effects of radiation on tissue and tumors depends
on the balance of inactivation of cells with the prolif-
eration of cells taking place during the treatment
course. It has been shown that for the same dose per
fraction and number of fractions (and therefore the
same total dose), the amount of time over which that
total dose is delivered has an impact on response,
even when there is sufficient time between fractions
for full repair of sublethal damage. It has also been
shown that normal tissues and tumors can poten-
tially undergo acceleration of repopulation after
radiation damage. This repopulation varies by tissue
and tumor type; however, it is generally reported to
be slow during the first 2 weeks but accelerates
between the 3rd and 7th week of conventional ther-
apy and may result in the effective loss of 0.5–0.7 Gy
per day when treatment schedules are extended. The
importance of overall treatment time is much greater
in more rapidly growing tumor types (Trott and
Kummermehr, 1991; Harari and Huang, 2006;
Bernier et al., 2009).
Modern radiation fractionation schemes are
based on manipulating repopulation and repair to
maximize tumor cell kill relative to normal tissue
toxicity, particularly in late-responding tissues.
Redistribution
Tumor cell populations proliferate asynchronously
with uneven distribution through the phases of the
cell cycle. Many tumors have a relatively short cell
cycle duration of 1–2 days. S phase typically lasts
about 1/3 of the cell cycle length. Since cells in S
phase are about three times more radioresistant
than cells in M phase, there is a significant popula-
tion of these more radioresistant cells at any time
(Bentzen, 2003; Marcu et al., 2015). Fractionated
radiation overcomes this resistance challenge due
to cells moving into a different phase of the cell
cycle between consecutive doses of radiation.
Reoxygenation
Tumor oxygenation is a major factor in radiation
response, with the presence of tumor hypoxia cor-
responding to poorer tumor control. Acute hypoxia
exists when blood vessels are transiently occluded,
and chronic hypoxia occurs when cells exceed the
maximum oxygen diffusion distance from capillar-
ies (100–150 μm). The oxygen status of cells varies
with time. Acute hypoxia is transient by its nature,
but chronically hypoxic cells can also change their
status through a course of radiation therapy due to
decreased oxygen consumption by the tumor,
tumor shrinkage, and/or vascular remodeling
(Bayer et al., 2011; Harada, 2011). Accordingly,
fractionating radiation helps to overcome tumor
resistance secondary to hypoxia due to the phe-
nomenon of reoxygenation.
Intrinsic radiosensitivity
Populations of normal cells and tumor cells have
different levels of radiosensitivity. This is generally
thought to be due to differences in intracellular
pathways including those involved in DNA damage
responses, cell cycle, and cell proliferation. As
tumor cells must have aberrations in these path-
ways, there is significant variability in radiosensi-
tivity between two different tumors.
Rejection by the immune system
The role of the immune system in tumor response
to radiation is incompletely understood but studies
showed reduced therapeutic efficacy of radiation in
mice lacking T cells (Stone et al., 1979; Boustani
et al., 2019). Innate and adaptive immune responses
are induced by the cellular damage caused by radia-
tion. Radiation has been shown to counteract
tumor immune evasion by upregulating major
histocompatibility complex (MHC) class 1 expression
of tumor cells, thus allowing tumor cell recognition
by cytotoxic CD8 T cells (Park et al., 2014). These
immunostimulatory effects are mitigated by the
microenvironment of many cancers, which is often
14 	I. Gordon

-- 30 of 258 --

15	Radiation Therapy
highly immunosuppressive. The impact of radiation
dose on immune response is complex as radiation
has well-described anti-inflammatory effects, par-
ticularly at low doses of 1 Gy and below, but higher
radiation doses to tumors may be more stimulating
of a tumor immune response (Bedford, 1991; Frey
et al., 2015).
Remodeling of the tumor microenvironment
Ionizing radiation can alter the interactions between
tumor cells and the tumor microenvironment. One
of the most well demonstrated of these effects is the
impact of radiation on tumor microvasculature,
although these effects are dose dependent. Low-dose
radiation may stimulate neovascularization and
result in tumor vessel relaxation, improving oxy-
genation (Kim et al., 2015). High doses of radiation
(>10 Gy per fraction) are associated with severe
vascular damage, leading to marked changes in the
tumor microenvironment (Park et al., 2012; Hellevik
and Martinez-Zubiaurre, 2014; Song et al., 2014).
This damage occurs through endothelial cell apopto-
sis. Accordingly, tumors treated with fractionated
radiation show less vascular damage than tumors
treated with a single high dose of radiation. This
feature is complex or may have a paradoxical
impact considering that high-dose radiation treat-
ments may disrupt tumor vasculature, leading to cell
death, but may also generate increased regions of
hypoxia, which confers radiation resistance.
Remote bystander effects
Bystander effects were described previously and are
consequences to cells that are not directly “hit” by
radiation. These effects can include DNA damage
or cell death in nontargeted cells and are thought to
be due to extracellular signals that are emitted by
targeted cells (Gerweck et al., 2006; Ponnaiya
et al., 2007; Maeda et al., 2016; Autsavapromporn
et al., 2019). Observed abscopal effects where an
irradiated tumor causes unirradiated distant lesions
to regress is a similar phenomenon (Collen and
Mayer, 2006; Kim et al., 2008).
Biology of Low-Dose or Finely
Fractionated versus High-Dose Per
Fraction Radiation
An increasing number of veterinary cancer patients
are being treated with relatively hypofractionated,
high-dose protocols, especially with SRT tech-
niques. This shift has occurred largely as a result of
technological advances in radiation equipment
reaching more of the veterinary field in combina-
tion with the interest of many pet owners in mini-
mizing the number of visits and anesthetic episodes
involved in a radiation treatment course for their
pet. As many of the factors that influence radiation
response described in the previous section are
impacted by fractionation and/or fractional radia-
tion dose, there is renewed effort to assess whether
radiation response is fundamentally different bio-
logically at high doses or primarily an extension of
previously established concepts for fractionated
radiation (Golden and Formenti, 2014).
In high-dose radiation, shortened courses with
fewer numbers of fractions are associated with
decreased DNA repair, cell cycle redistribution, cell
repopulation, and reoxygenation between frac-
tions. One might anticipate that the relative bene-
fits of these aspects of fractionation in exploiting
differences between late-responding tissue and
tumor cells would decrease the therapeutic index of
high-dose radiation fractions. However, at least in
high-dose stereotactic radiation, this is mitigated by
relative dose sparing of normal tissues (although
potentially also to invasive tumor cells outside of
the 	gross 	tumor 	volume) 	by 	the 	treatment
technique.
Intrinsic radiosensitivity defines characteristics
inherent to cells that are independent of dose per
fraction but for tumor cells that have a high capac-
ity to repair sublethal damage (i.e., melanoma),
higher-dose fractions may be considerably more
cytotoxic (Bentzen et al., 1989).
It has been suggested that direct tumor cell death
does not completely account for the efficacy of
high-dose radiation and that this may be due to a
greater impact of these high-dose fractions on
rejection by the immune system and/or remodeling
of the tumor microenvironment. Radiation doses >
10 Gy per fraction induce more severe and sus-
tained vascular damage and occlusion, particularly
tumor blood vessels (Clement et al., 1978;
Anonymous, 2009; Kim et al., 2015). Consistent
with this mechanism of indirect tumor cell death
are mouse studies that have shown tumor cell sur-
vival over the days following radiation decreases
compared to day 0 with high-dose radiation (15–
20 Gy) but not at low doses (i.e., 10 Gy or less).
Because radiation damage is nearly instantaneous,
this enhanced delayed cytotoxicity at very high

-- 31 of 258 --

doses suggests an indirect cause of cytotoxicity
such as changes to vasculature or the microenvir-
onment (Frankenberg-Schwager et al., 1985).
However, there is conflicting data about these dif-
ferences in secondary cell killing due to changes in
the microenvironment and there is currently insuf-
ficient evidence to conclude that this is an import-
ant factor in tumor response to high-dose radiation
(Golden and Formenti, 2014).
It has also been shown that high-dose radiation
activates a greater antitumor CD8+ T-cell response
as well as increased antigenicity of tumors (Lee
et al., 2009). There is anecdotal clinical evidence of
immune rejection of metastatic distant tumors in
human patients with melanoma, but these reports
are sporadic, and it is unclear whether this repre-
sents a more general phenomenon or one limited to
a subset of melanoma (Golden and Formenti,
2014).
A key question is whether existing radiobiologic
modeling with the linear–quadratic equation and
resulting BED is adequate to explain the effects
seen at high doses or if changes in the factors listed
above change these paradigms. This topic was well
reviewed by Brown et al. (2014) and the conclusion
was that for most tumors, the standard radiobiol-
ogy concepts including the five Rs were sufficient
to explain the available data for high-dose radia-
tion although there likely are some tumors that
radiation may generate enhanced antitumor immu-
nity for. They also concluded that clinical improve-
ments in outcomes in patients with non-small-cell
lung tumors and brain metastases treated with
high-dose SRT appear to be due to the ability to
safely deliver higher BEDs and not due to new bio-
logic effects of those higher doses per fraction
(Golden and Formenti, 2014). Despite these con-
clusions, this is an active area of ongoing study.
Drugs that Modify the Radiation
Response (Radiation Sensitizers
and Protectors)
There are two reasons why tumors may fail to
respond or be controlled after radiation. The first is
geographic miss, which is the scenario when areas
occupied by tumor cells were not incorporated in
the treated volume. The second and more common
reason is that a population of tumor cells was
resistant to the radiation dose that was delivered.
The obvious approach to this common reason for
treatment failure is dose escalation as higher doses
of radiation to a target should result in increasing
rates of cytotoxicity and tumor control. The chal-
lenge to this solution is the tolerance of normal
tissues, which ultimately limits the maximum radi-
ation dose that can be safely delivered. In most
circumstances, the efficacy of radiation is primarily
limited by the tolerance of adjacent normal tissues.
The consequence of these radiation dose limita-
tions is that the rate of local tumor control for most
tumors is significantly less than 100%.
The concept of therapeutic index describes the
effect of a treatment (in this case, radiation dose)
that causes a desired effect relative to the risk that
it results in unacceptable toxicity. By convention,
radiation treatment protocols are often intended to
limit severe toxicity risk to a tolerable level (i.e.,
5% risk) while achieving a desired degree of local
tumor control in a substantial percentage of
patients. For certain aggressive diseases, a higher
rate of toxicity may be acceptable if there is at least
a corresponding increase in the rate of local tumor
control.
A different approach to widen the therapeutic
index of radiation is the use of drugs that selec-
tively sensitize tumor cells to radiation or selec-
tively protect normal tissues from the effects of
radiation. This selectivity is critical to the potential
utility of a radiation-modifying drug. This selectiv-
ity can be achieved by a variety of characteristics
including selective uptake, retention, or metabo-
lism/clearance of the agent. It can also be achieved
if the target of the drug is present specifically or in
much higher levels in the tumor (for radiosensitiz-
ers) or in normal tissues (for radioprotectors)
(Citrin and Mitchell, 2014).
Radiosensitizers are drugs that increase the abil-
ity of radiation to kill cells. A clinically useful
radiosensitizer must enhance the killing of tumor
cells without a corresponding increase in the
response of normal tissues, thus increasing the rate
of tumor control relative to normal tissue injury.
Most drugs that increase the ability of radiation to
kill cells also have some activity/toxicity as a single
agent. A true sensitizer should be synergistic with
radiation, resulting in a greater impact in cell kill-
ing than the sum of the drug and radiation inde-
pendently. 	Most 	radiation 	sensitizers 	target
pathways of cellular resistance to radiation such as
the cell cycle, DNA repair, or hypoxia. There are
also agents that are directly cytotoxic to tumor cells
that may have additive rather than synergistic
effects with radiation but may still improve tumor
16 	I. Gordon

-- 32 of 258 --

17	Radiation Therapy
control if toxicity is low. Some agents may have
multiple mechanisms of action.
Radioprotectors are agents that protect normal
tissues from adverse effects of radiation. Provided
that this protection does not provide a correspond-
ing degree of protection to the tumor, this should
also increase the therapeutic index, although it
should require radiation dose escalation to see
improved local tumor control. In most instances, it
is necessary for radioprotectors to be present in
tissue before or at the time of radiation delivery
but there are some agents that may lessen normal
tissue damage when given after radiation exposure
(Strom et al., 2015). Radioprotectors are different
from treatments that may reduce the severity of an
injury after it manifests. The vast majority of
radioprotectors work by scavenging free radicals,
which are responsible for the majority of DNA
damage after radiation. Amifostine is the only
radiation protector approved by the US Food and
Drug Administration (FDA) (King et al., 2020).
Amifostine exhibits selective protection due to
increased initial uptake in normal tissues, under-
scoring the importance of timing of administration
(Strom et al., 2015).
One of the challenges of developing clinically
effective radiosensitizers and radioprotectors is the
limitations of the laboratory models used to assess
them. There are significant differences in the het-
erogeneity, growth rates, and tumor microenviron-
ment between spontaneously occurring tumors in
patients and what is seen in cell culture and in
xenograft tumors in animal models. The radiation-
induced toxicities seen in rodent models may also
be different than those seen in veterinary cancer
patients.
It is disappointing that despite many years of
interest in radiation-modifying drugs, very few
have showed significant clinical utility. One of the
challenges of clinical implementation of successful
radiation-modifying drugs historically has been the
use of fractionated radiation protocols consisting
of many daily treatments. The dosing schedule of
these agents is likely important, and this has often
not been feasible in patients receiving many frac-
tions of radiation. If the field continues to shift
toward high-dose hypofractionated protocols, it
may be easier to overcome this challenge. There is
also reason for optimism that precision medicine
and genomics may aid in the identification of tar-
gets and agents that are associated with more selec-
tive radiosensitization.
New Biologic Frontiers in Radiation
Oncology
Our deeper understanding of cancer at the cellular
level continues to expand. We now have the ability
to find specific genomic alterations that can predict
the likelihood that a tumor will respond to specific
therapies. The field of personalized medicine
remains in its infancy in veterinary medicine. While
many of the advances focus on predicting response
of tumors to systemic or targeted drugs, there is
likely significant value in applying these advances
to the field of radiation.
Precision medicine and the
genomics of radiosensitivity
Many of the changes in radiation oncology in
recent decades have been driven by advances in
imaging and dosimetry while advances in medical
oncology have been driven by advances in the
understanding of tumor biology. Radiation proto-
cols and recommendations continue to be based
primarily on features such as clinical tumor stage,
histology, tumor size, lymph node status, and histo-
logic margins.
While radiation has become more precise in a
spatial and anatomic sense, the field has not bene-
fitted significantly from deeper understanding of
tumor biology. As we approach the limits of clini-
cally beneficial anatomic precision, it is likely that
future advances may depend more on biologic
precision. The lack of assays predictive of radiation
response is particularly challenging in veterinary
medicine due to considerations that pet owners
must weigh in electing whether to pursue radiation
for their pet or not, including the high costs of
therapy, logistic or quality-of-life concerns related
to serial hospital visits with sedation, and the
potential side effects of radiation. If there were
assays available that would better predict the
response of a tumor to radiation therapy, the radia-
tion oncologist would be able to provide a more
informed recommendation and prognosis and the
pet owner could more accurately weigh the
expected benefits versus risks of treatment.
The goal of precision medicine as relates to
radiation would most likely be to prospectively
apply tumor information to individualize treatment
decisions.
Radiation response is influenced by a variety of
DNA repair pathways in cells. It is likely a cellular

-- 33 of 258 --

signature could be used to assay DNA repair path-
way alterations as a basis to predict radiation
response. The radiosensitivity index is a 10-gene
signature developed by modeling cell survival
across a panel of cell lines from the National
Cancer Institute. This radiosensitivity index has
been found to correlate to radiation response and
treatment outcome in several cohorts of primary
tumors (Strom et al., 2015; Scott et al., 2017). In
addition, functional assays such as clonogenic sur-
vival of primary tumor cells irradiated ex vivo have
been associated with clinical outcomes (West et al.,
1997; Björk-Eriksson et al., 2000; Kamran and
Mouw, 2018). There have also been efforts to
establish patient-derived xenografts to test therapy
combinations against a tumor (Ben-David et al.,
2017). The expense and time-consuming nature of
some of these approaches limits current clinical
utility but cost and speed are likely to improve with
time (Björk-Eriksson et al., 2000).
One example of the application of this type of
personalized medicine to radiation therapy is
human glioblastoma multiforme (GBM). One of
the major advances in GBM therapy in the last
15–20 years was the discovery by Stupp et al. that
the addition of temozolomide chemotherapy to
radiation significantly improved overall survival
(Stupp et al., 2002). Temozolomide is a DNA
alkylating agent that causes cytotoxicity by adding
a methyl group to the O6 site on guanine in DNA,
which leads to subsequent insertion of a thymidine
instead 	of 	cytosine 	opposite 	methylguanine.
Methylated DNA can be repaired by base excision
or mismatch repair pathways. O6-methylguanine
methyltransferase (MGMT) is the enzyme that
reverses this methylation caused by temozolomide.
It has been found that a subset of GBM patients
have methylation of the MGMT promoter, leading
to its silencing (Hegi et al., 2005). Studies have
shown that patients with methylated MGMT do
not have a difference in outcome when treated with
radiation therapy alone but do have longer survival
when treated with radiation plus temozolomide
(Linz, 2010).
One of the first widely used gene expression sig-
natures was the Oncotype DX test, which measures
expression of a variety of genes involved in estro-
gen receptor signaling (Kang et al., 2020). This was
initially validated to predict whether adjuvant
chemotherapy was beneficial in estrogen-positive
breast cancer (Sparano et al., 2015). It was subse-
quently shown to effectively estimate the risk of
locoregional recurrence of radiation of ductal car-
cinoma 	in 	situ 	and 	invasive 	breast 	cancer
(Knopfelmacher et al., 2015). As similar types of
predictive signatures are identified in veterinary
oncology, radiation oncologists should look for
similar opportunities to assess whether they pro-
vide prognostic value for radiotherapy.
A feature of clinical radiation therapy that often
feels counterintuitive is that radiation is prescribed
primarily based on normal tissue tolerance and not
based on tumor sensitivity. In some instances,
tumor histology plays a role but typically, tumor
sensitivity is unknown. Therefore, the approach of
treating to maximal tolerable dose is assumed to
provide the best probability of tumor control and
therefore the best clinical outcome. More precise
biologic approaches could lead to an era where
tumor radiosensitivity is more predictable and
therefore radiation dose and course can be pre-
scribed to match. This could result in lesser toxicity
and treatment for more radiosensitive tumors and
for more aggressive radiation protocols when
appropriate. It could also result in identifying the
subset of tumors where an effective tumoricidal
dose cannot be achieved without unacceptable
toxicity.
Adverse effects of radiation also vary signifi-
cantly between patients and can depend upon the
presence of comorbidities, concurrent medical
treatments, field size, and treatment location. In
addition, a significant component of this risk is
variable and likely genetic. There are rare extreme
examples of radiation sensitivity syndromes associ-
ated with genetic mutations but in most patients,
this sensitivity is driven by a combination of
genetic and other factors. It is likely that assays
could be developed to better predict individual
patient sensitivity to normal-tissue effects of radia-
tion, resulting in changes to how radiation is pre-
scribed to those patients.
As discussed previously, there are likely some dif-
ferences in tumor responses to conventional frac-
tionated doses of radiation and high-dose radiation
fractions. There are differing impacts of factors like
repair, 	repopulation, 	reoxygenation, 	immune
effects, and changes to the tumor microenviron-
ment. It is not currently known whether there are
tumor genomic features that could be predictive of
the most effective radiation dose and fractionation
scheme or technique.
Another area of interest in oncology that could
be specifically beneficial in radiation oncology is
18 	I. Gordon

-- 34 of 258 --

19	Radiation Therapy
the development of minimally invasive techniques
to monitor disease status and response. Assessing
of circulating tumor DNA and circulating tumor
cells could have the potential to provide an early
and sensitive assessment of disease activity and
response (Björk-Eriksson et al., 2000). While many
of the efforts surrounding these techniques have
focused on the monitoring of metastatic disease
and systemic therapy, there are recent reports dem-
onstrating the utility of these techniques in moni-
toring response from treatment of localized disease,
which may precede clinically detectable recurrence
by many months. One of the clinical challenges
faced by radiation oncologists is that due to the
kinetics of radiation response, it is typically not
possible part way through a radiation course to
accurately predict or assess whether a patient is
responding favorably. Instead, the course must be
completed, and the patient followed for months or
longer. It would be tremendously valuable if a test
could be performed part way through a treatment
course that indicated the degree to which a tumor
was responding. This could allow personalization
of the remaining treatment course or could allow
for the decision to discontinue an ineffective treat-
ment early and before reaching doses causing the
most severe adverse effects.
One of the current challenges in analysis of
genomics is distinguishing between prognostic and
predictive factors. Many genomic events are associ-
ated with a worse (or better) clinical outcome
independent of how patients are treated. In addi-
tion, there are factors that are predictive of whether
a patient will respond to a given therapy or radia-
tion course. It is likely that some profiles may be
associated with a worse prognosis but a greater
response (or a greater prognosis but lesser response).
Distinguishing between these in assessing molecu-
lar profiles will require well-designed and multi-
armed clinical studies.
In addition to molecular profiling of tumors to
personalize radiation treatment, functional imaging
has the potential to improve tumor targeting and
personalization of radiation therapy. The ability to
image areas of high metabolic activity, DNA repli-
cation, and/or hypoxia within tumors via MRI or
positron emission tomography (PET) imaging
could allow for new treatment approaches. For
example, biologically modulated radiation therapy
that boosts dose to hypoxic areas as visualized by
18F-fluoromisnidazole could be considered to over-
come hypoxic radioresistance. Functional imaging
during therapy could allow for much earlier assess-
ment of treatment effectiveness.
Conclusion
Radiation therapy remains a major component of
cancer treatment. The field has evolved signifi-
cantly in the past 20 years in veterinary medicine,
primarily as a function of advances in radiation
technology and computing. However, as we reach
the limits of clinical improvements from anatomic
precision in radiation, the next frontier of clinical
advancement in radiation is likely to be from
improved understanding of radiation biology.

KELVIN KOW*

Introduction: History of Chemotherapy
The focus of this chapter lies in the foundational
principles and biologic rationale of cancer chemo-
therapy and is not intended to be an all-encompassing
review of the technical or clinical aspects, nor a
summary of different chemotherapy protocols uti-
lized in veterinary oncology that are well covered
elsewhere, such as in Withrow & MacEwen’s Small
Animal Clinical Oncology (Vail et al., 2020).
Comparatively, chemotherapy is a relatively recent
development in the treatment strategies available
for the treatment of cancer. The earliest documenta-
tion of cancer treatment dates to Egypt in 3000–2500
bc, where cautery via a “fire-drill” was presented as
a modality of treatment of ulcerated breast tumors
(Breasted, 1930). Practical utilization of radiation
therapy started in the 1930s and radiation com-
bined with surgery dominated the treatment of
cancer until the 1950s.
Between 3000 bc and the 1900s, there were no
practical or helpful chemotherapeutics. Indeed,
systemic cancer treatments included herbs, miner-
als, and animal parts, including arsenic, falcon
feces, crab eyes, animal bones, mandrake juice, and
boiled viper’s flesh. A detailed history of these and
other treatments for cancer has recently been
assembled (Hajdu, 2005, 2011a,b). From this start,
the modern era of Western chemotherapeutics
began in the 1950s and 1960s following the tragic
events in Bari Harbor, Italy in 1943. German bomb-
ing of Allied naval vessels there led to the acciden-
tal release of nitrogen mustards after the US cargo
ship, the John Harvey, carrying nitrogen mustards
warheads was hit, leading to wide airborne and
waterborne dissemination to military personnel
and the surrounding civilians (Krumbhaar and
Krumbhaar, 1919; Smith, 2017). The clinical and
postmortem observations of these exposures
revealed severe myelosuppression in the exposed,
which led to the landmark studies by Gilman and
Goodman at Yale showing the therapeutic benefit
of these drugs in cancer models. The lymphoprolif-
erative diseases were logically the first neoplastic
conditions treated based upon these early observa-
tions and the evolution of chemotherapy as a whole
is largely dependent on what we have learned from
these diseases (DeVita and Chu, 2008).
Colonel Cornelius Rhoads of the US Army
Chemical Warfare Service, a peacetime pathologist
and oncologist at NY Memorial Hospital, was con-
vinced of the clinical utility of these agents for
lymphoma/leukemia based upon the Bari bombing
data and pushed for funding and research into
these agents. He later became the first director of
the newly formed Sloan–Kettering Institute at NY
Memorial Hospital whose goal was to further
study and synthesize clinical nitrogen mustards and
other chemotherapeutics. The first of these drugs
was mechlorethamine, which was approved by the
US Food and Drug Administration (FDA) in 1949
and became the standard of care for the treatment
of non-Hodgkin’s lymphoma. This coincided with
the discovery and development of the folic acid
analog, methotrexate, by Dana Farber in 1948, as
well as the observations of clinical response of lym-
phoid neoplasia after the use of adrenocorticotropic
hormone (ACTH) and cortisone in the 1940s and
1950s. The 1960s brought about the discovery of
vincristine by scientists at Eli Lily and procarbazine
by Brunner and Young, which ultimately led to the
25
*Email: kkow@ethosvet.com

DOI: 10.1079/9781789245820.0002

-- 41 of 258 --

MOPP (mechlorethamine, vincristine (Oncovin),
procarbazine, prednisone) protocol by DeVita et al.
The anthracycline drugs were also discovered in the
late 1950s by DiMarco et al. (1964) from the
Farmitalia Research Labs in Italy that culminated
in the development of CHOP (cyclophosphamide,
doxorubicin 	(hydroxydaunomycin), 	vincristine
(Oncovin), prednisolone)-based therapy in the late
1970s and 1980s for non-Hodgkin’s lymphoma
(DeVita, 2003; DeVita and Chu, 2008).
Biological and Clinical Rationale
for Chemotherapy Use
High-dose chemotherapy, also known as conven-
tional chemotherapy, is still the basis of much of
medical oncology even with the advent of targeted
therapies and immunotherapy. The basic principle
of high-dose chemotherapy is derived from maxi-
mal tolerated dose (MTD) therapy in humans. The
National Cancer Institute (NCI) definition of MTD
is: “The highest dose of a drug or treatment that
does not cause unacceptable side effects” (https://
www.cancer.gov/publications/dictionaries/cancer-
terms/def/maximum-tolerated-dose, 	accessed 	3
March 2023). The willingness and ability to man-
age side effects in veterinary patients results in
much lower MTD as the same drugs used in human
patients. Dose intensity is defined as the dose of
chemotherapy per unit of time (Lyman, 2009). As
an example of ideal dose-intense MTD chemo-
therapy, each cycle of CHOP chemotherapy for
human diffuse large B-cell lymphoma (non-Hodg-
kin’s lymphoma) consists not just of higher doses
but also that each cycle of treatment occurs over a
single sitting. For most human patients, cyclophos-
phamide is routinely dosed at 500 mg/m2, vincris-
tine at 1.4 mg/m2, and doxorubicin at 50 mg/m2.
Undoubtedly, the major advantage of the human
approach is a higher cure/survival rate compared to
veterinary medicine with the trade-off being a com-
promise in quality of life during treatment. In vet-
erinary oncology, not only are our treatments
distributed on a single drug basis per treatment, but
we also utilize doses that are essentially 50% of
MTD in humans.
The first and most important principle of chemo-
therapy taught to veterinary students and oncology
trainees is that the vast majority of our patients
have an excellent quality of life with few exhibiting
major side effects of treatment. It is oft quoted that
80% do well with few to no major complications,
15% develop side effects requiring medical atten-
tion, 5% requiring hospitalization, and a fatality
rate of approximately 1% (G. Mauldin, Louisiana,
2001, personal communication). When patients do
exhibit side effects, the vast majority of them are
short-lived and rarely chronic or debilitating. These
statistics, while largely anecdotal, serve as the basis
of our decision-making and clinical recommenda-
tions to clients. Furthermore, the patient and quality-
of-life driven focus in veterinary oncology gives
clients and oncologists far more control over deci-
sions on dose intensity, treatment modification, and
even discontinuation of therapy (self-described as
“communicative cancer medicine”) compared to
the “algorithmic approach to oncology” provided
to most human cancer patients. Nonetheless, even
with this less dose-intense approach to chemother-
apy, long-term survivors for most veterinary can-
cers 	do 	occur 	but 	are 	rarely 	mentioned,
communicated, or measured. Recent efforts are
underway to expand communication of outcomes
in veterinary oncology to include this perspective
on survivorship (C. Khanna, Washington DC,
2022, personal communication).
With the exception of lymphoma where chemo-
therapy is the primary treatment modality, most
chemotherapy in veterinary oncology is adjuvant in
nature after local control has been achieved for
solid tumors such as osteosarcoma, soft tissue sar-
coma, and mast cell tumors. There is, however, a
disconnect in biologic rationale. The demonstration
of activity for a drug following the observation of
response should not be the only basis to predict
activity in the adjuvant setting. Evidence of adju-
vant activity in clinical trials is necessary for the
adjuvant use of these conventional drugs, in the
same way that novel antimetastatic agents must be
validated in appropriate adjuvant studies (see
Amato, Chapter 5, this volume, 2023). In addition,
chemotherapy may be used prior to definitive
therapies as a means to down-stage a primary
tumor prior to surgical resection (so-called neoad-
juvant chemotherapy). This is rarely performed in
veterinary medicine, other than in canine mast cell
tumors. Palliative chemotherapy is utilized to
improve quality of life when primary treatment is
not chosen, with indications in veterinary medicine
including reducing effusions in carcinomatosis and
mesothelioma symptomatic management of lym-
phomas with l-asparaginase and steroids.
For the lymphoproliferative diseases, we use the
terms induction, consolidation, and maintenance
26 	K. Kow

27	High-Dose Conventional Chemotherapy
chemotherapy. Induction chemotherapy refers to
the initial treatments used to achieve a complete
remission, while consolidation refers to the remain-
ing cycles of treatment to eliminate microscopic
disease burden. Maintenance chemotherapy is that
used long-term beyond the consolidation period to
maintain a remission. This chapter will focus on the
foundational biology of conventional chemother-
apy. Specific protocols and treatment recommenda-
tions are already well reviewed and covered
elsewhere.
The Cell Cycle
The basis of high-dose chemotherapy is the disrup-
tion of growth of rapidly dividing cancer cells. One
key challenge of chemotherapy, however, is that in
addition to the presence of rapidly dividing neo-
plastic cells, there are relatively resistant cancer
cells in a terminal, non-dividing state as well as
those that are quiescent and resist therapy for a
number of known and unknown reasons (collec-
tively described as “drug persister cells”). Since
some normal cells also exhibit rapid cell division,
overlapping toxicity can be expected unless precise
targeting of dysregulated elements controlling can-
cer cell division can be achieved (Chabner and
Longo, 2018, pp. 6–8; see Fig. 2). Considering the
cell cycle, cells in G1 phase have just completed cell
division while those in S phase are undergoing DNA
synthesis. G2 is a period of rapid cell growth and
proliferation in preparation for cell division in the M
phase. These phases of the cell cycle are regulated by
cyclins and cyclin-dependent kinases (CDKs) as well
as various checkpoint proteins. The phases of the
cell cycle and the mechanisms controlling the cell
cycle are disease targets for both conventional
chemotherapy and targeted therapies.
Cell cycle specific chemotherapy drugs mostly
work to interrupt DNA replication (S phase) or
mitosis (M phase) whereas non-cell cycle specific
drugs target rapidly dividing cells in any phase of
the cell cycle. An “ideal” conventional chemother-
apy protocol would consist of cell cycle specific
and nonspecific drugs. Combination protocols
containing both cell cycle specific and non-cell
cycle specific chemotherapeutics should in theory
lead to better treatment outcomes, best illustrated
by the improved outcome with CHOP versus sin-
gle-agent therapy in canine lymphoma. Cell cycle
specific drugs commonly utilized in veterinary
medicine include the vinca alkaloids and nucleoside
analogs. The vinca alkaloids are more active within
the M phase while the nucleoside analogs are more
S-phase specific. Bleomycin and the epipodophyllo-
toxins such as etoposide are more active in G2.
Examples of non-cell cycle specific drugs include
the alkylating agents, anthracyclines, and platinum
drugs.
Tumor Kinetics: Models of Cancer Growth
Tumor kinetics play an important role in the likeli-
hood of a response to chemotherapy and our
understanding of this is fundamental to predict and
design appropriate treatments. The early models of
tumor cell kinetics were heavily influenced by data
generated by Howard Skipper at the Southern
Institute largely based upon L1210 murine leuke-
mia models. This model of tumor growth assumes
exponential growth. Theoretically, under perfect
conditions, a single tumor cell creates two daughter
cells and could reach a clinically detectable state of
1 billion cells (1 cm3) after only 30 cell divisions.
The behavior of this model is the foundation of
the log kill/fractional kill hypothesis, which pre-
dicts that each cycle of treatment kills a constant
fraction of cells regardless of the cancer burden.
With this hypothesis, a theoretical starting cancer
burden of 1 cm3/1 billion (1 × 109) cells treated
with five cycles of chemotherapy with a 99% cell
kill will result in < 1 remaining cells at the comple-
tion of treatment. This also means that, mathemati-
cally, a true zero is never reached. The elimination
of a constant fraction of cancer cells also means
that the starting tumor burden is key to the efficacy
of treatment. With the example given above, it is
not difficult to see that a 2–3 cm3 or even larger
mass treated with a similar five-cycle protocol
would result in a higher remaining tumor burden.
This principle is also why tumor cytoreduction of
solid tumors with surgery and/or radiation therapy
is most likely to deliver an optimal chemotherapy
response. Although fundamental, the failure of
these models includes the heterogeneity of cancer
cells in a tumor and the resulting heterogeneity of
cell susceptibility to a given chemotherapy or treat-
ment protocol. This is further complicated by the
fact that part of this cancer heterogeneity evolves
during the described cellular doubling.
Nonetheless, all models are useful when used
appropriately, and the fractional kill hypothesis is
the basis for the number of cycles of high-dose/
conventional chemotherapy in most treatment

-- 43 of 258 --

protocols. Skipper’s principles were particularly
applicable and influential in the development of
modern conventional chemotherapy protocols for
lymphomas/leukemias and for adjuvant treatment
of solid tumors, but the observation of a lympho-
proliferative disease in a murine model does not
extrapolate well to solid tumors in a gross disease
setting where chemotherapy responses have been
largely disappointing. This is largely due to the
issue of broad exposure of “liquid” tumors and
microscopic solid tumors to chemotherapeutics
versus solid tumors, where there is less exposure of
the tumor to drugs in addition to the challenges of
tumor hypoxia (DeVita and Chu, 2008; DeVita
et al., 2011; Chabner and Longo, 2018, pp. 8–9).
Gompertzian Kinetics
In contrast to lymphoproliferative cancers where
growth kinetics are exponential, the growth charac-
teristics of solid tumors tend to have rapid, expo-
nential initial growth followed by a period of
slowing growth as the total cell number increases
eventually reaching a plateau. The shape of this
growth curve is the classic sigmoid-shaped curve.
One of the first people to describe this type of curve
was a British actuary, Benjamin Gompertz, in 1825
(Gompertz, 1825). In this model, growth fraction is
not constant as in the exponential growth model
but rather it decreases exponentially with time. This
model predicts that the peak growth fraction occurs
at ~37% of the maximum cellular burden and that
treatment with chemotherapy should ideally occur
at or before that fraction. However, this is rarely
when most solid tumors are evaluated clinically.
This explains the low efficacy of neoadjuvant
chemotherapy for large solid tumors where the
growth fraction is already at a low or plateau phase
of the sigmoid-shaped growth curve. Tumors in this
setting have a large fraction of cells in the G0 phase
in addition to poor vascularity. Cell cycle specific
drugs, with some exceptions, would be especially
poor choices for neoadjuvant chemotherapy of
solid tumors. Conversely, non-cell cycle specific
drugs such as the alkylators, anthracyclines, and
platinum agents are typical choices for neoadjuvant
treatment. Once the initial tumor burden is
decreased with non-cell cycle specific neoadjuvant
chemotherapy, surgery, or radiation therapy, cell
cycle specific drugs are expected to have a better
chance of antitumor effects (DeVita et al., 2011;
Chabner and Longo, 2018, pp. 6–8).
Pharmacologic Basis of High-Dose
Chemotherapy
Beyond the effect of chemotherapeutics on cancer
cells, the determining and limiting factor for high-
dose chemotherapy is the narrow therapeutic
index. Chemotherapeutics cause toxicity to normal,
rapidly dividing cells including bone marrow,
gastrointestinal cells, and hair follicles. These
dose-limiting toxicities (DLTs) are balanced out
against the MTD. The therapeutic index is defined
as the ratio of the “dose required to produce a
given … toxicity and the dose required to give a
defined effect against the tumor” (Tannock et al.,
2013, p. 406).
These toxicities to normal tissues are affected by
the dose/concentration of the chemotherapeutic,
age, drug interactions, genetics, drug absorption,
metabolism, and clearance. Clearance includes all
the processes that contribute to drug elimination
including hepatic metabolism and renal clearance
(Chabner and Longo, 2018, p. 8; Horde and
Gupta, 2020). Pharmacokinetics allows the deter-
mination of maximum serum concentration (Cmax)
and area under the concentration curve (AUC) that
plots the concentration of a drug in plasma over
time, which is an indicator of total drug exposure.
This is determined via Phase I clinical trials where
the adverse effects and pharmacokinetics is often
determined.
Outside of the recent veterinary oncology
approvals, with few exceptions, treatment regimens
are extrapolated empirically from human studies
and limited animal toxicity studies rather than via
well-controlled clinical trials. For example, with
the canine CHOP protocol (Wisconsin protocol)
the typical chemotherapy doses for vincristine,
cyclophosphamide, and doxorubicin were set at
~50% of the typical doses used in human medicine
with each drug given separately over a 1- to 2-week
interval. This varies with human oncology-based
CHOP protocols where these drugs are given at
significantly higher doses over a single day (DeVita,
2003).
Goldie–Coldman Hypothesis
Treatment failure is defined by the NCI’s Surveillance,
Epidemiology, and End Results (SEER) Program to
be: “The treatment modalities did not destroy or
modify cancer cells” (Adamo et al., 2018). There
are certainly patient/client-related factors such as
28 	K. Kow

-- 44 of 258 --

29	High-Dose Conventional Chemotherapy
comorbidities and toxicity from treatment but also
unique to veterinary oncology, the conscious choice
for suboptimal protocols. However, the larger issue
in treatment failure is resistance of cancer cells to
chemotherapy.
The Goldie–Coldman hypothesis states that due
to tumor heterogeneity, inherently resistant cells
are present and as that tumor grows, the fraction of
these resistant cells increases. The presence of even
a single resistant cell may lead to treatment failure.
Hence, large tumors and treatment delays are
expected to have a higher fraction of resistant cells
and a higher chance of treatment failure. This con-
versely also means that small tumors are less likely
to have resistance and have a higher chance of a
cure. The challenge at present is that our detection
index for these small, curable tumors is low and we
invariably set ourselves out for failure with the
treatment of bulky, clinically detectable disease.
Despite an instinctive allure of an early cancer diag-
nosis, well-controlled prospective studies will be
needed to demonstrate clinical value of an early
diagnosis to patients. Indeed, the certainty of the
value of an early cancer diagnosis is limited to a
relatively narrow set of circumstances, rarely seen
in veterinary patients. The Goldie–Coldman model
also predicts that two or more drugs with different
mechanisms of action would be superior to single-
agent therapy especially when given in an alternat-
ing (nonsequential) manner (Goldie and Coldman,
1984).
Biologic Rationale for Combination
Therapy
Lymphoproliferative diseases were the first cancers
treated with chemotherapy after the development
of mustargen and methotrexate in the late 1940s.
Although there were remarkable improvements in
outcome, they were rarely durable due to treatment
resistance largely via the selection for survival of
resistant clones as well as the presumed presence of
cancer stem cells (CSCs) (Tannock et al., 2013,
p. 299; Chabner and Longo, 2018, p. 8). Within a
particular type of cancer, it was also observed that
there was significant heterogeneity in response. The
Goldie–Coldman hypothesis predicts that the use
of multiple agents, each with different mechanisms
of action, decreases the number of resistant clones
and was first utilized for lymphoproliferative dis-
eases with protocols such as MOPP and CHOP.
These protocols dramatically improved outcomes
for the lymphoproliferative diseases, with complete
remission rate going from zero to 80% within a
time frame of 20 years for Hodgkin’s disease
(DeVita, 2003). Most pediatric acute lymphoid
leukemias are cured at present when it was univer-
sally a fatal disease in the 1940s (DeVita and Chu,
2008).
A key component in developing combination
chemotherapy is the concept of summation dose
intensity (SDI), which allows the determination of
the impact of combination chemotherapy based
upon the responses seen from monotherapy (Frei
et al., 1998; Chun et al., 2005).
In veterinary oncology, CHOP-based therapies
continue to be the standard of care for lymphoblas-
tic lymphoma and are clearly superior to single-
agent therapy. Paradoxically, combination therapy
has not been shown to be superior in canine osteo-
sarcoma (Chun et al., 2005; Skorupski et al.,
2016). However, from examining Chun et al.’s
paper, and as the authors also point out, the SDI of
the combination protocol did not exceed that of
the fractional dose intensity of the drugs as single
agents and accordingly predicts the failure of this
attempt at combination therapy.
The integration of targeted therapy and immu-
notherapy to conventional chemotherapy holds
great promise as a means to decrease cancer cell
resistance and improve outcomes. Indeed, these
novel approaches have become integrated into the
standard of care of treatment of various cancers in
human patients. For example, non-small-cell lung
cancer is routinely treated with a combination of
pembrolizumab (Keytruda®) and a platinum agent.
Human epidermal growth factor receptor 2
(HER2)-positive breast carcinomas are treated
with a combination of trastuzumab (Herceptin®)
and taxanes/platinum agents. The rationale for
such successful combination is not necessarily
intuitive or transferable from one cancer setting to
another and therefore will require carefully exe-
cuted prospective studies in relevant veterinary
cancers.
Chemotherapy Resistance Mechanisms
The two overall reasons for chemotherapy resist-
ance are acquired and inherent resistance. Inherent
resistance is largely due to the existence of self-
renewing cells or CSCs, more recently described as
drug persister cells (Hangauer et al., 2017). The
evolution away from the term “cancer stem cells” is

-- 45 of 258 --

the result of recognition that the origin and biology
of these resistant cells are unknown but the pheno-
type of “persister” is clearly evident. Nonetheless,
irrespective of terminology, characteristics of these
cells include plasticity, capacity for self-renewal,
pluripotency, and tumorigenicity (Seno et al., 2019).
There are several known mechanisms of acquired
cancer drug resistance and its impact on treatment
outcome is significant. It is therefore not surprising
that novel therapeutics have and will emerge to
block these resistance mechanisms and provide a
biologic rationale for novel combination therapy
approaches. Some of these mechanisms of acquired
resistance include the following.
Decreased drug uptake
One example displaying this mechanism are the
solute carrier (SLC) proteins, which are members
of the membrane transport protein superfamily
that mediate the influx of nutrients, neurotransmit-
ters, and hydrophilic drugs. Point mutations in one
of the SLCs, the reduced folate carrier 1 (RFC1),
which is crucial for methotrexate uptake, are respon-
sible for reduced influx of methotrexate. These
mutations have been identified in human acute
lymphoblastic leukemias (Huang, 2007; Tannock
et al., 2013, p. 447).
MDR-mediated chemotherapy efflux
The best-known example of multidrug resistance
(MDR) results from the overexpression of the
MDR1 gene that codes for P-glycoprotein (P-gp)/
ATP-binding cassette (ABC) subfamily B member 1
(ABCB1), which leads to increased efflux of chemo-
therapeutics from the intracellular space. The
chemotherapeutics that are substrates for this
efflux are natural-product xenobiotics including
doxorubicin, etoposide, mitoxantrone, actinomycin
D, and the vinca alkaloids. Beyond P-gp/ABCB1,
other efflux pumps exist including breast cancer
resistance 	protein 	(ABCG2/BCRP), 	ABCB5,
ABCB8, ABCC3, and ABCC5.
It is widely believed that pretreatment of canine
lymphoma patients with corticosteroids is associ-
ated with treatment resistance to chemotherapy
and while the suspected mechanism is some form of
MDR-mediated efflux, the actual mechanism of
this anecdotal phenomenon remains unclear.
In a study by Levi et al., P-gp/ABCB1 was expressed
in 85% of inflammatory carcinomas compared to
39% of Grade III noninflammatory carcinoma.
A similar trend is seen in human mammary carcino-
mas and this may partly explain their overall poor
response to adjuvant chemotherapy (Levi et al.,
2019). P-gp mRNA upregulation has also been
found to be higher in gastrointestinal lymphoma
compared to multicentric lymphoma, which may in
part explain their resistance to chemotherapy. Other
studies in canine lymphoma have shown that P-gp
expression was lower prior to induction of chemo-
therapy than at treatment relapse (Zandvliet and
Teske, 2015; Zandvliet et al., 2015). In addition to
P-gp/ABCB1, ABCG2/BCRP mRNA has also been
found to be upregulated in canine lymphoma
patients found to be drug resistant. It is likely that
there is a wider role of other yet unidentified MDR
mechanisms or other yet undescribed drug resist-
ance mechanisms beyond the ABC transporter
family.
Increased repair
DNA damage is not limited to that caused by
chemotherapeutics as it is daily occurrence second-
ary to mutagens/chemicals, radiation, and oxidative
damage. It is estimated that humans can have up to
1 million mutations per day (Clancy, 2008).
Endogenous DNA repair mechanisms direct base
repair, nucleotide excision repair, base excision repair,
mismatch 	repair, 	homologous 	recombination
repair, and nonhomologous end joining. A diverse
array of mechanisms for cancer cells to increase
repair of DNA damage have been described, most
often specific to the specific type of DNA damage.
For example, one mechanism of action of alkylating
agents is to bind to guanine; O6-methylguanine
methyltransferase (O6-MGMT) directly repairs this
damage by removing/transferring the alkyl groups
to cysteine residues on the enzyme itself. O6-
MGMT has been found to be upregulated in human
glioblastoma/gliomas and is responsible for resist-
ance to temozolomide therapy (Cabrini et al., 2015).
Poly(ADP-ribose) polymerase 1 and 2 (PARP1
and PARP2) are in the family of enzymes that have
a key role in the DNA damage response, particularly
in their ability to repair single-strand breaks. PARP1
binds to single-strand breaks leading to a process
called PARylation that involves other DNA repair
proteins such as X-ray repair cross-complementing
protein 1 (XRCC1) (Lord and Ashworth, 2017).
PARP is overexpressed in some cancers, leading
to increased repair/survival. On the surface, PARP

31	High-Dose Conventional Chemotherapy
inhibition would be a useful treatment strategy to
be exploited for cancer treatment. Combinations of
PARP inhibitors and temozolomide have been
found to have increased antitumor activity but the
challenge for many cancers is that the repair mech-
anisms have not been clearly defined (Zaremba and
Curtin, 2007). Furthermore, the benefit of PARP
inhibition is predictably linked to very specific
mechanisms of repair and resistance. The proteins
encoded by BRCA1 (BReast CAncer gene 1) and
BRCA2 (BReast CAncer gene 2) are key compo-
nents of DNA double-strand break repair via
homologous recombination and germline muta-
tions in these genes are well known to lead to an
elevated risk of breast cancer. There is a complex
interplay between BRCA1/2 and PARP for essential
strand break repair and PARP inhibitors have hence
been identified as a treatment strategy for patients
with these mutations, with example drugs including
olaparib and niraparib (Lord and Ashworth, 2017).
The activity of these agents beyond BRCA1/2-
altered tumor cells remains unclear.
Resistance to apoptosis
Apoptosis resulting from chemotherapy is largely
through the induction of the intrinsic pathway of
apoptosis 	via 	the 	release 	of 	mitochondrial
cytochrome c, binding of APAF-1 and caspase 9
activation, and subsequently caspase 3 activation
(execution pathway). The ability of a cell to resist
apoptosis can result from mutations, up- or down-
regulation of the various proteins involved such as
p53 upstream of the mitochondria, BCL-2 family
at the mitochondria, and also those further down-
stream such as Survivin, an apoptosis-inducing
factor (Kaufmann and Earnshaw, 2000; Zandvliet
and Teske, 2015). Survivin is a member of the
inhibitor of apoptosis (IAP) family that is antiapop-
totic and is often increased in rapidly dividing cells.
High expression of Survivin has been shown to be
a negative prognostic factor for dogs with osteosar-
coma and lymphoma. A Phase I clinical trial utiliz-
ing a Survivin inhibitor has recently been performed
in canine lymphoma and may be a promising thera-
peutic target (Shoeneman et al., 2016).
Alterations of drug target
The efficacy of a chemotherapeutic is dependent
upon its ability to bind to its target and induce
necessary alterations of these targets,Topoisomerase
inhibitors such as doxorubicin and mitoxantrone
work by altering DNA structure, leading to single-
and double-strand breaks. The effects of these
drugs can be blunted by mutations in topoisomer-
ase as well as reductions in topoisomerase expres-
sion. Increased dihydrofolate reductase (DHFR)
expression as well as mutated DHFRs can negate
the effects of methotrexate. Microtubule inhibitors
such as the vinca alkaloids and taxanes function by
binding to the microtubular structure and inhibit-
ing mitotic progression leading to cell arrest and
apoptosis. Resistance to these drugs occurs via
mutations in βI-tubulin as well as increased expres-
sion of βIII-tubulin. Increases in the microtubule-
associated protein, tau, have been shown to cause
chemotherapy resistance in human breast and
prostate cancer. Tau functions by stabilizing micro-
tubules and promoting polymerization and binds
to β-tubulin at the same location as the taxanes
(Smoter et al., 2011; Tannock et al., 2013, p. 454;
Housman et al., 2014; Zandvliet and Teske, 2015).
Epithelial–mesenchymal transition
Although not directly related to mechanisms of cancer
drug resistance, the process of epithelial–mesenchy-
mal transition (EMT) may transiently alter drug
sensitivity in a cancer cell. This is a reversible hypo-
thetical process whereby epithelial cells are able to
transform to a mesenchymal morphology impor-
tant in embryogenesis and wound healing but also
in the malignant progression of epithelial cancers.
These cells not only acquire the morphology of
mesenchymal cells, but also express markers associ-
ated with mesenchymal cells such as vimentin and
fibronectin while losing expression of epithelial
markers such as E-cadherin. These changes confer
a mesenchymal phenotype to epithelial neoplasms
with characteristics such as increased ability to
migrate, a more invasive nature, and increased pro-
duction of extracellular matrix. These cells also
become more resistant to apoptosis and anoikis.
There is also good evidence showing that the
reverse process, mesenchymal–epithelial transition,
occurs after metastatic cells colonize a distant
metastatic site. Sorenmo and co-workers have dem-
onstrated these characteristics occur in a grade-
dependent manner in canine mammary carcinoma
but also that metastatic lesions differ from their
primary sites in expression of the E-cadherin/
vimentin 	regulators, 	SNAIL/SLUG 	(Raposo-
Ferreira et al., 2018).
