Intracellular Chemotherapy
Compartmentalization
A very recent addition to our foundational know-
ledge regarding chemotherapy activity has come
from the realization that chemotherapy drugs are
not evenly distributed within a cell but rather are
unevenly distributed within intracellular compart-
ments. This uneven distribution is independent of
the mechanism of action of the drug but rather a
chemical feature of the drug. Accordingly, even
drugs within a similar mechanism of action (e.g.,
topoisomerase inhibition) may experience very dif-
ferent intracellular distribution than other mem-
bers of the same drug class (i.e., mitoxantrone and
doxorubicin), resulting in unpredictably distinct
activities against a cancer. The clinical significance
of this new knowledge is that an apparent resist-
ance by a cancer to a drug class (defined by mecha-
nism of action) does not necessarily predict
resistance to all drugs in that class, based on pre-
sumed mechanisms of action or presumed mecha-
nisms of resistance. Predictors of intracellular
distribution remain poorly understood, but this
knowledge will likely become part of the clinician’s
decision-making with regard to the choice of rescue
therapy in the setting of what may appear to be
drug resistance.
Chemotherapy Classes
Antimetabolites
The antimetabolites function by interfering with
DNA synthesis, mostly as either purine or pyrimi-
dine analogs or as antifolates. The cytidine analogs,
gemcitabine and cytarabine, are the classic nucleo-
side inhibitors in veterinary oncology and exert
their effects in a cell cycle specific manner by com-
petitively inhibiting DNA polymerase. Their effi-
cacy is dependent on the duration of exposure
more than peak concentration, and hence they are
most ideally administered as long infusions or as
constant-rate infusions (CRIs).
Rabacfosadine (Tanovea) is a novel antimetabo-
lite with recent FDA approval for canine lym-
phoma. It is a guanine double prodrug analog with
its active intracellular metabolite being 9-(2-phos-
phonylmethoxyethyl)guanine 	(PMEG) 	diphos-
phate. While effective in both a naïve and rescue
setting, its clinical use is most often as a lymphoma
rescue chemotherapy, but arguably it may replace
other treatment approaches as a frontline therapy.
Rabacfosadine does have unique side effects includ-
ing idiosyncratic pulmonary fibrosis, especially in
West Highland Terriers, and a transient dermatopa-
thy. These side effects are a good reminder that
even within an established family of chemothera-
peutics, mechanism of action does not always pre-
dict adverse events (Thamm et al., 2017; Cawley
et al., 2020; Saba et al., 2020).
Nitrogen-based alkylating agents
Alkylating agents are so named because they contain
alkyl groups (C 	) and function by alkylating	nH2n+1
DNA. Chemically they are actually alkyl halides, in
that they all have had a hydrogen replaced with chlo-
rine (CH2Cl). Once taken up, they are metabolized to
a highly reactive (electrophilic) aziridinium intermedi-
ate that serves as the alkylating agent. They function
by binding to the N-7 position of guanine, leading to
interstrand cross-linking in a non-cell cycle-specific
manner. They are not, as a class of drugs, particularly
specific in their site of action, which is why they tend
to be more myelosuppressive compared to the cell
cycle specific drugs. The binding of the alkyl group
leads to DNA fragmentation, DNA strand breaks,
cross-linking, and nucleotide pairing mismatch
(Tannock et al., 2013, p. 422; Lehmann and Wennerberg,
2021).
Mustargen, the first chemotherapeutic agent
available, is the prototype of the nitrogen mustards
alkylating agents with many others developed
since, including cyclophosphamide, dacarbazine,
ifosfamide, chlorambucil, melphalan, and lomus-
tine. Mustargen is still in use to this day, most com-
monly as part of the MOPP protocol for lymphoma.
It is too reactive for oral administration and can
only be administered intravenously.
Chlorambucil and melphalan are second-generation
alkylating agents, being structurally very similar to
and derived from mustargen. They are much more
stable than mustargen due to addition of an electron-
withdrawing aromatic ring, allowing them to be
administered orally. Additionally, this aromatic ring
makes the interaction with DNA slower compared to
the first-generation alkylators such as mustargen. For
this reason, chlorambucil and melphalan are often
referred to as “slow” alkylators. They also function by
alkylating the N-7 position of guanine, similar to other
agents of this class.“Fast” and “slow” alkylators refers
to the speed of chemical interaction with DNA and
should not be confused with the clinical activity of the
drugs in patients.
32 	K. Kow

-- 48 of 258 --

33	High-Dose Conventional Chemotherapy
Cyclophosphamide is a prodrug that is activated
via cytochrome p450 into 4-hydroxycylophospha-
mide that is then further metabolized intracellu-
larly to acrolein and phosphoramide mustard,
which is the active metabolite that binds DNA.
Acrolein is the toxic principle for sterile hemor-
rhagic cystitis. Cyclophosphamide is a standard
component of the CHOP protocol and frequently
also utilized in metronomic chemotherapy proto-
cols (see Matsuyama and Mutsaers, Chapter 3, this
volume, 2023).
Lomustine is a nitrosourea alkylating agent often
used as a rescue protocol in canine and feline lym-
phoma but also useful because it crosses the blood–
brain barrier and hence can be helpful for cases of
primary brain tumor as well as central nervous
system (CNS) lymphomas. Its ability to cross the
blood–brain barrier is due to its lipid-soluble
nature. Lomustine is particularly hepatotoxic in
canine patients; the mechanism of toxicity is poorly
understood but suspected to be due to lipid peroxi-
dation and glutathione depletion. Concomitant use
of denamarin has been demonstrated to signifi-
cantly decrease hepatotoxicity (Skorupski et al.,
2011). Anecdotally, α-lipoic acid is also purported
to reduce lomustine-related hepatotoxicity and
there is at least some in vitro data that supports its
hepatoprotective benefits via the reduction of oxi-
dative stress (Zicker et al., 2002; Shmalberg, 2014;
Abdulrazzaq et al., 2019).
Antitumor antibiotics
The prototype drug in this class, daunorubicin, is a
natural product isolated from Streptomyces in the
1950s. Doxorubicin is a hydroxylated analog of
daunorubicin. The distinctive red color is a result of
the production of a red pigment by the Streptomyces
strain used in doxorubicin fermentation. Doxorubicin
is arguably one of the most important tools avail-
able to clinical oncologists due to its broad spec-
trum of clinical application that is partly explained
by the multiple mechanisms of action. It is utilized
against a broad range of neoplasms in veterinary
medicine ranging from the solid tumors to hemato-
logic malignancies.
Despite their long history of use, the specific
mechanisms of action for this class of drugs con-
tinue to evolve. Described mechanisms include free
radical-mediated damage to DNA, topoisomerase
II inhibition leading to DNA damage and apopto-
sis, histone displacement, DNA alkylation, and
intercalation of DNA that causes DNA strand
breaks. Secondary mechanisms of action include
disruption of calcium homeostasis and thioredoxin
inhibition. Potent free radical-mediated damage
may have a greater role in its cardiotoxicity and
extravasation injury than any direct antitumor
benefit (Tannock et al., 2013, p. 433; Wander et al.,
2020).
Dexrazoxane reduces doxorubicin-induced free
radical-mediated damage by its iron-chelating
properties and has been demonstrated to be cardio-
protective with no reduction in efficacy in human
cancer patients, which supports the less important
role of free radical-mediated cancer cell death. A
secondary use of dexrazoxane is the treatment of
extravasation-related injuries in a peracute setting
(Langer, 2007; Venable et al., 2012). Feline patients
appear resistant to secondary dilated cardiomyop-
athy (DCM) but are more prone to develop renal
toxicity following doxorubicin administration.
Mitoxantrone is technically an anthracenedione
with many mechanistic properties of the classic
anthracyclines, with topoisomerase II inhibition
and DNA intercalation being the main mechanisms
of action. It is utilized in veterinary oncology for
primary therapy of transitional cell carcinoma but
also as an adjuvant therapy for anal sac apocrine
gland adenocarcinoma and as a substitute for
doxorubicin for canine patients with DCM and
feline patients with underlying renal dysfunction.
The substitution of mitoxantrone for doxorubicin
translates into a shorter survival time in canine
lymphoblastic lymphoma compared to a standard
CHOP protocol but this is less clear in feline
patients (Marquardt et al., 2019).
Actinomycin is another fermentation product of
Streptomyces that functions via its ability to target
transcription via inhibition of RNA polymerase. It
is predominantly utilized as a substitute for doxo-
rubicin or as part of canine lymphoma rescue pro-
tocols such as DMAC (dexamethasone, melphalan,
actinomycin D, cytosine arabinoside).
Mitotic inhibitors/vinca alkaloids
The taxanes, derived from the bark and needles of
yew trees, inhibit microtubule disassembly, which
leads to mitotic arrest. The microtubules are
responsible for formation and separation of the
mitotic apparatus and disruption of this leads to
mitotic arrest and cell death. It is standard-of-care
therapy for human head and neck tumors, non-small-cell

-- 49 of 258 --

lung, ovarian, and breast carcinomas, but of
unknown utility in veterinary oncology. The tax-
anes have very poor solubility that is overcome by
use of carriers: Cremaphor for paclitaxel and
Polysorbate 80 for docetaxel. Cremaphor causes a
severe hypersensitivity in veterinary patients.
Docetaxel is less toxic in our patient population,
but it nonetheless can also have very significant
hypersensitivity reactions. Oral versions of pacli-
taxel may be of greater utility in veterinary medi-
cine, but bioavailability continues to limit its use
thus far with most existing formulations. The con-
current use of cyclosporine with oral paclitaxel
improves its bioavailability and has shown poten-
tial benefit for canine oral squamous cell carci-
noma; however, it is not clinically practical as
administration requires anesthesia and paclitaxel
delivery by gavage. A new formulation of paclitaxel
delivered along with a P-gp inhibitor, encequidar, is
currently in clinical trials. If proven effective, it may
become the first practically administered taxane in
veterinary oncology (C. Khanna, Washington DC,
2022, personal communication).
In veterinary oncology there is widespread use of
the vinca alkaloids, particularly vincristine and vin-
blastine. Similar to the taxanes, they are naturally
derived: in this case, from the periwinkle plant. They
function at a different binding site to microtubulin
compared to the taxanes, inhibiting polymerase, lead-
ing to metaphase arrest and subsequently to cell cycle
specific death. They are considered to be strong vesi-
cants and are given as rapid intravenous boluses with
the exception of vinorelbine, which is typically admin-
istered over 5 minutes.
Vincristine is predominantly utilized in canine and
feline lymphomas and is a standard component of
COP (cyclophosphamide, vincristine (Oncovin), pred-
nisone)/CHOP therapy. Vinblastine is often substi-
tuted for vincristine in feline CHOP protocols with
potentially lower rates of gastrointestinal toxicity. Its
main use is as adjuvant therapy for high-grade and/or
metastatic mast cell tumors as well as for primary
therapy of canine transitional cell carcinomas.
Vinorelbine is a semisynthetic vinca alkaloid
with use mainly as a rescue agent for canine mast
cell tumors and also as an adjuvant therapy for
primary lung tumors. In humans, the lung concen-
tration of vinorelbine is 300-fold that in serum;
however, it is unclear if this clearly contributes to
improved outcome in canines or humans with pri-
mary lung tumors. Vinorelbine is available in
Europe as an oral agent and could prove useful in
metronomic protocols (Levêque and Jehl, 1996;
Poirier et al., 2004; Grant et al., 2008; Wouda
et al., 2015).
Platinum agents
These are synthetic, non-cell cycle specific agents, with
cisplatin the prototype agent in this class. It is still
considered standard-of-care therapy for human uro-
genital and gynecological tumors as well as for solid
tumors such as osteosarcoma. The introduction of
cisplatin led to dramatic improvement in outcome for
testicular cancer with cure rates improving from 10 to
75% when used in combination with bleomycin and
vinblastine. These agents function very similarly to
alkylating agents and covalently bind to guanine and
adenine, leading to cross-linking of DNA (Einhorn,
1990; Chabner and Longo, 2018, p. 235). The “cis” in
cisplatin refers to the cis configuration, i.e., the chlo-
ride functional groups are on same side of the planar,
platinum-containing complex. For carboplatin, car-
boxylate (carboxylic acid) replaces the chloride func-
tional groups found in cisplatin. These leaving groups
are important in understanding the biological differ-
ences of cisplatin versus carboplatin as the added
complexity of the carboxylate group in carboplatin
reduces its reactivity, hence reducing the renal and
ototoxicity associated with cisplatin (Tannock et al.,
2013, p. 425).
Prior to carboplatin being available as an FDA-
approved generic, cisplatin was the platinum agent
of choice in veterinary oncology and standard-of-
care therapy for adjuvant therapy of canine osteo-
sarcoma. It induces significant emetogenic and
renal toxicity in dogs as well as fatal pulmonary
edema in cats (Knapp et al., 1987) in addition to
being nursing intensive due to the need for aggres-
sive diuresis. Carboplatin has mostly replaced cis-
platin due to its significantly reduced side effects,
relative safety in cats, and ease of administration. It
has been observed (S. Lana, Colorado, 2005, per-
sonal communication) that carboplatin can have a
nadir at 10–14 days and/or as late as 21 days post
administration. Dose reductions are indicated in
the presence of renal dysfunction and should ide-
ally be performed based upon iohexol clearance
(Bailey et al., 2009).
Chemotherapy-Related Toxicity
The success and failure of chemotherapy is due not
only to the inherent sensitivity or resistance to
34 	K. Kow

-- 50 of 258 --

35	High-Dose Conventional Chemotherapy
treatment but also to patient toxicity, which is
invariably a result of interpatient differences in
pharmacogenomics. An important component in
evaluating and comparing toxicity has been the
adoption of the Veterinary Cooperative Oncology
Group (VCOG) common terminology criteria for
the most common toxicities seen. In this set of cri-
teria, a Grade 1 toxicity is considered mild while a
Grade 	5 	is 	death 	resulting 	from 	treatment
(Anonymous, 2016).
Bone marrow toxicity is possible with any chemo-
therapeutic, with the neutrophil nadir of most
drugs being around 7 days except for carboplatin,
where the nadir is at either 10–14 days or as late as
21 days. In veterinary patients, neutropenias are
much more clinically relevant compared to anemias
and thrombocytopenias, whereas in human oncol-
ogy, chemotherapy-related anemias are far more
frequent. In one study of 41,000 patients in
Europe, 67% of patients suffered anemias (Boyle
et al., 2004; Lustberg, 2012). While we do not have
clear incidence data in veterinary patients, the fre-
quency of anemia is far less common most likely
due to the lower dose and schedule intensity. The
use of growth factors is uncommon in veterinary
patients, unlike in human oncology, but also partly
due to the lack of commercially available recombi-
nant canine or feline products.
Within veterinary oncology, there are some differ-
ences of opinion and comfort level in the minimum
neutrophil count for safe chemotherapy. Certainly,
utilizing a lower acceptable neutrophil cutoff empiri-
cally translates to greater dose intensity; however, evi-
dence of a therapeutic value from dose intensification
requires purposeful prospective studies, not completed
to date. Based upon how most veterinary clinical
oncologists are trained, a routine practice is to per-
form dose reductions of approximately 20% if unac-
ceptable side effects are noted (S. Lana, Colorado,
2005, personal communication). However, dose
reductions and treatment delays are significant con-
tributors to treatment failure, and it has been noted
that as little as a 20% dose reduction may translate to
up to a 50% reduction in cure rates (DeVita et al.,
2011). Guidelines for the appropriate dose modifica-
tions are available in other texts such as Withrow and
MacEwen’s Small Animal Clinical Oncology (Vail
et al., 2020). Until we have better pharmacogenetic
and pharmacogenomic tools to help inform treatment,
calculations of SDI are likely the best way for us to
improve 	treatment 	outcomes 	with 	multidrug
protocols.
Pharmacogenomics and
Pharmacogenetics
Pharmacogenomics is the “study of genetic variation
of drug-metabolizing enzymes, receptors, transporter
and targets” (Crews et al., 2012, p. 467) and the
impact of these variations on treatment response and
toxicity. The terms “pharmacogenetics” and “pharma-
cogenomics” are often used interchangeably but phar-
macogenetics, strictly speaking, is a narrower
evaluation of the impact of single-nucleotide polymor-
phisms, insertions, and deletions on drug therapy,
while pharmacogenomics is a broader-based study of
the complex interplay of multiple genes.
The best example of pharmacogenetics in veteri-
nary oncology is found among herding breeds,
which have a well-documented dysfunction in P-gp
resulting from a 4 bp mutation in the gene encod-
ing MDR1/ABCB1. This plasma membrane protein
is responsible for the efflux of xenobiotics – ranging
from drugs such as ivermectin and loperamide to
xenobiotic chemotherapeutics such as the vinca
alkaloids, doxorubicin, mitoxantrone, and actino-
mycin D – from the intracellular space. This P-gp is
found in especially high concentration in intestinal
epithelial cells, the blood–brain barrier, and the
biliary system, which correlates with organs/tissues
that clearly need protection from potentially dan-
gerous xenobiotics. In dogs, MDR mutations lead
to increased exposure of the body to the deleterious
effects of xenobiotic agents, particularly if they are
homozygous for the mutated alleles. This has the
most significant impact on canine lymphoma
patients as it markedly increases the risk of gastro-
intestinal toxicity and myelosuppression with 2/3
of the chemotherapeutics in the protocol. Dogs
heterozygous for the mutated alleles are at lower
risk and may do well with significant dose reduc-
tions, but this likely translates to a poorer outcome.
The herding breeds including Collies, Border
Collies, Shetland Sheepdogs, and Old English
Sheepdogs should ideally be tested for the mutation
through Washington State University’s Clinical
Pharmacology lab. While results are pending, it is
recommended that non-MDR substrate chemo-
therapeutic agents be started first, such as l-aspar-
aginase or cyclophosphamide (Mealey et al., 2003,
2008; Mealey, 2004; Geyer and Janko, 2012). The
rigor of studies and evidence around these herding
breed mutations should be a template for the delivery
of new innovations in the fields of pharmacogenomics
and precision medicine in veterinary oncology.

-- 51 of 258 --

Broader pharmacogenomic-driven chemotherapy
decision-making is in its infancy in veterinary medi-
cine. An ex vivo chemosensitivity platform for canine
lymphoma is available to help predict the efficacy of
commonly utilized lymphoma chemotherapeutics
including vincristine, cyclophosphamide, doxorubicin,
lomustine, rabacfosadine, and other drugs. Lymphoma
cells are plated and exposed to various chemothera-
peutics followed by cell viability analysis with a resa-
zurin-based assay. This information is analyzed via a
proprietary artificial intelligence (AI) assay and the
information combined with phenotyping information
from flow cytometry & PCR for Antigen Receptor
Rearrangement (PARR) with the goal of helping clini-
cians be more precise in choosing efficacious drugs. In
a study of 242 canine lymphoma patients, this
AI-based assay does appear to have predictive value
for outcome in evaluating progression-free survival in
both B- and T-cell lymphoma patients (Bohannan
et al., 2021; Koo et al., 2021).
There are commercially available next-generation
sequencing platforms to identify gene alterations in
known cancer genes promoted to help improve
treatment outcome, but strong evidence in support
of the therapeutic and prognostic value to patients
is not available at this time (see Fenger, Chapter 11,
this volume 2023).
The allure of these genomic and drug-matching
approaches to veterinary oncology is strong. It is
important to recognize that the adoption of these
approaches in human oncology has been largely
driven by the motivation of patients and not the
result of physician adoption into the standard of
care. Indeed, it has been surprisingly difficult to
demonstrate the value of many precision oncology
approaches in humans at this time. Important gaps
in knowledge must be addressed in human oncol-
ogy before the value of these approaches can be
expected to be delivered. It is not surprising that
demand for these products by veterinary oncology
consumers is strong, especially given public mis-
conception of the widespread use and adoption as
a standard in human patients.

3 	Metronomic Chemotherapy
ARATA MATSUYAMA AND ANTHONY MUTSAERS*
Ontario Veterinary College, University of Guelph, Guelph, Ontario, Canada
Introduction
Metronomic chemotherapy is a unique therapeutic
approach designed to administer conventional
chemotherapeutic agents in a manner that opti-
mizes their potential effects on the tumor microen-
vironment, particularly their antiangiogenic and
immunomodulatory activities (Fig. 3). While cyto-
toxic chemotherapeutic drugs are commonly
administered at their maximum tolerated dose
(MTD) intermittently to induce lethal damage to
actively proliferating neoplastic cells, metronomic
chemotherapy is administered chronically at rela-
tively lower doses without a break period. The
therapeutic window of MTD is narrow, resulting in
rare but potentially serious adverse events and the
subsequent requirement of a treatment break
period to allow for healthy cell recovery from the
cytotoxicity 	(Chabner 	and 	Longo, 	2011).
Unfortunately, the prolonged drug-free intervals of
MTD chemotherapy allow cancer recovery, includ-
ing reestablishing blood supply to the cancer tis-
sues. To address the challenge, two research groups
tested shortened drug-free intervals at varying
doses and demonstrated antiangiogenic properties
of low-dose chemotherapeutic agents such as cyclo-
phosphamide in rodent models (Browder et al.,
2000; Klement et al., 2000). In reference to these
studies, the term “metronomic chemotherapy” was
first coined in a letter by Hanahan et al. (2000).
While 	metronomic 	chemotherapy 	was 	later
reported to deplete regulatory T cells (Tregs),
thereby reducing cancer-induced immune suppres-
sion (Ghiringhelli et al., 2007), immunologically
based tumor regressions following injections of
low-dose cyclophosphamide have been docu-
mented as early as the 1980s both in mouse and
human cancers (Hengst et al., 1981; Berd and
Mastrangelo, 1988). These indirect anticancer
mechanisms of metronomic chemotherapy appear
to be evident in canine species, and together with
generally low side effect incidences and availability
of orally administrable protocols, there have been
increasing numbers of preclinical and clinical trials
published in both human and veterinary oncology.
Therefore, this chapter describes the mechanisms
and rationale for therapeutic application of metro-
nomic chemotherapy and outlines the existing gaps
between biologic theory and clinical evidence in
veterinary oncology.
Chemotherapeutic Targeting
of the Tumor Microenvironment
Alkylating agents, such as cyclophosphamide and
chlorambucil, are most commonly used in metro-
nomic chemotherapy protocols in both human and
veterinary patients (Lien et al., 2013; Cramarossa
et al., 2014). Their primary mechanism of action is
covalent binding of alkyl groups to cellular mole-
cules, such as DNA, RNA, and proteins. These
bindings are mediated by reactive intermediates
formed by the parent compounds, resulting in
cross-linking and subsequent cell death (Chabner
and Longo, 2011). Both vascular endothelial cells
and Tregs are sensitive to chronic exposure to low
doses of these agents, leading to antiangiogenic and
immunomodulatory effects, respectively.
The vascular endothelial cell is a critical compo-
nent of tumor biology and targeting these cells has
been a successful goal of antiangiogenic therapies.
Indeed, low-dose cyclophosphamide with a shorter
drug-free interval induces prolongation of the S
phase of the cell cycle, decreases cell migration,
and induces apoptosis of vascular endothelial cells
*Email: mutsaers@uoguelph.ca
© CAB International 2023. Therapeutic Strategies in Veterinary Oncology (C. Khanna ed.)
DOI: 10.1079/9781789245820.0003
41

-- 57 of 258 --

(Browder et al., 2000). One reported key mediator
of cyclophosphamide-induced endothelial cell
apoptosis is the endogenous antiangiogenic peptide
thrombospondin 1 (TSP-1). Vascular endothelial
cells and certain cancer cells increase TSP-1 pro-
duction upon exposure to low-dose cyclophospha-
mide. The released TSP-1 molecules bind to CD36
receptors on the endothelial cell surface with sub-
sequent induction of apoptosis (Bocci et al., 2003;
Hamano et al., 2004). The unique cytotoxicity to
endothelial cells results in decreased microvessel
density (MVD), reduced circulating progenitor
endothelial cells, modulation of tumor hypoxia,
and increased tumor necrosis (Browder et al.,
2000; Bertolini et al., 2003; Shahrzad et al., 2008;
Burton et al., 2011). Reduction in tumor produc-
tion of vascular endothelial cell growth factor A
(VEGF), a potent inducer of endothelial cell prolif-
eration and migration, has also been reported both
in vitro and in vivo/preclinical trials using metro-
nomic chemotherapy (Colleoni et al., 2006; Aktas
et al., 2012; Mainetti et al., 2013). In dogs, statisti-
cally significant changes in circulating TSP-1 and
VEGF were not observed in a study of 30 cancer-
bearing dogs following 2- to 4-week exposures to
alkylators (Denies et al., 2017). It is possible that
the lack of significant alterations observed in that
study may relate to the chosen dose of cyclophos-
phamide (12.5 mg/m2) and/or the heterogeneity of
cancer types included. While circulating levels of
TSP-1 and VEGF were not specifically evaluated,
reduced MVD was documented in canine soft tis-
sue sarcomas (STS) following treatment with a
higher dose (15 mg/m2) of cyclophosphamide but
not at 12.5 mg/m2 (Burton et al., 2011).
Metronomic cyclophosphamide impacts the
makeup of lymphoid subsets. Tregs, which suppress
the immune response, are frequently activated and
increased in cancer patients. These Tregs are par-
ticularly sensitive to cyclophosphamide. Tregs carry
low intracellular ATP levels and subsequent low
glutathione 	expression 	(Zhao 	et 	al., 2010).
Glutathione is a key detoxifier of alkylating agents,
especially for cyclophosphamide metabolites, and
as a result, Tregs accumulate higher levels of active
cyclophosphamide metabolites within the cell
(Zhao et al., 2010). In addition, these cells may be
less likely to extrude these metabolites, as expres-
sion of the drug efflux transporter ATP-binding
cassette (ABC) subfamily B member 1 (ABCB1)
was shown to be reduced in Tregs (Dimeloe et al.,
2014). While alkylating agents are not known
ABCB1 substrates, increased apoptosis was never-
theless observed following ABCB1 blockade by
verapamil in CD4+ lymphocytes, whereas Treg
susceptibility did not change regardless of the addi-
tion of verapamil (Dimeloe et al., 2014). Treg-
specific depletion by oral cyclophosphamide has
been clinically confirmed to be dose-dependent in
human advanced cancer patients, where a higher
dose (200 mg/day) induced nonspecific lymphocyte
depletion as opposed to a lower-dose metronomic
regimen (100 mg/day) (Ghiringhelli et al., 2007).
Similarly, reduced circulating Treg number was
demonstrated in dogs with STS following a 4-week
exposure to metronomic cyclophosphamide with-
out affecting the remaining lymphocyte subsets and
other peripheral blood cells, although the follow-
up was limited to the 1-month period (Burton
et al., 2011). Upon drug cessation, a rapid and
complete restoration of decreased peripheral Treg
count induced by metronomic cyclophosphamide
was observed over a 3-month period in metastatic
human breast cancer patients (Ge et al., 2012).
While this result would urge long-term evaluation
of the immunomodulatory effects of metronomic
cyclophosphamide in canine species, it is notewor-
thy that the clinical responses as well as circulating
tumor reactive T-cell levels were maintained despite
the Treg restoration (Ge et al., 2012).
The antiangiogenic and immunomodulatory
effects of metronomic chemotherapy may also be
interactively related. Circulating Tregs express
higher levels of VEGF receptor 2 (VEGFR-2) com-
pared to other CD4+ lymphocytes and Treg num-
bers expand in response to VEGF exposure, the
effect of which can be counteracted by a neutraliz-
ing VEGF antibody (Wada et al., 2009). Similarly,
the innate immune response induced by low-dose
cyclophosphamide was reversed by VEGF receptor
(VEGFR) blockade with the tyrosine kinase inhibi-
tor axitinib in a preclinical model (Doloff and
Waxman, 2012). This phenomenon is clinically
evident as shown by reduction of Treg proportion
in both peripheral circulation and the tumor micro-
environment with anti-VEGF antibody therapy
(Roland et al., 2009; Wada et al., 2009; Terme et al.,
2013). The VEGFR blockade also induced in situ
immunologic reactions such as increased intratumoral
interleukin-1β (IL-1β) expression and decreased mye-
loid-derived suppressor cell infiltrate (Roland
et al., 2009; Wada et al., 2009; Terme et al.,
2013). Similarly, toceranib phosphate, a veterinary
approved small-molecule inhibitor of multiple
42 	A. Matsuyama and A. Mutsaers

-- 58 of 258 --

43	Metronomic Chemotherapy
tyrosine kinase receptors, including VEGFR-2, can
deplete Treg in cancer-bearing dogs with and with-
out the addition of metronomic cyclophosphamide
(Mitchell et al., 2012). In that study, the Treg
exhaustion was inversely correlated to serum
interferon-γ level.
Vascular normalization induced by antiangio-
genic therapy is another known mechanism that
would enable enhanced immune cell infiltration
into the tumor through normalized blood vessels
with improved blood flow and tissue perfusion
(Shrimali et al., 2010). While it seems counterintui-
tive that antiangiogenic therapies that inhibit tumor
vasculature would result in improved blood flow
and tumor perfusion, vascular normalization has
been demonstrated in multiple scenarios, including
clinically (Willett et al., 2006). However, many
other studies of antiangiogenic agents show
increased hypoxia within the tumor microenviron-
ment, and therefore the exact nature of blood flow
disruption or enhancement with antiangiogenic
therapies, including metronomic chemotherapy,
remains to be fully resolved.
In addition to the antiangiogenic and immuno-
modulatory effects, other potential antineoplastic
mechanisms may exist with the use of low-dose
cytotoxic chemotherapeutic agents. Those mecha-
nisms include induction of tumor dormancy,
chemosensitization of cancer stem cells (Folkins
et al., 2007), inhibition of tumor stromal cell acti-
vation (Chan, T.S. et al., 2016), and potential direct
cancer cell killing, highlighted in a recent review
article (André et al., 2017). However, scientific evi-
dence for these proposed theories is currently lim-
ited and further research is warranted to validate
the relative contribution of these mechanisms to
the anticancer effects observed.
In addition to continuous dosing of conventional
chemotherapeutic drugs, other agents with the
potential to target cancer cells and/or the tumor
microenvironment are often utilized in metronomic
chemotherapy combination protocols. For exam-
ple, 	nonsteroidal 	anti-inflammatory 	drugs
(NSAIDs) are frequent components of metronomic
chemotherapy protocols in both humans and dogs.
The primary target of NSAIDs is cyclooxygenase
(COX), a prostaglandin H synthase, which facili-
tates cancer progression through multiple path-
ways. An inducible COX isoform, COX-2, plays
key roles in the inflammatory/angiogenic tumor
microenvironment by regulating production of
proangiogenic factors, such as VEGF and nitric
oxide (Dormond and Rüegg, 2001). Subsequent
inhibition of these factors by NSAIDs results in
indirect anticancer effects through antiangiogene-
sis. In addition, NSAIDs also have direct antineo-
plastic activity by suppressing COX-2-induced
BCL-2, matrix metalloproteinase (MMP), and αvβ3
integrin expression in cancer cells, proteins which
contribute to apoptosis resistance and increased
cell invasion and migration (Gately and Li, 2004).
In canine species, several studies have demon-
strated COX-2 expression in carcinomas (urogeni-
tal, mammary, apocrine gland anal sac, nasal, and
squamous cell carcinoma) and osteosarcoma (OSA)
(Wolfesberger et al., 2006; Impellizeri and Esplin,
2008; Cekanova et al., 2013; Knudsen et al., 2013;
Millanta et al., 2016; Carvalho et al., 2017). Given
the increased COX-2 activity in neoplastic condi-
tions, compared to the ubiquitous COX-1 expres-
sion in normal tissues, COX-2-selective drugs have
been increasingly investigated in cancer research. In
addition to the potential for better anticancer activ-
ity, higher COX-2 selectivity decreases the risk of
side effects associated with inhibition of homeo-
static COX-1 functions, such as gastrointestinal
ulceration and renal failure. However, the clinical
oncologic significance of selecting drugs with
higher COX-2 affinity has yet to be demonstrated,
and older nonselective COX inhibitors such as
piroxicam are widely used in dogs and have shown
antineoplastic activity with acceptable toxicity in a
variety of cancers (Knapp et al., 1992, 1994; Lana
et al., 2007; Elmslie et al., 2008; Spugnini et al.,
2014; London et al., 2015; Cancedda et al., 2016;
Eichstadt et al., 2017; Finotello et al., 2017; Polton
et al., 2018; Rossi et al., 2018; Treggiari et al.,
2020). It is also noteworthy that COX-independent
activities of NSAIDs and their metabolites have
also been shown to contribute to chemopreventive
effects in canine cancers (Baek et al., 2009).
Thalidomide is another anticancer agent that is
potentially effective as a component of metronomic
chemotherapy protocols. Thalidomide and two
later-developed analogs (lenalidomide and poma-
lidomide) are classified as immunomodulatory
agents that produce both antiangiogenic and
immunomodulatory effects. Thalidomide binds to
multiple proteins including cereblon, which is a
substrate receptor of the E3 ligase complex, and
subsequent degradation of Ikaros family proteins,
exerting both antimyeloma effects and teratogenic-
ity (Ito et al., 2010; Krönke et al., 2014). The direct
anticancer effects of thalidomide are mediated by

-- 59 of 258 --

inhibition of cyclin-dependent kinases and down-
regulation of nuclear factor-κB (NF-κB) with
accompanying cell cycle arrest and suppression of
proneoplastic molecules such as urokinase plas-
minogen activator receptor (Kobayashi et al.,
2005). Thalidomide also inhibits endothelial sprout
formation and cell migration by a different mecha-
nism, characterized by reductions in tumor necrosis
factor-α (TNF-α), VEGF, and basic fibroblast
growth factor (bFGF) production by bone marrow
stromal cells (Quach et al., 2010). The anti-TNF-α
effect, combined with T-cell co-stimulation and
natural killer (NK) cell activation, contribute to
its immunomodulatory effects, and is considered
one of the primary antimyeloma mechanisms.
Lenalidomide and pomalidomide appear to be
more potent immunomodulatory agents with a
direct anti-Treg effect both in vitro and in vivo,
which is a mechanism that is absent with thalido-
mide (Galustian et al., 2009). Despite the increas-
ing 	interest 	in 	combining 	thalidomide 	with
chemotherapy in metronomic protocols, mechanis-
tic investigation of these drug combinations is cur-
rently lacking in veterinary patients.
Approaches to Clinical Application
Chemotherapy drug selection
Metronomic chemotherapy was first predominated
by use of cytotoxic drugs such as alkylators, vinca
alkaloids, or antimetabolites at attenuated doses
and inter-dosing intervals. The wide availability of
clinically similar but functionally different chemo-
therapy agents has not only enabled drug substitu-
tion to avoid adverse effects unique to specific drug
types but also permitted incorporation of multiple
drugs with different mechanisms of action into
combination protocols, in line with oncologic prin-
ciples of combination chemotherapy. The relatively
low toxicity profile that has been demonstrated
with these drugs at metronomic dosing also may
encourage clinical concurrent usage. Optimizing
drug dose and interval has been the focus of a num-
ber of preclinical and clinical studies, whereas the
selection of effective drug combinations has been
entirely empirical due to the extremely limited cur-
rent evidence and the wide array of possible mecha-
nisms of action for metronomic approaches, which
confounds the development of biomarkers of effec-
tive exposure. While it is possible (but unlikely)
that antiangiogenesis and immunomodulation with
metronomic chemotherapy may impact the tumor
microenvironment more or less ubiquitously across
different tumor types, specific drug-type depend-
ency of anticancer activity as well as the presence
of drug antagonism have been reported (Fioravanti
et al., 2009; Aktas et al., 2012; Chow et al., 2014).
For instance, addition of metronomic 5-fluoroura-
cil and oxaliplatin to low-dose irinotecan signifi-
cantly inhibited its in vitro cytotoxicity and
prevented the reduction in tumor growth and
MVD seen with single-agent treatment (Fioravanti
et al., 2009). Regardless, efficacy of multiple chem-
otherapy drug metronomic protocols with or with-
out addition of targeted drugs such as toceranib
phosphate, thalidomide, NSAIDs, and/or doxycy-
cline, and even in combination with other treat-
ment modalities such as MTD chemotherapy or
immunotherapy, has been reported.
Combination with targeted drugs
Toceranib phosphate is a veterinary approved
tyrosine kinase receptor inhibitor that blocks mul-
tiple receptors, including VEGFR and platelet-
derived growth factor receptor (PDGFR) (Liao
et al., 2002). Given the proangiogenic role of these
tyrosine kinase receptors, toceranib may be clini-
cally used to target the cancer microenvironment,
sometimes in conjunction with conventional chem-
otherapeutics (Mitchell et al., 2012; Robat et al.,
2012; Pan et al., 2016; Pellin et al., 2017; Wouda
et al., 2018). A combination of toceranib with
MTD chemotherapy protocols can effectively tar-
get certain cancers with aberrant constitutive
expression of relevant targets such as KIT expres-
sion in mast cell tumors and may also facilitate
effective drug delivery to tumor sites via vascular
normalization (Taguchi et al., 2008; Robat et al.,
2012; Pan et al., 2016). Toceranib can be concur-
rently used with MTD chemotherapy protocols
with mild dose reductions, where myelosuppres-
sion is frequently the dose-limiting toxicity (Robat
et al., 2012; Pan et al., 2016; Pellin et al., 2017;
Wouda et al., 2018). On the other hand, studies
investigating concurrent use of toceranib with oral
metronomic cyclophosphamide have been imple-
mented safely at the standard doses for both agents
(Mitchell et al., 2012; London et al., 2015). Such
combination therapy may activate a suppressed
host immune system associated with increased cir-
culating Treg (Mitchell et al., 2012). While both
toceranib and metronomic chemotherapy inhibit
44 	A. Matsuyama and A. Mutsaers

-- 60 of 258 --

45	Metronomic Chemotherapy
angiogenesis, partly via downregulation of the
VEGFR-2 signaling pathway, they do not appear to
be antagonistic, perhaps because of the lower affin-
ity of toceranib for VEGFR-2 and the presence of
multi-receptor targeting (Doloff et al., 2014). In
mouse glioma models, the innate immune response
induced by metronomic cyclophosphamide was
inhibited by the potent VEGFR-2 inhibitor axitinib
or specific antibody but not by sorafenib, which is
functionally and structurally similar to toceranib
(Doloff and Waxman, 2012; Doloff et al., 2014).
Therefore, while clinical evidence is lacking, caution
is needed when combining metronomic chemother-
apy with small-molecule signaling inhibitors (see
Rönnberg, Chapter 6, this volume, 2023), as they
typically inhibit multiple targets and may create
harm, inclusive of accelerating cancer progression.
Immunotherapy
Given the current expansion of knowledge regard-
ing targeting the immune system to treat cancers
that is leading to successful clinical application (see
Mason and Dow, Chapter 8, this volume, 2023),
coupled with the demonstrated immunomodula-
tory effects of metronomic chemotherapy, an
opportunity exists to investigate such combination
approaches across multiple immunotherapy strate-
gies. For example, low-dose cyclophosphamide has
been shown to boost oncolytic viral immunother-
apy in mouse models of metastatic melanoma (Pol
et al., 2020). The movement of oncolytic virother-
apy and other immunotherapies into veterinary
clinical investigation, such as targeting of the pro-
grammed cell death-1/programmed cell death-1
ligand (PD-1/PDL-1) signaling pathway, could
allow for further study into whether these
approaches are more efficacious following precon-
ditioning of the tumor microenvironment with
metronomic chemotherapy.
Disease setting
Metronomic chemotherapy studies have been con-
ducted in dogs in both macroscopic and micro-
scopic disease settings. While specific tumor and
patient characteristics are likely important factors
in response to treatment, it seems clear that metro-
nomic chemotherapy generally exerts any antineo-
plastic effects gradually over time, and therefore
would not appear suitable as a sole therapy for a
case that requires urgent relief of clinical symptoms
or is at high risk of death due to the presence of
gross disease. Rapidly effective cytoreductive local
therapies, such as surgical resection of the tumor,
need to be considered, when possible, then low-
dose metronomic (LDM) chemotherapy may be
started in smaller tumor burden or adjuvant/
microscopic disease settings. The exact relation-
ship between tumor burden and tumor response to
metronomic chemotherapy is unclear. Within the
tumor microenvironment, angiogenesis is a crucial
factor for both microscopic and macroscopic
tumors to progress. While lack of vascularization
within the core of a tumor can result in hypoxia,
necrosis, or even apoptosis, microscopic disease
requires gain of angiogenic profiles (the so-called
“angiogenic switch”) to progress to a gross disease
state (Holmgren and Folkman, 1995; Naumov
et al., 2006). The log kill hypothesis of cytotoxic
chemotherapy favors the use of MTD protocols in
smaller tumor burdens and shows maximum effect
in microscopic disease settings (Emens and Jaffee,
2005; Gulley et al., 2011). The same principle may
(and perhaps should) apply to antiangiogenic
therapy or LDM chemotherapy, yet to date, scien-
tific data to support this assumption is absent. In
fact, many metronomic chemotherapy applications
are considered for palliation in patients that are
not deemed suited to conventional therapy due to
advanced disease status and/or comorbidities. As a
result, many studies have shown sustained stable
disease of gross tumor burden in advanced cases,
while evidence for improvement of outcome in
adjuvant settings is limited. The same may be said
for certain direct antiangiogenic strategies, such as
bevacizumab (Avastin) that showed anticancer
effects in early trials of metastatic disease that
were not observed when the drug was moved into
the adjuvant setting. Postoperatively, immune sup-
pression and potential acceleration of angiogenesis
can occur in association with pain and surgical
and anesthetic procedures (Perry and Douglas,
2019). It is possible that such detrimental effects
may be reduced by the perioperative application of
metronomic chemotherapy. However, before this
theory is tested clinically, metronomic chemother-
apy treatment benefits in microscopic settings
should be confirmed prospectively, while develop-
ing and validating disease-monitoring biomarkers.
In the absence of measurable gross disease, anti-
cancer effects are challenging to measure against
untreated control populations, particularly for
slowly progressive tumors that may take months

-- 61 of 258 --

to years to progress to macroscopic disease, like
low- to intermediate-grade canine STS.
Patient selection
Given that pharmacokinetic and in vitro studies
have demonstrated difficulty in achieving cytotoxic
doses directly to neoplastic cells, characterizing the
angiogenic and/or immunosuppressive profiles of
individual patients may lead to more logical patient
selection compared to selection by histologic tumor
type. A similar but more robust approach to preci-
sion medicine has been successfully used to select
patients for relevant targeted therapies in human
oncology, such as HER2/neu expression in breast
cancer and BRAF gene mutation in melanoma. In
veterinary medicine, the feasibility of a precision
medicine strategy using excised tumor samples has
been tested with timely transcriptomic assessment
(Monks et al., 2013; Paoloni et al., 2014). Less-
invasive patient selection approaches that may
apply to metronomic chemotherapy include blood
sample collection for quantification and transcrip-
tomic characterization of circulating cells such as
Treg and/or endothelial progenitor cells, and/or
analysis of serum angiogenic marker expression.
These assays do not require a biopsy or surgical
removal of tumor tissues. Such an approach must be
prospectively evaluated for clinical significance but
can be effectively performed through creation of
algorithms that take both angiogenic and immune
cell factors into consideration. Identification of
pharmacodynamic biomarkers would facilitate
more effective and logical tumor response evalua-
tion than volumetric tumor measurements.
Studies in Veterinary Oncology
Over 30 clinical trials of metronomic chemother-
apy in dogs have been reported since 2007. These
studies commonly utilized alkylators based on
reported preclinical evidence and wide drug avail-
ability, yet the types, dosing, and frequency of the
alkylators are diverse. While LDM chemotherapy is
more commonly studied in carcinomas in human
oncology, particularly breast cancers, sarcomas are
the most common cancers reported in canine spe-
cies, including hemangiosarcoma (HSA), OSA, and
STS. This difference may be related to the higher
sarcoma prevalence in dogs.
Canine visceral HSA is one of the most studied can-
cers for the efficacy of metronomic chemotherapy,
perhaps due to its extremely high metastatic rate,
poor prognosis, and angiogenic cellular origin
(Lamerato-Kozicki et al., 2006). In a study of adju-
vant daily cyclophosphamide with alternating
etoposide and piroxicam in nine dogs with stage II
splenic HSA, significantly longer median survival
time (MST) was reported by the addition of daily
cyclophosphamide (Lana et al., 2007). The results
of the study were encouraging; however four sub-
sequent retrospective studies showed no survival
benefit by the addition of low-dose oral cyclophos-
phamide +/– NSAIDs to MTD chemotherapy in
dogs with splenic HSA (Wendelburg et al., 2015;
Matsuyama et al., 2017a; Alexander et al., 2019;
Treggiari et al., 2020). The reported MST in these
studies ranged from 4 to 7 months with adjuvant
MTD followed by metronomic cyclophosphamide.
Although a study by Treggiari and colleagues
reported comparable outcomes with postoperative
MTD anthracyclines versus LDM chemotherapy
for stage I/II splenic HSA, the LDM group had a
higher proportion of stage I disease, which was a
positive prognostic factor in the studied population
(Treggiari et al., 2020). Survival analysis was not
performed on an intent-to-treat basis, indicating
the possibility of case selection bias. In contrast,
two studies have reported favorable outcomes in
canine stage II but not III splenic HSA when treated
with thalidomide (Finotello et al., 2017; Bray et al.,
2018). The lack of benefit in advanced-stage dis-
ease may be related to the duration of time needed
before the antineoplastic effects of the metronomic
chemotherapy occur and/or the persistent risk of
spontaneous bleeding from lesions in stage III dis-
ease, where cytostatic effects may have little clinical
significance. As of April 2023, thalidomide availa-
bility is limited for veterinary clinical use in North
America due to its teratogenicity, and a canine
clinical trial using thalidomide was postponed in
Canada due to this restriction (Woods et al., 2005).
Therefore, to date, published studies using thalido-
mide have been primarily conducted in Europe or
Oceania. 	Regardless, 	prospective 	pharmaco-
dynamic assessment of thalidomide including a
control group is needed.
OSA is another highly metastatic sarcoma, where
increased serum VEGF levels and circulating Tregs
are documented in affected dogs (Thamm et al.,
2008; Biller et al., 2010). While three studies have
assessed adjuvant metronomic cyclophosphamide
in canine appendicular OSA following standard of
care, the outcome was not encouraging (Bracha
46 	A. Matsuyama and A. Mutsaers

-- 62 of 258 --

47	Metronomic Chemotherapy
et al., 2014; London et al., 2015; Matsuyama et al.,
2018). In a multi-institutional prospective trial of
126 OSA-bearing dogs, the reported median pro-
gression-free interval (PFI) and MST with the use
of metronomic cyclophosphamide +/– toceranib
phosphate were 7 to 8 months and 8 to 10.5
months respectively, which are not superior to the
outcomes with standard of care (London et al.,
2015). Similar outcomes (PFI of 6 to 6.5 months)
were also reported in a study of concurrent MTD
carboplatin/doxorubicin with daily cyclophospha-
mide and piroxicam in dogs with appendicular
OSA (Bracha et al., 2014). Another study that ret-
rospectively compared the prognosis with standard
of care +/– daily metronomic cyclophosphamide
and meloxicam also did not report statistically sig-
nificant differences in outcome (Matsuyama et al.,
2018). Power analysis in that study showed a need
for 107 dogs to detect a minimum 8-month differ-
ence in PFI, while the study included only 39 dogs,
leaving the possibility of a type II error. Like canine
HSA, applying metronomic chemotherapy in gross
disease settings could be clinically challenging in
canine OSA; however, measurable shrinkage of a
recurrent bone lesion (n = 1) and stabilized gross
disease (n = 2) have been reported in limited cases
(Tripp et al., 2011; Leach et al., 2012; Spugnini
et al., 2014). Duffy et al. examined the outcome of
86 dogs with OSA receiving palliative radiotherapy
on gross disease with or without daily oral lomus-
tine, and no survival benefit was detected (Duffy
et al., 2018). These results indicate that currently
the clinical benefit of commonly utilized LDM
chemotherapy protocols in canine appendicular
OSA is limited.
Canine STS is a locally invasive cancer, where
local tumor recurrence after incomplete resection is
a common clinical challenge. Canine STS is a
highly angiogenic tumor that frequently produces
focal hypoxia and subsequent necrosis (Dennis
et al., 2011; de Queiroz et al., 2013; Zornhagen
et al., 2015). The biologic activity of metronomic
chemotherapy against canine STS was prospec-
tively documented via reduction in MVD and circu-
lating Tregs following daily LDM cyclophosphamide
for 4 weeks (Burton et al., 2011). Clinically, a sig-
nificant delay in tumor recurrence following incom-
plete STS resection was reported with daily
cyclophosphamide and piroxicam treatment in 85
dogs (Elmslie et al., 2008). While less than 20% of
the treated dogs developed local recurrence, all 55
dogs in the control group developed local recurrence
with the median PFI of 211 days, resulting in a
significant difference in PFI between the groups
(410 versus 211 days). Even complete remission of
a canine STS case in the macroscopic disease setting
has been reported within a study of a daily chlor-
ambucil protocol (Leach et al., 2012). When com-
bined with radiation therapy on gross disease, a
metronomic chemotherapy protocol incorporating
cyclophosphamide, thalidomide, and piroxicam
also showed improvement in MST (Cancedda
et al., 2016).
Immunologic profiling of canine carcinoma
patients has shown increased circulating Treg pro-
portion, hence it is possible that certain canine car-
cinomas may be also effectively treated with
metronomic therapy, similar to human patients
(O’Neill et al., 2009; Lien et al., 2013; Cramarossa
et al., 2014). Individual clinical tumor responses
have been documented in dogs with transitional cell
carcinoma, pulmonary carcinoma, and mammary
carcinoma with varying metronomic protocols
(Schrempp et al., 2013; Spugnini et al., 2014;
Polton et al., 2018). Other sporadically reported
histologies with measurable tumor volume reduc-
tion include nasal tumors (n = 4), inflammatory
mammary carcinoma (n = 2), anal sac adenocarci-
noma (n = 2), primary hepatic cancer (n = 2), mast
cell tumor (n = 1), thyroid carcinoma (n = 1), histio-
cytic sarcoma (n = 1), oral malignant melanoma
(n = 1), and lingual squamous cell carcinoma (n = 1)
(Leach et al., 2012; Marchetti et al., 2012; Spugnini
et al., 2014). Partial responses were also reported in
four of four dogs with inflammatory mammary
carcinoma that underwent a combination of pallia-
tive radiotherapy, toceranib phosphate, thalido-
mide, and piroxicam (Rossi et al., 2018).
While metronomic chemotherapy is relatively
less toxic compared to MTD treatments, some
harmful side effects have been reported in accord-
ance with the various mechanisms of action of each
drug in the protocol and the duration of treatment.
One of the most well-recognized adverse effects of
cyclophosphamide is sterile hemorrhagic cystitis
(SHC), which is caused by urinary accumulation of
the cyclophosphamide metabolite acrolein, induc-
ing irritation of the urinary bladder mucosa. The
incidence of SHC with metronomic cyclophospha-
mide varies from 0 to 80% with a reported median
time to SHC development of 3–9 months in dogs
(Lana et al., 2007; Elmslie et al., 2008; Mitchell
et al., 2012; London et al., 2015; Finotello et al.,
2017; Harper and Blackwood, 2017; Matsuyama

-- 63 of 258 --

et al., 2017b; Ekena et al., 2018; Matsuyama et al.,
2018; Treggiari et al., 2020). The variation in
reported SHC incidence rates may be secondary to
differences in the cumulative doses of cyclophos-
phamide in each study, which is a reported risk
factor for SHC development (Matsuyama et al.,
2017b; Ekena et al., 2018). Individual variation in
glutathione S-transferase (GST) function is a
known SHC risk factor in human patients, and a
recent study investigated genetic GST polymor-
phisms in dogs (Ekena et al., 2018). Drug conjuga-
tion with glutathione by normally expressed GST
decreases cyclophosphamide toxicity, hence the
potential risk of fatal side effects and impact on
outcome with certain GST polymorphisms (Naoe
et al., 2002). Although Ekena et al.’s study did not
show significant associations between GST poly-
morphisms and incidence of cyclophosphamide
side effects, the lack of association may originate in
the lower cyclophosphamide dose used in dogs
compared to humans and/or dose variations sec-
ondary to drug compounding. Interestingly, 16 of
20 (80%) of dogs developed SHC with cumulative
cyclophosphamide doses of 330 to 14,715 mg/m2.
Other factors, such as administering the drug in the
morning, encouraging urination frequently, ensur-
ing water access, and addition of diuretics, may
also be clinically important factors to eliminate
acrolein from the bladder and avoid SHC. In fact,
a considerably reduced SHC incidence (3.6–10.2%)
has been reported with the addition of furosemide
to a metronomic cyclophosphamide protocol
(Chan, C.M. et al., 2016; Setyo et al., 2017). These
results may justify the routine use of diuretics with
regular monitoring of blood renal profile, urine
concentration ability, and blood electrolytes. Other
reported side effects of metronomic cyclophospha-
mide protocols have been mostly low-grade self-
limiting gastrointestinal signs, such as inappetence,
vomiting, and diarrhea, which could have been
influenced by concurrent administration of NSAIDs
(Elmslie et al., 2008; Harper and Blackwood, 2017;
Matsuyama et al., 2017b). Neutropenia or throm-
bocytopenia has been rarely reported with daily
dosing of cyclophosphamide at 10 to 25 mg/m2.
In contrast to the reported results with cyclo-
phosphamide, chronic administration of chloram-
bucil can induce myelosuppression but does not
result in urologic side effects. The bone marrow
progenitor cell injury by cytotoxic drugs accumu-
lates over time and can result in gradual long-term
depletion of the stem cells and clinically detectable
cytopenias (Testa et al., 1985). Both neutropenia
and thrombocytopenia have been reported with
chronic chlorambucil exposures in a potentially
dose-dependent manner (Hanot and de Lorimier,
2014; Custead et al., 2017). In a study of 36 dogs
treated daily with chlorambucil at 4 mg/m2, no
incidence of hematological toxicity was reported
for a follow-up range of 8–798 days (Hanot and de
Lorimier, 2014), while another study reported an
incidence of up to 50% at the 3-month recheck
with a higher dose (8 mg/m2) (Custead et al., 2017).
Similarly, two additional studies reported treatment
discontinuation due to thrombocytopenia in 11 out
of 28 dogs after 8 to 16 months (Bentley et al.,
2018). Chlorambucil-induced thrombocytopenia
can occur irreversibly, emphasizing the need for
close hematological monitoring, especially in
patients with a history of other myelosuppressive
therapy or bone marrow infiltrative disease (Hanot
and de Lorimier, 2014; Custead et al., 2017). Low-
grade gastrointestinal side effects, such as inappe-
tence and vomiting, are uncommon, with reported
incidences of 11 to 24% (Leach et al., 2012;
Schrempp et al., 2013; Custead et al., 2017).
Lomustine may exert renal toxicity when given
as a lower-dose regimen, while myelosuppression
and hepatotoxicity are the most common major
side effects when the drug is given at the MTD
(Hosoya et al., 2009; Heading et al., 2011). In a
prospective 	study, 	LDM 	lomustine 	induced
azotemia in eight out of 52 dogs when used at a
dose of 2.84 mg/m2 every 24 hours (Tripp et al.,
2011). The azotemia was mild in seven dogs, while
the other dog developed severe fatal renal toxicity.
Renal toxicity was also reported in one out of 43
cases treated with the same regimen following pal-
liative radiotherapy for treatment of appendicular
OSA (Duffy et al., 2018). The degree of azotemia
was reported to be dose-limiting in that patient,
although the treatment details were not reported.
In addition, myelosuppression, gastrointestinal tox-
icity, and elevations in alanine transaminase were
observed in up to 25% of patients, indicating the
necessity for protocol modification, such as dose or
administration frequency reduction and/or active
supportive care along with the treatments, espe-
cially in dogs with advanced-stage disease (Tripp
et al., 2011).
The toxicity of NSAIDs appears to be unchanged
when given as a part of metronomic protocol com-
pared to sole therapy. Reduction in prostaglandin
synthesis secondary to COX-1 inhibition can alter

the gastrointestinal mucosal barrier and reduce
renal blood flow, with subsequent ulceration, renal
necrosis, and interstitial nephritis (Knapp et al.,
1992, 1994). No studies have specifically investi-
gated whether aggregated toxicity occurs when
NSAIDs are used with metronomic alkylators, but
caution should be taken, especially with concur-
rent lomustine, due to the potential for renal toxic-
ity (Tripp et al., 2011; Duffy et al., 2018). The
anti-inflammatory effects of NSAIDs can be thera-
peutic for cyclophosphamide-induced SHC, but
are unlikely prophylactic (Matsuyama et al.,
2017b). When piroxicam is solely used without
alkylators, dosing at 0.3 mg/kg daily or 0.5 mg/kg
every other day resulted in gastrointestinal toxicity
in 4.3 to 18.8% of dogs, which resolved with drug
discontinuation (Knapp et al., 1992, 1994; Schmidt
et al., 2001). In a recent large retrospective study,
Eichstadt et al. reported increasing age and use of
gastroprotectants as risk factors for piroxicam-
induced gastrointestinal toxicity in cancer-bearing
dogs (Eichstadt et al., 2017). The majority of
patients (85%) concurrently received MTD chemo-
therapy, and the use of gastroprotectants could
have been merely an intermediate factor. Diagnosis
of transitional cell carcinoma was also found to be
a risk factor for serum creatinine increase in dogs
receiving piroxicam, which is likely related to urin-
ary tract obstruction and/or increased risk of
urinary tract infection by the tumor (Eichstadt
et al., 2017).
Teratogenicity is a well-characterized side effect
of thalidomide and has been the cause of drug
withdrawal from the market for morning sickness
(de Campos et al., 2016). The drug can also affect
the nervous system, leading to sedation/hypnosis,
and indeed sedation is the only reported side
effect among reported doses for dogs, ranging
from 1 to 20 mg/kg every 24 hours (Woods et al.,
2005; Cancedda et al., 2016; de Campos et al.,
2016; Finotello et al., 2017; Bray et al., 2018;
Polton et al., 2018; Rossi et al., 2018; Marconato
et al., 2019; Treggiari et al., 2020). Dose-dependent
sedation can clinically occur for a few hours after
administration, and it can last longer and become
moderate at higher doses (de Campos et al.,
2016). Thalidomide appears to be otherwise well
tolerated. No clinically significant changes on
complete blood count or serum biochemistry were
reported after 3 months of thalidomide treatment
in 29 dogs with mammary tumors (de Campos
et al., 2016).
The Future of “Metronomics”
What role(s) may the low-dose, continuous appli-
cation of cytotoxic chemotherapy drugs have in the
future treatment of veterinary cancers? Does the
favorable toxicity profile and convenient applica-
tion lead to their continued use in strictly palliative
clinical scenarios, where the prognosis is deemed
poor and the most important goal is to maintain
quality of life, while doing no harm, despite a lack
of formal clinical evidence to support anticancer
benefit? Is it more likely that strategic coupling of
LDM chemotherapy with targeted agents based on
validated biomarkers will provide superior benefit
in a subset of patients selected in a personalized
medicine approach? As the field of immunotherapy
advances clinically, will its benefits be improved by
concomitant immunomodulation provided by the
use of concurrent metronomic chemotherapy? Of
course, the answers to these questions are currently
unknown and require further study in well-designed
clinical trials and rigorous preclinical experiments.
What is clearer perhaps, is that a deeper under-
standing of the roles that various components of
the tumor microenvironment play in the response
and resistance to oncologic therapies, including
cytotoxic chemotherapy, will evolve into novel
treatment approaches that are not solely focused
on the cancer cell as a therapeutic target.

Fig. 4. Cancer Metabolism Dependencies: Targeting Building Blocks and Sources of Energy.

-- 72 of 258 --

4 	Targeting Cancer Metabolism
Dependencies
KAYLA HARDING*
Ethos Vet Health, Wheat Ridge, Colorado, USA
Introduction
The development and progression of cancer relies
upon several well-characterized metabolic alterations
that confer proliferative and survival advantages.
These alterations arise as a result of two non-
mutually exclusive driving forces: the need for energy
production in the form of ATP and the requirement
for building blocks in the production of proteins,
lipids, and DNA. As a means of feeding accelerated
cell growth, proliferation, and survival, cancer cells
upregulate cell surface receptors for glucose and
other amino acids. Furthermore, cancer cells alter
metabolism to preferentially utilize glycolysis, the
breakdown of glucose, which yields ATP and pyruvic
acid. This metabolic shift has been termed the
“Warburg effect” and occurs in the presence or
absence of oxygen. The importance of altered energy
metabolism is highlighted by its inclusion in the
updated Hallmarks of Cancer 2011 in which
Reprogramming Energy Metabolism was proposed
as an emerging hallmark of cancer (Hanahan and
Weinberg, 2011). This hallmark is sufficiently mature
for therapeutic targeting, and to be an important
concept for clinical consideration. This chapter will
explore key metabolic derangements in cancer that
may be exploited therapeutically (Fig. 4). Existing
and developing therapeutics will be covered along
with areas of future exploration.
Targeting the Warburg Effect
In normal tissues, approximately 90% of energy is
derived from oxidative phosphorylation, whereas
cancer cells derive only about 40% of their ATP
production from oxidative phosphorylation and
approximately 60% from aerobic glycolysis,
although this can be highly variable depending on
the cancer (Nakashima et al., 1984). There are several
reasons why cancer cells may benefit from this
metabolic shift. Glycolysis can occur under hypoxic
conditions and removes the necessity for adequate
oxygen delivery for cell proliferation and survival.
This alone does not explain the Warburg effect,
however, as many cancer cells will preferentially
use glycolysis even in the presence of oxygen (aero-
bic glycolysis) (Hanahan and Weinberg, 2011). The
proliferation of cancer cells is often occurring at
rapid rates and these cells prefer to utilize the fast-
est and most efficient approach for energy and
biosynthetic pathways (often referred to as “meta-
bolic flexibility”). Indeed, glycolysis offers fast
energy production from the metabolism of lactate
from glucose, occurring ten to 100 times faster
than the complete oxidation of glucose in the mito-
chondria (Liberti and Locasale, 2016). Furthermore,
glycolysis provides a rich carbon source that can
then be utilized for biosynthetic pathways includ-
ing the production of amino acids and lipids. It is
also possible that tumor cells benefit from acidifi-
cation of the tumor microenvironment that occurs
with lactic acid production. An acidic microenvir-
onment may promote further tumor invasion
(Estrella et al., 2013). In addition, utilization of
glucose may limit this nutrient for tumor-infiltrating
lymphocytes that would otherwise have an inhibi-
tory effect on tumor growth (Chang et al., 2015).
Finally, glycolysis may provide benefit in driving
redox potential and homeostasis, as well as modu-
lation of other key intracellular pathways such as
histone acetylation and deacetylation (Evertts
et al., 2013; Cluntun et al., 2015).
57
