Glycolytic Inhibitors
The glycolytic inhibitors 2-deoxy-d-glucose (2-DG)
and citrate have both been evaluated as potential
therapeutic strategies for targeting the Warburg
effect. These compounds have demonstrated cyto-
toxic effects in vitro but have not been further
explored in the in vivo setting. In contrast,
3-bromopyruvate (3BP) is a glycolytic inhibitor that
has demonstrated significant antineoplastic effects in
animal models (Ko et al., 2004). 3BP is a structural
analog of pyruvate that works as an alkylating agent
toward some proteins and enzymes. It is proposed
that 3BP influxes through upregulated monocar-
boxylate transporters (generally used to efflux excess
lactate) or through simple diffusion driven by aber-
rant pH changes in the tumor microenvironment.
3BP may also be specific to cancer cells due to over-
expression of hexokinase 2 (HK2) on mitochondrial
membranes and enhanced glycolysis in these tissues.
The drug then inhibits glycolysis and mitochondrial
ATP production via inhibition of HK2 and GAPDH,
leading to ATP starvation and apoptosis (Lis et al.,
2016, p. 2; Fan et al., 2019). The clinical use of 3BP
has been reported in two human patients with
advanced cancer highly resistant to standard thera-
pies (Ko et al., 2012; El Sayed et al., 2014).
Metformin
Metformin is another strategy that has been uti-
lized to target enhanced glucose utilization in cancer
cells. Metformin is approved as an oral antihyper-
glycemic agent with effects including inhibition of
gluconeogenesis, decreased glucose absorption
from the small intestines, and reduction in insulin
resistance (Rena et al., 2017). Although metformin
has classically been used in the treatment of type 2
diabetes mellitus, numerous preclinical studies have
demonstrated antineoplastic effects and clinical
research into this medication in the treatment of
cancer is ongoing. Metformin modulates or inter-
acts with several cancer pathways and is proposed
to exert antineoplastic effects through a variety of
mechanisms. A primary antineoplastic mechanism
of action is through metformin’s inhibitory effect
on mammalian target of rapamycin (mTOR), an
important regulator of cell growth and survival.
Metformin can also blunt the Warburg effect and
have immune-modulatory effects such as enhanc-
ing survival of CD8+ tumor-infiltrating lympho-
cytes and enhanced effector memory T-cell survival
(Chae et al., 2016; Vancura et al., 2018). Numerous
retrospective studies, including meta-analyses, have
demonstrated reduced risk of cancer development
in patients with diabetes treated long-term with
metformin (Gandini et al., 2014). Currently, clini-
cal trials are underway evaluating metformin used
alone or in combination with cytotoxic chemo-
therapy for numerous cancer types including breast,
colorectal, lung, melanoma, pancreatic, prostatic,
and other advanced cancers (Chae et al., 2016).
Amino Acid Addiction
Many studies have shown relative dependence on
specific amino acids in cancer cells compared to
normal tissue. Some of the better-characterized
amino acid addictions include asparagine, arginine,
and glutamine, although additional amino acid
addictions have also been reported such as methio-
nine, glycine, serine, proline, tyrosine, and phenyla-
lanine. Amino acid starvation leads to cellular
aberrations including initiation of the amino acid
control pathway in which cells attempt to maintain
homeostasis (Fung and Chan, 2017). This occurs via
alterations in cell surface receptors, and changes in
metabolic enzyme and growth hormone expression.
In addition, induction of autophagy for recycling of
intracellular organelles and proteins can occur. If
homeostasis cannot be achieved by these mecha-
nisms, then reduction in protein synthesis, growth
suppression, and programmed cell death will ensue.
Amino acid addiction in cancer can be targeted
as a therapeutic strategy through a variety of
mechanisms. The best-known and utilized approach
is the use of l-asparaginase to deprive cancer cells
of asparagine. With the use of recombinant tech-
nology, high-efficiency bacterial enzymes can be
manufactured in large quantities which offer a
specific and fast-acting means of depriving neoplas-
tic cells of necessary nutrients. Enzymatic therapies
are also being utilized to target glutamine and argi-
nine addictions in a variety of cancers. Several
other therapeutic strategies are under development
or currently in use as a means of targeting altered
glucose metabolism and utilization in cancer cells.
Asparagine depletion
Mechanism of action
l-Asparagine is a nonessential amino acid. Cells
have the ability to produce asparagine via asparagine
58 	K. Harding

-- 74 of 258 --

59	Targeting Cancer Metabolism Dependencies
synthetase, an enzyme that catalyzes the synthesis of
asparagine from aspartate in an ATP-dependent
manner (Lomelino et al., 2017). Once inside the cell,
asparagine plays many important physiologic func-
tions such as regulating uptake of other amino acids
including arginine, histidine, and serine; suppression
of apoptosis caused by glutamine starvation; and
coordination of protein and nucleotide synthesis.
Most importantly, asparagine is a major contributor
to protein synthesis, which is necessary for the
growth and division of cells (O’Connor and Imperiali,
1996; Zhang et al., 2014; Krall et al., 2016).
l-Asparaginase is an enzyme that catalyzes the
conversion of asparagine into l-aspartate and ammo-
nia in the serum, thus depleting circulating asparagine
levels. Asparagine then effluxes from cells into the
serum where it is also destroyed. While most cells
have the ability to produce asparagine from aspartate,
lymphoid malignancies often lack asparagine syn-
thetase and thus rely on exogenous asparagine for cell
survival and growth. Exogenous asparagine depletion
thus leads to death in cells lacking asparagine syn-
thetase. Death may be induced by protein depletion
leading to cessation of proliferation and subsequent
triggering of apoptosis (Story et al., 1993).
The 	l-asparaginase 	enzyme 	obtained 	from
Escherichia coli also contains approximately 1–4%
activity against glutamine, which results in its conver-
sion to glutamate (Capizzi et al., 1970; Valerius et al.,
1999). Glutamine has been shown to be a critical
nutrient for cancer cells and plays important func-
tions in the production of energy, glutathione, and
amino acid synthesis. It is suspected that that activity
against glutamine may contribute to l-asparaginase’s
anticancer effects; however, this mechanism may also
contribute to toxicity associated with the drug.
Sources
l-Asparaginase is found in many organisms including
mammals, microorganisms (yeast, bacteria, proto-
zoa, fungi, actinomyces), and plants. Interestingly,
l-asparaginase was first discovered as a therapeutic
enzyme with the discovery that guinea pig serum
could lead to regression of lymphoma in mice
transplanted with malignant lymphoid cells (Kidd
et al., 2015). Several years later, l-asparaginase was
determined to be the antineoplastic agent present
within guinea pig serum (Broome, 1963). Due to
difficulty in obtaining large amounts of l-asparagi-
nase from guinea pig serum, other sources of the
enzyme were established for therapeutic potential,
with bacterial sources presenting many advantages
such as rapid growth on simple and inexpensive
substrates, easy genetic modification to increase
efficiency of production, good stability, ability to
preserve enzymatic activity ex situ, and economic-
ally feasible production and purification (Lopes
et al., 2017).
Bacterial l-asparaginase enzymes have been
characterized as two main types: type I and type II.
Type I is expressed constitutively and has activity
against asparagine and glutamine, while type II
expresses high specificity for asparagine. Type II
asparaginases are exclusively used therapeutically.
Currently, industrial-scale production solely utilizes
E. coli and Erwinia chrysanthemi as bacterial
enzyme sources (Batool et al., 2016). l-Asparagi-
nase enzymes originating from E. chrysanthemi
generally are less immunogenic, however these
formulations have shorter half-lives. Generally,
formulations derived from E. coli are used as first-
line treatments, whereas formulations from E.
chrysanthemi are reserved for patients who have
developed hypersensitivity reactions to the native
E. coli enzyme (Keating, 2013; Horvat et al., 2016;
Fung and Chan, 2017). While bacteria offer many
advantages for the production of large amounts of
l-asparaginase, disadvantages include the need for
rigorous purification to prevent bacterial contami-
nation and the immunogenic properties of bacterial
enzymes administered to mammalian species.
Novel asparaginase formulations
To address hypersensitivity reactions and drug neu-
tralization, PEGylated forms of l-asparaginase
have been produced by the covalent binding of
polyethylene glycol (PEG) groups to ε-amino acids
in the lysine residues of the asparaginase enzyme.
This coupling significantly reduces immunogenicity
and prolongs half-life in the serum (Abuchowski
et al., 1984). These alterations confer a treatment
advantage by allowing increased dosing intervals
and maintenance of elevated levels of active aspara-
ginase in the serum, which correlates with clinical
efficacy of the drug (Asselin, 1999). PEGylated
forms of asparaginase, pegasparagase, are now the
primary forms of asparaginase available for clinical
use, with the cessation of native E. coli asparagi-
nase occurring in 2012. While PEGylated forms of
asparaginase have been shown to be less immuno-
genic than native forms, allergic reactions are still
possible and pose a considerable barrier to treatment

-- 75 of 258 --

in some patients. It has also been demonstrated
that antibodies can be formed against the PEG
conjugate, although studies in immune-competent
mice suggest that these antibodies do not affect the
pharmacokinetics of asparaginase in the serum
(Poppenborg et al., 2016). Interestingly, a recent
case report in humans described the successful use
of native l-asparaginase in two patients who were
unable to tolerate PEGylated forms of the enzyme,
which suggests that immune reactions to the PEG
conjugate 	can 	also 	be 	clinically 	significant
(Fernandez et al., 2014). Another mechanism of
hypersensitivity to PEGylated formulations of
asparaginase may occur due to instability in the
succinimidyl succinate linker that joins the PEG
groups to the asparaginase enzyme, allowing
release of free bacterial enzyme into the serum. In
2018, the US Food and Drug Administration (FDA)
approved a new form of asparaginase in which this
linker is replaced with a more stable succinimidyl
carbamate bond. This new formulation is called
calaspargase pegol-mknl and is sold under the
trade name CALASP. Although CALASP appears to
have similar efficacy, preliminary studies suggest
that hypersensitivity reactions occur in similar fre-
quency to traditional PEGylated forms of asparagi-
nase (Li et al., 2020).
Commercially 	available 	formulations 	from
E. chrysanthemi are sold under the name crisantas-
pase and include the trade names Erwinase and
Erwinaze. l-Asparaginase formulations from E. coli
are sold under the name colaspase and include the
trade names Elspar, Kidrolase, Leunase, and Spectrila.
PEGylated versions of colaspase are called pegaspar-
gases, and Oncospar and CALASP are the commer-
cially available formulations of these products.
Glutamine depletion
Glutamine is a nonessential amino acid that plays
important roles in energy production, the develop-
ment of glutathione to relieve oxidative stress, and
serves as a building block for protein production.
Glutamine enters the cells via the glutaminase
transporter. Once inside the mitochondria, glu-
tamine may be converted to glutamate by the
enzyme glutaminase. Glutamate may then enter the
cytoplasm for conversion into glutathione or enter
the tricarboxylic acid (TCA) cycle where it is con-
verted to α-ketoglutarate and then ATP for energy
production. Other key molecules that come from
glutamate’s entry into the TCA cycle include
malate, which can be converted to lactate in aero-
bic glycolysis; oxaloacetate, which can be con-
verted to aspartate for nucleic acid synthesis; and
citrate, which can be utilized for amino acid and
lipid synthesis (Fung and Chan, 2017). Glutamine
is also an essential component for the activation of
mTORC1, an important regulator of cell growth
(Nicklin et al., 2009). Glutamine’s critical role in
energy production and as a precursor for protein,
nucleic acid, and lipid production makes it indis-
pensable to a rapidly proliferating population of
cancer cells.
Glutamine depletion for cancer therapy is a logi-
cal therapeutic goal, although the successful
employment of this therapeutic approach is still in
its infancy. Glutamine depletion may be achieved
through glutaminase inhibition, glutamine membrane
transporter inhibition, or glutamine depletion within
the serum. The best-known glutamine-depleting
agent is l-asparaginase, which has cross-reactivity
against glutamine and results in its conversion to
glutamate in the serum (Emadi et al., 2018). However,
there is significant debate regarding the role and
extent of glutamine breakdown associated with
asparaginase treatment with some in vitro studies
reporting that success of treatment correlated with
glutamine depletion, whereas others show that glu-
tamine depletion does not affect therapeutic outcomes
(Wu et al., 1978; Chan et al., 2014). An alternative
approach to glutamine starvation is inhibition of
the glutaminase enzyme, preventing the production
of glutamate for subsequent entry into the TCA
cycle. Several molecules have been developed
including BPTES, 968, and CB-839 in which anti-
cancer activity has been studied in vitro or in vivo
(Song et al., 2018). CB-839 is the furthest devel-
oped with Phase I and II clinical trials in humans
showing tolerable side effects in patients with lym-
phoma, non-small cell lung cancer, and triple-negative
breast cancer (Riess et al., 2021).
Glutamine membrane transporter inhibition has
also been explored as a means to suppress intracel-
lular glutamine concentrations. A major glutamine
transporter is the SLC1A5 (also known as ASCT2)
transporter, which has been shown to be highly
expressed in many different malignancies (van
Geldermalsen et al., 2016; Cormerais et al., 2018;
Lin et al., 2018, p. 1; Zhang et al., 2020). Several
preclinical trials have evaluated the efficacy of vari-
ous compounds in blocking the activity of this
transporter with many showing promise for in vitro
and murine models (Schulte et al., 2018). Development
60 	K. Harding

-- 76 of 258 --

61	Targeting Cancer Metabolism Dependencies
of glutamine membrane transport inhibitors has
not progressed to human trials at this point.
Arginine depletion
Arginine is a semi-essential or conditionally essen-
tial amino acid. The majority of plasma arginine
originates from dietary sources and protein break-
down, although the synthesis of arginine occurs
under specific conditions (Castillo et al., 1993;
Morris, 2016). This amino acid is classified as con-
ditionally essential because de novo synthesis does
not meet demands under periods of physiologic
stress including renal and/or intestinal disease
states (Morris, 2016). Arginine is an important
component in normal physiology with key func-
tions that include its role as a building block for
protein synthesis and as a precursor for several
molecules including nitric oxide (NO), urea, and
creatinine (Morris, 2016). Arginine can be synthe-
sized from aspartate and citrulline via the actions
of arginosuccinate synthetase 1 (ASS1) and argino-
succinate lyase (ASL). ASS1 is constitutively
expressed in most tissues, and its expression is
particularly important in the liver and kidneys for
urea cycling and endothelial cells for the produc-
tion of NO (Husson et al., 2003).
Several studies have documented minimal to
absent ASS1 expression in various tumor types,
making arginine a conditionally essential amino
acid in these tissues (Dillon et al., 2004; Delage
et al., 2012). Decreased ASS1 expression often
results from methylation-dependent transcriptional
silencing although other mechanisms also play a
role in some tumors (Delage et al., 2012). Arginine-
degrading enzymes have been developed as a means
of targeting arginine dependency in tumor cells
lacking ASS1. Arginine depletion alone can lead to
both caspase-mediated and caspase-independent
mechanisms of apoptosis and autophagy resulting
from an inability to synthesize proteins and nucleic
acids (Kim et al., 2009; Delage et al., 2012).
Additional metabolic derangements associated
with arginine depletion and arginase therapy are
also important in cell death. For example, consider-
able crosstalk between arginine and glutamine
exists and the presence of arginine in the serum
appears to have a sparing effect for glutamine in
the synthesis of pyrimidines. Some of the cytotoxic
effect from arginase therapy may arise as a result of
alterations in glutamine availability for nucleotide
synthesis (Long et al., 2013; Phillips et al., 2013).
Furthermore, arginine deiminase downregulates
expression of mTOR and modulates phosphoi-
nositide 3-kinase (PI3K) via suppression of phos-
phatase and tensin homolog (PTEN) activity
(Phillips et al., 2013).
Arginase forms that are currently under develop-
ment or in clinical trial stages include a recombinant
human arginase enzyme and mycoplasma-derived
arginine deiminase. As with l-asparaginase, thera-
peutic forms are PEGylated to reduce immunogenicity
and improve pharmacokinetic and pharmaco-
dynamic parameters. The arginase enzyme that is
furthest along in development is ADI-PEG20, which
is a PEGylated recombinant enzyme cloned from
Mycoplasma hominis. Preclinical research and
modeling have demonstrated cytotoxic effects of
arginine depletion in numerous tumor types includ-
ing hepatocellular carcinoma, melanoma, small cell
lung cancer, pancreatic carcinoma, and leukemia
(Dillon et al., 2004; Kim et al., 2009; Delage et al.,
2012). ADI-PEG20 has undergone Phase I and II
clinical trials for patients with hepatocellular
carcinoma and melanoma. Not surprisingly, in
patients with metastatic melanoma, responses were
confined to patients who had ASS1-negative tumors
(Feun et al., 2012).
Limitations to arginine deprivation are similar to
those reported for asparagine deprivation and
include induction of immune responses leading to
drug inactivation, hypersensitivity reactions, and
induction of ASS1 expression. Arginine deprivation
is likely to be included in multi-agent protocols to
maximize clinical benefit from this treatment.

Fig. 5. Surgical and Medical Innovations for Metastasis Management.

5 	Antimetastatic Therapy
NICOLE S. A MATO*
Ethos Veterinary Health, Woburn, Massachusetts, USA
Introduction
The ability of cancer cells to metastasize is the pri-
mary cause of solid tumor-related morbidity and
mortality in most human and veterinary cancer
patients (Guan, 2015; Abu-Helil and van der
Weyden, 2019). Traditionally, the approach to the
treatment of malignant solid cancers has been to
manage the primary tumor with surgery and/or
radiation therapy, followed by the use of cytotoxic
drugs that are intended to target micro metastases,
or upon relapse, to treat macro metastatic lesions
with a similar cytotoxic approach (DeVita and
Chu, 2008; Palumbo et al., 2013). This approach to
therapy has delivered measurable benefit in select
cancer 	histologies; 	however, 	further 	clinical
improvements are unlikely to come from this same
approach (Crawford, 2013; Anderson et al., 2019).
Indeed, new drug development strategies and
approaches are now needed to address this contin-
ued unmet need for most cancer patients (Khanna
et al., 2014; Anderson et al., 2019). Specifically,
new antimetastatic progression therapeutics (i.e.,
therapeutics that target metastatic progression
rather than shrink overt tumors) that are mechanis-
tically distinct from those available today are nec-
essary (Khanna et al., 2014; Fontebasso and
Dubinett, 2015).
This chapter will explore the concept of anti-
metastatic progression therapy, revisiting the con-
ventional metastatic cascade, the premetastatic
niche (PMN), dormancy, and the concept of meta-
static endurance (Stewart et al., 2019) as a means
to understand potential disease targets/processes
for the development of these much-needed novel
therapeutics. We will review the basic classification
of these potential agents and the important chal-
lenges that remain for their development. We will
then include a discussion of the use of comparative
oncology as a means to de-risk investment in this
challenging area of drug development. Indeed,
comparative oncology has been proposed as a
potential solution to some of these recognized chal-
lenges in the study and development of antimeta-
static therapies for all species (Paoloni and Khanna,
2007; Gordon et al., 2009; Fan et al., 2020; van der
Weyden et al., 2020). Lastly, although the systemic
prevention and treatment of metastatic progression
is the focus of this chapter, we will address the
intersection between antimetastatic therapy and
the treatment of measurable metastatic lesions once
they have developed, including the potential role
and risks that surgery plays in the management of
established metastatic tumors, using the examples
of pulmonary metastasectomy (PM) and lymph
node dissection and resection (Fig. 5).
Antimetastatic Therapy: Fulflling
an Unmet Need
Historically, most cytotoxic cancer therapeutics
have been developed based on their biologic activ-
ity against cell proliferation or induction of apop-
tosis, not the biology of metastasis (Gandalovicˇová
et al., 2017; Falzone et al., 2018). Even if remark-
ably effective against these processes in their ability
to shrink measurable cancer lesions, such agents
are less likely to add significant value in preventing
metastasis, the primary cause of mortality in cancer
patients overall (Falzone et al., 2018). Accordingly,
most cancer drug development today is misaligned
with the greatest need of cancer patients, which is
the development of drugs that address the problem
of the metastatic progression (Khanna et al., 2014;
Fontebasso and Dubinett, 2015; Anderson et al.,
*Email: namato@ethosvet.com
© CAB International 2023. Therapeutic Strategies in Veterinary Oncology (C. Khanna ed.)
DOI: 10.1079/9781789245820.0005
69

-- 85 of 258 --

2019). Nonetheless, given that a small part of
metastatic progression includes a need for cell pro-
liferation and evasion of apoptosis, there have been
hints of activity derived from this misaligned
approach. For example, the use of cytotoxic chem-
otherapy given in the adjuvant setting to humans
and dogs with localized osteosarcoma (OSA) has
been shown to deliver a benefit by delaying the
progression of metastasis (Mauldin et al., 1988;
Berg et al., 1992, 1995; Thompson and Fugent,
1992; Jafari et al., 2020; Marconato et al., 2021).
However, it is reasonable to believe that a drug
development effort directed against the broader
biology of metastatic progression will deliver more
meaningful value to patients than observed with
agents that target the narrow biologic overlap
between measurable tumor formation and meta-
static progression (i.e., apoptosis and cell prolifera-
tion) (Khanna et al., 2014).
As our understanding of the biology of metastatic
progression has expanded there are currently new
opportunities to develop or repurpose a wide variety
of therapeutics for potential use as drugs that may
uniquely target this process (Anderson et al.,
2019). For instance, the value of recent forms of
immunotherapy in cancer treatment has been the
result of their dual activity in shrinking measurable
tumors and targeting metastasis simultaneously
(Borcoman et al., 2018). Similar serendipitous drug
development will slowly deliver additional therapeu-
tics to patients at risk for metastasis; however, until
very recently, there has been little to no intentional
or purposeful efforts to develop antimetastatic drugs
that pointedly target the biology of metastatic pro-
gression in humans or animals (Lu et al., 2018;
Koons et al., 2021). The relative lack of advances in
this category compared to the vast numbers of can-
cers that metastasize delivers an impetus to discover
noncytotoxic-based antimetastatic therapies that
inhibit metastatic progression, improve patient out-
comes, and align cancer drug development with the
most important needs of patients.
The Problem of Metastasis
Benign tumors are generally slow growing and
noninvasive in nature, often allowing curative-
intent treatment with surgical resection or radio-
therapy (Talmadge and Fidler, 2010). Malignant
tumors by contrast can grow relatively quickly,
show varying degrees of invasion into surrounding
tissue, and are not always amenable to surgical
resection and curative-intent procedures (Talmadge
and Fidler, 2010). These tumors are inherently het-
erogeneous in composition, possessing both tumor
and nontumor cellular constituents that collectively
contribute to the emergence of metastatic proclivity
in 	select 	metastatic 	cellular 	subpopulations
(Mendoza and Khanna, 2009).
Cancer metastasis is a clinical challenge from
every standpoint. For reasons not entirely under-
stood, treating measurable metastases is distinct
and additionally challenging when compared to
treating the primary tumor alone (Qian et al.,
2017). It remains unclear if metastatic lesions are
intrinsically resistant to therapies effectively used in
the management of the primary tumor (surgery or
radiation therapy) or if some metastatic cancers
would benefit from a similar locoregional approach
that 	would 	reprioritize 	surgery 	and 	other
approaches of measurable tumor control for estab-
lished 	metastatic 	lesions 	(Hellman 	and
Weichselbaum, 1995; Weichselbaum and Hellman,
2011). Pediatric OSA is one type of cancer that is
characterized by a surprisingly high proportion of
patients who, following the development of lung
metastases, are essentially cured using PM (Croteau
and Heaton, 2019). It is unclear but important to
learn whether this strategy could be successful for
other types of cancers once macro metastatic
lesions develop, as well as understanding the bio-
logic reasons that explain and may predict the
value of metastasectomy in other cancers.
Notwithstanding these understood exceptions,
with most cancers, the value and rationale for
curative-intent therapy (surgery and radiation ther-
apy) are reduced and not prioritized for most
patients with metastatic disease. Accordingly, clini-
cians must rely on systemic treatment to a greater
extent. Unfortunately, either due to intrinsic or
acquired resistance, most macro metastases are not
responsive to the current systemic treatments (Qian
et al., 2017; Wang et al., 2019) and the prevention
of metastatic progression has become even more
important for patients.
Metastatic Progression Drug
Development Challenges
It is clear that the problem of cancer metastasis and
metastatic cancer progression represents the great-
est unmet need to cancer patients. Despite this
simple matter of fact, there continues to be a
misalignment between the need for drugs that
70 	N.S. Amato

-- 86 of 258 --

71	Antimetastatic Therapy
target metastatic progression and the persistent
focus on the development of drugs that target can-
cer cell proliferation or induction of apoptosis (Fan
et al., 2020). This misaligned approach is challeng-
ing to overcome at many levels. First, preclinical
assays and drug screens specifically for antimeta-
static drugs have only recently been developed and
used (Koons et al., 2021). Second, even if these
drugs are developed and target the unmet need of
metastatic cancer progression, they are unlikely to
be successful at shrinking measurable tumors, and
thus are unlikely to advance successfully through
conventional early-phase human clinical trials
(Sleeman and Steeg, 2010; Khanna et al., 2014;
Anderson et al., 2019). Subsequently, if these drugs
fail in early-phase clinical trials, it is doubtful that
they will be prioritized to advance into such later-
phase trials (Anderson et al., 2019), where cancer
drugs that target metastatic progression have the
potential to be most successful. Accordingly, in the
conventional cancer drug development approach,
the most necessary drugs are destined to fail.
From this perspective, to be successful in the
future, alternative approaches to cancer drug devel-
opment and testing must evolve (Khanna et al.,
2014). Recognition of these drug development
challenges has been made in some types of human
cancers and modifications have been instituted.
Most noteworthy, in pediatric OSA, creative Phase
II trials that circumvent these challenges have been
recently designed and successfully completed
(Bishop et al., 2016). Furthermore, the opportunity
to de-risk the human Phase II trial decision with
parallel data from canine OSA trials of antimeta-
static agents has been recognized, endorsed, and
now must be optimized (Khanna et al., 2014).
Historical Approaches to Target
Metastatic Progression
Historically, there has been a somewhat haphazard
and circuitous path of cancer drug development
that has included the problem of metastasis. These
efforts have resulted in limited successes. Indeed,
the resulting therapeutic agents have serendipitous,
but not purposeful antimetastatic activity.
Invasion inhibitors
The ability for a cancer cell to acquire an invasive
phenotype has been believed to be an important
feature of malignancy (Hanahan and Weinberg,
2011) and has historically been a target for cancer
therapy. As a result of cellular evidence in support
of the role for invasion in metastasis, many early
drug development programs targeting cellular inva-
sion were launched, including those interrogating
matrix 	metalloproteinase 	(MMP) 	inhibitors
(Martin and Matrisian, 2007). Although shown to
be initially promising in preclinical trials, they per-
formed poorly in Phase II and Phase III clinical tri-
als for numerous identified reasons (Vandenbroucke
and Libert, 2014). In retrospect, the failure of this
drug class to effectively target metastatic progres-
sion can now be predicted based on the new
knowledge that matrix invasion is not indepen-
dently sufficient for metastasis (Martin and
Matrisian, 2007). Furthermore, the design of the
clinical trials may have contributed to the failure,
since these agents were tested on patients with
advanced, measurable metastatic disease, whereas
the preclinical trials examined use of the drug early
in the metastatic process (Vandenbroucke and
Libert, 2014). For this class of drugs to have been
successful, it would have needed to be administered
to the patient before invasion occurred, not after it
was established, a scenario that is challenging due
to the fact that dormant micro metastases are likely
present well before treatment onset with current
drug dosing regimens.
Failures of this drug class does provide important
lessons for current and future drug development
paths that seek to target and inhibit metastatic pro-
gression. Beyond the shortcomings in knowledge
surrounding invasion and cancer metastasis, the
development of invasion inhibitors highlighted the
challenge to appropriately define dose and schedule
of these agents outside of the conventional maxi-
mally tolerated dose approach of cytotoxic drugs (Li
et al., 2013). In addition, the failure of this drug class
also points to the need and challenge of identifying
patient subsets most likely to respond to therapy
(i.e., MMP target expression levels or activity)
(Martin and Matrisian, 2007). Reemergence of the
development of drugs that target invasion will
require solutions to these challenges and an improved
knowledge of disease targets and biomarkers that
represent dependencies in the metastatic cascade.
Angiogenesis and antiangiogenesis therapy
In general, angiogenesis refers to the formation of
new capillaries that form from existing blood ves-
sels (Patan, 2004). This process rarely occurs after

-- 87 of 258 --

postnatal development, with adult vasculature
being relatively stable and rare to proliferate
under physiologic conditions (Eelen et al., 2020).
In certain pathological situations however, such as
in cancer, angiogenesis does occur partially in
response to the growing need of these pathologi-
cally expanding cancerous masses (primary or
secondary tumors) for oxygen and the nutrients
needed to survive (Nishida et al., 2006; Muz
et al., 2015).
Antiangiogenic therapy, as a strategy for cancer
therapy, does include but is not limited to metasta-
sis, since inhibiting angiogenesis has a dual effect of
regressing measurable tumors and potentially tar-
geting metastatic progression (Cao, 2016). The
early development of drugs that focused on block-
ade of the vascular endothelial growth factor
(VEGF) pathway, as an antiangiogenic tactic,
included 	a 	conventional 	drug 	development
approach based on tumor regression in conven-
tional Phase II human clinical trials as well as some
subsequent innovative trial designs, particularly in
human renal cancer patients (Vachhani and George,
2016). These efforts resulted in the initial approvals
of the anti-VEGF receptor (VEGFR) antibody,
bevacizumab, in human cancer patients (Montero
et al., 2012). Subsequently, bevacizumab gained
approvals for renal and other cancers, as an antian-
giogenic approach to preventing metastatic pro-
gression (Kurkjian and Kim, 2012; Montero et al.,
2012). The subsequent and widespread targeting of
VEGFR kinase through small-molecule drugs has
furthered this dual-activity approach to metastatic
progression, which includes both tumor response
and inhibition of metastatic progression simultane-
ously (Vasudev and Reynolds, 2014).
Vascular targeting therapy
Once blood vessels form via angiogenesis and vas-
culogenesis in the tumor microenvironment, the
result is a vascular network that is morphologically
and possibly functionally distinct from normal vas-
cular networks (Konerding et al., 1995). Indeed,
this new tumor vasculature has been found to be
primitive and chaotic in nature (Konerding et al.,
1995; Teleanu et al., 2019) and has been the basis
to develop therapeutic approaches that may target
and destroy established tumor vasculature since
these vessels are essential for tumor growth and
progression (Siemann and Horsman, 2009).
Vascular disruptive agents
Distinct of antiangiogenic agents, vascular disrup-
tive agents (VDAs) consist of two main classes: (i)
ligand-based therapies, which deliver toxins, proco-
agulant, or proapoptotic effectors to tumor-associ-
ated vessels; and (ii) small-molecule VDAs that may
also target spindle filaments, known to be essential
for endothelial cell function and resistance to apop-
tosis (Siemann and Horsman, 2009). Although
these therapeutic approaches are distinct from
most anticancer therapeutics, they are not consid-
ered to be uniquely antimetastatic nor specifically
disruptive of metastatic progression.
Disease Targets for Drug Development
within the Metastatic Cascade
To better align the unmet needs of cancer patients
with a coherent drug development path that draws
lessons from historical successes and failures, sev-
eral innovations are needed. As mentioned previ-
ously, since it is true that both metastatic progression
and measurable cancer lesions require cell prolif-
eration and evasion of apoptosis, there will be a
narrow overlap of benefit delivered by drugs devel-
oped for these conventionally valued cancer pro-
cesses that may benefit both measurable cancer
lesions and metastatic progression simultaneously.
Although much is not known, we do know what
processes/dependencies are associated with meta-
static progression (Fares et al., 2020). Given the
unquestioned shortcomings of conventional cancer
drug development to deliver drugs that effectively
prevent metastatic progression, there is an urgency
to reimagine cancer drug development to develop
new drugs that target these distinct processes
(Gandalovicˇová et al., 2017).
More specifically, there is a need to focus on the
dependencies for metastatic progression with the
metastatic cascade (Khanna et al., 2014; Anderson
et al., 2019; Fan et al., 2020). In this setting
“dependencies” refer to targets or processes that are
necessary or essential for the progression of metasta-
sis. As exemplified with the flawed development on
cancer invasion inhibitors, there is a need to prior-
itize the targeting of these processes.
Although the conventional and historical per-
spective of the metastatic cascade consists of sev-
eral sequential steps (cellular mobilization, invasion,
intravasation, transit within the vasculature, arrest,
72 	N.S. 	Amato

-- 88 of 258 --

73	Antimetastatic Therapy
survival at the secondary site (part of metastatic
endurance), entry exit from metastatic dormancy,
extravasation, angiogenesis, and eventual macro
metastatic lesion growth) (Fidler, 2003; Gupta and
Massagué, 2006; Talmadge and Fidler, 2010;
Anderson et al., 2019), the PMN, metastatic dor-
mancy, and metastatic endurance represent impor-
tant new dependencies for metastatic progression
and should be the focus of future cancer drug
development efforts. They are now summarized in
further detail below.
Metastasis and the Premetastatic
Niche
Although it was once believed that the first step in
metastasis was the entry of tumor cells into the
circulation, it is now hypothesized that select pri-
mary tumor cells play a direct role in preparing the
future metastatic microenvironment of the second-
ary site for eventual dissemination and subsequent
arrival of disseminated metastatic cells (Peinado
et al., 2011, 2017). This microenvironment is
termed the “premetastatic niche” or PMN and is
defined as a microenvironment within a secondary
organ that is primed specifically by the primary
tumor for metastasis to occur and to be successful
(Peinado et al., 2011, 2017). The PMN was first
described by Kaplan et al. in 2005 and expands
upon the “seed and soil” hypothesis proposed by
Steven Paget in 1889, which sought to explain the
inherent organ-tropism of metastasis (Ribatti et al.,
2006). In the Kaplan model, the PMN is cultivated
by primary tumor-derived components that mobi-
lize bone-marrow-derived cells (BMDCs) and the
local stromal components of the microenvironment
of the host to increase the chance of metastatic
tumor survival within specific anatomic regions of
the secondary microenvironment (Kaplan et al.,
2005; Liu and Cao, 2016). Furthermore, the con-
cepts of metastatic endurance described below may
be closely aligned with the PMN, through the con-
cept of permitting metastatic cells to adapt and
survive at the secondary metastatic site (Liu and
Cao, 2016).
Although a detailed assessment of the biology of
the PMN is beyond the scope of this chapter, its
addition to our growing understanding of the biol-
ogy and molecular events of metastasis provides
additional disease targets for a purposeful metasta-
sis-specific drug development approach.
Metastatic Dormancy
During the multistep process that comprises the
metastatic cascade, it is widely known that only a
small fraction of disseminating tumor cells (DTCs)
acquire the necessary genetic and epigenetic altera-
tions to move between states/stages (Neophytou
et al., 2019). Of those few DTCs that are successful
at traversing the metastatic cascade, some may
arrive and colonize a secondary site but do not
proliferate (Sosa et al., 2014). Instead, these cells
may remain in a quiescent state of dormancy
(Hadfield, 1954; Aguirre-Ghiso, 2007; Goddard
et al., 2018; Neophytou et al., 2019). These dor-
mant cells may include one singular tumor cell or a
cluster of micro metastatic cells that exist in a bal-
anced state of proliferation and apoptosis (Hadfield,
1954; Holmgren et al., 1995; Aguirre-Ghiso, 2007;
Goddard et al., 2018).
It is presumed that the development of metasta-
ses in general is due to outgrowth of these micro-
scopic cells that may be lying dormant at a
secondary metastatic site (e.g., the lung) or in a
transient ‘sanctuary’ site (e.g., the bone marrow)
waiting to be activated to form overt metastatic
lesions at some point in the future (Tsao et al.,
1997; Karrison et al., 1999; Aguirre-Ghiso, 2007;
Goddard et al., 2018; Neophytou et al., 2019).
These dormant cells may start dividing as a result
of poorly understood signals from the tumor
microenvironment and eventually lead to the devel-
opment of measurable lesions, months, years, or
even decades following a patient’s initial treatment
(McNichols et al., 1981; Tsao et al., 1997; Karrison
et al., 1999; Freedland and Moul, 2007).
As mentioned previously, the problem of dor-
mancy in terms of metastatic progression and can-
cer therapy is twofold. First, cancer cells at this
stage are undetectable by traditional diagnostic
means (Sauer et al., 2021). Second, since these
DTCs may be in an essentially nonproliferative
state, they are capable of evading the cytotoxicity of
traditional chemotherapeutics (Sosa et al., 2014;
Sauer et al., 2021). A drug development effort to
target the processes that permit dormancy or a
break from dormancy may be uniquely helpful
adjuvant agents for cancer patients (Neophytou
et al., 2019). Furthermore, targeting DTCs at sec-
ondary sites may provide a means to delay or pre-
vent metastasis or reduce the frequency of recurrence
(Barkan et al., 2010; Neophytou et al., 2019).

-- 89 of 258 --

Metastatic Endurance
Independent of or as part of the process of dor-
mancy, a requirement of successful DTCs is to
adapt and survive a variety of stressors experienced
in the new microenvironment of the secondary site.
It is hypothesized that the stress conditions encoun-
tered upon arrival may require efficient stress
detection, and then early stress adaptation mecha-
nisms and programs that result in cell survival,
dormancy, and/overall 	metastatic 	progression
(Stewart et al., 2019). This concept of metastatic
endurance describes the combination of stress
adaption, survival with or without dormancy that
is characteristic of DTCs that can successfully
reside at secondary metastatic sites and form overt
metastases (Stewart et al., 2019).
Metastatic endurance has been shown to be a
dependency of cancer metastasis in a diverse set of
cancer models and is considered a phenotype con-
sistently displayed by highly metastatic cells that
allows these cells to adapt to their foreign microen-
vironment (“nonpermissive soil”) and initially sur-
vive the attrition known as “metastatic inefficiency”.
These cells need to be able to detect a variety of
poorly understood cellular stressors, allowing them
to survive and progress, whereas metastatic cells that
do not express the metastatic endurance phenotype
will die without causing a clinical problem.
A recent perspective on the biology of metastatic
endurance now includes the collaboration of hetero-
geneous populations of metastatic cells that may
cooperate based on phenotypic diversity to allow
stress adaptation and survival (Schild et al., 2018).
This hypothesis has been recently and best charac-
terized in OSA by the discovery of “anchor cells”,
which have been described as hypoproliferative,
cytokine-producing cells that have the ability to
survive early attrition in the early stages of metasta-
sis and promote metastatic progression (Reinecke
et al., 2020). Through the production of cytokines,
these cells have the ability to alter the surrounding
lung tissue in a manner that promotes subsequent
colonization by other OSA tumor cells with prolif-
erating phenotypes (i.e., “growth cells”). These
growth cells then divide to form measurable and
clinically relevant metastases (Reinecke et al., 2020).
Targeting metastatic endurance
Although cellular processes of metastatic endur-
ance have been recognized and studied in the past
two decades, and a picture of the underlying biol-
ogy is beginning to emerge, they have yet to be
widely integrated into cancer drug discovery and
development efforts. In addition to various aberra-
tions associated with the structure and activity of
genes and proteins of various associated pathways
and networks, there is evidence to support the
regulation of metastatic endurance at the epigenetic
level and data supportive of targeting the epigenetic
regulatory apparatus (“metastasis super-enhanc-
ers”) to prevent metastatic progression (Yokoyama
et al., 2016; Morrow et al., 2018; Peng et al.,
2019). With these factors in mind, it is reasonable
that targeting metastatic endurance may also
uncover new or repurposed drugs that may be
valuable in preventing the progression of meta-
static disease.
Preclinical Modeling in the Study
of Metastasis
Understandably, the complex interactions of the
DTCs with host cells make the preclinical study of
metastasis challenging (Sauer et al., 2021). For this
and other reasons, the preclinical identification of
drugs with potential antimetastatic activity is not
simple using conventional preclinical cancer mod-
els (Sauer et al., 2021). This shortcoming further
limits the opportunity to develop drugs aligned
with the greatest needs of patients, i.e., agents that
target metastatic progression (Khanna et al., 2014),
and has provided the impetus for more novel strat-
egies of drug development.
Naturally occurring canine cancer: a model
to de-risk the development of drugs
that target metastatic progression
Keeping in mind the challenges that exist in the
development of novel drugs that target metastatic
progression, comparative oncology is an emerging
discipline that offers an opportunity to circumvent
some of the preclinical modeling challenges needed
for successful metastasis drug development efforts
(LeBlanc and Mazcko, 2020).
Comparative oncology has found its greatest
traction within the human drug development path
when critical questions about the development of a
new drugs remain unanswered or unanswerable
within either human clinical trials or conventional
preclinical models (Gordon et al., 2009; LeBlanc
and Mazcko, 2020; van der Weyden et al., 2020).
74 	N.S. Amato

-- 90 of 258 --

75	Antimetastatic Therapy
As a result of the costs and consequences of not
having answers to these critical questions, there is
a great value derived from answering these ques-
tions in complex and biologically similar diseases
that naturally develop in the pet dog with cancer
(Gordon et al., 2009; LeBlanc et al., 2016; LeBlanc
and Mazcko, 2020; van der Weyden et al., 2020).
Indeed, there is potentially no greater value from
the field of comparative oncology than the rela-
tively rapid and robust assessment of the potential
activity of antimetastatic therapeutics that can be
translated from pets to the treatment of metastatic
progression in humans (Gordon et al., 2009;
LeBlanc et al., 2016; LeBlanc and Mazcko, 2020).
For example, the unique activity of a drug to
inhibit metastatic cancer in dogs may be coupled
with conventional or creative Phase II human data
to prioritize agents for additional human Phase II
or III studies. The opportunities and use of com-
parative oncology in cancer drug development have
been reviewed extensively elsewhere; however, it is
important to note the prospect for this cross-
species assessment that has been actively considered
and pursued in canine OSA (Khanna et al., 2014).
The recent rise of the animal health biotech and
pharmaceutical industry’s interest in veterinary
oncology has created the opportunity for a self-
funded, bidirectional approach to comparative
oncology and a novel cross-species drug develop-
ment that can answer critical human drug develop-
ment questions and simultaneously create revenue
and data in support of a veterinary approved drug
that may be licensed from human pharma for vet-
erinary approval (LeBlanc et al., 2016; Fenger
et al., 2020). This comparative oncology approach
to drug development does not aim to replace tradi-
tional strategies but serves to augment and
strengthen the essence of this important work.
Antimetastatic Therapies
What will a therapeutic approach that targets
metastatic progression look like?
Despite the recognition that metastases and meta-
static progression are significant problems for most
solid tumor cancer patients, as discussed, there are
currently no oncology drugs that uniquely target
the rich biology understood to be necessary for
metastatic progression in humans or animals. The
current observation of cancer drug activity against
metastatic progression is the result of the narrow
overlap (referenced above) of cell proliferation and
apoptosis evasion, common to measurable tumors
and the steps associated with the metastatic cas-
cade. More meaningful improvements in patient
outcome should be expected from successful drug
development efforts that that uniquely target the
biology of metastatic progression.
Once developed, the predicted profile of a suc-
cessful antimetastatic drug will be one that is orally
bioavailable with highly favorable tolerability.
These new drugs will likely best be administered
chronically, starting from the neoadjuvant period,
concurrent with adjuvant therapy and then for
extended periods of time after the completion of
chemotherapy.
Until the development and availability of drugs
that fit this description, there will be more immedi-
ate access to the following non-mutually exclusive
approaches for managing metastasis:
1. Repurposed drugs: Those taken from cancer
and from therapeutic areas unrelated to cancer but
repurposed for metastasis as a result of phenotypic
metastasis drug screens or selected based on mecha-
nisms of action aligned with metastasis processes
(e.g., rapamycin) (Zhang et al., 2020).
2. Immuno-oncology drugs: Historically, immuno-
therapy drugs were believed to have the greatest
utility in the setting of minimal residual disease
(e.g., liposome-encapsulated muramyl tripeptide-
phosphatidylethanolamine (L-MTP-PE)); however,
the surprising activity of novel immunotherapy
drugs (e.g., immune checkpoint inhibitors; see
Mason and Dow, Chapter 8, this volume, 2023)
against measurable tumors has provided the oppor-
tunity for their use as antimetastatic drugs similar
to other pluripotent agents (Robert, 2020).
3. Pluripotent drugs: Anticancer drugs with a multi-
plicity of mechanisms of action that allow them to
frst succeed in the setting of measurable cancers,
but simultaneously demonstrate activity against
metastasis due to overlapping mechanisms that also
target metastasis (i.e., sorafenib, and other multi-
targeting receptor tyrosine kinase (RTK) inhibitors)
(Petrelli and Giordano, 2008).
Many of the pluripotent drugs with activity
against metastatic progression have distinct mecha-
nisms of action compared to conventional chemo-
therapy (Zhong et al., 2021). Whereas conventional
chemotherapy primarily functions to disrupt cell
proliferation or induce apoptosis, most pluripotent
drugs are inhibitors of molecular signaling and

-- 91 of 258 --

often paradoxically described as “targeted thera-
pies”. The inhibition in cellular signaling generates
pluripotent activities for these drugs for several
reasons including:
● a multiplicity of biologic actions resulting from
inhibited cellular pathways (i.e., mTOR and
rapamycin) (Petrelli and Giordano, 2008); and
● often “dirty” inhibitors (i.e., toceranib) inhibit
more than one target (i.e., in the case of tocer-
anib: c-KIT, VEGFR, and platelet-derived growth
factor (PDGF) receptor (PDGFR)) (Pleyer and
Greil, 2015).
Most of the current targeted therapies of interest
are either small-molecule inhibitors of signal trans-
duction or monoclonal antibodies. Numerous
small-molecule inhibitors and antibodies have been
approved to treat human cancer (Shahid et al.,
2019; Zhong et al., 2021) and are currently in
development or approved in veterinary patients
(Beltrán Hernández et al., 2021).
Pluripotent targeting cell signaling in cancer
As mentioned above, numerous processes involved
in the growth, progression, and metastasis of solid
cancers have been found to be mediated by abnor-
malities in growth factor signaling pathways (see
Rönnberg, Chapter 6, this volume, 2023).
The credentials of signaling targets in cancer has
evolved since they were first recognized as drugga-
ble. It is clear that target expression or overexpres-
sion is likely insufficient for the optimal cancer
target and that a cancer addiction or cancer depend-
ency on a signaling protein is more likely if that
target is mutated and driving the cancer phenotype
(Torti and Trusolino, 2011). The complexity of tar-
get credentialing is beyond the scope of this chapter
and has been reviewed extensively elsewhere.
Specifc Receptor Tyrosine Kinase
Small-Molecule Inhibitors
RTKs take part in the signaling pathway that
involves protein kinases that use ATP to phospho-
rylate themselves and other proteins (Zwick et al.,
2002; Du and Lovly, 2018). The prominence of
RTK and their inhibitors in oncology is presented
in Rönnberg (Chapter 6, this volume, 2023); how-
ever, some specific agents are described in this
chapter due to the hypotheses that they may target
metastatic progression.
Toceranib
Toceranib is a classic example of an RTK small-
molecule inhibitor (Palladia; Pfizer, New York, NY,
USA) and is approved for use in dogs with mast cell
tumors. Toceranib is an oral multi-kinase inhibitor
of the split tyrosine kinase family that blocks sev-
eral RTKs (VEGFR-2, PDGFRα, and c-KIT). By
reversible competitive inhibition of ATP binding,
toceranib suppresses receptor phosphorylation and
subsequent downstream signaling of many impor-
tant cancer-associated signaling proteins (London
et al., 2003, 2009, 2012; Yancey et al., 2010a,b).
This pluripotential targeting of an RTK by a single
inhibitor and its target spectrum, including both
VEGFR and PDGFR, has been the basis to consider
this agent for potential activity against metastatic
progression (London et al., 2003, 2012).
Although toceranib is labeled for the use in treat-
ment of mast cell tumors, the pluripotency described
above provides a biologic rationale and may pre-
dict the observed evidence of its biologic activity in
other types of tumors including thyroid carcinoma,
apocrine gland anal sac adenocarcinoma, nasal
carcinoma, gastrointestinal stromal tumor (GIST),
and other tumors both in the measurable disease
and micro metastatic settings (London et al., 2012).
Nonetheless, this pluripotency may be associated
with potential patient risk, through the develop-
ment of evasive resistance (Halsey et al., 2014).
Evasive resistance refers to the acceleration of
metastatic progression following the sustained
inhibition of VEGFR (Halsey et al., 2014), often
concurrent with measurable tumor responses
(Casanovas et al., 2005). Evasive resistance is
believed to be mediated through mitogen-activated
protein kinase (MAPK) activation and is most
harmful in cancers that are not driven by a target
blocked by the pluripotent kinase inhibitor in use
(Haibe et al., 2020).
Sorafenib
In vivo and in vitro studies have shown that the
synthetic, oral multi-kinase inhibitor, sorafenib,
inhibits tumor growth and disrupts tumor micro-
vasculature through antiproliferative, antiangio-
genic, and proapoptotic effects (Gollob et al., 2006;
Wilhelm et al., 2008). Sorafenib has been found to
target the RAF serine/threonine kinases (RAF-1,
wild-type BRAF, and oncogenic b-raf V600E) and
RTKs (VEGFR-1, VEGFR-2, VEGFR-3, PDGFRβ,
76 	N.S. 	Amato

-- 92 of 258 --

77	Antimetastatic Therapy
FLT-3, and c-KIT) that have been associated with
tumorigenesis, tumor progression, and metastasis
(Wilhelm et al., 2008). Sorafenib may also induce
apoptosis by an MEK/ERK-independent mecha-
nism (Liu et al., 2006; Wilhelm et al., 2008).
Sorafenib inhibits tumor angiogenesis in xenograft
models, including a renal cancer model (Chang
et al., 2007), and inhibits tumor growth in preclini-
cal models of human melanoma, renal, colon, pan-
creatic, 	hepatocellular, 	thyroid, 	and 	ovarian
carcinomas as well as non-small-cell lung cancer
(NSCLC) (Wilhelm et al., 2008). The result of com-
bined VEGFR and MEK/ERK inhibition suggests a
potential advantage of sorafenib compared to
agents that do not possess this specific dual activity,
and therefore it may deliver improved antimeta-
static activity by avoiding evasive resistance-medi-
ated acceleration of metastasis (described above).
Early preclinical studies have examined sorafenib
in canine in vitro and in vivo studies (Wolfesberger
et al., 2010). Recently, the safety profile of sorafenib
was interrogated for use in dogs and this tolerabil-
ity study identified a dose for use in future pharma-
cokinetic studies (Foskett et al., 2017; Cawley
et al., 2022).
Non-receptor tyrosine kinase
small-molecule inhibitors
Although a lot of focus has been given to RTKs and
their ligands, non-RTK targets should not be over-
looked. The potential therapeutic value of the intra-
cellular non-RTK Src and other members of the Src
family kinases (SFKs) has been heavily investigated
in people and may have activity in dogs.
Src, a protein kinase, is a member of a large fam-
ily of structurally related kinases now termed “Src
family kinases” or SFKs (Thomas and Brugge,
1997). Src and other SFKs play an important role
in regulating signaling from cell surface receptors
in a number of cancers (Thomas and Brugge,
1997). These mechanisms are known to drive many
fundamental cellular processes, including cell
growth, differentiation, cell shape, migration, and
survival, and specialized cell signals (Parsons and
Parsons, 2004). It has also been shown that Src
represents a point of signaling convergence down-
stream of many RTKs (Parsons and Parsons, 2004).
In studies with epidermal growth factor receptor
(EGFR), SFKs were shown to physically interact
with EGFR, and this mutual interaction was crucial
for full activation of the receptor (Biscardi et al.,
1999; Citri and Yarden, 2006). Similar occurrences
between SFKs and other RTKs including PDGFRs,
fibroblast growth factor receptor (FGFR), and
insulin-like growth factor 1 receptor (IGF-1R) have
also been documented (Thomas and Brugge, 1997).
Thus, treatment with small-molecule inhibitors that
disrupt these RTK–Src interactions may prove to be
a more effective antimetastatic strategy versus tar-
geting one or the other alone (Zhang and Yu, 2012).
Dasatinib
Dasatinib is another tyrosine kinase inhibitor with
multiple targets, including the SFKs (SRC, LCK,
YES, and FYN), the BCR-ABL, and to a lesser
extent, c-KIT, PDGFRβ, and EPHA2 (Steinberg,
2007). Studies have shown dasatinib’s ability to
block signaling through both PDGFRβ and c-KIT,
resulting in targeting a wider number of tyrosine
kinases compared to imatinib (Lombardo et al.,
2004). Other studies investigating the cooperation
between RTKs and Src suggest that dasatinib use
may offer an approach to overcome acquired resist-
ance that has been seen with most single-agent uses
of small-molecule inhibitors (Wheeler et al., 2009).
Although dasatinib has been investigated in
many human cancers (Kantarjian et al., 2010,
2012; Benjamini et al., 2014; Safdari et al., 2014;
Spreafico et al., 2014), its clinical therapeutic value
in veterinary species is less understood. There is,
however, mounting evidence for its use as a novel
small-molecule inhibitor in certain canine cancers
(Dickerson et al., 2013; Marley et al., 2015).
In one in vitro study (Dickerson et al., 2013)
investigating imatinib and dasatinib in canine
hemangiosarcoma, dasatinib inhibited in vitro pro-
liferation of canine hemangiosarcoma cells several
orders of magnitude greater than imatinib, and the
concentration needed to inhibit the phosphorylation
of PDGFRβ was approximately 1000 times less than
that needed by imatinib. Another study noted that
dasatinib facilitated in vitro growth suppression of
cultured malignant canine mast cells (Gleixner et al.,
2007), illustrating another potential use.
Rapamycin
Rapamycin is a drug that has been repurposed
from its original use as an immune suppressant in
transplant patients. Several lines of evidence have
supported its development as an anticancer agent
and more recently for the treatment of metastatic

-- 93 of 258 --

progression of sarcomas in dogs and people
(Gordon et al., 2008; Paoloni et al., 2010; Zhou
et al., 2010; Vemulapalli et al., 2011; Xie et al.,
2013; Wang et al., 2014). Rapamycin is an inhibi-
tor of mTOR, a serine/threonine kinase that plays
roles in the signaling of a variety of downstream
kinases, thought to play a role in the metastasis of
OSA and other cancers (Ciuffreda et al., 2010;
Vemulapalli et al., 2011; Lainetti et al., 2021). In
murine model of metastatic OSA, rapamycin
decreased the development of pulmonary metasta-
sis by inhibition of the mTOR/S6K1/4E-BP-1 path-
way (Wan et al., 2005). Inhibition of this pathway
is also found to decrease cell motility, growth, and
migration, induce apoptosis, and decrease angio-
genesis (Wan et al., 2005). For these reasons and
other supportive data, mTOR and its downstream
signaling have been thought to be a possible target
for human and canine OSA treatment and metasta-
sis inhibition. However, a recent large-scale canine
study was disappointing and found that adjuvant
treatment with rapamycin (Sirolimus) administered
following amputation and concurrent with adju-
vant chemotherapy to pet dogs with appendicular
OSA did not significantly improve disease-free
interval (DFI) or survival over amputation and
chemotherapy alone (LeBlanc et al., 2021). Further
studies with designs that can overcome potential
shortcomings of the aforementioned study will be
needed to fully understand the potential role of
rapamycin for the treatment of this and other sar-
comas in people and dogs.
Antimetastatic Immunotherapy
Although the specific details and mechanisms of
cancer immunotherapy are explored elsewhere and
in other chapters (see Mason and Dow, Chapter 8,
this volume, 2023), it is reasonable to consider the
role of immunotherapy in managing metastases.
One notable antimetastatic immunotherapy,
which has been explored in canine patients, uses
the activation of macrophages and monocytes in
targeting micro metastatic progression in OSA
(MacEwen et al., 1994). L-MTP-PE has been
shown to activate macrophages and monocytes to
target the destruction of OSA neoplastic cells
(MacEwen et al., 1994). Investigation into the use
of L-MTP-PE in OSA in dogs included a rand-
omized, double-blind study in which patients first
underwent limb amputation and then were rand-
omized into two groups: one group was administered
L-MTP-PE and the other administered a placebo
(MacEwen et al., 1989). Dogs receiving L-MTP-PE
were found to have survived significantly longer
(222 days) as compared to dogs receiving placebo
(77 days) (MacEwen et al., 1989).
Since this benchmark study, further studies evalu-
ated the treatment of dogs with OSA using L-MTP-PE,
alongside adjuvant chemotherapy (MacEwen et al.,
1994; Kurzman et al., 1995). In one study (MacEwen
et al., 1994), patients were initially treated with limb
amputation followed by four treatments of cisplatin.
After chemotherapy, these patients were randomized
into two groups, one receiving L-MTP-PE and one
receiving placebo. Dogs receiving L-MTP-PE had a
significantly longer median DFI and median survival
time as compared to dogs receiving placebo
(MacEwen et al., 1994). Following this study, two
randomized, double-blind clinical trials showed the
benefit of L-MTP-PE (after amputation and cispl-
atin) with longer survival times versus placebo; how-
ever, administration of L-MTP-PE concurrently with
cisplatin did not demonstrate a survival advantage
(Kurzman et al., 1995). Intravenous L-MTP-PE was
found to be well tolerated in dogs.
The use of L-MTP-PE in pediatric OSA has also
been reported to show improvement in event-free
survival in both localized and metastatic disease
and is approved for use in Europe for the treatment
of OSA in people (Meyers et al., 2005, 2008; Mori
et al., 2008). It is noteworthy that the diminished
therapeutic signal seen in dogs treated with concur-
rent L-MTP-PE and chemotherapy was not effec-
tively translated into the design of human trials.
This agent was not granted approval by the US
Food and Drug Administration (FDA) for use in
children (Harrison and Schwartz, 2017).
Treating Macro Metastatic Lesions:
Treatment of Gross Metastatic Disease
Although the development of antimetastatic thera-
pies that target the development and progression of
metastasis is essential to combat the morbidity and
mortality associated with most cancers, there remains
another unmet need for strategies that are aimed at
treating metastases once they are established. Since
many veterinary and human cancers have been found
to have metastasized at the time of diagnosis, anti-
micro metastatic therapies need to be employed
alongside macro metastatic therapies for a holistic
approach to treatment. Most notably this may
include the use of surgery in some patient use cases.
78 	N.S. Amato

-- 94 of 258 --

79	Antimetastatic Therapy
Although numerous metastasectomy procedures
have been described in people, pulmonary and
lymph node metastasectomy are most frequently
described (Kawada and Taketo, 2011; Cheung
et al., 2019; Handy et al., 2019). This is likely due
to the fact that these sites are generally more amen-
able to surgical resection as compared to the liver,
bone, and other organs where metastasis can also
develop (Rees et al., 2008; Mohammad and Balaa,
2009; Staehler, 2011; Lu et al., 2015).
Pulmonary Metastasectomy
Given that the lungs are a common site for metas-
tasis in people, PM is most commonly performed.
Although numerous types of cancers metastasize to
the lung, colorectal cancer is the most comprehen-
sively studied in regard to PM in humans (Treasure
et al., 2014), followed by pediatric OSA, and a
short list of other cancer types. The accepted onco-
logic criteria to justify the use of PM as a therapeu-
tic approach in people have been reported
(Erhunmwunsee and Tong, 2016) as:
● the primary cancer needs to be controlled or
controllable;
● no extrathoracic metastases exist, whether they
are controlled or controllable;
● all of the pulmonary tumor or tumors must be
resectable with adequate pulmonary reserve
retained; and
● there are no other alternative options with lower
morbidity available to the patient.
Regardless of tumor type, intrathoracic lymph
node involvement is associated with decreased sur-
vival after PM, with the most convincing data
found in colorectal and renal cell cancer, and there
is limited evidence as to whether or not removing
mediastinal nodes helps improve survival concur-
rent with PM (Veronesi et al., 2007; Reinersman
and Wigle, 2016).
Pediatric osteosarcoma and pulmonary
metastasectomy
Pediatric OSA is an example of human cancer
where pulmonary metastases are less responsive to
and often resistant to conventional chemothera-
pies, but responsive to surgical resection in the
form of metastasectomy (Croteau and Heaton,
2019). In this profoundly unique case, treating the
secondary tumors behaves much like treating the
primary tumor, with removal of all secondary
metastatic tumors creating the opportunity for
long-term survival in some patients (Salah et al.,
2013; Croteau and Heaton, 2019). This observed
surgical benefit for patients with nonlocalized dis-
ease is potentially unique among human cancers.
Although there are limited studies to date, there
is some evidence that PM confers a survival advan-
tage to canine OSA patients as well, when combined
with primary tumor resection (O’Brien et al., 1993;
Turner et al., 2017). Prognostic factors were identi-
fied in one study and included DFI and the number
of metastatic nodules present at the time of surgery
(O’Brien et al., 1993). It was found that dogs with
fewer than three nodules and a DFI > 300 days at
the time of metastasectomy had a better prognosis
than other dogs without these variables (O’Brien
et al., 1993). Since this was a retrospective study
without a control comparator, the significance of
the survival benefit remains unclear.
In another retrospective study of dogs with OSA
(Turner et al., 2017), the investigators found that
PM was associated with a longer median stage III
survival time (232 days) versus those that had no
metastasectomy (49 days). Using similar criteria as
O’Brien et al., for dogs with fewer than three pul-
monary nodules visible on thoracic radiographs and
a pre-PM DFI > 275 days, a survival advantage was
believed to exist. Although this was another retro-
spective study, when considering the close parallels
between canine and pediatric OSA in terms of bio-
logic behavior and response to treatment, PM may
prove to be a significant means of controlling meta-
static disease in canine patients in the future.
Both video-assisted thoracic surgery (VATS) and
open thoracotomy techniques have been described
and are accepted as appropriate means for per-
forming PM in people. Proponents for an open
approach argue that this technique allows for more
thorough detection of metastases by palpation of
possible deeply embedded lesions in the lung paren-
chyma (Downey and Bains, 2016). Proponents for
VATS consider this approach more valuable since it
allows for a quicker return to function and a much
less invasive procedure (Numan et al., 2016). The
morbidity challenges associated with this PM has
limited the necessary robust assessment of this
approach in dogs; however, work is underway to
determine the value of VATS to deliver using a
minimally invasive approach to PM in dogs
(C. Thomson et al., MIMIC Trial, personal com-
munication, 2021).

Metastatic Lymph Node Management
Although PM is not a common treatment in veteri-
nary medicine yet, removal of presumed metastatic
lymph nodes is routinely performed. Nonetheless,
the therapeutic value and optimal use for lymph
node removal remain unclear.
The complexity in the management of metastatic
lymph nodes stems from the open question of what
lymph node metastasis represents in the overall
process of the metastatic progression and what
defines lymph node metastasis (i.e., cytologic find-
ings from an aspirate versus a clinically effaced and
altered lymph node). It is largely unknown if meta-
static cells that are trapped by lymph nodes repre-
sent a risk to the patient sufficient to remove the
immunomodulatory function of the lymph node or
if they represent a secondary lesion that warrants
resection (Schlag, 1998). There is some evidence
that lymphogenous metastasis is not an important
route of metastasis, but instead lymph node metas-
tasis is propagated through hematogenous spread
to lymph nodes (Reiter et al., 2020).
Theories of lymph node metastasis
One well-studied disease entity in relation to meta-
static lymph node management is breast cancer in
women. Local therapy in the form of radical mas-
tectomy with lymph node dissection and local
radiation therapy was historically the mainstay of
treatment to control local recurrence and prevent
metastatic spread (Plesca et al., 2016). With ongo-
ing research on the various clinical entities of this
cancer, divergent clinical viewpoints of lymph node
metastasis have evolved, and three divergent theo-
ries of lymph node metastasis have now been pro-
posed (Kawada and Taketo, 2011).
Although originally described for breast cancer
in women, these theories can be broadly applied to
various cancer histologies and exemplify the need
for an understanding of each theory as it relates to
a specific cancer, in formulating the management of
metastatic lymph nodes in individual patients:
1. The Halstedian theory: William Halsted set forth
the widespread notion that breast cancer is primarily
a local disease that spreads from the primary tumor
to regional lymph nodes via lymphatics and then sys-
temically to distant organs in a predictable, stepwise
manner (Halsted, 1907). This theory laid the foun-
dation for the justifcation of radical breast-cancer
surgery with extended lymph node dissection.
2. The systemic theory: Although many found
merit in the Halstedian approach, others proposed
the theory that interprets breast cancer as pre-
dominantly a systemic disease even early on in its
progression (Hellman, 1994). Proponents of the
systemic theory believe that lymph node metastasis
is useful for prognostic signal alone and that lymph
node dissection does not affect overall survival.
This suggests that hematogenous dissemination of
metastases to vital organs (liver, lungs, etc.) may be
more important and unrelated to lymphatic spread
(Fisher, 1980). Accordingly, effective systemic ther-
apies were employed alongside local strategies in
breast-cancer treatment, which improved overall
survival.
3. The spectrum theory: This compromise between
the Halstedian and systemic theories argues that
metastatic potential may emerge early as part of a
systemic disease, but recognizes that genomic and
metastatic evolution occurs over time and that at
some point an effaced metastatic lymph node may
become an active source for ongoing evolution
(Hellman, 1994).
Keeping all theories in mind, it is likely that the
approach will vary depending upon the cancer his-
tology and biologic behavior in question. Some
tumors may follow the Halstedian approach, while
others will follow the other theories. Current clini-
cal evidence is insufficient to apply these models to
veterinary cancers at this time. Not surprisingly,
disease-specific studies are needed to guide deci-
sion-making surrounding lymph node removal.
Regardless of the current open questions, in the
setting of a clinically effaced metastatic lymph node
there is likely a clear benefit to node resection.
What we do not know, however, is whether micro-
scopic lymph node metastasis is sufficient to guide
node resection and if such node resection will
enhance metastatic progression by removing these
sites of potential immunotherapy or improve
patient outcome by removing a source of cancer
evolution in the patient. These questions will need
to be answered before the value of lymph node
resection or sentinel node dissection can be under-
stood on a cancer-by-cancer basis.
Future Directions of Antimetastatic
Therapies
Despite substantial advancements in the under-
standing of the mechanisms of metastasis, as of this
80 	N.S. 	Amato

-- 96 of 258 --

81	Antimetastatic Therapy
writing, drugs that specifically target metastatic
progression do not exist in human and veterinary
medicine. Only a small handful of compounds have
been investigated in veterinary patients and even
fewer have been employed clinically.
Although this work is in its infancy, numerous
novel compounds, existing drugs, and drug combi-
nations are currently being explored to combat
metastatic disease.
The future success in developing these agents,
will require preclinical studies and clinical trials
in patients with no measurable disease to
advance this specific drug development path.
This is, in itself, a steep challenge and one of the
reasons for the lack of therapeutics available
today. The use of comparative oncology as a
means to examine these drug development chal-
lenges should be fostered to advance this path
across species.
