6 	Signal Transduction Inhibitors
HENRIK RÖNNBERG*
Swedish University of Agricultural Sciences (SLU), Uppsala, Sweden
Introduction: Defnitions
Several significant discoveries in the 1950s launched
a revolution that laid the foundation for a new field
of research, dramatically increasing our knowledge
of how cell signaling is initiated in cell membrane
receptors and propagated through cytoplasmic
intermediaries as part of well-regulated signaling
pathways. Ultimately this creates a nuclear signal
(see London, Chapter 7, this volume, 2023) that
alters gene expression and alters the cellular pheno-
type, and the biology of the cancer in the patient.
Fundamentally, signal transduction molecules are
responsible for chemically or physically generating
cellular signals that result in nearly all cellular
responses, such as cell growth, cell division, migra-
tion, angiogenesis, and apoptosis. In most cases,
cell signaling occurs through the transfer of phos-
phorous residues between signaling proteins. This
often results in conformational changes that are
responsible for activation of signaling proteins.
Phosphorylation is catalyzed by protein kinases.
When phosphorylation occurs through action on
the amino acid tyrosine, the protein kinase is
referred to as a “tyrosine kinase”, in the same way
that serine/threonine protein kinases phosphorylate
either serine or threonine. These pathways and
their dysregulation are involved in most steps in
oncogenesis and cancer progression. The under-
standing of both normal and aberrant cellular sig-
nal transduction is necessary to understand cancer
biology and translate this knowledge to cancer
prevention, early detection, and treatment (Fig. 6).
Apoptosis was one of the first cellular processes
in which signal transduction was studied. Apoptosis
is an essential cellular process that breaks down
cells through a controlled mechanism in order to
control cell number, and in specific instances, to
preserve their building blocks for reuse in new
structures; it can be likened to the natural phenom-
enon of trees shedding their leaves in the fall and
reabsorbing their nutrients into the trunk. For this
reason the process was named after the Greek word
for leaves dropping off trees, apoptosis (Kerr et al.,
1972). Subsequently, an intricate signaling network
mainly involving caspases (CASP3 and CASP9) was
discovered where the cellular pathways require
protein kinases for regulation. Apoptosis proved to
be important not just in the regulation of normal
cell functions and embryonal development, but also
of great importance in cancer (Hanahan and
Weinberg, 2011). From these origins in apoptosis,
signal transduction is now recognized to be a part
of nearly all aspects of cancer biology. This chapter
will focus on the foundational biology of signal
transduction and its inhibition with novel thera-
peutics, so as to guide clinical decision-making on
the use of current and future inhibitors of signal
transduction in veterinary patients.
Normal Function of Protein Kinases
The protein kinase complement of the human
genome encodes for about 500 protein kinases, and
accounts for 2% of the total number of genes
(Manning et al., 2002). The majority of these are
serine/threonine protein kinases, while the remain-
der largely consist of tyrosine kinases. As men-
tioned elsewhere, most protein kinases are highly
specific, but less-specific enzymes that are able to
phosphorylate several different amino acids exist.
Once an amino acid is phosphorylated its activity
(inhibition or activation) changes, as does its asso-
ciation with other proteins, and its subcellular
localization. Kinases modulate many cellular activi-
ties, especially those that regulate signal transduc-
tion. Stimulation is usually initiated by growth
89
*Email: henrik.ronnberg@slu.se
© CAB International 2023. Therapeutic Strategies in Veterinary Oncology (C. Khanna ed.)
DOI: 10.1079/9781789245820.0006

-- 105 of 258 --

factors (GFs) or other extracellular substances.
Receptor tyrosine kinases (RTKs) are tyrosine
kinases localized at the surface of the cell and acti-
vated through binding with GFs. Signaling through
intracellular protein kinases is fundamental in reg-
ulation of normal cell differentiation, cell growth,
and survival. To date, some 60 RTKs have been
identified, which can be divided into 20 subclasses
(Robinson et al., 2000).
Unlike RTKs, non-receptor protein tyrosine
kinases (NRTKs) lack a transmembrane domain.
They are mainly located in the cytoplasm and carry
out signal transduction by interacting with trans-
membrane receptors such as cytokines, GFs, and
hormones (Gocek et al., 2014), and carry signals
through the cytoplasm toward the nucleus.
Receptor Tyrosine Kinases
RTKs are a class of transmembrane receptor pro-
teins. When a signal molecule (ligand) binds to the
receptor, phosphorylation occurs and two mono-
mers often form a dimer structure, which subse-
quently initiates signal transduction (Hunter, 2009).
RTKs are often structurally divided into three dis-
tinct segments: (i) an extracellular domain that
contains structures for ligand binding; (ii) a hydro-
phobic transmembrane α-helix region; and (iii) an
intracellular component possessing protein kinase
activity (Lemmon and Schlessinger, 2010).
In each subgroup of RTKs, the extracellular
domain has a unique sequence and structure that
defines ligand specificity. Each receptor has differ-
ent types and numbers of specific protein structures
(motifs), such as the leucine-rich domain (L-domain),
fibronectin type 3 (Fn3)-like domain, immunoglob-
ulin-like (Ig) domain, or cysteine-rich (CR) domain
(Robinson et al., 2000). The tyrosine kinase func-
tion is localized to the intracellular region in the
C-terminal region. The C-terminal domain also
varies among the RTK families and thereby deter-
mines specificity and diversity of downstream cell
signaling (Ullrich and Schlessinger, 1990). In addi-
tion, downstream signals are not necessarily exclu-
sive or linear. This can result in “crosstalk” between
signals at the membrane with cytoplasmic and
juxta-membrane partners, the result and magnitude
of which may be cell type defined. The common
steps in signal transduction for RTKs are described
in detail below. Knowledge of these steps is para-
mount to design drugs interacting and blocking
distorted RTK signaling in cancer.
● Receptor–ligand interaction: As noted above, in
physiologic conditions, RTKs rest as inactive
monomers. Once a ligand attaches, a dimer and
heterodimerization may occur.
● Cytoplasmic tail activation: This process leads
to phosphorylation of the tyrosine in the
C-terminal kinase.
● Protein complex formation: The next phase gen-
erates association of signal molecules that con-
tain the Src homology 2 domain and the phos-
photyrosine-binding region to accumulate. These
molecules include kinases (phosphatidylinositol
3-kinases (PI3K), SRC), adaptor proteins (SHC,
GRB2), transcription factors (signal transducer
and activator of transcription (STAT)), ubiquitin
ligases, and phospholipases (PLC-γ).
● Downstream cytoplasmic activation: In turn,
these then activate downstream signal cascades
such 	as 	RAS/RAF/mitogen-activated 	kinase
(MAP), PI3K/AKT/mammalian target of rapa-
mycin (mTOR), PLC-γ/protein kinase C, and the
Janus kinase (JAK)/STAT signal pathways.
● Nuclear response/transcription factor activation
(see London, Chapter 7, this volume, 2023):
Ultimately, signal transduction impacts various
biologic responses within the cell through tran-
scription factors that either induce or inhibit
gene expression that may be additionally modi-
fied via epigenetic (see Cawley, Chapter 10, this
volume, 2023) changes (Yarden and Pines,
2012). These processes must be carefully coordi-
nated so that cellular homeostasis as well as
normal function of the entire organism is main-
tained. In the process of neoplastic transforma-
tion, these normal protein kinase functions are
often altered or dysregulated.
Protein Kinases in Cancer
The discovery that protein kinases often are over-
expressed in tumors and appear to be of central
importance in oncogenesis created an interest in the
development of therapeutic approaches to target
these kinases. Initially, some felt that there were too
many potentially altered protein kinases in a given
tumor, which would make it difficult to find a
driver/dependency. In addition, it was feared that
protein kinase targeting would result in significant
side effects, since protein kinases are fundamental
to normal cell metabolism. In the 1950s cytogenet-
ics began to provide a basis for a subsequent
biologic rationale that therapeutic targeting of a
90 	H. Rönnberg

-- 106 of 258 --

91	Signal Transduction Inhibitors
cancer dependency could be linked to dysregulated
signal transduction. David Hungerford and Peter C.
Nowell investigated chronic myelogenous leukemia
(CML), where a constant small chromosome was
apparent in most CML patients, soon named
Philadelphia chromosome, from the city of the dis-
covery (Nowell, 2007). In the 1970s Janet Rowley
discovered that the Philadelphia chromosome was
actually a chromosomal translocation of parts on
Chr9 and Chr22 (Rowley, 1973). The identification
of the genes involved came in 1983, where researchers
found the c-abl oncogene on Chr9, that was translo-
cated to be part of the Philadelphia chromosome
(Heisterkamp et al., 1983). The final step to develop-
ing targeted therapy came when groups identified the
function of the disease-specific chromosomes. This
oncoprotein was a dysregulated tyrosine kinase (Lugo
et al., 1990). Soon thereafter a BCR-ABL inhibitor
was identified in a screen and then launched in clini-
cal trials. Brian Druker and his colleagues reported a
complete remission in 53 out of 54 patients with
CML (Druker et al., 2001). The discovery of STI-571
(signal transduction inhibitor-571, i.e., imatinib)
changed everything and gave rise to a completely new
approach to treatment in oncology, based on target-
ing altered signal transduction.
Imatinib revolutionized cancer therapy and
launched the concept of targeted therapy. In this
case the target was unique to cancer cells as a result
of the cancer-specific translocation. In addition, the
target was a genetic dependency or “driver” of CML
that predicted tumor response to its inhibitor. This
constellation of attributes predicts the success of
imatinib and defines the challenges predicted for
future successful drugs and targets in the context of
targeted therapy in oncology. Aberrant signal trans-
duction is principally inhibited by two different
approaches: either by small-molecule tyrosine kinase
inhibitors (TKIs) or by monoclonal antibodies
(mAbs). Monoclonal antibodies generate cytotox-
icity by directing the immune system against the
tumor-specific target by direct target degradation
and through both antibody-dependent cellular cyto-
toxicity and complement-dependent cell-mediated
cytotoxicity directed at the target expressing cell. In
contrast, the small-molecule inhibitors target the
activation of the altered target gene. For certain
gene targets, both TKIs and mAbs have been approved
in human patients. Indeed, the resistance pattern
differs between these distinct approaches, even if
the target is identical. For example, the presence of
activating mutations within the ATP-binding cleft of
the epidermal growth factor receptor (EGFR) kinase
domain is associated with the sensitivity of non-
small-cell lung cancer (NSCLC) to the small-molecule
inhibitor gefitinib, but not to the mAb cetuximab.
By contrast, cetuximab shows a clinical benefit for
colorectal cancers that overexpress EGFR in a
manner independent of EGFR mutations (Imai and
Takaoka, 2006). There is hence a rationale to
develop both TKIs and mAbs to overcome resist-
ance and also to optimize efficacy. Finally, some
patients may not tolerate a specific drug class and
may be treated with the other modality. The com-
bination of distinct classes of signal transduction
inhibitors may increase their efficacy and may
overcome resistance.
A great deal about a cancer’s dependency on an
altered signaling pathway has been uncovered since
the launch of imatinib. In the early days, the defin-
ing feature of a cancer dependency was believed to
be the simple observation of an activating mutation
in the gene. Since then we have learned that the
dependency of an altered gene must be interpreted
within the biologic context of a given cancer (see
Fenger, Chapter 11, this volume, 2023). For exam-
ple, the V600E mutation in b-raf seems to predict
response of a BRAF inhibitor in human melanoma;
whereas the identical inhibitor used against the
identical b-raf V600E mutation in human colon
cancer delivers no similar therapeutic value and
may accelerate cancer progression. The responsive-
ness of these agents may be predicted by concurrent
alterations in other genes (i.e., EGF amplification)
in colon cancer; however, we should not expect
additional genomics analysis, in the absence of an
understanding of disease-specific context, to be suf-
ficient to predict these responses. As such, predict-
ing genomic dependencies for drug matching using
results from cancer genomic data in one cancer
should not be expected to necessarily predict thera-
peutic value in another cancer. This new knowledge
likely explains some of the challenges in success-
fully developing Precision Medicine approaches in
human oncology. Clearly the requirement for trans-
lation of questions of biologic context across spe-
cies will further complicate the promise of precision
medicine drug matching in veterinary oncology,
until veterinary cancer contexts are studied and
understood. The allure of a pan-cancer “single tar-
get/single drug” approach has faded based on the
realities of cancer-specific biologic context and is
now recognized to be more complicated by our
growing understanding of tumor heterogeneity.

-- 107 of 258 --

Specifically, even before any drug exposure, we
have now learned of the preexistence of drug-
resistant clones, which is only further complicated
by the additional complexity of understanding
cancer as an “organ”, where even nontumor sup-
portive structures are altered and then influence
tumor biology and drug response in disease-specific
manners (Cox et al., 2012; Quail and Joyce, 2013).
In this setting “dirty” kinase inhibitors and other
nuances of kinase selectivity by distinct kinase
inhibitors may provide a solution (Fojo, 2008; Guo
and Ma, 2021). For example, in human gastrointes-
tinal stromal tumor (GIST), c-kit is often mutated.
Both imatinib and sunitinib target the same gene
(c-kit), but may act as different drugs, defined by
c-KIT targeting differences, and other less under-
stood drug and target variables (Gajiwala et al.,
2009). Hence, although very similar in target pro-
file, imatinib is a first-line agent and sunitinib is
approved and often active as a second-line agent
(Wang et al., 2011). Selection, ordering, and combi-
nations of these highly similar agents alone and
with mAbs will likely be necessary to deliver opti-
mal therapeutic value even when one altered cancer
dependency is identified in a cancer, let alone when
multiple alterations are found in a tumor or an
individual cell. Current data suggest that the “art”
of oncologists will continue to be necessary to guide
optimal therapy for patients, collective of these vari-
ous complexities and those not yet understood.
By the 1990s, researchers had gained sufficient
knowledge and synthetic chemistry capabilities to
initiate use of rational drug design (RDD). The
identification of TKIs based on the knowledge of
the specific structure of the target enzyme’s ATP-
binding pocket is part of RDD.
Gefitinib (Iressa; AstraZeneca) initially failed to
demonstrate improved effect compared to placebo
for treatment of NSCLC. However, a subgroup
analysis showed that a selected patient group
clearly experienced beneficial effects compared to
the controls. An egfr mutation (exon 19 deletion or
exon 21 (L858R) substitution) was demonstrated
within this group and expanded studies focusing on
this mutation showed that gefitinib was signifi-
cantly more efficacious, in the presence of these
alterations. Gefitinib was the first selective TKI to
be approved that was shown to have an effect on
the egfr-mutated tyrosine kinase. This was rapidly
followed by erlotinib (Tarceva; Roche), which has
also found use against pancreatic cancer (in combi-
nation with gemcitabine) after a modest survival
advantage was observed compared to gemcitabine
treatment alone (median survival of 6.4 versus
6.0 months). Pancreatic cancer patients who devel-
oped a skin rash during treatment with erlotinib
demonstrated longer median survival compared to
those who did not develop skin lesions (7.2 versus
5.0 months).
Although the promise of constructing targeted
therapies from a discovered gene alteration in a
specific tumor is alluring, there are many chal-
lenges in this process and subsequent steps to
develop an active drug (Twomey et al., 2017). The
“one biomarker/one drug” concept model is chal-
lenging, as many trials have shown that other cel-
lular changes can co-occur with discovered signal
transduction alterations and predict treatment
failure or early development of resistance. In
Herceptin-treated human epidermal growth factor
receptor 2 (HER2)-positive breast-cancer patients
it was determined that low levels of phosphatase
and tensin homolog (PTEN), a negative regulator
of PI3K signaling, and PTEN loss during treatment
may be an early predictive marker for drug resist-
ance (Zhang et al., 2015). Moreover, the epithelial–
mesenchymal transition (EMT) gene signature has
been shown to predict resistance to EGFR, PI3K/
AKT, and HER2 pathway inhibitors (Byers et al.,
2013; Burnett et al., 2015). The future development
of targeted therapies must include studies of the
tumor heterogeneity, monitor the cancer progres-
sion continuum, describe the mutations created or
enriched by the targeted therapy itself, and also
identify surrogate (protein) biomarkers (see below)
that may help in predicting potential mechanisms
of targeted therapy resistance (Twomey et al., 2017).
Classifcations of Tyrosine Kinase
Inhibitors and their Mechanisms of Action
Imatinib is an example of what is known as a small-
molecule TKI. Many classification systems have been
applied to type these molecules; most common
approaches include Types I–III or Types I–IV. The clas-
sification is based on how and where the molecule
binds and inactivates the function of the tyrosine
kinase. A knowledge of TKI classifications mirrors the
essentiality of an oncologist’s knowledge of conven-
tional chemotherapy mechanisms of action to appro-
priately manage a cancer patient:
● Type I: TKIs that serve as competitive inhibitors
by binding to the ATP pocket in the activated
92 	H. Rönnberg

-- 108 of 258 --

93	Signal Transduction Inhibitors
protein. This type inhibits phosphorylation and
inactivates the tyrosine kinase. Examples of
Type I TKIs include bosutinib (BCR-ABL1 and
Src), 	cabozantinib 	(c-MET 	and 	vascular
endothelial growth factor receptor 2 (VEGFR-
2)), and gefitinib (EGFR).
● Type II: TKIs that bind to a hydrophobic pocket
that forms within the inactive Asp–Phe–Gly
(DFG) motif, therefore known as DGF-out. Type
II often demonstrates more specific kinase inhi-
bition and also blocks enzymes for a longer
period of time than Type I. Well-tested sub-
stances in this class include imatinib (BCR-
ABL1) and the multi-targeted kinase inhibitor
sorafenib (vascular endothelial growth factor
receptor (VEGFR), platelet-derived growth fac-
tor receptor (PDGFR), and RAF).
● Type III: Molecules that exhibit allosteric inhi-
bition through binding in the proximity of the
ATP-binding domain. An example is the MEK,
MAPK/ERK inhibitor trametinib, which is used
to treat malignant melanoma in humans. Type
III kinase inhibitors demonstrate the highest
selectivity, as they use binding sites and physio-
logic mechanisms that are specific to each indi-
vidual kinase. Type III inhibitors are completely
noncompetitive since their activity is not depend-
ent on the presence of ATP or degree of kinase
activation. A greater focus is likely to be placed
on allosteric TKIs in the future, as they are con-
sidered to have a better side-effect profile, higher
specificity, and can perhaps be expected to pro-
vide a longer interval before resistance develops.
● Type IV: These inhibitors are defined as non-
ATP-competitive molecules that bind to the sub-
strate-specific domain on the tyrosine kinase.
Few examples of such inhibitors can be found
today, but studies indicate that ONO12380 has
an 	effect 	on 	imatinib-resistant 	cell 	lines
(Gumireddy et al., 2005).
● Type V: TKIs of this type form a covalent bond
with the amino acid cysteine. Over 200 tyrosine
kinases contain a cysteine chain adjacent to the
ATP-binding region, which creates enormous
potential for development of new drugs within
this group. The advantages of Type V TKIs
include delayed dissociation from the enzyme,
which provides improved pharmacodynamics,
fewer off-target side effects, and the potential to
use a lower dose. Several Type V TKIs, such as
afatinib and ibrutinib, have been shown to over-
come EGFR resistance seen in patients treated
with first-generation EGFR TKIs such as gefi-
tinib and erlotinib (Liao, B.C. et al., 2015).
Knowledge of the small-molecule inhibitor classifi-
cation is an important part of predicting optimal
combinations and optimal sequencing of inhibitors
for patients following the emergence of resistance.
Distinct of the above classes of small-molecule
inhibitors, a diverse array of agents that target sig-
nal transduction pathways have been developed
and used in cancer patients. The classical substance
for inhibition of mammalian or mechanistic target
of rapamycin (mTOR) is rapamycin, which has
long been used for immunosuppression (Markman
et al., 2010; Vilar et al., 2011). Rapamycin inhibits
the function of mTOR complex 1 (mTORC1) by
binding to FKBP-12, thereby forming a complex
with mTOR. This leads to several signal interac-
tions such as inhibition of phosphorylation of
protein kinase S6K1 and other proximate targets,
which has an effect on protein synthesis and other
aspects of cell metabolism (Tavares et al., 2015).
The 	rapamycin 	analogs 	(rapalogs) 	currently
approved for clinical use in oncology include siroli-
mus (Rapamune; Pfizer), everolimus (Afinitor;
Novartis), and temsirolimus (Torisel; Pfizer), and
have been evaluated or used to treat skeletal and
soft tissue sarcomas, renal cancer, neuroendocrine
tumors, and breast cancer (Magaway et al., 2019).
As monotherapy, their efficacy is unpredictable in
the setting of measurable disease, and they may
have distinct roles as part of combination therapy
approaches or as antimetastatic agents (see Amato,
Chapter 5, this volume, 2023). Accordingly, it is
crucial to discover better predictive biomarkers for
this drug class (Tian et al., 2019) in cancer.
Hedgehog (HH) pathway signaling is often dys-
regulated in human cancer (Carpenter and Ray,
2019). The normal function of HH is closely linked
with embryonic development and is essentially
turned off after birth, although it plays a role in
governing 	stem 	cell 	functions 	(Ingham 	and
McMahon, 2001). Although HH signaling does not
initially stem from protein kinases, downstream
signaling is dependent on several key protein kinase
cascades (Montagnani and Stecca, 2019). The HH
family consists of three ligands – Sonic (SHH),
Indian (IHH), and Desert (DHH) Hedgehog –
where SHH is the most commonly expressed and
also the most important for dysregulation and
cancer development (Pathi et al., 2001; Amakye
et al., 2013). The receptor for the HH protein is the

-- 109 of 258 --

transmembrane protein Patched1 (PTCH1), which
normally inhibits signaling from Smoothen (SMO)
(Ingham and McMahon, 2001). When such inhibi-
tion is disrupted (through HH–PTCH1 binding), a
process is initiated that releases, increases expres-
sion of, and translocates GLI proteins (GLI1, 2,
and 3) to the nucleus, where these transcription
factors stimulate expression of a variety of genes
that affect proliferation, survival, angiogenesis, and
differentiation (Carpenter and Lo, 2012). There are
many protein kinases that regulate the HH path-
way. Protein kinase A (PKA) and casein kinases
(CK1 and to a lesser degree also CK2) phosphoryl-
ate SMO, which leads to activation of GLI and also
Wnt/β-catenin (Jia et al., 2010; Zema et al., 2020).
Phosphorylation of GLI1 by the protein kinase
S6K1 (p70 ribosomal protein S6 kinase 1) releases
GLI1 from its inhibitory binding to SUFU
(Suppressor of Fused) (Wang et al., 2012). Once
again, this demonstrates how initiation of mTOR/
S6K1 signaling plays a central role in cancer devel-
opment through its impact on cell mechanisms. The
HH pathway is also governed by classical oncoge-
netic signaling pathways such as protein kinase C
(PKC), mitogen-activated protein kinase kinase
kinases 	(MAP3Ks, including 	genes 	encoding
MEKK1, MEKK2, and MEKK3), as well as through
NOTCH regulation of cancer-associated fibro-
blasts and angiogenesis (Cai et al., 2009; An et al.,
2013; Goruppi et al., 2017; Antonucci et al., 2019;
Huang et al., 2019). There are two approved HH
inhibitors (vismodegib and sonidegib), both focused
on inhibition of SMO for the indication treatment-
refractory basal cell carcinoma, as a result of aberrant
SHH pathway activation (Axelson et al., 2013; Casey
et al., 2017). SMO inhibitors are, however, associated
with troublesome side effects and development of
resistance, which means that future efforts concerning
HH inhibition will be aimed at identifying crucial
steps in GLI activation, as described above, and for
which several protein kinase inhibitors have already
been 	approved, 	albeit 	for 	other 	indications
(Montagnani and Stecca, 2019).
Signal Transduction Blockade
by Monoclonal Antibodies
In addition to small-molecule inhibitors, signal
transduction inhibition in tumor cells can be affected
through mAbs. These may vary significantly in mode
of action and must usually be administered intraven-
ously, as opposed to small-molecule inhibitors,
which are usually given orally (Imai and Takaoka,
2006). Antibodies exert their effect on the tumor cell
surface. They bind to specific epitopes on the kinase
receptor, which can result in receptor internalization/
degradation resulting in pathway blockade or which
may result in direct tumor cell destruction via induc-
tion of apoptosis (Mandal et al., 1998; Liu et al.,
2000) or from immune system activation. Tumor
treatment options include monotherapy, as well as in
combination with other antibodies, immunotherapy,
chemotherapy, and/or hormone therapy (Hynes and
Lane, 2005). These antibodies can be used “as is” or
bound to cytotoxic payloads, including radionuclides
or cellular toxins (antibody–drug conjugates). They
can also be conjugated with cytokines to call in an
immune-mediated attack on the tumor. Initially, these
mAbs were developed through hybridoma technology
using cells derived from mouse spleen. Administration
of these mouse-derived mAbs in humans led to
rapid inactivation of the immune system and had
little effect on the tumor. Subsequently, recombi-
nant technology was used to develop more human-
ized antibodies with few or no nonhuman gene
sequences. Their impact on disease has dramati-
cally improved and today an array of mAbs have
been approved for tyrosine kinase inhibition in
tumors when necessary characteristics of depend-
ency in specific cancers are defined. The suffix of
the name of the generic antibody reveals what type of
antibody it is – monoclonal mouse antibodies have
the suffix “momab”, chimeric antibodies “ximab”,
humanized antibodies “zumab”, and completely
human “umab.” The first mAb to treat tumors was
approved in 1994, i.e., rituximab, for treatment of
non‐Hodgkin’s lymphoma (NHL). Rituximab is
not a TKI but targets B cells expressing CD20,
expressed on target cells. The antibody was initially
used to treat patients with indolent NHL. All of the
antineoplastic mechanisms exerted by rituximab,
as well as those resulting from its anti-inflammatory
effect, have yet to be completely clarified, but it is
known to initiate and have an effect on apoptosis,
as well as to inhibit cell division within tumors
through various protein kinases, such as protein
kinase B (PKB, aka AKT) and extracellular signal-
regulated kinase 1 and 2 (ERK 1/2), as well as to
inhibit mitogen-activated protein kinases (MAPKs)
(Weiner, 2010).
The first specific tyrosine kinase-inhibiting mAb
to treat cancer was trastuzumab, which was approved
in 1998 and was used at the time in combination
with the chemotherapeutic drug paclitaxel to treat
94 	H. Rönnberg

-- 110 of 258 --

95	Signal Transduction Inhibitors
metastatic HER2-positive breast cancer in women
(Slamon et al., 2001). More than a decade earlier,
the first reports had been published describing a
specific tyrosine kinase that was overexpressed in
many cases of breast cancer (King et al., 1985;
Schechter et al., 1985). Today, trastuzumab
(Herceptin) is included on the World Health
Organization’s list of essential medicines.
Monoclonal antibodies have been used to treat
an array of tumors beyond leukemia and breast
cancer. Antibodies specific for EGFR epitopes, in
particular, have proven successful in the treatment
of several solid tumors. Currently, four mAbs
aimed at various EGFR targets have been approved
for human use. They are cetuximab, panitumumab,
nimotuzumab, and necitumumab (Cai et al., 2020),
which have been used to treat NSCLC, colorectal
cancer, pancreatic cancer, malignant glioma, and
head and neck squamous cell cancer (HNSCC). Not
only do mAbs that interfere with EGFR signaling
share their mode of action with their corresponding
TKIs (afatinib, erlotinib, gefitinib, and osimertinib),
they also regulate expression using additional mech-
anisms that are linked to the immune system.
Side Effects from Treatment with Signal
Transduction Inhibitors
Despite the discovery of several promising central
control mechanisms for tumor transformation and
the identification of key enzymes, there was ini-
tially little interest in developing therapies aimed
at inhibiting signaling pathways since their func-
tions were deemed to be of central importance to
essentially all normal cell processes and interfering
with these mechanisms was therefore predicted to
cause unacceptable side effects. Following the dis-
covery of imatinib and reports of the impressive
responses in treating chronic leukemias, in the
absence of predicted toxicity, interest surged;
today, most new treatments approved in oncology
are based on the identified dysregulations associ-
ated with cell signaling. The previously raised
concerns related to side effects of these treatments
are of course still relevant, and it is important to
understand these risks in order to be able to select
patients or prevent/minimize side effects (Keefe
and Bateman, 2011).
Conventional chemotherapy is primarily associ-
ated with reactions from organs containing rapidly
dividing cells, since most drugs directly or indirectly
affect cell division. These include the classic side
effects seen in hematopoiesis and the immune sys-
tem, as well as those on mucous membranes, hair,
and skin. In addition, adverse effects on the kidney,
liver, and central and peripheral nervous system
may occur from distinct mechanisms.
Many of the side effects that develop during
treatment with signal transduction inhibitors are
identical to conventional chemotherapy, while oth-
ers are unique.
Bone marrow suppression
Bone marrow suppression is the most common
hematologic side effect of signal transduction
inhibitors. In contrast to conventional chemother-
apy, however, serious high-grade febrile neutro-
penias are less common. Dogs treated with TKIs
also demonstrate the same type of hematologic side
effects (Hahn et al., 2008; London et al., 2009; Dos
Santos Horta et al., 2018; Weishaar et al., 2018). It
is likely that cytopenias arise because the treat-
ments target normal hematopoietic progenitor
cells; for example, c-KIT and FLT-3 are important
for development of hematopoietic stem cells (Dy
and Adjei, 2013).
Gastrointestinal toxicity
Gastrointestinal side effects are common with both
conventional chemotherapy and treatment with
signal transduction inhibitors. These may vary
from pain without visible erosions in the orophar-
ynx to pronounced mucosal inflammation of the
stomach and intestine. EGFR/RAF/MEK, PI3K/
AKT/mTOR, and VEGFR are known to be involved
in physiologic processes concerning cell prolifera-
tion and mucous membrane repair in the gastroin-
testinal tract. The development of goblet cells from
undifferentiated crypt cells in the intestinal mucosa
is dependent on NOTCH and serves as one of the
explanations for TKI-mediated diarrhea (van Es
et al., 2005).
Impact on circulation
In human patients, hypertension commonly occurs
during treatment with signal transduction inhibi-
tors that target VEGF/VEGFR, since these sub-
stances are normally involved in synthesis of nitric
oxide and thereby in regulating vascular plasticity.
(Smith and Dunn, 1985; Bhargava, 2009). Drugs

-- 111 of 258 --

in this class do not cause these side effects com-
monly in veterinary patients.
Cutaneous toxicity
Alopecia is a common side effect of systemic
chemotherapy. With TKI treatment, cutaneous tox-
icity is common; however, these skin reactions are
distinct (Dy and Adjei, 2013), including pruritus,
erythema, acne, folliculitis, thinning of the skin,
and palmar-plantar erythrodysesthesia (PPE) or
hand–foot skin reaction (HFSR) (Robert et al.,
2012). This is likely due to extensive expression of
several protein kinases in the skin. This is especially
true for EGFRs, where more than 50% of patients
undergoing EGFR inhibitor treatment experience
skin side effects. In severe cases, such conditions are
treated with skin softeners, topical corticosteroids,
clindamycin, tetracyclines, and antihistamines.
Such side effects may be severe and dose limiting to
the point that the medication must be discontinued
(Lacouture et al., 2018). The presence of cutaneous
side effects is strongly associated with a good thera-
peutic response to EGFR therapy (Kogawa et al.,
2015). c-KIT inhibitors may cause reversible hypo-
pigmentation, thought to result from disruption of
the c-KIT/MITF (microphthalmia-associated tran-
scription factor) pathway for melanin production
(Kitamura et al., 2004).
Combination Therapy
Over 40 years ago, the idea that surgery alone
could be supplemented with a combination of
other treatments to improve prognosis and survival
in cancer patients began to gain acceptance (Forbes,
1982). Similarly, signal transduction inhibitors as
part of multimodal protocols have been shown to
optimize therapy for an array of cancers. Specifically,
these signal transduction inhibitors have been
shown to have both radiosensitizing, chemother-
apy-enhancing effects and to potentiate immuno-
therapy (see Mason and Dow, Chapter 8, this
volume, 2023).
One example is the first specific tyrosine kinase-
inhibiting mAb for cancer treatment, trastuzumab,
which was used in combination with taxanes to
treat metastatic HER2-positive breast cancer in
women (Slamon et al., 2001).
Signal transduction inhibitors themselves can
also be combined to optimize treatment and hit
several targets simultaneously, thereby obtaining a
more potent and lasting response while also over-
coming resistance development. In CML the
expression of Bcr-Abl oncogene is often associated
with several additional signaling pathway altera-
tions, including JAK/STAT, MAPK/ERK, and PI3K/
AKT/mTOR. Accordingly, a biological rationale
exists to combine imatinib with mTOR inhibitors
to potentiate the response and minimize the risk of
resistance (Singh et al., 2021).
Resistance Development
While the idea of using targeted therapies to dis-
rupt key dependencies in tumors that drive cancer
development presents an alluring opportunity, the
dynamic evolution of dependencies in cancer cre-
ates the problem of resistance. Interestingly, the
pattern of resistance is often influenced by the ini-
tial targeting approach. Once targeted treatment is
initiated, an inevitable process of selective pressure
occurs, in which cancer cells within a heterogene-
ous population selectively survive and circumvent
the treatments that have been initiated.
Resistance development against targeted thera-
pies occurs through several mechanisms:
1. Specifc changes in receptors can lead to mAb
resistance. The receptors can either mutate to reduce
binding affnity or completely cease to express the
extracellular domain and thereby become resist-
ant to such drugs (Liao, H.W. et al., 2015; Pan
and Magge, 2020). The receptors can also increase
expression to thereby overcome competitive inhibi-
tion (Del Re et al., 2019).
2. In molecules aimed at the ATP-binding domain,
resistance develops when mutations cause this
affnity to be altered (Zhang et al., 2020). Second-
and third-generation substances have been devel-
oped for several TKIs to address this problem.
Nevertheless, new generations of TKIs do not
always result in survival benefts, even when they
are initiated, and continued research is needed to
bridge the gaps and improve survival in the face of
TKI resistance (Hochhaus et al., 2020).
3. The hypothesis regarding cancer resistance or
recurrence, variably described as the “cancer stem
cell” or “drug persister cell” hypothesis, includes
mechanisms of resistance against signal transduc-
tion inhibitors (Giani et al., 2020).
4. The targeting of altered signaling genes in cancer
lends itself to monitoring the emergence of drug-
resistant clones by analysis of small quantities of
96 	H. Rönnberg

-- 112 of 258 --

97	Signal Transduction Inhibitors
tumor-derived nucleic acid in the blood, known as
circulating tumor DNA (ctDNA) or cell-free tumor
DNA (cftDNA). The utility of this approach is
challenging in the setting of low disease burden but
holds important potential value, by informing drug
selection during tumor evolution and treatment
resistance.
Clinical Use of Kinase Inhibitors
in Veterinary Oncology
Three TKIs are currently approved for veterinary
medical use. All three are oral, small-molecule
inhibitors. Oclacitinib (Apoquel; Zoetis) is a Janus
kinase – a JAK1/JAK2 inhibitor that targets several
processes related to pruritus and inflammation in
allergies. It is approved for use in atopic dermatitis
in dogs and will not be further described (Cosgrove
et al., 2013).
The remaining two have been approved for treat-
ment of tumors in dogs, primarily based on c-KIT
targeting in canine mast cell tumors. The first sub-
stance is toceranib (Palladia; Zoetis), which was
approved in 2009 for treatment of grade II or III
Patnaik recurrent, cutaneous mast cell tumors in
dogs, with or without regional lymph node involve-
ment, and regardless of c-kit mutation status
(London et al., 2009).
Toceranib is an orally administered, class I multi-
kinase TKI with activity against VEGFR-2, VEGFR-
3, PDGFRα/β, KIT, CSF1R, FLT-3, and RET
(Papaetis and Syrigos, 2009). Toceranib is related
to sunitinib (Sutent; Pfizer). Based on rodent model
studies, toceranib was initially developed for its
antiangiogenic potential and for its inhibition of
VEGFR and PDGFR (London, 2014). Because
toceranib had an effect on other key signaling path-
ways (c-KIT and FLT-3), it was believed to have
direct effects on some cancer cells and was there-
fore included in clinical trials of dogs with measur-
able tumors. In an initial Phase I study evidence of
activity was seen in 54% of patients (London et al.,
2003). Tumors that responded to this therapy
included sarcomas, carcinomas, and hematologic
neoplasias, including dogs with mast cell tumors. In
canine mast cell tumors c-kit is mutated in about
30% of cases and considered to contribute to
oncogenesis.
Based on knowledge of the c-kit mutation in
dogs with mast cell tumors, the mode of action of
toceranib, and prior experience from the clinical
Phase I study, a randomized, blinded study on dogs
with inoperable grade II and III mast cell tumors
was initiated (London et al., 2009). The study
included a total of 149 dogs. In the blinded phase,
response was seen in 37.2% (complete response,
n = 7; partial response, n = 25) of dogs that were
given toceranib, compared with 7.9% of those
given the placebo. The dogs in the placebo arm
were offered toceranib after the completion of the
blinded phase or in the case of progression. Based
on this study, in 2009 the US Food and Drug
Administration (FDA) approved use of this drug in
dogs with inoperable grade II and III mast cell
tumor, regardless of c-kit mutation status.
Since that prospective study, the independent
role of c-kit mutation status in the prognosis of
canine mast cell tumors has been questioned. It is
reasonable that the biologic role of c-kit mutation
in dogs with mast cell tumors complicates the ques-
tion of toceranib activity with and without muta-
tion of c-kit (Weishaar et al., 2018; Thamm et al.,
2019). These disparate data in the setting of a sin-
gle presumed genomic driver underscore the
required rigor and depth of analysis of biomarker
validation and credentialing studies (see below).
Following registration, an array of studies has
been published concerning the off-label use of
toceranib for tumors other than mast cell tumor.
Most often these studies were not conducted with
a clear perspective of the disease target or its role in
the biology of the disease. Distinct studies appro-
priately asked questions about combinations of this
new veterinary drug with other medications and/or
radiation therapy. Toceranib has also been used in
cats with tumors, alone or in combination with
other treatments (Harper and Blackwood, 2017;
Merrick et al., 2017; Olmsted et al., 2017; Wiles
et al., 2017; Berger et al., 2018). The extent of oral
bioavailability of toceranib in cats remains largely
unclear, as does whether achieved exposures actu-
ally modulate relevant disease targets. Although
reported to be well tolerated in prescribed doses,
the lack of controlled trials means that toceranib
treatment in cats is yet to be optimized.
An increased awareness of the potential negative
impact of sustained targeting of VEGFR in both
human and murine studies has been raised, based
on the concept of evasive resistance (see Matsuyama
and Mutsaers, Chapter 3, this volume, 2023;
Amato, Chapter 5, this volume, 2023). Evasive
resistance has been used to describe a treatment-
induced acceleration of cancer metastasis following
VEGFR inhibition, even if a benefit is measured in

-- 113 of 258 --

the primary tumor. The evasive resistance hypothesis
recognizes that objective responses against measur-
able tumors are distinct from and do not predict
activity of the same drug in the same patient with
minimally residual disease. Based on this hypothe-
sis, sustained VEGFR blockade, by any method,
should be avoided unless there is a known genomic
driver present in the tumor cell also targeted by the
chosen inhibitor. Accordingly toceranib use in a
minimal residual disease setting may not only be
ineffective but may accelerate metastasis in patient
subsets who do not express driving mutations in
disease targets blocked by toceranib. Furthermore,
this hypothesis does not suggest the same caution
in the use of toceranib in canine mast cell tumors in
either measurable or minimal residual disease set-
tings. Although examined in human clinical trials,
the impact of the evasive resistance hypothesis
requires further study in veterinary patients.
The second TKI developed for veterinary oncol-
ogy was also used in canine mast cell tumors.
Masitinib is an orally administered small-molecule
inhibitor mainly targeting mutated c-kit, but also
PDGFRα/β, lymphocyte-specific kinase (LCK),
LCK/YES-related protein (LYN), fibroblast growth
factor receptor 3 (FGFR3), and focal adhesion
kinase (FAK) (Marech et al., 2014). It has been
approved by the European Medicines Agency
(Masivet; AB Science), while prior conditional
approval by the FDA (Kinavet) has been with-
drawn. In vitro studies and rodent models have
shown antitumoral effect in human cancer cell lines
(Humbert et al., 2010). KIT affinity in vitro has
also been confirmed (Dubreuil et al., 2009).
One prospective, randomized, blinded, placebo-
controlled study on dogs with non-metastasized
grades II and III mast cell tumors included 202
dogs (Hahn et al., 2008). The response did not dif-
fer significantly between masitinib and placebo
(11.2% versus 4.9%), but median survival was
longer in the subgroup of dogs with the c-kit muta-
tion compared with the placebo group (417 versus
182 days). This led to the approval of masitinib for
grades II and III mast cell tumors with confirmed
c-kit mutation. As noted above this is distinct to
toceranib, which was approved for both wild-type
and mutant c-kit-expressing tumors (London,
2014). Side effects from treatment with masitinib
are generally mild and transient and mainly involve
toxicity to the gastrointestinal tract, but a serious
kidney damage has been rarely reported (Hahn
et al., 2008).
In addition to the approved indication of masto-
cytoma, off-label use of masitinib has also been
reported (Holtermann et al., 2016). The responses
seen beyond mast cell tumor were not predicted or
understood based on signal transduction pathways
active or dysregulated in these tumors. Interestingly
masitinib has been shown to potentiate doxoru-
bicin activity in vitro and potentially reverse doxo-
rubicin resistance in dog tumor cell lines (Zandvliet
et al., 2013; Milovancev et al., 2016).
Recent studies have identified a potentially path-
ogenic BRAF alteration in dogs with transitional
cell carcinoma (TCC). BRAF is a serine/threonine
protein kinase that affects the MAPK/ERK signal-
ing pathway, which is involved in most important
cell functions including cell division, differentia-
tion, and secretion (Cope et al., 2018). A large
proportion of dogs with TCC and prostate cancer
display a b-raf mutation that can be analyzed in
urine samples (Mochizuki et al., 2015). This find-
ing provides a biologic rationale for clinical studies
using the selective BRAF inhibitor vemurafenib
(Zelboraf; Genentech, San Francisco, California) in
dogs with this mutation in TCC (Wiley et al.,
2019). As described earlier this genomic data lacks
the necessary biologic context to predict the role of
this b-raf mutation in canine TCC, or the therapeu-
tic consequence of its targeting with an appropri-
ately administered inhibitor, again underscoring the
concept of understanding target biology and bio-
logic inhibition (i.e., context) as part of therapeutic
decision-making in cancer.
Several other kinase inhibitors have been exam-
ined on a smaller scale in dogs and cats. Imatinib is
reported to be well tolerated in both dogs (Isotani
et al., 2008, Yamada et al., 2011) and cats (Lachowicz
et al., 2005; Isotani et al., 2006, 2010) with masto-
cytoma. Studies using the PI3K inhibitor RV1001
have demonstrated beneficial effects in hematologic
neoplasia in dogs, with hepatotoxicity as the dose-
limiting side effect (Gardner et al., 2018). Bruton
tyrosine kinase (BTK) plays a central role in the
function of the B-cell antigen receptor and other cell
surface receptors that are involved in proliferation
and cell survival (Burger, 2019). Ibrutinib and acala-
brutinib are BTK inhibitors and have been approved
for treatment of human B-cell tumors. Both have
been studied in canine B-cell lymphoma (Honigberg
et al., 2010; Harrington et al., 2016).
In addition to the large protein kinase inhibitor
group, several other types of signal transduction
inhibitors have also been used and developed
98 	H. Rönnberg

-- 114 of 258 --

99	Signal Transduction Inhibitors
in veterinary oncology. These include nuclear trans-
port proteins (see London, Chapter 7, this volume,
2023).
Biomarkers and Protein Kinases
in Clinical Oncology
Altered signal transduction genes have utility in
cancer beyond therapeutic targeting. Within oncol-
ogy, biomarkers are usually defined as being diag-
nostic, predictive, and/or prognostic. Biomarkers
are measurable indicators of a biologic condition
that can be analyzed from body fluids, exhaled air,
and expression in tissue. Usually, they are proteins
or nucleic acids that have been modified in some
way. At the turn of the millennium, the National
Cancer Institute (NCI) launched the Early Detection
Research Network (EDRN) initiative, with the
purpose of gathering expertise and conducting
studies aimed at discovering new cancer biomark-
ers that would be validated and clinically useful
(Srivastava and Rossi, 1996). Diagnostic biomark-
ers are among the best understood and validated
and can be used to discover and define cancer and
help distinguish it from other illnesses with similar
symptoms in affected patients. Examples of widely
used biomarkers in human patients include pros-
tate-specific antigen (PSA) found with prostate
cancer in men; cancer antigen 125 (CA-125), which
occurs in ovarian cancer among women; and highly
elevated calcitonin, which is diagnostic for medul-
lary thyroid cancer. Such biomarkers have found
additional clinical uses and may be more useful for
monitoring burden of disease over time. Similar to
the earlier reference regarding biologic context of
altered genes and therapeutic response during tar-
geting, the impact and value of a biomarker is often
cancer dependent.
A recent development in the biomarker field
includes the analysis of cftDNA that has leaked
into the bloodstream from the tumor, known as
“liquid biopsy”. In the setting of TKIs, monitoring
the presence and emergence of resistant clones
using cftDNA liquid biopsy approaches could be a
useful part of therapeutic monitoring in cancer
(Diao et al., 2020).
Similarly, drug-response biomarkers are used to
determine whether a specific treatment is suita-
ble/effective for a given diagnosed tumor (see
Fenger, Chapter 11, this volume, 2023). The quin-
tessential example here is, of course, imatinib in
patients with CML, where 95% of patients dem-
onstrate an acquired specific chromosomal trans-
location, known as the Philadelphia chromosome
(Nowell, 2007) that is the target of imatinib. The
Bcr-Abl1 fusion serves as a diagnostic biomarker
of CML and can be used to monitor burden of
disease on therapy. Furthermore, sequencing of
this locus can guide the selection of signal trans-
duction inhibitors during therapy and at thera-
peutic failure.
A prognostic biomarker is most valuable in the
management of a patient when it independently
influences the outcome and prognosis of a patient.
In some cases, overexpression of tyrosine kinases
can be prognostic. Absence of RTK can also be
prognostic. A typical example of this is the worse
prognosis for women with breast cancer who do
not express the RTK HER2/neu. To some extent,
this can be explained by the predicted inactivity of
HER2/neu inhibitors like Herceptin in these
patients. However, biologically, these tumors also
appear to be more aggressive.
Future Perspectives and
New Diagnostic Tools
Many cancer drugs today are approved for a spe-
cific biomarker linked with the drug’s effect, which
helps to optimize effect and target treatment. As
clinical experience mounts for all new targeted
therapies, it is becoming clear that resistance devel-
opment remains a significant dilemma, even for
targeted treatments. Moreover, it is now known
that the same kind of mutation does not necessarily
mean the drug will work in the same way in rela-
tion to different types of cancer. For example, tras-
tuzumab, an inhibitor of erythroblastic oncogene B
ErbB-2 (which encodes HER2), is not effective for
treatment of ERBB-positive gastroesophageal can-
cer, even though it works well against ERBB-
positive breast cancer (Maron and Bass, 2020).
The likely explanation for such varying responses
in different tumors with the same type of mutation
is unclear and requires the study of each genomic
alteration in each cancer to understand the bio-
logic context of the alteration in that cancer.
Cancer is not simply a disease of altered genes and
cannot be understood through a pan-cancer genomic
lens. Furthermore, genomic heterogeneity in cancer
further complicates the value of any genomic
variant identified in a patient sample. Indeed,
tumor heterogeneity has many sources and may be

-- 115 of 258 --

categorized as: intratumoral, intertumoral (between
patients with the same subtype), intrametastatic,
and intermetastatic (between different metastases
in the same patient), resulting from geographic
heterogeneity 	and 	evolutionary 	heterogeneity
(Jamal-Hanjani et al., 2015). Sometimes the intra-
tumoral heterogeneity even exceeds the heterogene-
ity seen between the tumors in different patients
(Bonin and Stanta, 2020). This has been demon-
strated in gastroesophageal cancer, where tumor
expression in histologic sections from biopsies
obtained just 0.67 mm apart differed to the point
that one qualified the patient for inclusion in an
FGFR2-selected study and the other did not (Chao
et al., 2020). Moreover, the simple pragmatics of
sample collection for genomic analysis is compli-
cated and deserving of additional study. For exam-
ple, the timing of sample fixation of biopsies in
RNA-sparing medium is complex and influenced
by both cancer type and collection procedure (von
Euler et al., 2005).
In summary, there is a great need to develop
improved biomarkers to guide selection of optimal
therapy and to aid in dynamic and reliable monitor-
ing of resistance development so that a new treat-
ment can be initiated as early as possible in cases of
therapeutic failure. Liquid biopsies are a promising
technology to aid in earlier detection of resistant
mutations and thereby provide an informative
guide for clinicians to select new therapy for a
patient (Del Re et al., 2019). The clinical setting in
which a biomarker is used requires validation in
that use case. Furthermore, results from one use
case should not be used to support validation in a
distinct use case. Recently, a cftDNA assay has been
advanced in dogs as a cancer screening biomarker
of asymptomatic dogs. The value from such a can-
cer screening test has yet to be determined. Distinctly,
a similar approach has been used in a cancer diag-
nostic setting. A cancer signal (using cftDNA) was
found in blood samples in nine out of 11 cancer-
bearing dogs, with next-generation sequencing
(NGS) identifying the same mutations in blood as in
the surgical cancer specimens investigated (Kruglyak
et al., 2021). This diagnostic clinical use case must
be understood as unrelated to the cancer surveil-
lance/screening use case that was the subject of a
study of over 1000 dogs. The sensitivity/specificity
to detect cancer signal in blood varied with cancer
type. Overall, the liquid biopsy test demonstrated a
54.7% (95% confidence interval (CI): 49.3–60.0%)
sensitivity and a 98.5% (95% CI: 97.0–99.3%)
specificity (Flory et al., 2022). A handful of asymp-
tomatic dogs were also found to have a cancer sig-
nal in blood before overt tumor symptoms were
detected. The usefulness of this NGS technique in
detecting cftDNA remains unclear. Studies are now
needed to understand if such a screening result adds
value or not to asymptomatic patients screened for
cancer using these approaches.
Tumor RNA may not be as helpful with tumor
detection from blood samples as cftDNA, since it is
indistinguishable from RNA in normal cells. On
the other hand, tumor RNA tissue panels are useful
for the analysis of drug resistance, which can help
guide selection of the correct drug to treat the indi-
vidual tumor (Katogiritis and Khanna, 2019).
MicroRNA (miRNA) has emerged as a highly
promising marker for diagnosing tumors and mak-
ing a prognosis. These are short, 18–25 nucleotide
segments that do not code for protein sequences.
Instead, their main function is to contribute to gene
regulation by binding to mRNA, thereby affecting
its activity. A deeper understanding of the role of
miRNA in relation to processes such as metastasis
could potentially lead to the development of new
targeted cancer therapies (Niu et al., 2021).
In a cancer lesion, tumor and nontumor cells
release extracellular vesicles, called exosomes.
Exosomes, containing signal transduction mole-
cules, cftDNA, and/or RNA (Quail and Joyce,
2013), provide a relatively stable substrate for
biomarker analyses and the potential is currently
being investigated in many studies.
Conclusions
The discovery of imatinib and its benefits in the
treatment of CLL in humans launched a revolution
in the field of targeted cancer therapy. Expectations
were and remain high in finding specific substances
that halt the altered cellular signaling pathways
that promote development of cancer, while simulta-
neously minimizing the off-target effects on normal
cells and reducing negative impact and side
effects. Over time, insight has grown concerning
the presence of several simultaneously active sig-
naling pathways in each cancer, which has
increased understanding for resistance mechanisms
associated with the use of signal transduction
inhibitors. Concomitant use of multi-targeted
kinase inhibitors and combination therapies with
other chemotherapeutic agents, immunotherapy,
and radiation therapy have enabled potentiation of
100 	H. Rönnberg

-- 116 of 258 --

101	Signal Transduction Inhibitors
the effect of new cancer drugs. The development of
improved technologies to identify biomarkers in
tumors will accelerate the development of new
effective cancer drugs, while improving the use of
those already available.

CHERYL L ONDON*
Tufts University, North Grafton, Massachusetts, USA
Introduction: Regulation of Nuclear
Transport
The exchange of proteins between the nucleus and
cytoplasm is a tightly regulated process critical for
maintaining cellular homeostasis (Floch et al.,
2014). In particular, efficient transmission of sig-
nals from the cell surface into the nucleus typically
requires movement of transcription factors from
the cytoplasm into the nucleus where they act to
modulate gene expression (Fig. 7). Although small
molecules can diffuse through the nuclear pore
complex (NPC), larger cargos (including RNAs and
proteins) must utilize a transport system that
involves various receptors (Wente and Rout, 2010).
These are further classified into importins (nuclear
import), exportins (nuclear export), and trans-
portins (bidirectional movement), all of which
require energy provided by the GTPase Ran (Ras-
related nuclear protein, RanGTP) (Cagatay and
Chook, 2018; Azizian and Li, 2020; Azmi et al.,
2021). Most of the nuclear transport proteins
belong to the karyopherin family (Kaps, from the
Greek karyon, nucleus and pherein, to bring). Kaps
recognize specific signals within their respective
cargo proteins including a nuclear localization sig-
nal (NLS) and/or a nuclear export signal (NES)
(Cagatay and Chook, 2018; Azizian and Li, 2020;
Azmi et al., 2021). The human genome encodes
more than 20 Kaps; members of this protein family
possess tandem huntingtin, elongation factor 3,
protein phosphatase 2A, and mechanistic target of
rapamycin (HEAT) repeats in their secondary pro-
tein structure that contain ~40–45 amino acids and
form two antiparallel α-helices linked by a loop
(Cooley et al., 2002; Kosyna and Depping, 2018).
As previously mentioned, the GTPase Ran works
with importins and exportins to regulate the movement
of proteins across the NPC. The concentration of
RanGTP is higher in the nucleus, while RanGDP
predominates in the cytoplasm, driving directional-
ity of transport (Moore and Blobel, 1994; Gorlich
and Mattaj, 1996; Cook et al., 2007; Guttler and
Gorlich, 2011; Matsuura, 2016). Briefly, RanGTP,
exportins, and nuclear cargo (flagged through a
NES) collectively bind/interact creating a ternary
complex in the nucleus that initiates the process of
export. Once translocated to the cytoplasm,
RanGTP is converted to RanGDP by the cytoplas-
mic proteins RanGAP1 and RanB1/BP2, which
causes the complex to dissociate, releasing the
cargo into the cytoplasm. The opposite process
occurs for nuclear import; cargos containing an
NLS bind importins and move through the NPC
into the nucleus where the concentration of
RanGTP is high. Release of cargo occurs when
RanGTP binds tightly to the importin.
Regulation of cargo movement across the nuclear
membrane is a tightly controlled process that plays
a key role in cellular homeostasis through modula-
tion of gene expression, protein translation, and
protein function. The functional diversity of Kap-
dependent transport influences a variety of pro-
cesses such as signal transduction, immune response,
cellular differentiation, and circadian rhythm,
among others (Harel and Forbes, 2004; Quan et al.,
2008; Kosyna and Depping, 2018). The diverse
functional properties of Kaps require that they
interact with a wide array of cargo; indeed, one Kap
protein can associate with different proteins using
distinct binding sites and/or specific conformational
states. Beyond their roles in regulating traffic across
the nuclear membrane, several non-transport func-
tions have been associated with Kaps. For example,
it is now clear that some importins can function as
*Email: Cheryl.London@tufts.edu

cytoplasmic chaperones by essentially covering spe-
cific domains of a protein and preventing their
aggregation (Jakel et al., 2002). Others have been
linked to direct regulation of gene expression
through binding to specific gene promoters (Yasuda
et al., 2012). Lastly, certain Kaps can regulate mito-
sis through their involvement in mitotic spindle
assembly (Forbes et al., 2015).
CRM1, Nuclear Transport, and Cancer
Dysregulation of nuclear transport involving spe-
cific cargo proteins is associated with many disease
states including inflammation, viral infection, and
neurodegeneration; however, it has been best char-
acterized in the setting of cancer (Turner and
Sullivan, 2008; Nguyen et al., 2012; Turner et al.,
2012; Kosyna and Depping, 2018). Aberrant
nuclear–cytoplasmic shuttling of oncogenes and
tumor suppressor genes has been demonstrated in
carcinomas, sarcomas, and hematopoietic neopla-
sia (Cagatay and Chook, 2018), and evidence sug-
gests that Kaps comprehensively impact the ten
hallmarks of cancer (Hanahan and Weinberg,
2011). While all Kaps likely influence tumorigene-
sis, CRM1 (also known as XPO1) represents the
most completely characterized of these with respect
to both cancer biology and therapeutic potential.
CRM1 is an exportin that regulates a wide range
of cellular processes through its transport of over
220 proteins and multiple RNA species including
mRNAs and microRNAs, among others (Xu et al.,
2012; Okamura et al., 2015). As several known
tumor suppressors and growth regulatory proteins
including p53, p75, Rb, p21, p27, STAT3, FOXO,
BCR-ABL, PI3K/AKT, and IκB are substrates of
CRM1, it has been widely believed that aberrant
protein localization mediated by CRM1 (e.g.,
nuclear export of tumor suppressor proteins) con-
tributes to tumor development and progression
(Gravina et al., 2014; Kim et al., 2016; Wang and
Liu, 2019). However, recent proteomic studies of
CRM1 cargos undertaken across yeast, frog oocytes,
and human cells identified greater than 700 poten-
tial export substrates (Kirli et al., 2015). Analysis of
these proteins suggests that CRM1 has a far
broader influence on cellular function including
regulation of centrosomes, autophagy, cytoskeleton,
ribosome maturation, and mRNA degradation. As
such, CRM1-mediated protein export is likely to be
a promiscuous process affecting multiple aspects of
cell biology that are dysregulated in cancer.
Overexpression of CRM1 has been documented
in several human cancers including carcinomas
(pancreatic, ovarian, lung, gastric, prostate, colo-
rectal) (Noske et al., 2008; Huang et al., 2009;
Zhou et al., 2013; Gravina et al., 2015; Chen et al.,
2017; Gupta et al., 2017; Saulino et al., 2018;
Subhash et al., 2018; Aladhraei et al., 2019), sarco-
mas (osteosarcoma, several soft tissue sarcomas)
(Yao et al., 2009; Bertucci et al., 2016), gliomas
(Shen et al., 2009), and hematologic malignancies
(chronic lymphocytic leukemia (CLL), diffuse large
B-cell lymphoma (DLBCL), multiple myeloma
(MM), acute 	myelogenous 	leukemia 	(AML))
(Kojima et al., 2013; Schmidt et al., 2013; Cosson
et al., 2017; Reddy et al., 2017), in most cases cor-
relating with a poor prognosis. However, the driv-
ers of CRM1 overexpression have not been well
characterized. Some studies have demonstrated
that MYC overexpression and/or loss of p53 func-
tion play a pivotal role in driving enhanced CRM1
gene transcription (Golomb et al., 2012). More
recently, mutations in CRM1 have been identified
in both solid and hematopoietic tumors, with the
highest incidence in lymphomas. Specifically,
somatic point mutations (E571, R749, and D624)
were identified in B-cell malignancies and Hodgkin
lymphoma, with the E571 most prevalent (Taylor
et al., 2019). Importantly, the E571K CRM1
mutant appears to cooperate with MYC and BCL2
in promoting the development of lymphoma
(Camus et al., 2017; Azizian and Li, 2020). Lastly,
several CRM1 binding partners and/or adapter
proteins are also overexpressed in human cancers
and may cooperate with CRM1 to affect nuclear
export (Azizian and Li, 2020). Accordingly, thera-
peutic targeting of CRM1 may be of value in the
setting of CRM1 overexpression as well as in situ-
ations where overexpression of specific binding
partners leads to dysregulation of function.
The functional consequences of CRM1 overex-
pression are believed in part to be driven by forced
aberrant localization of proteins. Specifically, the
enhanced export of multiple tumor suppressor pro-
teins impairs their ability to constrain tumor cell
growth. However, it is now evident that CRM1
binds a broad array of cargo including multiple
oncoproteins such as cyclins, Survivin, and BCR-
ABL, making it more likely that increased CRM1-
driven nuclear export functionalities are required
by cancer cells to support their growth and energy
requirements. The effects of CRM1 mutation, spe-
cifically E571, have only recently been interrogated.

113	Nuclear Transport Inhibitors
In a mouse model of B-cell CLL, the E571 CRM1
mutation was capable of driving leukemogenesis by
priming the preneoplastic lymphocytes for acquisi-
tion of additional genetic and epigenetic abnor-
malities that collectively resulted in malignant
transformation (Walker et al., 2021).
Inhibitors of CRM1
Attempts at developing inhibitors of CRM1 began
in the early 1980s resulting in the development and
evaluation of several small molecules, most of
which did not move into the clinical realm. The
first of these was leptomycin B, which was isolated
from Streptomyces initially as an antifungal agent
(Hamamoto et al., 1985). Leptomycin B demon-
strated antitumor activity both in vitro and in
murine tumor models and was subsequently found
to bind CRM1 covalently and irreversibly at
Cys528 located in the NES binding groove (Nishi
et al., 1994). Unfortunately, a Phase I study in peo-
ple demonstrated little clinical activity and the trial
was terminated early due to significant toxicity
including malaise and anorexia (Newlands et al.,
1996). Leptomycin B analogs have been evaluated
including ratjadones, anguinomycins, and KOS2464;
these also covalently bind to Cys528 and typically
demonstrate greater potency in vitro and in vivo
with a significantly reduced toxicity profile in mice
(Koster et al., 2003; Mutka et al., 2009; Sun et al.,
2013). However, these agents require intravenous
delivery, limiting the frequency of drug administra-
tion, and they have not moved forward for clinical
development.
More recently, novel, drug-like, orally bioavaila-
ble, small-molecule selective inhibitors of nuclear
export (SINEs) that bind to CRM1 at the reactive-
site Cys528 residue have been developed including
KPT-251, KPT-276, KPT-335 (verdinexor), and
KPT-330 (selinexor) (Parikh et al., 2014). These
compounds are slowly reversible with a half-life of
~24 hours, and lead to functional inactivation of
the CRM1 protein as well as transient proteosome-
mediated degradation. SINEs induce apoptosis and
block proliferation in an array of cancer cell lines
with corresponding activity in mouse models,
including carcinomas, sarcomas, and hematopoietic
malignancies, while sparing normal cells (Walker
et al., 2013; Zhang et al., 2013; Sun et al., 2014;
Tai et al., 2014; Wang et al., 2014; Green et al.,
2015; Etchin et al., 2016; Azmi et al., 2020).
Importantly, SINEs showed good oral bioavailability
and tolerability when evaluated in mouse models of
cancer (Lapalombella et al., 2012; Ranganathan
et al., 2012; Azmi et al., 2013; Inoue et al., 2013;
Zhang et al., 2013; Tai et al., 2014).
The lead SINE, selinexor, has since been evalu-
ated alone or in combination with other agents
across several clinical trials in people. In the setting
of solid tumors (carcinomas, sarcomas) little single-
agent activity has been noted in either Phase I or
Phase II trials, and several of these studies were
associated with fatigue, anorexia, nausea, and
other dose-limiting toxicities (Abdul Razak et al.,
2016; Gounder et al., 2016; Wei et al., 2018;
Shafique et al., 2019; Nilsson et al., 2020; Vergote
et al., 2020; Azmi et al., 2021). In contrast,
selinexor has demonstrated consistent single-agent
activity in the setting of heavily pretreated hemato-
logic malignancies including B-cell lymphomas,
AML, and MM (Alexander et al., 2016; Garzon
et al., 2017; Kuruvilla et al., 2017; Chen et al.,
2018; Vogl et al., 2018; Wang et al., 2018; Zhang
et al., 2018; Chari et al., 2019; Jakubowiak et al.,
2019; Bhatnagar et al., 2020; Grosicki et al., 2020;
Kalakonda et al., 2020; Azmi et al., 2021) In
refractory or relapsed AML, selinexor treatment
resulted in a greater than 50% decrease in bone
marrow blasts and was associated with a signifi-
cant improvement in overall survival in responders
versus non-responders (9.7 versus 2.7 months)
(Garzon et al., 2017). Similarly, a Phase I trial of
people with relapsed or refractory B-cell lymphoma
showed an objective response rate of 31% (22/71
patients) (Kuruvilla et al., 2017). Selinexor has now
received approval from the US Food and Drug
Administration (FDA) for the treatment of relapsed/
refractory MM and DLBCL.
Attempts to define biomarkers of response to
CRM1 inhibition with the goal of better selecting
those patients most likely to benefit from therapy
have proven challenging. In the STORM trial that
served as the basis for approval of selinexor in
MM, CRM1 mRNA levels isolated from CD138+
bone marrow cells and blood samples of patients
along with the levels of glucocorticoid receptor in
the nucleus were correlated with response to treat-
ment (Malandrakis et al., 2020). A preliminary
analysis also demonstrated a four-master-gene sig-
nature including IRF3, ARL2BP, ZBTB17, and ATRX
that was highly predictive of outcome (Vogl et al.,
2018; Chari et al., 2019). However, no other clear
molecular or genomic correlates of response have
yet been defined. Future studies will be necessary to

-- 129 of 258 --

more precisely characterize drivers of response and
resistance to CRM1 inhibition.
Studies of Verdinexor in Canine Cancer
SINEs have also been studied in canine tumor cells/
cell lines where single-agent activity has been dem-
onstrated. KPT-185 (one of most potent SINE
compounds limited by poor oral bioavailability)
and verdinexor (KPT-335) both reduced the viabil-
ity of the canine DLBCL cell lines (CLBL1) and
primary canine DLBCL samples at low nanomolar
concentrations of drug (London et al., 2014).
Furthermore, a preliminary analysis of three addi-
tional canine tumor cell lines (mast cell tumor,
osteosarcoma, melanoma) using an earlier SINE
(KPT-214) demonstrated inhibition of cell growth,
with IC50 values ranging from 70 to 450 nM.
Additional work was subsequently conducted
in vitro using four canine melanoma cell lines
(Breit et al., 2014). Verdinexor inhibited the prolif-
eration of all cell lines tested, with IC50 values rang-
ing from 71 to 330 nM. Verdinexor also inhibited
colony formation, promoted upregulation and
nuclear localization of p53 and p21, and induced
apoptosis in the melanoma lines at drug concentra-
tions in the nanomolar range. Last, while expres-
sion of CRM1 protein was reduced following
exposure to verdinexor, a compensatory upregula-
tion of CRM1 mRNA was noted.
An expanded investigation of verdinexor was
undertaken in several additional canine osteosar-
coma cell lines, where dose-dependent growth
inhibition and activation of caspases 3 and 7 were
noted at low nanomolar concentrations. The com-
bination of verdinexor with doxorubicin resulted
in synergistic growth inhibition and increased
γH2A.X foci (an indicator of DNA damage) when
compared to verdinexor or doxorubicin alone
(Breitbach et al., 2021). In another study, both ver-
dinexor and KPT-185 were tested in one canine
transitional cell carcinoma (TCC) and in two
canine mammary cell lines (Grayton et al., 2017).
Verdinexor inhibited the growth of all three lines
with an IC50 of approximately 1.5 μM, while KPT-
185 was less effective. As with the melanoma lines,
verdinexor enhanced expression of both p53 and
p21, and promoted nuclear localization of p53.
A Phase I clinical trial of verdinexor (KPT-335)
was performed in 17 dogs with lymphoma (naïve
or relapsed), mast cell tumor, and osteosarcoma
(London et al., 2014). The maximum tolerated
dose was 1.75 mg/kg given orally 2×/week,
although biologic activity was noted at doses as
low as 1 mg/kg. Clinical benefit including partial
response to therapy (PR, n = 2) and stable disease
(SD, n = 7) was documented primarily in dogs with
lymphoma for a duration of 35–256 days. In an
additional cohort of six dogs with lymphoma given
1.5 mg/kg verdinexor 3×/week, clinical benefit was
documented in four dogs for a duration of 35–354
days. Adverse events were primarily anorexia,
weight loss, vomiting, and diarrhea, and were
manageable with supportive care; dose modulation
and administration of low-dose prednisone to
stimulate appetite was often effective. The dose-
limiting toxicities were hepatotoxicity, anorexia,
and weight loss.
Following positive results in dogs with lym-
phoma from the Phase I trial, a Phase II study was
conducted to expand clinical experience and better
define the biologic activity of verdinexor in dogs
with this disease (Sadowski et al., 2018). Fifty-eight
dogs with previously untreated or progressive/
relapsed B-cell and T-cell lymphoma were enrolled
in this prospective study across ten different study
sites. Verdinexor was administered orally in one of
three dosing groups (1.5 mg/kg 3×/week, 1.25 mg/
kg 3×/week, and 1.25–1.5 mg/kg 2×/week). For all
dogs, the objective response rate (complete response
(CR)/partial response (PR)) was 37% (20/54) in the
evaluable patient population. Interestingly, dogs
with T-cell lymphoma had a higher objective
response rate (71%). While the median time to pro-
gression was relatively short (29 days, range: 7–244
days), 36% of dogs treated remained on study for
at least 2 months. Lastly, although case numbers are
small, it is interesting that the objective response
rate did not vary between previously untreated ver-
sus relapsed dogs with lymphoma, suggesting that
mechanisms driving typical resistance to chemo-
therapy do not induce cross-resistance to CRM1
inhibition. The most common adverse events across
all dose groups related to verdinexor treatment
included anorexia (45%), weight loss (31%), vomit-
ing (26%), lethargy (17%), and diarrhea (12%).
Most were grade 1 or 2 (95%) in nature and gener-
ally responsive to supportive care. These data sup-
ported FDA Minor Use Minor Species approval of
verdinexor for the treatment of canine naïve or
relapsed B- and T-cell lymphoma.
As noted above, anorexia was the most common
adverse event noted in both the Phase I and II stud-
ies in dogs with lymphoma. Many of the dogs in

both trials had substantial disease burden at the
time of treatment, making it challenging to distin-
guish between drug-induced versus disease-related
clinical signs. However, drugs such as leptomycin B
that target CRM1 have historically induced loss of
appetite in both mice and people. The mechanism
of this effect is not entirely clear, although in the
case of selinexor and verdinexor, their ability to
penetrate the blood–brain barrier indicates that
some of this effect may be centrally mediated
(Gandhi et al., 2018). In the canine studies, tradi-
tional anti-nausea/anti-vomiting agents such as
5HT3 and neurokinin 1 receptor antagonists
(ondansetron and maropitant, respectively) were
relatively ineffective at mitigating anorexia (London
et al., 2014; Sadowski et al., 2018). Recommen-
dations for preventing selinexor-induced gastroin-
testinal toxicity in humans include ondansetron
administration the day of and the day after
selinexor treatment in addition to neurokinin 1
receptor antagonists and cannabinoids if needed
(Malandrakis et al., 2020). Interestingly, in both
species, glucocorticoid administration appears to
be the most effective approach for improving appe-
tite (London et al., 2014; Gandhi et al., 2018;
Sadowski et al., 2018). Because the centrally acting
ghrelin agonist capromorelin was not available for
use during the prior canine studies, it will be inter-
esting to see if this drug class has efficacy in treat-
ing verdinexor-induced anorexia.
Conclusions and Future Considerations
A substantial body of data across in vitro studies,
mouse models, and canine as well as human cancer
patients supports CRM1 as a relevant target for
therapeutic intervention. In the setting of canine
cancer, additional studies will be necessary to help
define the molecular/genomic correlates of response
to treatment in T- and B-cell lymphomas. While
both MYC and BCL2 overexpression are com-
monly found in canine B-cell lymphomas, muta-
tions in CRM1 have not been identified (C.
London, 2022, unpublished results), suggesting
that the potential cooperation between MYC/BCL2
and E571K CRM1 thought to drive human lym-
phomagenesis may not be relevant for the canine
disease. Recent improvement in genomic tools such
as RNA sequencing/single-cell RNA sequencing
and the development of canine-specific reagents
such as the NanoString Canine Immuno-Oncology
panel, as well as availability of curated canine
tumor genomic data through the Integrated Canine
Data Commons, will facilitate future biomarker
interrogation. Lastly, as experience with CRM1
inhibitors broadens, it is attractive to consider the
distinct and potentially nonoverlapping adverse-
event profiles of these agents compared to conven-
tional treatment approaches to advance rational
combination approaches that enhance activity
without exacerbating toxicities for both hemato-
logic malignancies and solid tumors.
