Introduction: Promise and Challenges
of Cancer Immunotherapy
In 2018, the Nobel Prize in Physiology or Medicine
was jointly awarded to James Allison and Tsuku
Honjo for their respective work on the immune
checkpoint molecules CTLA-4 and PD-1 and the
recognition that their inhibition can generate
potent and durable antitumor immune responses.
Clinical development of monoclonal antibodies
targeting checkpoint molecules, including ipili-
mumab (anti-CTLA-4) and pembrolizumab (anti-
PD-1), rapidly followed their discoveries and these
therapies have revolutionized the treatment of both
solid and hematologic cancers, firmly cementing
immunotherapy as the fourth pillar of cancer ther-
apy in the human oncology arena. Nonetheless,
challenges remain, including improving and broad-
ening overall efficacy while at the same time avoid-
ing significant immune-mediated toxicities.
The immune system plays an essential role in
protecting the body from invading pathogens and
transformed cells. Both innate and adaptive arms
of the immune system partake in immune surveil-
lance, seeking out pathogens or abnormal cells and
specifically targeting them for destruction. Antigen-
specific activation and killing of virus-infected cells
or tumor cells is mediated primarily by appropri-
ately primed T cells that undergo clonal expansion
to generate and sustain antigen-specific responses
(Burnet, 1976). Tumor cell clearance is also depend-
ent in part on the participation of innate immune
cells, including natural killer (NK) cells and appro-
priately activated macrophages and dendritic cells
(DCs), that results in both antigen-specific and
nonspecific effects. Upon resolution of infection or
elimination of transformed cells the immune
response contracts, and memory B and T cells are
formed that are capable of responding more rap-
idly and with a heightened intensity upon future
exposure to the same target antigen (Janeway,
2001). These key properties of naturally occurring
tumor immunity, namely immune surveillance,
antigen-specific tumor elimination, and generation
of long-lasting immune memory, render the immune
system an ideal weapon in the oncologic armamen-
tarium. Strategies to induce effective antitumor
immunity must first overcome the basic principles
of immune tolerance in order to generate high-
affinity, antigen-specific T cells against what in many
cases are tumor-expressed self-antigens, including
differentiation and developmentally regulated anti-
gens that constitute, in part, overexpressed tumor-
associated antigens (TAAs). Indeed, many factors
that influence the generation of effective antitumor
immunity are now well known and can be manipu-
lated to drive antigen-specific immune responses
against transformed cells as part of a purposeful
anticancer therapeutic strategy.
The rapidly growing field of cancer immuno-
therapy and the availability of new tools such as
immune checkpoint molecule-blocking antibodies
and chimeric antigen receptor (CAR)-T cell thera-
pies have already revolutionized the treatment of
cancer in humans (Maude et al., 2014; Hamid
et al., 2019; Gellrich et al., 2020). However, major
immunologic and physical barriers to effective can-
cer immunotherapy remain and will need to be
addressed before immunotherapy can fulfill its full
curative potential. Ironically, many of these barriers
arise from the complex interaction between the
patient’s immune system and the tumor itself (Fig. 8).
For example, immune targeting of tumor antigens

leads to antigen downmodulation, editing, and/or
complete loss, resulting in tumor “immune escape”
(Sotillo et al., 2015; O’Rourke et al., 2019). In
another example, coercion of the immune response
by the tumor leads to the development of immune
suppressive networks and upregulation of check-
point molecules that together create a hostile tumor
microenvironment (TME) for effective antitumor
immunity (Binnewies et al., 2018). Furthermore,
intrinsic T-cell defects and acquired T-cell exhaus-
tion can significantly impair effective antitumor
responses against a number of different cancers
(Ahmadzadeh et al., 2009; Baitsch et al., 2011;
Tagawa et al., 2016).
Currently there is intense focus on the immune-
suppressive TME and strategies that modify this
environment, including immune checkpoint-targeted
agents and depletion or modification of immune-
suppressive myeloid cell populations in the TME
(Cascini and Chiodoni, 2021; Mazzaschi et al.,
2021; Roulleaux Dugage et al., 2021). In addition,
certain types of radiation therapy (RT) and selected
chemotherapy drugs that induce immunogenic cell
death (ICD) are being actively explored in combi-
nation with immunotherapeutic approaches to
augment antitumor immunity (reviewed in Wang
et al., 2018; Opzoomer et al., 2019). The use of RT
and chemotherapy as immune modulators to
enhance antitumor immunity represents a signifi-
cant departure from the previously held views that
proposed that chemotherapy and RT are always
immune suppressive and detrimental for concur-
rent immunotherapies. The challenge going for-
ward will be to discover the optimal dose, timing,
and sequence of combination therapies to maxi-
mize antitumor immunity.
The Emerging Field of Immuno-oncology
and Implications for Veterinary Oncology
This chapter is intended to provide a foundational
understanding of cancer immunology and the
mechanistic underpinnings of emerging immuno-
therapeutic strategies. More practically, the review
presented in this chapter will provide the oncology
clinician with a better understanding of currently
available or soon-to-be-licensed immunotherapy
options, and guidance on incorporating these
immunotherapeutics into daily practice. The first
approved veterinary cancer biologic was the DNA
vaccine for the treatment and prevention of mela-
noma in dogs, approved by the US Department of
Agriculture (USDA) in 2009. The vaccine (Oncept)
was labeled for use in dogs with stage II or stage III
oral melanoma following local disease control with
surgical excision. Since then, additional cancer vac-
cines, monoclonal antibodies, biologic response
modifiers, and cell-based immunotherapies have
been introduced for veterinary oncology. Thus, the
advent of immunotherapy to treat cancer in com-
panion animals is upon us and encouraging results
from several pilot studies are stimulating veterinary
pharmaceutical development, paving the way for
immunotherapy to become the fourth principal
modality of veterinary cancer therapy. As the next
generation of immunotherapeutics is developed
and launched, it will increasingly fall to veterinary
oncologists to understand mechanisms of action
and to make informed decisions regarding rational
combination therapies, using the foundational
knowledge provided here and elsewhere. The ulti-
mate payoff from immunotherapy will be realized
once this new modality is fully incorporated into
comprehensive cancer treatment programs and
protocols.
Tumor Immunogenicity: Neoantigens
and Tumor Mutational Burden
Genomic instability, deficiencies in DNA mismatch
repair, and failure of apoptosis are characteristics
of many cancers and all lead to an accumulation of
both synonymous and nonsynonymous mutations
within the tumor cell population. Nonsynonymous
mutations can result in the formation of novel
(neoantigenic) peptides not previously seen by the
host immune system, which can then serve as effec-
tive targets for recognition by effector CD4 and
CD8 T cells (Davies et al., 2002; Campbell et al.,
2004; Mochizuki et al., 2015; Schumacher and
Schreiber, 2015). Tumor mutational burden (TMB)
describes the total number of somatic coding muta-
tions present within a tumor and varies signifi-
cantly between different cancer types (ranging from
0.001 to as high as 400 mutations per megabase)
and even within the same tumor type (Alexandrov
et al., 2013; Chalmers et al., 2017). In humans,
tumors such as non-small-cell lung cancer and
melanoma that result from exposure to environ-
mental factors such as smoke and ultraviolet light
tend to exhibit higher TMB and are more respon-
sive to treatment with immune checkpoint inhibi-
tion (ICI) (Alexandrov et al., 2013; Yarchoan et al.,
2017; Samstein et al., 2019). Generally, a positive
122 	N. Mason and S. Dow

-- 138 of 258 --

123	Cancer Immunotherapy
correlation has been observed between TMB and
cytotoxic CD8 T-cell infiltrates in different tumor
types in humans, and in some cancer types these
CD8 T-cell infiltrates are associated with improved
overall survival (Rooney et al., 2015).
Microsatellite instability (MSI) in tumor cells
results in defective mismatch repair and is associ-
ated with high TMB and neoantigen load. MSI-
high tumors have been shown to respond favorably
to ICI because of the large preexisting T-cell response
(Zhao et al., 2019; Marabelle et al., 2020). In
human patients, TMB has been used independently
of MSI status or PD-L1 expression status as a bio-
marker for predicting response to ICI in melanoma,
urothelial carcinoma, and deficient mismatch
repair (dMMR) colorectal cancers (Samstein et al.,
2019). However, it should be noted that TMB
alone is not considered a universally robust, vali-
dated predictor of response to ICI and its relevance
as a correlative biomarker in veterinary species
remains to be determined (see below).
The gold standard for measuring TMB remains
whole-exome sequencing (WES); however, in the
human field, TMB is now more routinely estimated
using targeted sequencing panels that evaluate sev-
eral hundred target genes (Fancello et al., 2019).
These panels are more cost-effective and less labor-
intensive to run and analyze than WES, report
TMB as mutations per megabase, and have been
shown to correlate with WES when a 1.5 to 3
megabase targeted genome is covered (Garofalo
et al., 2016; Fancello et al., 2019). TMB and onco-
genic drivers have been evaluated by WES, whole-
genome sequencing (WGS), and targeted sequencing
panels in canine hemangiosarcoma (HSA), mam-
mary carcinoma, osteosarcoma (OSA), glioma, and
lymphoma (Liu et al., 2014; Wang et al., 2017;
Gardner et al., 2019; Alsaihati et al., 2021). These
studies have generally found comparable TMB
between tumors in dogs and humans. For example,
HSA in dogs was found to have a low TMB, com-
parable to human sarcomas and ovarian carcinoma
(Megquier et al., 2019; Wang et al., 2020). The
TMB in canine OSA was 1.98 mutations per
megabase, similar to the TMB in pediatric OSA
(Gardner et al., 2019), and was shown to positively
correlate with increasing age but not with breed,
sex, or tumor location in the dog (Sakthikumar
et al., 2018). Comparably low mutational loads
were identified in both canine and pediatric glio-
mas (Amin et al., 2020). Studies that investigate
correlations between TMB, CD8 T-cell infiltrates,
and survival are needed in canine cancers and
might reveal a role for TMB assessment (and in
future, neoantigen prediction algorithms) in prog-
nostication and stratification for immunotherapy
studies (Igase et al., 2020). With the ongoing devel-
opment of advanced immune monitoring tools
such as gene expression profiling (GEP) via RNA
sequencing or NanoString technology, and canine-
specific antibodies to quantify immune cell infil-
trates and checkpoint molecule expression, we can
expect that canine oncology trials in the future will
routinely assess TMB and immune cell infiltrates as
potential biomarkers of therapeutic response and
prognosis.
Mechanisms of Tumor Immune Evasion
and Resistance to Immunotherapy
Neoplastic cells subjected to immune pressure will
respond with multiple different cellular adapta-
tions to avoid immune elimination. These adaptive
immune evasion responses therefore present an
inherent challenge to immunotherapy and must be
factored into optimal treatment protocols. To help
circumvent these barriers in the future we can
expect 	to 	see 	combined 	immunotherapeutic
approaches being employed routinely. The major
mechanisms responsible for cancer immune eva-
sion are discussed below.
Failure of tumor antigen presentation
T cells recognize their cognate antigens as peptides
presented on either major histocompatibility com-
plex (MHC) class I molecules (for CD8 T-cell rec-
ognition) or MHC class II molecules (for CD4
T-cell recognition) (MHCI and MHCII respec-
tively). Mutations in the antigen processing and
presentation machinery of neoplastic cells can lead
to reduced surface expression of peptide–MHC
complexes and an inability of effector T cells to
engage and eliminate the target cell (Cai et al.,
2018; Bandola-Simon and Roche, 2019). Indeed,
mutations in the MHCI molecule and downregula-
tion of transporter proteins associated with antigen
processing have been reported in many different
spontaneous tumors in humans and in mouse mod-
els (Seliger and Ferrone, 2020). Loss of MHCII
expression has also been reported in malignant B
cells (Rimsza et al., 2004), along with downregula-
tion of pathways necessary for MHCII antigen
processing and presentation (Rimsza et al., 2004),

-- 139 of 258 --

and decreased MHCII expression has been shown
to correlate with poor outcome in dogs with B-cell
lymphoma (BCL) (Rao et al., 2011).
Loss of dominant tumor antigens
Strong T-cell responses against dominant tumor
antigens often lead to outright elimination of
nearly all tumor cells, only to be replaced by anti-
gen loss variants of tumor cells lacking expression
of the original target antigen, in a process referred
to as “immune editing”. Immune editing can also
lead to the downregulation of target antigen
expression, without complete genetic loss of the
antigen. The end result of both processes is the
emergence of immune-edited tumor clones that are
essentially invisible to the T-cell arm of the immune
system. This phenomenon explains the apparent
paradox of nonimmunogenic tumors arising in the
setting of strong immune competence (Shankaran
et al., 2001). This phenomenon has perhaps been
most clearly documented in human patients with
B-cell malignancies receiving CAR-T cells targeting
CD19, wherein following initial clinical responses,
patients relapse with tumors that lack the CD19
molecule (Maude et al., 2014). The same antigen-
escape phenomenon has been reported in a canine
patient with stage Va B-cell non-Hodgkin lym-
phoma (B-NHL) treated with CD20-targeting
CAR-T cells (Panjwani et al., 2020). Sequencing of
CD20 in the CD20– population of neoplastic B
cells in this patient revealed the presence of a splice
variant lacking exons 4 and 5 that encode the sec-
ond extracellular loop of CD20 that contains the
original CAR-T cell target epitope. The phenome-
non of immune editing supports the use of strate-
gies that generate antitumor responses against
more than one epitope, such as bi-specific CAR-T
cells or multi-epitope vaccines.
Immune Suppression Within the Tumor
Microenvironment
Increasingly, the TME and its cellular and extracel-
lular matrix components is viewed as an essential
regulator of overall tumor immunogenicity and
responses to immunotherapy. The tumor stroma
comprises host cellular components (both immune
and nonimmune cells such as fibroblasts and
endothelial cells) as well as connective tissues and
extracellular matrix proteins. All of these components
together contribute to an immune environment in
solid tumors that significantly impairs both adap-
tive and innate immune responses.
Immune cells that regulate the immune-
suppressive tumor microenvironment
The TME contains an abundant population of
immune cells (macrophages, myeloid-derived sup-
pressor cells (MDSCs), neutrophils, T cells, DCs,
NK cells) as well as nonimmune cells (endothelial
cells and fibroblasts), all of which contribute to an
environment that is often extremely inhibitory to
immune responses (Biswas et al., 2013). For most
tumors, tumor-associated macrophages (TAMs)
constitute the most abundant host immune cell
population, comprising more than 50% of all cells
in some tumors. The density of TAMs generally
positively correlates with poor prognosis (Malfitano
et al., 2020; Carvalho et al., 2021), although there
are occasional exceptions to this rule, as reported
for example in primary OSA in dogs (Withers et al.,
2019). In general, TAM populations in tumors are
classified functionally as anti-inflammatory mac-
rophages, otherwise referred to as M2 macrophages
(Parisi et al., 2021). However, it is also recognized
that macrophage polarization is a dynamic state,
and that the functional phenotype of macrophages
within the TME can be readily shifted by cytokines
and therapeutic innate immune stimuli such as
muramyl tripeptide (Kurzman et al., 1995). TAMs
suppress tumor immunity via multiple, distinct
mechanisms including the secretion of immune-
suppressive cytokines (e.g., transforming growth
factor-β (TGF-β); interleukins (ILs) including IL-10
and IL-4; and vascular endothelial growth factor
(VEGF)). The TAMs can also suppress the TME
immune environment by production of metaboli-
cally active enzymes that deplete necessary sub-
strates for T cells, including overproduction of the
enzyme arginase, which depletes the necessary
amino acid l-arginine, and the enzyme indoleamine
2,3-deaminase (IDO), which depletes the essential
amino acid tryptophan that T cells require for
effector functions and survival (Goulart et al.,
2012; Gabrilovich, 2017). Tumor macrophages
also produce VEGF, which not only drives tumor
angiogenesis, but is directly immunosuppressive
through its ability to inhibit DC maturation and
contribute to cytotoxic T-cell exhaustion (Lee et al.,
2020). In addition, macrophages secrete highly
active oxidant molecules (reactive oxygen and
nitrogen intermediates) that interfere with T-cell
124 	N. Mason and S. Dow

-- 140 of 258 --

125	Cancer Immunotherapy
function and promote tumor genetic instability
(Goulart et al., 2012). Not surprisingly, TAMs are
a target for multiple different immune-modulatory
approaches, including use of depleting agents (e.g.,
liposome-encapsulated bisphosphonates), repro-
gramming by activating TAM from an M2 to an
M1 profile (e.g., administration of Toll-like recep-
tor (TLR) or Nod-like receptor (NLR) ligands such
as CpG oligonucleotides (TLR9 agonist) or mura-
myl tripeptide (NLR2 agonist)), use of enzyme
inhibitors (e.g., IDO inhibitors), and use of sus-
tained inflammatory monocyte migration inhibi-
tion (e.g., CCR2 antagonists) (Kurzman et al.,
1999; Guth et al., 2013; Ammons et al., 2022;
Regan et al., 2022).
Within the TME and lymphoid tissues, a second
major myeloid cell population consists of MDSCs,
which comprise a dual population of monocytic-
MDSCs and PMN (neutrophilic)-MDSCs that each
contribute to both local and systemic immune sup-
pression (Goulart et al., 2012, 2019; Gabrilovich,
2017; Mazzaschi et al., 2021; Roulleaux Dugage
et al., 2021). MDSC numbers are greatly expanded
in tumor and lymphoid tissues and in circulation in
cancer patients, and increased numbers are gener-
ally associated with poorer prognosis (Diaz-
Montero et al., 2014; Goulart et al., 2019).
Generation of MDSCs and their release from the
bone marrow is regulated by cytokines associated
with chronic inflammation (e.g., granulocyte-mac-
rophage colony-stimulating factor (GM-CSF), IL-3,
IL-6), and they are present in other chronic inflam-
matory conditions as well as cancer (Gabrilovich,
2017). Their release in response to adrenergic stress
has also been described recently. Several studies
have reported the phenotypic and function proper-
ties of MDSCs in dogs with cancer (Sherger et al.,
2012; Goulart et al., 2019). While there is general
overlap between the immune-suppressive mecha-
nisms utilized by MDSCs and tumor macrophages,
MDSCs are particularly important sources of reac-
tive nitrogen and oxygen species production, with
neutrophilic MDSCs producing more reactive
nitrogen species versus monocytic MDSCs, which
produce reactive oxygen intermediates. In dogs
with cancer, PMN-MDSCs have been described as
the most abundant population of circulating
MDSCs, and they suppress immune responses in
part by producing reactive nitrogen intermediates
(Goulart et al., 2012, 2019). MDSCs can be tar-
geted therapeutically by nonselective tyrosine kinase
inhibitors (e.g., sunitinib and toceranib) and by
β-adrenergic receptor blockers (e.g., propranolol)
(Qiao et al., 2018; Chen et al., 2020; Duckett et al.,
2020). These drugs act in part by blocking MDSC
mobilization from the bone marrow (e.g., pro-
pranolol) and by reprogramming their immune-
suppressive properties (e.g., sunitinib and toceranib)
(Ozao-Choy et al., 2009; Mohammadpour et al.,
2019).
Tumor-associated DCs play a key role in sup-
pressing the generation of effector T cells and pro-
moting the development of dysfunctional T cells,
referred to variously as “exhausted”, “anergic”, or
“tolerogenic” T cells. Tumor-associated DCs are
generated within the TME in response to immune-
suppressive factors produced locally. The DC
immune-suppressive phenotype is manifested by
upregulation of immune inhibitory checkpoint
molecules (e.g., PD-L1, TIM-3, LAG-3) and down-
regulation of co-stimulatory molecules such as
CD86 and MHCII. Tumor DCs also secrete
immune-suppressive cytokines and molecules such
as IDO and galectins. In some cases, it is possible to
reprogram these DCs through strategies such as
immune-suppressive cytokine neutralization, meta-
bolic inhibitors, and activation by TLR ligands or
immune-activating cytokines.
Neutrophils are the fourth major immune-
suppressive myeloid cell population found in tumors
and draining lymph nodes that contribute to the
immune-suppressive TME. Immune-suppressive
neutrophils promote tumor growth through multi-
ple mechanisms, including platelet activation and
thrombosis, stimulation of angiogenesis, and sup-
pression of T-cell responses by secretion of IL-23
and production of arginase (Singel and Segal, 2016;
Carnevale et al., 2020). In dogs with cancer, includ-
ing lymphoma and OSA, the numbers of circulating
neutrophils are positively correlated with shorter
survival times (Sottnik et al., 2010; Perry et al.,
2011; Mutz et al., 2015). Neutrophils can be tar-
geted therapeutically by blocking migration with
CXCR1 and CXCR2 antagonists, with metabolic
reprogramming agents (e.g., STAT3 inhibition with
toceranib), and by arginase inhibitors.
Nonimmune-cell regulation of the tumor
microenvironment
Cancer-associated fibroblasts (CAFs) are generated
by exposure to immune-suppressive factors in the
TME and serve as important drivers of the epithelial
to mesenchymal transition typical of immunologically

-- 141 of 258 --

“cold” tumors such as glioma and OSA (De et al.,
2021; Peng et al., 2021). This transition is mediated
in part by secretion of cytokines such as IL-6.
Therapeutically, fibroblasts have been challenging
to target directly with immunotherapy, although
disrupting the immune-suppressive TME by manip-
ulating other cell populations can relieve or reverse
the immune-suppressive effects of CAFs (Peng
et al., 2021). Interestingly, CAR-T cells directed
against the membrane protease fibroblast activa-
tion protein (FAP), that is expressed by cancer
associated stromal cells including CAFs, have been
shown to disrupt tumor stroma and are now being
employed in combination strategies to improve
penetration of tumor-specific CAR-T cells (Lo
et al., 2015).
The extracellular matrix deposited within the
TME can also suppress tumor immunity in several
ways. First, the dense collagen and extracellular
matrix serve as a physical barrier to the entry of
effector T cells and NK cells. Disruption of this
matrix pharmacologically has been shown to pro-
mote T-cell entry and enhance overall tumor immu-
nity (Martín-Otal et al., 2022). The extracellular
matrix can also serve as a depot for binding and
sustained release of cytokines that may be immune
suppressive, such as VEGF and IL-4 (Marigo et al.,
2008; Zhang et al., 2021). Finally, the extracellular
matrix can also regulate cytokine signaling and
communication between effector T cells and APCs
in the TME, ultimately disrupting generation of
effector T-cell responses (Pickup et al., 2014).
The role of checkpoint molecules in
suppression of antitumor immunity
Molecules secreted or expressed by tumor cells
themselves also contribute significantly to the
immunologically cold landscape of the TME,
including especially sarcomas. A great deal of
attention in recent years has focused on expression
of immune-suppressive checkpoint molecules such
as PD-L1 expressed by tumor cells, TAMs, and
other tumor-infiltrating immune cells (TIICs).
Expression of PD-L1 is important because it is the
primary ligand for PD-1 expressed on T cells, and
their interaction is a major driver of T-cell suppres-
sion in cancer. Indeed, one of the principal predic-
tive 	factors 	governing 	clinical 	responses 	to
checkpoint inhibition is the overall level of PD-L1
expression particularly on TIICs and TAMs (Herbst
et al., 2014). The PD-1 (programmed cell death
protein 1) and PD-L1 (programmed death ligand
1), axis is a key component of what is referred to
as the “adaptive tumor immune evasion process”,
since cytokines (especially interferon-γ (IFN-γ) and
tumor necrosis factor-α (TNF-α)) secreted by effec-
tor T cells infiltrating the TME lead to strong
upregulation of PD-L1 expression, which in turn
potently suppresses T-cell function by binding to
T-cell expressed PD-1 (Hartley et al., 2017). The
end result of this counter-regulatory process is the
generation of exhausted T cells. “Exhausted T cells”
refers to T cells that exist in a state of unresponsive-
ness to activation by antigen-presenting cells
(APCs) or tumor cells. The exhausted T-cell state
develops following prolonged exposure to the
immune-suppressive 	TME. 	Characteristics 	of
exhausted T cells include upregulated expression of
immune-suppressive checkpoint molecules (e.g.,
PD-1, TIGIT, TIM-3), lack of effector cytokine pro-
duction (e.g., decreased or absent production of
IFN-γ, IL-2, TNF-α), mitochondrial dysfunction,
and acquisition of both reversible and irreversible
epigenetic changes (Wherry and Kurachi, 2015).
Therapeutic strategies for reversing T-cell exhaus-
tion include directly targeted strategies such as
antibodies to block checkpoint molecule signaling
as well as indirect approaches including the TME
immune modification approaches discussed here.
Myeloid cells within the TME express multiple
additional immune co-inhibitory checkpoint mole-
cules capable of suppressing both APCs as well as
effector T cells and NK cells, including lymphocyte-
activation gene 3 (LAG-3), T-cell immunoglobulin
and mucin domain 3 (TIM-3), T-cell immunorecep-
tor with Ig and ITIM domains (TIGIT), V-domain
Ig suppressor of T-cell activation (VISTA), and B7
homolog 3 protein (B7-H3). All of these molecules
are potential targets for blockade with therapeutic
monoclonal antibodies, and numerous trials in
humans are underway to elucidate the effectiveness
of blocking each pathway. The metabolic environ-
ment typical of tumors is also very inhibitory to
normal functioning of effector T cells and NK cells.
For example, high levels of lactate within the TME
can suppress normal T-cell function by altering
glucose metabolism (Brand et al., 2016). In addi-
tion, local tumor hypoxia also suppresses T-cell and
DC proliferation and function and leads to a state
of local immune paralysis and T-cell exhaustion.
Thus, we can appreciate that a complex mix of
cellular, physical, and biochemical features within
the TME contributes to overall tumor immune
126 	N. Mason and S. Dow

127	Cancer Immunotherapy
suppression. The sheer complexity of processes
involved, many of which elicit overlapping effects,
illustrates the challenges faced in selecting targets
to attack to significantly modify the immune-
suppressive TME. However, focusing on certain
fundamental immune regulatory processes, such as
expression of co-inhibitory checkpoint molecules,
or on key populations of immune regulatory cells
such as TAMs, can provide a framework upon
which to build effective combinatorial cancer
immunotherapy protocols. The challenge facing the
field today is identification of readily implemented
approaches that are not only additive in their effec-
tiveness, but ideally also synergistic, as well as fully
compatible with the concurrent delivery of conven-
tional cytotoxic and targeted cancer agents and RT.
Generating Effective Cancer Immunity:
The Cancer–Immunity Cycle
The overall goal of cancer immunotherapy is to initi-
ate, enhance, and broaden a self-propagating cycle
of largely T-cell-mediated responses that eliminate
tumor cells and sustain tumor-specific memory
responses to prevent tumor recurrence. Chen and
Mellman elegantly described the key steps involved
in this process, which they termed the “cancer–
immunity cycle” (Chen and Mellman, 2013). Most
effective cancer immunotherapy approaches to date
act at one or more aspects or stages of the cycle. Key
initial stages in the cycle include tumor antigen
release, antigen uptake and processing by APCs,
antigen presentation to effector T cells, and T-cell
and NK-cell activation. However, simply generating
large numbers of tumor-specific T cells is not suffi-
cient to produce effective and sustained antitumor
immunity. Appropriately primed, tumor-specific T
cells need to traffic to the tumor, extravasate, and
function within a hostile, immune-suppressive
microenvironment. Furthermore, generation of a
pool of self-renewing, tumor-specific memory T cells
is necessary to protect against molecular and clinical
relapse. However, the immunologic rules that govern
generation of effective T-cell immunity to cancer, and
why only a subset of patients respond to immune
checkpoint inhibitors, remain largely undefined.
Generating tumor-specifc
cytotoxic effector cells
Two principal approaches are currently employed
to generate effector T-cell immunity: (i) active
immunization (i.e., cancer vaccines); and (ii) adop-
tive transfer of ex vivo expanded cytotoxic cells.
Active immunization
Active immunization involves the administration of
TAAs together with an immune adjuvant or appro-
priate delivery system, to prime antigen-specific
T cells and induce generation of long-term memory
T cells. A number of different vaccine approaches,
including the use of antigens comprising intact
tumor cells, tumor cell lysates, or tumor recombi-
nant proteins, administered together with a variety
of different vaccine adjuvants, have been evaluated
in dogs with cancer. Many of these small-scale
studies have reported some success but to date, no
large-scale, randomized trials have been reported to
conclusively demonstrate the effectiveness of can-
cer vaccines alone in inducing antitumor immunity
and mediating durable therapeutic responses. It is
also important to note that no effective conven-
tional cancer vaccines have been identified with
consistent antitumor activity in humans, despite
decades of effort. Attention in the human field has
therefore shifted to focus on combining tumor vac-
cines with synergistic approaches including radia-
tion, immune checkpoint molecule blockade, and/
or TME modification strategies.
One of the greatest challenges in developing
effective cancer vaccines in veterinary medicine has
been identifying TAAs that can serve as safe and
effective targets for vaccination. That problem has
been partially solved in the human arena by devel-
opment of bioinformatic tools that allow rapid
identification of true cancer neoantigens that are
unique to individual patient tumors and can pro-
vide attractive targets for vaccination. However, in
the veterinary field we currently lack the necessary
tools to identify cancer neoantigen peptides or to
predict their ability to bind to canine MHCI mole-
cules. Thus, cancer vaccine efforts for dogs still
largely focus on the use of TAAs previously identi-
fied in human oncology. Among the TAAs evalu-
ated in trials in dogs as cancer vaccine candidates
include: (i) developmentally expressed cancer testis
(CT) antigens such as melanoma antigen gene
(MAGE) and New York esophageal squamous cell
carcinoma 1 (NY-ESO-1); (ii) tissue differentiation
antigens such as CD20 (B cells), tyrosinase and
GD1 and GD2 (melanoma), and prostate-specific
antigen (PSA) (prostatic epithelial cells); and (iii)
overexpressed normal tissue antigens such as

-- 143 of 258 --

human epidermal growth factor receptor 2 (HER2)/
neu, Survivin, human telomerase reverse tran-
scriptase (hTERT), and p53, where differential
overexpression by tumor tissues is sufficient to
break immune tolerance and induce targeted elimi-
nation of tumor cells, while sparing normal cells
with reduced or restricted expression of these same
antigens.
TUMOR CELL AND CELL LYSATE VACCINES 	The most
commonly evaluated cancer vaccines consist of
either whole inactivated tumor cells, or lysates pre-
pared from these cells. Tumor cell sources include
autologous tumor cells or allogenic tumor cell
lines. This approach is appealing because it does
not require knowledge of the tumor antigens, has
the potential to generate immunity against a broad
array of antigens rather than single antigens, and it
is comparatively easy to implement. A number of
studies have reported results from tumor cell vac-
cine studies, and there are ongoing trials of several
different tumor cell vaccines in veterinary medicine
(Finocchiaro et al., 2019; Thalmensi et al., 2019;
Flesner et al., 2020; Goodrich et al., 2020; Lucroy
et al., 2020; Xiong et al., 2020; Klingemann, 2021;
Musser et al., 2021). Previously reported small
pilot studies have documented improvement in
survival and in some cases tumor regression fol-
lowing administration of cell lysate vaccines (e.g.,
melanoma, HSA vaccines) (Alexander et al., 2006;
U’Ren et al., 2007; Lucroy et al., 2020). However,
tumor cell vaccines alone have not been particu-
larly successful, in either veterinary or human tri-
als, despite promising results from rodent studies.
While it may be possible to demonstrate induction
of tumor-specific T cells and antibodies follow-
ing vaccination, clinical responses are uncommon
and rarely complete or durable. Reasons for the
lack of efficacy include immune blockade from
co-inhibitory checkpoint molecules such as PD-L1,
tumor-specific T-cell exhaustion, and the inhibitory
effects of the highly immune-suppressive TME,
which can completely inhibit effector T-cell func-
tion. Thus, the tumor cell or tumor cell lysate vac-
cine approach will likely need to be combined with
other immune-modulatory therapies, including
checkpoint molecule blockade and TME-modifying
immunotherapy, to improve efficacy (Olin et al.,
2019).
AUTOLOGOUS ANTIGEN - PRESENTING CELL VACCINES
To improve the effectiveness of tumor vaccines,
autologous DCs or B cells loaded ex vivo with
an antigenic payload have been used as natural
delivery platforms. DCs are highly effective at
generating both CD4 and CD8 T-cell responses
and have been widely employed in human can-
cer vaccine trials. Tissue culture-derived DCs are
generated by culture of blood monocytes in high
concentrations of GM-CSF, along with various
other cytokines and activating stimuli, to upregu-
late co-stimulatory molecules, avoid the induction
of anergy, and promote an effective cell-mediated
immune response. Two different cell-based pro-
fessional APC vaccination strategies, using either
autologous DCs or CD40-activated autologous
B cells, have been evaluated in small numbers of
canine cancer patients, which provides important
proof-of-concept information.
In pilot canine studies, autologous DCs either
pulsed with tumor lysates or fused to allogeneic or
autologous tumor cells were employed to effi-
ciently deliver TAAs. In these studies, DC vaccina-
tion was found to be safe and antigen-specific
cell-based responses were elicited in some dogs
(Gyorffy et al., 2005; Bird et al., 2008; Tamura
et al., 2008; Konduri et al., 2019). Tumor regres-
sions were identified in dogs with transmissible
venereal tumors (TVTs) (Pai et al., 2011) and pro-
longed survival was reported in a subset of patients
with mammary tumors (Mito et al., 2010), HSA,
and melanoma.
Despite the promise of DC vaccines, their use
clinically 	has 	proven 	technically 	challenging.
Generating autologous DCs in vitro is labor-inten-
sive and expensive. Large volume leukapheresis is
often required to procure sufficient numbers of
monocytes to generate enough differentiated DCs
for vaccine generation. As an alternative to DCs, B
cells are also professional APCs and can be readily
expanded in vitro in the presence of CD40 cross-
linking antibodies and IL-4 (Sorenmo et al., 2011).
Like DCs, CD40-activated B cells can be loaded
with tumor lysate or RNA (the antigenic payload)
and used to trigger polyvalent T-lymphocyte
responses against multiple TAAs in vitro (Mason
et al., 2008; Sorenmo et al., 2011). The use of RNA
to produce tumor antigens avoids the need to purify
protein antigens and allows a multiple-antigen-
targeting approach with autologous B cells or DCs.
A small, prospective clinical trial using autolo-
gous CD40+ B cells electroporated with autologous
tumor RNA following successful induction chemo-
therapy was conducted in dogs with BCL (Sorenmo

et al., 2011). Results of that study demonstrated
the feasibility of the approach and the ability to
induce antitumor cell-based responses. However,
clinical outcomes were not altered as the disease-
free interval was not increased compared to histori-

vaccinated patients led to a statistically significant
improvement in overall survival, underscoring a
recurring yet poorly understood concept that res-

immune modulation in both human and canine
patients (Sorenmo et al., 2011).
CANINE CANCER VACCINES DELIVERED USING PLASMID DNA
VECTORS 	The first DNA vaccine to be licensed
for use in dogs with malignant melanoma encodes
human tyrosinase and is delivered using a plas-
mid DNA vector by intramuscular electropora-
tion (Bergman et al., 2006; Wolchok et al., 2007).
Although similar to canine tyrosinase, the encoded
human tyrosinase protein is sufficiently different
that it is immunologically perceived as an “altered
self-antigen” and can generate cross-reactive immu-
nity to native canine tyrosinase. Rodent studies
have shown that such a strategy can generate effec-
tive cross-reactive immune responses against mela-
noma (Naftzger et al., 1996; Weber et al., 1998;
Bowne et al., 1999).
These findings were translated into a Phase I
clinical trial involving nine dogs with melanoma,
which showed that repeated vaccine administration
was safe and was associated with prolonged overall
survival with documented regression of metastatic
disease in one dog (Bergman et al., 2003). Follow-up
studies confirmed the induction of anti-tyrosinase
antibodies in dogs with melanoma, as well as
T-cell-mediated 	IFN-γ 	responses 	in 	research
Beagles, following vaccination (Liao et al., 2006;
Goubier et al., 2008). A multi-institutional trial to
evaluate the safety and efficacy of this approach in
58 dogs with locally controlled, stage II/III oral
melanoma demonstrated a statistically significant
increase in survival for vaccinated dogs over his-
torical outcomes. These results led to the USDA
licensure of the vaccine (Oncept) as an adjunctive
treatment for stage II/III oral melanoma in dogs
(Anonymous, 2010; Grosenbaugh et al., 2011).
However, subsequent studies have not replicated
the original study findings. For example, a smaller
retrospective study failed to find evidence of clini-
cal efficacy in 15 dogs treated with Oncept (Ottnod
et al., 2013). Stage, completeness of margins, and
delay in administration of vaccine after surgery
were shown not to statistically influence overall or
progression-free survival in 32 dogs evaluated ret-
rospectively (Treggiari et al., 2016). Another larger
retrospective case series of 151 dogs with oral
malignant melanoma (OMM) suggested there was
no survival benefit to receiving adjuvant therapies,
including Oncept (n = 14) postoperatively (Boston
et al., 2014). Many factors may have contributed to
these discrepancies, including cohort size, retro-
spective study design, use of concurrent medica-
tions, and the presence or absence of local tumor
control. What can be concluded is that a subset of
dogs likely experiences benefits from Oncept, and
that like all forms of immunotherapy, better predic-
tors of response are needed to identify patients
most likely to realize this benefit. In the future,
combination of Oncept vaccination with check-
point inhibitors and/or TME modifiers is likely to
increase the overall success of this and other cancer
vaccines.
Additional cancer vaccines have been developed
for veterinary use. Using the same plasmid DNA
vaccine as Oncept, an orthologous murine CD20
DNA vaccine has been developed for dogs with
BCL and this received USDA conditional licensure
in 2015. The vaccine was evaluated in a prospec-
tive, multi-institutional clinical trial where it was
administered as a series of four doses in the setting
of minimal residual disease following CHOP
(cyclophosphamide, doxorubicin (hydroxydauno-
mycin), vincristine (Oncovin), prednisolone)-based
chemotherapy; however, the results of that study
have not been published. Intramuscular adminis-
tration of a DNA plasmid vaccine encoding human
p62, a protein involved in selective autophagy in
cancer cells, was shown to increase T-cell infiltrates,
induce a desmoplastic reaction, and reduce tumor
size in a small pilot study in dogs with mammary
carcinoma (Gabai et al., 2014).
Vaccines targeting telomerase have also been
shown to elicit humoral and cellular immune
responses in dogs with lymphoma and to signifi-
cantly prolong time to progression and survival
(Thalmensi et al., 2019). Other orthologous DNA
vaccines evaluated in tumor-bearing dogs include
the chondroitin sulfate proteoglycan-4 (CSPG4)
vaccine for dogs with OMM (Riccardo et al., 2014;
Piras et al., 2017) and heat shock protein 70
(HSP70) vaccines for dogs with TVT (Yu et al.,
2011). A similar electrovaccination approach has
been evaluated in a small number of healthy cats

-- 145 of 258 --

using either a HER2 gene derived from black bears,
a chimeric human–rat HER2 gene, or a point-
mutated feline HER2 gene (Perry et al., 2011). In
these studies, four of ten immunized cats mani-
fested T-cell responses against wild-type feline
HER2 (Gibson et al., 2015). It is important to note
that responses of vaccinated cats against the xeno-
geneic target (i.e., black bear HER2) were more
robust and consistent than those against the native
feline HER2 gene.
ADENO-ASSOCIATED VIRUS-VECTORED VACCINES TAR-
GETING TELOMERASE REVERSE TRANSCRIPTASE 	Active
telomerases are necessary to maintain the unlimited
proliferative capacity of neoplastic cells thus con-
tributing to their immortality. As such, telomerase
serves as a promising “universal” target for cyto-
toxic T cells. Aurisicchio’s group pioneered the
use of plasmid DNA electroporation (DNA-EP)
prime with full length, codon optimized telomerase
reverse transcriptase (TERT) DNA, followed by
boosting with an adenovirus serotype 6 (Ad6) vector
expressing TERT vaccine to elicit telomerase-specific
T-cell responses in healthy dogs (Peruzzi et al.,
2010b). The TERT DNA-EP vaccination alone
elicited TERT-specific IFN-g responses that were
significantly augmented by the Ad6-TERT boost.
The same group demonstrated that following
Ad6-TERT priming, TERT-specific T-cell responses
were induced and subsequently maintained by
TERT DNA-EP electroporation in dogs with BCL
(Peruzzi et al., 2010a). In a small prospective,
clinical study, this immunization regimen admin-
istered to 21 dogs with BCL after a successful
6- to 8-week COP (cyclophosphamide, vincristine
(Oncovin), prednisolone) induction regimen and
concurrently with maintenance chemotherapy, led
to the expansion of canine TERT-specific T cells,
without adverse effects (Gavazza et al., 2013).
Although there was no significant prolongation of
disease-free interval in the vaccinated group, over-
all survival of vaccinated patients was prolonged
when compared to a control arm of 21 dogs that
received no immunotherapy after COP induction.
All relapsed dogs were treated with doxorubicin.
This phenomenon of improved overall survival fol-
lowing rescue chemotherapy in patients that have
received prior immunotherapies has been observed
in other immunotherapy trials in dogs (Sorenmo
et al., 2011) and in humans. The mechanisms behind
this phenomenon have not been fully elucidated.
Nonetheless, induction of ICD by cytotoxic agents
such as doxorubicin, cyclophosphamide, and pacli-
taxel may reinforce or augment prior antitumor
immunity. It is important to note that this phe-
nomenon of enhanced survival can be missed if
progression-free survival is the primary endpoint
of trial design and overall survival data is not also
recorded.
LISTERIA- AND SALMONELLA-VECTORED CANCER VAC-
CINES 	As suggested by William Coley’s early work,
bacteria and their secreted products can serve as
powerful antitumor agents, not only through their
vaccine adjuvant effects but also by reprogram-
ming immune-suppressive myeloid cells in the
TME. Facultative and obligate anaerobic bacteria
such as Listeria, Clostridium, and Salmonella
have natural tumor-homing capabilities and exert
tumoricidal and immune-modulatory effects on
the TME, mediated by activated macrophages and
NK cells. Both Listeria monocytogenes (Lm) and
Salmonella have been used as TAA or cytokine
delivery systems in dogs and humans (Thamm
et al., 2005; Mason et al., 2016). Listeria is an
intracellular bacterium that preferentially infects
mononuclear cells, thus making it an ideal vector
to deliver an antigenic payload to prime CD4+ and
CD8+ T cells. The ability of Lm to induce potent,
antigen-specific cytotoxic T cells relies on secretion of
a pore-forming lysine, listeriolysin O (LLO), which
enables the organism to escape the phagosome and
enter the cytosol. In the cytosol, TAAs produced
as recombinant antigens in engineered Listeria are
fused to LLO so that they are processed via both
MHCI and MHCII pathways, resulting in the gen-
eration of TAA-specific CD8+ and CD4+ T cells respec-
tively. A genetically engineered, recombinant Lm
expressing a chimeric human HER2/neu induced
potent and effective cytotoxic T-cell responses
in murine models of HER2-expressing cancers.
Several human studies and one canine study indi-
cate that HER2/neu is expressed in 40–60% of
human OSA cases and in 40% of canine OSA cases
(Musser et al., 2021). Nevertheless, the literature
supports the notion that HER2/neu may serve as
a clinically relevant T-cell target for the prevention
and treatment of metastatic OSA.
A Phase I clinical trial in dogs to identify the
maximum tolerated dose (MTD) of intravenously
delivered, highly attenuated Lm-LLO-HER2/neu
and to assess the ability of the vector to safely elicit

HER-2/neu-specific T-cell immune responses and
antitumor immunity was performed in 18 dogs
with appendicular OSA following amputation and
adjuvant carboplatin chemotherapy (Mason et al.,
2016). Immune monitoring data demonstrated
induction of HER2/neu-specific T-cell responses
(against human HER2/neu), and vaccine adminis-
tration produced a significant increase in time to
tumor progression and overall survival time (OST)
in treated dogs when compared to historical con-
trols (Mason et al., 2016). Transient, low-grade
adverse events were observed 2–4 hours after
attenuated Lm-LLO-HER2/neu administration and
included lethargy, fever, nausea, and vomiting.
Overall survival in that study correlated with early
indicators of innate immune activation at 24 hours
following treatment.
Unfortunately, a change in the vaccine prepara-
tion process in subsequent trials resulted in the
appearance of unacceptable cytokine-mediated side
effects that were lethal in at least one instance
(Musser et al., 2019). Furthermore, failure to include
post-treatment antibiotics to eliminate residual bac-
teria after immunization likely contributed to two
reports of Listeria-induced abscesses in treated dogs.
A multi-institutional, prospective, clinical trial with
a control arm using the original vaccine formulation
is currently underway though the National Institutes
of Health (NIH) Comparative Oncology Trials
Consortium (COTC) with the aim of vaccinating 80
dogs to evaluate safety and efficacy and identify cor-
relative biomarkers of response.
Attenuated Salmonella typhimurium has been
engineered to express IL-2, CD40L, and cytosine
deaminase as a novel cancer vaccine platform. In a
Phase I safety trial in dogs, the engineered
Salmonella vaccine was administered intravenously
to 41 dogs with seven different tumor types includ-
ing sarcoma, carcinoma, and round cell tumors, all
with significant disease burdens (Thamm et al.,
2005). Dose-dependent adverse effects of fever,
vomiting, and diarrhea were observed in most
dogs. Leukocytosis and hepatic transaminitis were
identified in 34% and 15% of treated cases. One
death directly related to infusion occurred and bac-
terial abscessation at the tumor site was identified
in seven dogs, consistent with trafficking to tumor
site, which was previously observed in murine
models (Luo et al., 2001). An overall response rate
of 15% was observed, along with and overall clini-
cal antitumor activity in 25% of treated dogs. This
work further emphasizes the fact that bacterial traf-
ficking to tumors is expected and likely desired for
effective cancer immunotherapy (Thamm et al., 2005).
Adoptive cell therapies
The newest approach to cancer immunotherapy,
and one with arguably the most impressive clinical
benefit to date, is the use of adoptive cell therapies
(ACTs) using T-cell receptor (TCR) transduced
autologous T cells. Pioneering studies using CAR
(chimeric antigen receptor)-T cells engineered to
target the CD19 molecule expressed by acute leu-
kemias and BCLs demonstrated complete and
durable tumor responses following a single infu-
sion of autologous CD19 CAR-T cells in relapsed
patients refractory to all conventional treatment
approaches (Bourbon et al., 2021; Gauthier and
Turtle, 2021; Haslauer et al., 2021). The CAR-T
cell approach built on decades of preclinical studies
in rodent cancer models perfecting the approach
until it warranted testing in human patients. While
CAR-T cell approaches for leukemia and lym-
phoma have led the field, CAR-T cell therapies are
being developed to target a variety of different
cancer types, including both hematopoietic and
solid cancers.
The ultimate aim of most cancer immunothera-
pies is to generate large numbers of tumor-specific
CD4 and CD8 T cells that can function as serial
tumor cell killers capable of eliminating bulky
tumor disease and micro metastases, and of persist-
ing in the patient for years following a single cell
infusion. However, as described previously, it is
very difficult to generate effective, long-lived anti-
tumor immunity using conventional tumor vaccine
approaches, particularly in heavily pretreated can-
cer patients. Thus, an attractive solution to this
problem is the use of adoptive cell transfer, using in
most cases T cells that have been expanded in vitro
using optimized stimuli and cytokine cocktails
designed to generate active effector and memory
T cells. Currently, there is significant emphasis being
placed on T-cell adoptive transfer, using culture-
expanded T cells that have been either genetically
modified to express chimeric receptors or other-
wise enriched in antigen-specific cells. This process
of adoptive cell transfer first showed promise when
tumor-infiltrating lymphocytes (TILs) were isolated
from human malignant melanomas, expanded
ex vivo, and adoptively transferred to human

-- 147 of 258 --

patients, where they mediated impressive clinical
responses 	(Rosenberg, 	1986; 	Dudley 	and
Rosenberg, 2003). Since then, ACT with TIL has
been largely overshadowed by the success of geneti-
cally engineered CAR-T cells, particularly for the
treatment of hematological malignancies. In the
veterinary arena, adoptive cell transfer was first
described using the human cytotoxic TALL-104
cell line and has since advanced to the experimental
clinical use of autologous, polyclonally activated
and expanded canine T cells (O’Connor et al.,
2012; Flesner et al., 2020), CAR-T cells (Panjwani
et al., 2016, 2020), and ex vivo expanded canine
NK cells (Canter et al., 2017).
TALL-104 CELLS FOR ADOPTIVE IMMUNOTHERAPY IN
DOGS 	The first report of adoptive T-cell transfer
to treat cancer in dogs used a xenogeneic cell
therapy approach in which high doses (up to
108 cells/kg body weight) of lethally-irradiated
TALL-104 cells were administered. The TALL-104
cell lines is a human cytotoxic T-cell line derived
from the peripheral blood of a child with T-acute
lymphoblastic leukemia (T-ALL). The TALL-104
cells were administered to 19 dogs with various
advanced malignancies that included lymphoma,
malignant histiocytosis, melanoma, and squamous
cell carcinoma (Cesano et al., 1996). Concurrent
administration of cyclosporin was used to pre-
vent rapid rejection of the TALL-104 cells, which
were given repeatedly as intravenous infusions
over 5 weeks. Other than one anaphylaxis event,
administration was safe, with only low-grade
transient gastrointestinal toxicities and elevations
of alanine transaminase (ALT) being reported.
Cytokine release syndrome, a multisystemic tox-
icity associated potentially with essentially all
protocols involving adoptive cell transfer with T
cells, was not observed following TALL-104 infu-
sion, which might be explained in part by lack
of cross-reactivity and binding between human
T-cell cytokines such as IFN-γ and canine cytokine
receptors. Additional studies built upon this work
and despite the formation of both humoral and
cell-mediated immunity against the transferred
cells and their lack of detectable persistence, prom-
ising results were reported in dogs with malig-
nant histiocytosis (without visceral involvement)
(Visonneau et al., 1997), OSA (Visonneau et al.,
1999a), and one dog with metastatic mammary
carcinoma (Visonneau et al., 1999b). Technical
difficulties in growing these cells and generating
cryopreserved cell banks resulted in this approach
being generally surpassed by newer platforms for
adoptive cell transfer.
ACTIVATED POLYCLONAL T CELLS FOR CANINE IMMU-
NOTHERAPY 	Clinical and experimental evidence
in humans and mice confirms that tumor-specific
T cells are naturally generated in tumor-bearing
hosts, and that these cells can be expanded ex
vivo under proper conditions of nonspecific acti-
vation and cytokine support, with or without
tumor antigen-specific restimulation. This premise
forms the biologic rationale for the administra-
tion of polyclonal activated canine T cells for
cancer immunotherapy (O’Connor et al., 2012;
O’Connor and Wilson-Robles, 2014; Flesner et al.,
2020). Polyclonal activation and expansion of T
cells isolated from peripheral blood mononuclear
cells from dogs with BCL, using artificial APCs as
nonspecific T-cell-activating agents, resulted in the
generation of an activated CD3+CD8+ effector cell
population that, upon adoptive transfer to eight
dogs in clinical remission following CHOP therapy,
trafficked to lymph nodes and was associated with
prolonged tumor-free survival and overall survival
(O’Connor et al., 2012). In that report it was
hypothesized that improved survival in these dogs
was due to the adoptively transferred cells acceler-
ating T-cell recovery following CHOP treatment.
However, caution should be used in the interpreta-
tion of signals from this small single-arm study.
To more specifically augment tumor-specific T-cell
responses, Flesner et al. combined tumor-specific
T-cell priming via autologous tumor vaccination
with subsequent polyclonal ex vivo expansion of
post-vaccinal T cells obtained via apheresis, with
the goal of generating a T-cell product enriched
with tumor-specific effectors (Flesner et al., 2020).
The expanded T cells were given together with
systemic low-dose IL-2 delivery to 14 canine
OSA patients following amputation, but without
administration of standard adjuvant chemotherapy.
Median survival time of 415 days was reported
in the 14 treated dogs, with survival greater than
730 days in five of the 14 dogs. These reported
survival times are impressive in as much as these
animals did not receive adjuvant chemotherapy
and support the notion that OSA in some patients
is responsive to immunotherapies.
CAR - T CELLS 	Unprecedented clinical responses
have been observed in human hematological
132 	N. Mason and S. Dow

133	Cancer Immunotherapy
malignancies following administration of autolo-
gous T cells genetically redirected (i.e., edited; see
Wierson et al., Chapter 9, this volume, 2023) to
express a CAR (chimeric antigen receptor). CAR-T
cells recognize a surface expressed tumor antigen
through a single-chain antibody molecule on the
outside of the CAR construct that is linked to a
functional intracellular TCR signaling domain
internally. Engagement of the antibody domain of
the CAR construct (single-chain variable region
fragment (scFv)) with its cognate antigen expressed
by tumor cells leads to dimerization of the CAR
and subsequent delivery of signals required for
T-cell activation. CAR-T cells kill tumor target
cells by several cytotoxic mechanisms, including
insertion of perforin and granzyme into the tumor
cell, as well as engagement of apoptosis-inducing
molecules such as Fas and TRAIL.
Despite the success of CD19- and more recently
B-cell 	maturation 	antigen 	(BCMA)-targeting
CAR-T cells for the treatment of hematologic
malignancies such as B-cell malignancies and mul-
tiple myeloma respectively, responses to CAR-T cell
therapy have been disappointing in human patients
with solid tumors. Multiple new approaches to
CAR-T designs to improve CAR-T cell trafficking
into solid tumors and to counter the immune-
suppressive TME, which may induce T-cell exhaus-
tion, are currently undergoing clinical evaluation.
The spontaneous occurrence of several solid can-
cers in dogs such as OSA and glioma that present
comparable barriers to effective CAR-T cell ther-
apy has prompted consideration of studies in dogs
to evaluate next-generation human CAR-T strate-
gies (Mata et al., 2014; Yin et al., 2018; Panjwani
et al., 2020). To this end, several groups have
reported protocols for the successful expansion and
transduction of primary canine T cells (Panjwani
et al., 2016; Sakai et al., 2020; Rotolo et al., 2021;
Szopa, 2021) required for CAR-T product develop-
ment. Canine T cells redirected with a second-gen-
eration 	HER2-specific 	CAR 	demonstrated
antigen-dependent IFN-γ production and cytotox-
icity against canine OSA cell lines expressing
canine HER2/neu (Mata et al., 2014), as have
canine CAR-T cells targeting B7-H3 expressed by
OSA cell lines (Zhang et al., 2022).
Canine CAR-T cells directed against CD20 on
BCL cells have been successfully generated and
evaluated in vitro, where they have shown antigen-
dependent activation, proliferation, cytokine pro-
duction, and cytotoxicity (Panjwani et al., 2016,
2020; Sakai et al., 2020). Second-generation CD20-
redirected CAR-T cells administered to a small
number of canine patients with B-NHL were asso-
ciated with short-term responses, followed by
downregulation of CD20 expression on neoplastic
B cells and in one case, selection of neoplastic B
cells expressing a CD20 splice variant that lacked
the CAR epitope (Panjwani et al., 2020). The find-
ings of a positive correlation between CAR-T cell
expansion ex vivo and overall survival, and the
development of canine anti-mouse antibodies that
correlated with CAR-T cell loss, mirror those of
human patients treated with CD19-targeting
CAR-T cells and suggest that the dog will serve as
a valuable model to explore improved-efficacy
CAR-T cell therapy using next-generation CAR
designs.
Although promising, the expense and impracti-
calities of generating autologous CAR-T cell prod-
ucts for treatment of dogs significantly limits the
utility and practicality of this approach. However,
recent developments using gene editing technolo-
gies such as CRISPR/Cas9 (clustered regularly
interspaced short palindromic repeats (CRISPR)/
CRISPR-associated protein 9 (Cas9)) may now
pave the way to the use of in vitro gene editing and
the generation of fully allogeneic CAR-T cell prod-
ucts for cancer therapy (Zhou, 2020). In one appli-
cation of this approach, β2-microglobulin, class II
major histocompatibility complex transactivator
(CIITA), and TCRα have been edited out of the
transduced CAR-T cells to prevent their elimina-
tion via MHCI and MHCII recognition by allore-
active host T cells and to avoid the development of
graft-versus-host disease (GVHD) mediated by the
donor TCR attacking host tissues. Additional
CRISPR edits such as the removal of PD-1 have
been suggested to render CAR-T cell therapy more
resistant to the immune-suppressive TME (Ren
et al., 2017). Ultimately, successful editing of T cells
together with the expression of nonclassical MHC
class Ib decoy receptors to avoid killing NK cells
(see below) may provide a viable, on-demand, off-
the-shelf cellular product derived from healthy
donor T cells, an approach that will increase the
therapeutic reach of this technology (Thommen
and Schumacher, 2018).
NATURAL KILLER CELLS 	NK 	cells 	have 	been
employed as an alternative to T cells for adoptive
immunotherapy and, unlike T cells, they have the
broader appeal of not being MHC restricted for

-- 149 of 258 --

tumor cell killing (Hu et al., 2019). NK cells are
rapid and potent serial killers, employing an early
and fast release of granzyme B followed by a sub-
sequent switch to cytotoxic activity mediated by
death receptor pathways (Prager et al., 2019). To
exert their tumor cytotoxicity, NK cells must first
be activated, and that process of NK-cell activation
is determined by the sum total of signals received
from canonical activating and inhibitory recep-
tors (Lanier, 2008). For example, the interaction
of killer immunoglobulin-like receptors (KIRs)
and C-type lectin receptors with MHC class I
molecules, expressed on all healthy nucleated cells,
inhibits NK-cell activation. Conversely, downregu-
lation of MHCI on tumor cells removes this “self-
preservation” mechanism and enables NK-cell
activation and cytolytic function. Upregulation
of stress receptors such as MICA and MICB on
malignant cells can directly activate NK cells via
activating receptors such as NKG2D, DNAM-1,
and the natural cytotoxicity receptors NKp44 and
NKp46 (Martinet and Smyth, 2015). As such, NK
cells are well suited to serve as mediators of anti-
tumor immunity in adoptive transfer strategies and
given that they do not express a TCR, they can be
safely used in an allogeneic setting without risk of
causing GVHD. The development and validation
of an anti-canine NKp46 antibody (Foltz et al.,
2016) has enabled the isolation, characterization,
and subsequent expansion of canine NK cells for
ACT (Grondahl-Rosado et al., 2015; Gingrich
et al., 2019).
Successful ex vivo activation and expansion of
non-edited NK cells from healthy dogs and canine
OSA patients has been achieved via stimulation
with artificial APCs expressing cross-reactive
human co-stimulatory molecules such as CD86 and
4-1BBL (Foltz et al., 2016). In preclinical rodent
studies, transient control of a high-grade canine
fibrosarcoma was achieved in a PDX mouse model
by intratumoral administration of expanded, allo-
geneic canine NK cells. Canine OSA PDX models
supported the hypothesis that RT could enhance
NK-cell activity by increasing the homing of NK
cells to the tumor and enhancing their cytotoxicity
to control tumor growth. A first-in-canine clinical
trial to evaluate palliative RT followed by intra-
tumoral autologous NK cells in canine patients
with appendicular OSA showed the persistence of
transferred NK cells within the tumor for at least 1
week, limited systemic toxicity, a tendency toward
local infection at the injection site, and a favorable
interval free from pulmonary metastases in treated
patients when compared to historical controls
(Canter et al., 2017). As in human and canine
patients receiving autologous ex vivo expanded
T-cell products, significant variation was observed
in the degree of expansion of NK cells from differ-
ent canine patients and future studies are required
to determine whether, as in humans, this may serve
as a functional biomarker of cell product quality
and ultimately clinical outcome (Panjwani et al.,
2016; Canter et al., 2017; Fraietta et al., 2018).
LIMITATIONS OF ADOPTIVE CELL TRANSFER 	While
cell-based therapies have emerged as one of the
most exciting breakthroughs in the treatment of
cancer in human patients, CAR-T cells and NK cells
are highly susceptible to the detrimental effects of
the immune-suppressive TME present in many
solid neoplasms. Immune-suppressive cells such
as regulatory T cells (Tregs) (Sakai et al., 2018;
Ohue and Nishikawa, 2019), MDSCs (Goulart
et al., 2012; Roussel et al., 2017), and TAMs
(Gabrilovich, 2017; Pittet et al., 2022) inhibit
T- and NK-cell responses within the TME through
the production of immune-suppressive cytokines
including IL-10, TGF-β, IL-35, and other inhibitors
including IDO, VEGF, arginase, nitric oxide (NO),
and reactive oxygen species, as described above. An
increasing array of checkpoint molecule-targeted
therapeutics such as blocking antibodies for PD-1,
PD-L1, CTLA-4, TIM-3, and LAG-3 have been
identified and shown to reverse or block T-cell
exhaustion and apoptosis in the TME. NK cells
also express checkpoint molecules and the effects
of checkpoint inhibitors on NK-cell activity is an
area of active research. Furthermore, the tumor
stroma poses a significant physical and functional
barrier, with CAFs identified as a significant inhibi-
tory cell population, along with the matrix proteins
produced by the fibroblasts. Recognizing such bar-
riers underscores the need to intelligently evaluate
combinatorial approaches and genetic engineering
strategies that will improve the efficacy of adop-
tively transferred cells.
Nonspecifc tumor immunotherapy using
biologic response modifers
Effective antitumor immunity can also be induced by
nonspecifically activating the innate arm of the
immune system in patients with cancer. Indeed,
William Coley’s work pioneered the use of innate
134 	N. Mason and S. Dow

-- 150 of 258 --

135	Cancer Immunotherapy
immune activation for effective cancer immunother-
apy. Approaches employed for nonspecific immuno-
therapy include, but are not limited to, administration
of Toll-like and Nod-like receptor agonists, use of
cancer oncolytic viruses, and administration of
recombinant cytokines including IL-2 and IFN-γ.
Tumor immunotherapy using Toll-like and
Nod-like receptor-targeted immunotherapies
The field of cancer immunotherapy largely arose
from William Coley’s work using mixed bacterial
cultures (Coley’s toxin) to treat human sarcoma
patients at the turn of the 19th century. Although
unknown at the time, the mechanism of action of
this approach stemmed from innate and adaptive
immune activation following stimulation of TLR
(Toll-like receptors) and NLR (Nod-like receptors)
by bacterial cell wall and secreted components.
Since that time, great strides have been made in
defining the TLR and NLR signaling pathways and
identifying natural and synthetic ligands for these
receptors. A multitude of different immunothera-
pies targeting these pathways have been evaluated
for cancer immunotherapy in dogs.
Arguably the greatest immunotherapy success to
date for the treatment of cancer in dogs remains the
liposomal NLR2 agonist, which is a complex of
L-MTP-PE (liposomal muramyl tripeptide phos-
phatidyl ethanolamine) that targets activation of the
NLR2 pathway in lung macrophages (Kleinerman
and Jaffe, 1990; Kurzman et al., 1999). This syn-
thetic lipophilic analog of muramyl dipeptide,
which is a natural component of the Mycobacterium
cell wall, was extensively evaluated by McEwen
et al. in the mid to late 1980s, and L-MTP-PE treat-
ment demonstrated clear benefit in the adjuvant
immunotherapy of OSA in dogs, either alone or
when used in combination with cytotoxic chemo-
therapy (Kurzman et al., 1995). The mechanism of
action of intravenously administered L-MTP-PE
involved, at least in part, activation of alveolar
macrophages. L-MTP-PE was subsequently evalu-
ated in pediatric OSA patients at risk for lung
metastases and demonstrated clinical benefit in
randomized trials, which led to approval of the
drug (MEPACT, mifamurtide) for use in Europe
(Kleinerman et al., 1995). L-MTP-PE has yet to be
approved for human use in the USA and is not
approved for veterinary use.
The use of TLR9 agonists to activate antitumor
innate immunity has also been evaluated in dogs.
Complexes of charged liposomes and plasmid
DNA molecules enriched in CpG motifs have dem-
onstrated strong activation of innate immunity,
including IFN-γ production and NK-cell activation,
and increased survival times in dogs with meta-
static OSA (Dow et al., 2005). In addition, lipo-
some–TLR9 agonist complexes also significantly
suppressed tumor angiogenesis in dogs with soft
tissue sarcoma (Kamstock et al., 2006). It should
also be noted that repetitive activation of innate
immune pathways such as TLR 3, TLR7/8, and
TLR9 that are associated with production of type I
interferons can over time also generate effective
T-cell activation and expansion. Thus, these
approaches may be complementary and additive to
antigen-specific approaches such as tumor vaccines
or CAR-T cell therapies.
Other less well-characterized TLR- and NLR-
activating biological therapies have been evaluated
in the past as innate immune activators in
canine cancer patients. For example, a lysate of
Propionibacterium was evaluated for use in non-
specific cancer immunotherapy in dogs, although
controlled prospective studies were not reported.
Local tumor injection of an Aloe vera plant extract
(acemannan), thought to activate C-type lectin
receptor pathways, leading to macrophage activa-
tion, was also shown to trigger tumor-cell necrosis
in treated animals (Harris et al., 1991; King et al.,
1995).
Oncolytic viruses
Increased expression of viral entry receptors
together with defects in antiviral defense mecha-
nisms, including interferon and apoptotic path-
ways, have been identified in tumor cells. This has
led to the employment of wild-type, attenuated,
and genetically engineered oncolytic viruses that
can take advantage of these characteristics for
selective infection of tumor cells, direct lytic activ-
ity, and an inflammatory response that initiates and
promotes antitumor immunity (Atherton and
Lichty, 2013; Lichty et al., 2014). The approach
does not require the identification of specific TAAs
as lysis of tumor cells will release multiple TAAs to
initiate and expand tumor-specific T-cell responses.
Many oncolytic viruses including reoviruses,
myxoma viruses, and vaccinia have been evaluated
for their ability to infect and lyse canine tumor cell
lines in vitro and to infect and control canine
tumor xenografts in immune-compromised murine

-- 151 of 258 --

models. These viruses have induced cytolytic effects
and in some cases replication-dependent apoptosis
in canine mast cell tumor, lymphoma, mammary
gland, OSA, and melanoma cell lines, as well as in
primary canine tumor cells. Multiple proof-of-
concept, pilot clinical studies have been performed
in canine cancer patients using oncolytic viruses; a
full review of oncolytic viral therapies in canine
cancers is beyond the scope of this chapter but is
given elsewhere (Sánchez et al., 2018). However,
notably, VSV genetically engineered to secrete
human IFN-b (VSV-IFN-B-NIS), to increase safety
for nonmalignant tissues, was shown to be safe in
healthy Beagles with no detected shedding or neu-
rotoxicity (LeBlanc et al., 2013) and when used in
the first evaluation of a systemically administered
oncolytic virus in ten canine cancer patients, was
shown to induce transient constitutional signs and
transient partial responses in two dogs with T-cell
lymphoma (Naik et al., 2018). In a second study,
using a cellular virotherapy approach (ICOCAv17),
canine mesenchymal stem cells were infected with
a canine oncolytic adenovirus and used as a mask-
ing mechanism to reduce or prevent neutralizing
antibody production following intravenous admin-
istration. The approach was evaluated in 27 canine
cancer patients with a variety of different tumor
histologies including OSA, HSA, melanoma, and
fibrosarcoma. Although anti-adenoviral antibodies
were detected in the peripheral blood of patients,
the approach resulted in a 74% response rate and
14.8% complete response (Cejalvo et al., 2018). In
a follow-up study, ten dogs with high-grade glioma
were treated with weekly intravenous administra-
tions of ICOCAv17 for 8 weeks. Partial responses
occurred in two dogs and stable disease was
observed in three of seven dogs (Cloquell et al.,
2022). Future work will look to establish optimal
dosing and combinatorial use regimens, the overall
safety of the approach, and strategies to overcome
neutralizing antibody production.
Cytokine therapeutics (IL-2, IL-15)
There was a great deal of early interest in the use of
high doses of IL-2 to treat multiple different can-
cers in humans. However, toxicities, including pul-
monary capillary leak syndromes, quickly appeared
and became severely dose limiting. Eventually
lower-dose IL-2 therapy was approved for use in
treatment of melanoma and renal cell cancer in
humans. Low-dose IL-2 therapy to activate NK
cells has been evaluated in dogs in early studies
(Helfand et al., 1994a,b). Doses of human IL-2 that
were well tolerated clinically were identified, along
with evidence of NK-cell activation, but the studies
were not pursued. More recently, recombinant
human (rh) IL-2 (250,000 IU/kg) has been co-
administered with autologous NK cells injected
intratumorally in dogs with appendicular OSA.
There was limited systemic toxicity associated with
IL-2 administration, other than one dog which had
a grade 3 reaction of fever, excessive salivation, and
dehydration (Canter et al., 2017). To circumvent
the risks of significant toxicity expected to occur as
systemic doses of IL-2 are increased, rhIL-2 and
rhIL-15 have also been delivered by inhalation to
canine patients with pulmonary metastases. Khanna
et al. first demonstrated the safety and, in some
instances, clinical activity of inhaled IL-2 in dogs
with metastatic OSA (Khanna et al., 1996).
The use of inhaled rhIL-15 to induce NK-cell
activation has also been explored in dogs. A recent
study reported the repeated administration of
inhaled rhIL-15 in a 3 + 3 Phase I trial (n = 18) in
which dogs with pulmonary metastatic OSA were
dosed twice daily for 14 consecutive days. Dose-
limiting toxicities were observed at the 70 μg IL-15
dose and an overall clinical benefit rate of 39%
was reported with one sustained complete response
of over 1 year (Rebhun et al., 2022). The same
study reported increased cytotoxicity of peripheral
blood mononuclear cells against OSA and mela-
noma targets after treatment which correlated with
overall survival. These findings set the stage for
further exploration of combination therapies such
as systemic NK-cell adoptive transfer with inhaled
rhIL-5 to augment clinical responses in patients
with pulmonary metastatic disease.
Fas ligand gene therapy for modifying
the tumor microenvironment
The interaction of Fas ligand (FasL) expressed by
activated T cells with Fas expressed by tumor cells
can trigger rapid tumor apoptosis. Several studies
in dogs have sought to exploit this effect by in vivo
tumor 	transfection 	using 	adenoviral 	vectors
expressing the canine FasL gene (Modiano et al.,
2012). These studies determined that adenovirus-
delivered FasL induced a neutrophilic infiltrate
within the transfected tumor and was associated
with suppression of tumor growth in some treated
animals. Activation of the Fas/FasL pathway may
