also represent part of the mechanism of action of
L-MTP immunotherapy, which has been shown
previously to prevent or delay the development of
OSA pulmonary metastases.
Immunotherapies modifying the tumor
microenvironment
The immune-suppressive TME remains at present a
formidable and largely unsolved impediment to
effective cancer immunotherapy. As noted earlier,
key immune-modulatory cells within the TME
include tumor macrophages, MDSCs, stromal cells,
neutrophils, and Tregs, each of which can be tar-
geted with currently available agents. At present,
there are several approaches to targeting these cells
therapeutically to modify the TME. These approaches
have included specific depletion of tumor macro-
phages using the drug liposome-encapsulated clo-
dronate, or slow, sustained depletion of tumor
macrophages by disrupting the mobilization and
migration of CCR2+ monocytes into tumor tissues,
using repurposed agents such as angiotensin receptor-
blocking drugs. Other approaches currently
under investigation include the use of repurposed
drugs to block the mobilization of MDSCs and
reverse their immune-suppressive function, using
β-adrenergic antagonists. Other approaches include
modified dosing of immune-suppressive drugs
(e.g., rapamycin, mycophenolate) or metronomic
dosing of cytotoxic agents (e.g., cyclophospha-
mide, toceranib).
Macrophage depletion using
liposomal clodronate
Bisphosphonate drugs have been used for years to
deplete osteoclasts to assist in the management of
metastatic cancers to bone. The cytotoxic activity
toward highly phagocytic osteoclasts can be mark-
edly enhanced by incorporating the bisphospho-
nate drug into neutral liposomes, typically of a
diameter in the 1 μm range. Particles of this size are
effectively internalized by macrophages, resulting
in the cytoplasmic liberation of the active bisphos-
phonate, which is much more effective at disrupt-
ing 	ATP 	production 	when 	high 	cytosolic
concentrations are achieved. This phenomenon has
been capitalized on with liposomal clodronate,
which selectively depletes macrophages throughout
the body following intravenous administration
(Guth et al., 2013). In dogs, liposomal clodronate
was originally used to deplete macrophages and
block erythrocyte destruction in dogs with immune-
mediated hemolytic anemia (Mathes et al., 2006).
Concurrently, rodent studies demonstrated that
tumor macrophage depletion with liposomal clo-
dronate could significantly deplete spleen and
tumor macrophages and significantly inhibit tumor
growth. Importantly, follow-on studies of lipo-
somal clodronate as a cancer immunotherapy in
dogs demonstrated activity in animals with histio-
cytic sarcoma and in dogs with soft tissue sarcoma,
inducing regression of large lesions in some cases
(Hafeman et al., 2010). Avid uptake of liposomal
clodronate directly by canine histiocytic sarcoma
cells was also demonstrated in vitro.
Tumor macrophage depletion using monocyte
migration inhibitors (CCR2 antagonists)
Chemokine-C type receptor 2 (CCR2) is the pri-
mary chemokine receptor expressed at high levels
by inflammatory monocytes, and CCR2 regulates
monocyte migration into tissues at sites of inflam-
mation. Macrophage turnover rates are very high
in tumors, and consequently the tumor macrophage
population is almost entirely dependent on efficient
repopulation from inflammatory monocytes in the
blood. Thus, disrupting monocyte migration leads
within days to significant depopulation of tumor
macrophages. Rodent studies have demonstrated
that specific antagonists of CCR2 can deplete
tumor macrophages and slow tumor growth, and
human trials have demonstrated promising activity
(Noel et al., 2020; Wu et al., 2020, 2022). However,
their expense has precluded clinical evaluation in
dogs. Therefore, in silico screens were conducted to
identify existing drugs that could be repurposed as
CCR2 antagonists, and the angiotensin type I
receptor blocking (ARB) family of drugs was iden-
tified (Regan et al., 2019). Studies in rodent models
demonstrated that losartan (and other drugs in the
ARB class) functioned as potent CCR2 antagonists
and led to significant inhibition of monocyte
migration and depletion of tumor macrophages in
the TME, accompanied by inhibition of tumor
growth (Regan et al., 2019). Ongoing trials in dogs
with metastatic OSA and malignant glioma have
provided evidence of sustained monocyte migra-
tion inhibition with daily losartan therapy (together
with toceranib or propranolol), accompanied in
some cases by partial responses and tumor stable
disease (Regan et al., 2022). Thus, the ARB class of

-- 153 of 258 --

drugs has potential for use in broadly and specifi-
cally modifying the TME immune-suppressive cel-
lular content.
Myeloid-derived suppressor cell-targeted
immunotherapy
As noted previously, MDSCs constitute another
important myeloid cell population that regulates
tumor immunity, both within the TME and sys-
temically. There are currently several drugs that can
be repurposed to target MDSCs. The mixed-
function tyrosine kinase inhibitor sunitinib has
been shown in rodent studies to deplete MDSCs, in
part by inhibiting signal transducer and activator
of transcription 3 (STAT3) signaling pathways
(Regan et al., 2022). The closely-related drug tocer-
anib is thought to exert similar activity against dog
MDSCs, at least based on in vitro studies. In addi-
tion, MDSCs can also be targeted using β receptor-
blocking drugs. For example, excess β-adrenergic
stress in cancer is associated with mobilization of
MDSCs and is a driver of their functional matura-
tion into immune-suppressive cells (Chen et al.,
2020). By blocking β-adrenergic signaling through
the β-adrenergic receptor type I and II signaling
using the nonselective β-blocker propranolol, stud-
ies in rodents and humans have demonstrated the
potent immune-modulatory properties of this drug.
These effects have also been confirmed in vitro
using dog MDSC cultures, and the combination of
losartan and propranolol with a tumor vaccine
demonstrated antitumor activity (80% clinical
response rate) in dogs with glioma (Ammons et al.,
2022).
Regulatory T-cell depletion
using repurposed drugs
Tregs are potently immune suppressive and also
more numerous in tumor tissues than in normal,
noninflamed tissues. At present, there are few drugs
to specifically target and deplete Tregs for cancer
immunotherapy; however, certain commonly used
pharmacological agents have been shown to deplete
Tregs as an off-target effect. For example, Treg
depletion was observed in dogs treated with metro-
nomically dosed cyclophosphamide, suggesting
that continuous exposure may either deplete Tregs
directly, as was noted in vitro, or through an indi-
rect mechanism (Mitchell et al., 2012). It was also
observed that Treg depletion in blood occurred in
dogs treated with oral toceranib, suggestive of
another off-target immunological effect, similar to
the effect of toceranib on MDSC depletion (Burton
et al., 2011; Mitchell et al., 2012). Furthermore,
anti-CTLA-4 antibodies have also been shown to
deplete Tregs in mouse cancer models and human
cancer patients, which is thought to contribute to
their ability to augment antitumor immunity. It was
also demonstrated recently that intratumoral injec-
tion of an anti-canine OX40 antibody depleted
Tregs in dogs with oral cancers (Boss et al., 2022).
Thus, there are several options for pharmacologi-
cally depleting Tregs in dogs with cancer, as part of
a more comprehensive cancer immunotherapy
strategy. However, the therapeutic value of such
approaches remains unclear at this time.
Checkpoint inhibitors and
co-stimulatory agonists
Checkpoint molecules are a diverse family of
inhibitory and stimulatory molecules, and their
receptors are expressed by immune cells, especially
T cells, NK cells, macrophages, and DCs, as well as
tumor cells in some cases. This family of molecules
is broadly divided into two primary categories: co-
inhibitory checkpoint molecules and co-stimulatory
molecules. Within the co-inhibitory receptor fam-
ily are the well-known PD-1 (programmed cell
death protein 1; CD279) and CTLA-4 (cytotoxic T
lymphocyte antigen-4) molecules that with their
cognate ligands, PD-L1/PD-L2 and CD80/86
respectively, lead to potent immune suppression.
The family of co-stimulatory molecules is repre-
sented primarily by CD28, OX40, and CD137
(4-1BB), which when engaged lead to effector T-cell
activation. These molecules can be targeted for
therapeutic gain using monoclonal antibodies that
either block receptor–ligand interactions (e.g., anti-
PD-1 or anti-PD-L1) to prevent inhibitory T-cell
signaling, or stimulate co-stimulatory molecules
(e.g., anti-CD28 or anti-OX40) to augment T-cell
activation.
Co-inhibitory checkpoint molecules
CTLA-4 AS A THERAPEUTIC TARGET 	The co-inhibitory
checkpoint molecule CTLA-4 was the first such
molecule targeted therapeutically using human-
ized antibodies, and these early studies provided
seminal insights into the potential effectiveness of
138 	N. Mason and S. Dow

-- 154 of 258 --

139	Cancer Immunotherapy
checkpoint-targeted antibodies (i.e., ICI) for can-
cer immunotherapy (Leach et al., 1996). CTLA-4
blocking antibodies are now approved for treat-
ment of melanoma, renal cell carcinoma, colorectal
cancer, non-small-cell lung cancer, and several other
human cancers. Canine-specific CTLA-4 blocking
antibodies are currently under development and
their in vitro activity has been reported recently
(Mason et al., 2021). T cells expressing CTLA-4
are generally present in lymphoid tissues, which is
thought to be the primary site of action of CTLA-4
antibodies. Since CTLA-4 is also expressed by T
cells specific for antigens that are not related to
cancer, CTLA-4 antibodies can result in activation
of many more T cells than checkpoint molecule
antibodies that target PD-1 (see below). Thus, the
toxicity of CTLA-4 therapeutic antibodies is gener-
ally higher than that of PD-1-targeted antibodies,
with roughly equivalent antitumor activity.
PD -1 AND PD-L1 AS THERAPEUTIC TARGETS 	PD-1 is
a co-inhibitory checkpoint molecule expressed pri-
marily on the surface of activated T cells, NK cells,
and B cells (Patsoukis et al., 2020). Interaction of
PD-1 with PD-L1 (its primary ligand) expressed on
tumor cells, TAMs, DCs, and other stromal cells
inhibits a number of T-cell functions, including
proliferation and cytokine secretion, and promotes
T-cell apoptosis (Freeman et al., 2000; Dong et al.,
2002). The expression of both PD-1 on T cells
and PD-L1 on tumor cells and macrophages is
dynamic and strongly upregulated by inflamma-
tory cytokines including IFN-γ and TNF-α (Hartley
et al., 2017). The second PD-1 ligand, PD-L2, is
expressed constitutively at low levels by myeloid
cells and is thus not considered an attractive target
for checkpoint blockade. PD-1 serves as a key neg-
ative regulator of CD4 and CD8 T-cell responses
and normally protects the host from overexuberant
immune responses, a function that is underscored
by the development of severe autoimmunity in
PD-1-deficient mouse strains (Nishimura et al.,
1999, 2001). However, interaction of PD-1 with
PD-L1 significantly impairs antitumor immune
responses through multiple immune-suppressive
mechanisms. Blockade of the PD-1–PD-L1 inter-
action with anti-PD-1 or anti-PD-L1 antibodies
enhances antitumor immunity and has led to an
increase in TILs and impressive clinical responses
following monotherapy in human patients with
different tumor histologies including malignant
melanoma, non-small-cell lung carcinoma, and
renal cell carcinoma (Liu et al., 2021). However,
durable clinical responses are not observed in
all patients treated with PD-1 checkpoint antibod-
ies, leading to the development of multiple differ-
ent combination strategies with other ICI drugs
to improve overall response rates. These strategies
include combinations with CTLA-4, TIM-3, TIGIT,
and LAG-3 antibodies, and combined treatment
with ICI and cancer vaccines, CAR-T cell thera-
pies, RT, chemotherapy, and small-molecule inhibi-
tors. In veterinary medicine the use of checkpoint
inhibitors is in its infancy. Although several groups
have reported the development of anti-PD-1 and
anti-PD-L1 antibodies that can detect PD-1 and
PD-L1 respectively, there are only two reports of
the use of anti-PD-1 or anti-PD-L1 antibodies in
small trials in dogs (Maekawa et al., 2017; Igase
et al., 2020). Responses in these studies were
modest and it remains to be seen whether strati-
fication of patients based on TMB and/or PD-L1
expression on tumor cells or TIICs and/or combi-
nation with other immunotherapies will improve
response rates.
TIM -3, LAG -3, TIGIT AS ADDITIONAL CO - INHIBITORY
CHECKPOINT MOLECULE TARGETS 	The co-inhibitory
checkpoint molecules TIM-3, LAG-3, and TIGIT
present attractive targets for inhibitory antibodies
to relieve tumor immune suppression. Multiple
Phase I and II trials are currently underway in
human cancer patients to elucidate the true util-
ity of immunotherapies targeting these checkpoint
molecules, whether their efficacy is similar to that
observed with PD-1, PD-L1, and CTLA-4 antibod-
ies and whether their use in combination with
other checkpoint inhibitors may improve clinical
response.
Co-stimulatory molecules:
CD28, OX40, CD40, CD137
For 	every 	co-inhibitory 	checkpoint 	molecule
expressed by T cells and other immune effector
cells, there is at least one co-stimulatory molecule
counterpart. The more well-known molecules
include CD28, OX40, CD40, and CD137, the lat-
ter three of which are members of the TNF-receptor
superfamily of molecules. These molecules offer an
alternative mechanism for activation of effective
T-cell-mediated antitumor immunity using agonis-
tic antibodies. However, targeting of co-stimulatory
molecules can be a complex undertaking, and one

-- 155 of 258 --

potentially subject to greater risk than targeting
inhibitory receptors. For example, serious, fatal
toxicity was observed in early human trials of
CD28 agonistic antibodies, which illustrated the
potential dangers of the approach (Suntharalingam
et al., 2006). However, the newer checkpoint target
molecules (i.e., OX40, CD40, CD137) are primar-
ily expressed only by activated T cells or APCs and
clinical trials in human cancer patients thus far
have not demonstrated major safety signals. A
recent trial demonstrated that intratumoral deliv-
ery of an OX40-activating monoclonal antibody,
together with a TLR9 agonist, could deplete Tregs
locally and enhance tumor immunity in dogs with
oral melanoma and squamous cell carcinoma
receiving RT (Boss et al., 2022). As the develop-
ment of canine monoclonal antibodies becomes
more commonplace, agonistic antibodies such as
OX40 antibodies may find their way into the vet-
erinary oncologist’s armamentarium following
appropriate safety trials.
Inducers of immunogenic cell death
Radiation therapy
As a general principle, the most effective cancer
therapies will employ multiple different therapeutic
modalities used in strategic combinations. One
example is the combination of RT with immuno-
therapy. Depending on dose, timing, and fractiona-
tion, RT can induce systemic tumor immunity in
part by inducing ICD of tumor cells and by modu-
lating 	the TME 	(Portella 	and 	Scala, 2019;
Rodriguez-Ruiz et al., 2020). Critically, at present
there is no consensus on whether coarsely or finely
fractionated RT is more effective in eliciting antitu-
mor immunity, and the issue needs to be resolved
before routinely incorporating RT into overall
immune-based approaches to cancer. The effective-
ness of RT in generating systemic antitumor immu-
nity has been reported for a number of tumors in
humans, including impressive examples of distant
tumor regression known as the “abscopal effect”,
particularly in melanoma (D’Andrea and Reddy,
2020). Improving RT delivery to stimulate the
abscopal effect more consistently is a major focus
of ongoing RT studies. Numerous clinical trials in
human patients are currently in progress assessing
the effectiveness of combining RT with other
immunotherapeutic modalities, including local and
systemic delivery of checkpoint molecule blocking
(e.g., PD-1, PD-L1) or activating (e.g., OX40) anti-
bodies (Boss et al., 2022). Understanding how to
most effectively combine RT with concurrent
immunotherapy with respect to timing of adminis-
tration and dose, to leverage the effects of ICD and
induce potent synergistic effects, represents a piv-
otal challenge in improving patient outcomes
(Monjazeb et al., 2016; Hoopes et al., 2018).
However, it is likely that combination RT and
immunotherapy protocols will need to be opti-
mized for different cancer types and for different
immunotherapeutics.
Chemotherapy
Some commonly employed chemotherapy agents
(e.g., doxorubicin, cyclophosphamide, paclitaxel)
have been shown to induce ICD, which in turn
leads to induction of systemic antitumor immunity,
which augments the overall effectiveness of chemo-
therapy. Various mechanisms have been advanced
to further explain the immune-activating properties
of these chemotherapeutic agents. In the case of
doxorubicin, upregulation and/or secretion of cell
surface molecules (damage-associated molecular
patterns (DAMPs) such as calreticulin, HSP70, and
the high-mobility group box-1 (HMGB1) protein)
trigger tumor cell phagocytosis and activate DCs,
contributing to its observed immunogenic effects.
Similarly, cyclophosphamide has been shown to
induce immunogenic tumor apoptosis character-
ized by the release of calreticulin and HMGB1, and
in an IFN type I dependent manner, cyclophospha-
mide promotes expansion of CD8a+ DCs (in mice)
that efficiently take up apoptotic tumor cells and
cross-present TAAs to CD8+ T cells, resulting in
enhanced antitumor immunity (Schiavoni et al.,
2011).
Combination immunotherapy with inducers
of immunogenic cell death
The challenges in veterinary oncology will include
developing combination RT plus immunotherapy
or chemotherapy plus immunotherapy protocols
based on optimized dosing and timing of delivery
for maximum synergy. Moreover, optimal protocols
will likely need to be developed for specific tumor
types. Given the similarity in chemotherapeutic
agents and RT protocols for human and veterinary
patients, it is likely that the veterinary field will
extrapolate best practice approaches used in human
140 	N. Mason and S. Dow

141	Cancer Immunotherapy
clinical trials as a starting point for exploring com-
bination therapy protocols for canine trials.
However, further optimization is expected to be
needed and it remains to be seen whether human
studies can accurately inform canine combination
therapy trial regimens and vice versa.
Assessing Response to Immunotherapy
Development of effective new immunotherapy pro-
tocols will require more than simply measuring
tumor responses. Increasingly, use of sophisticated
biologic immune endpoints is viewed as an essen-
tial tool in immunotherapy drug development. Use
of such immune endpoint biomarkers is much fur-
ther advanced in human oncology, but new tools
are being developed to evaluate the same biomark-
ers in veterinary immuno-oncology and these will
increase the value of canine studies for comparative
work.
In contrast to tumor responses to conventional
chemotherapeutics, tumor responses to immuno-
therapy can have unique attributes that have
prompted 	a 	revision 	of 	traditional 	RECIST
(Response Evaluation Criteria in Solid Tumors)
guidance for evaluating responses to immunothera-
pies. Of particular importance is the phenomenon
of delayed tumor responses to immunotherapy,
preceded in some cases by apparent increase in
tumor size due to immune infiltrates and inflamma-
tion. Thus, with conventional RECIST criteria
many of these early immune responses would be
classified as progressive disease and treatment
halted. However, recognition of this effect, and the
often delayed clinical response to immunotherapy,
has led to the development of immune-related
RECIST (irRECIST) criteria and immune-modified
RECIST (imRECIST) criteria for use in immuno-
therapy clinical trials (Wolchok et al., 2009; Hodi
et al., 2018). Debate exists as to which criteria are
superior; however, irRECIST criteria are most read-
ily applied to the evaluation of responses in meta-
static disease, where numbers and sizes of tumor
nodules can be readily assessed over time.
Assessing biologic activity of cancer
immunotherapies in preclinical
or clinical studies
The effective development of new cancer immuno-
therapies relies heavily on a comprehensive under-
standing of their immunologic mechanisms of
action, as well as on the development of assays to
monitor immune and tumor responses and to pre-
dict which patients are most likely to respond, or
not, to a particular immunotherapy. A variety of
different immunologic tools and assays can now be
employed. A full discussion of immune assays is
beyond the scope of this chapter; however, a few
key assays discussed here should be considered in
clinical trial design where possible, depending on
the specific immune pathways being targeted.
In the case of antibody therapeutics (e.g., check-
point inhibitors, TAA-targeting antibodies), target
binding both in vitro and in vivo should be demon-
strated, along with evidence of biologic activity
such as activation or blockade of the relevant target
pathway or elimination of the target antigen-
expressing cells (e.g., B-cell aplasia with a CD20-
targeting antibody). For tumor vaccines, immune
responses to be monitored should ideally include
measures of cellular immune responses by assays
such as ELISpot, ELISA, TCR clonotyping, or gene
expression profiling, in addition to humoral
immune responses, before and after therapy.
However, it is also acknowledged that cellular
assays are technically challenging, and studies
should be designed with this in mind.
For evaluation of CAR-T cell therapies, valida-
tion of target engagement and evidence of tumor
antigen-specific cytotoxic activity are essential.
Validation is typically performed using target anti-
gen-expressing cell lines (engineered or natural
expressors) and primary T cells isolated, engi-
neered, and expanded from peripheral blood of
healthy donor animals. In addition, target expres-
sion modulation should be evaluated over time in
treated patients to the extent possible since tumor
antigen-escape variants are a common cause of
relapse in human CAR-T patients with hematologic
malignancies. Treated dogs should be monitored
during trials for evidence of cytokine-mediated
toxicity (so-called “cytokine release syndrome”)
using cytokine multiplexing assays to allow meas-
urement of multiple cytokines from single blood
samples (Panjwani et al., 2020). More in-depth
assessment of T-cell responses and functionality can
also be achieved using transcriptomic analysis tech-
nologies, including RNA sequencing and single-cell
RNA sequencing (sc-RNAseq). The use of sc-RNAseq
has been reported to assess NK-cell responses in
dogs, and to characterize T-cell responses in dogs
with OSA (Gingrich et al., 2021; D.T. Ammons,
R.A. Harris, L.S. Hopkins, J. Kurihara, K. Weishaar,

-- 157 of 258 --

and S. Dow, 2023, unpublished results). Utilization
of these technologies addresses many of the current
limitations imposed on analysis of canine and feline
immune responses by limited antibody availability,
and in the future they are likely to be used much
more commonly.
For immunotherapies that rely on induction of
innate immune responses, the innate immune
response elicited should be interrogated fully in vitro,
using newer immunologic tools, including multi-
plexed cytokine assays and bulk or single-cell
immune 	transcriptome 	analysis. Phagocytosis
assays and oxidative burst analysis may also be
performed to assess innate immune function at
baseline, which may be valuable to screen and/or
stratify patients. In vivo monitoring of responses to
nonspecific immunotherapies should also include
cytokine measurement in serum or plasma, along
with measurement of immune cell activation in vivo,
including analysis of circulating leukocyte responses
by flow cytometry, RNA sequencing, or NanoString
analysis.
New tools for cancer immunotherapy studies
should also include predictive measures of tumor
response, based on information gleaned from
human immune oncology trials. Thus, where pos-
sible, tumors should be profiled by immunohisto-
chemistry and/or flow cytometry to assess tumor
immune infiltrates. For example, tumor responses
to immunotherapy may correlate with the density
of T-cell infiltrates in tumor tissues, or inversely
correlate with the density of tumor macrophage
infiltrates and Tregs. Digital spatial profiling of
tumor tissues combines high-plex spatial profiling
of RNA and proteins and enables deep interroga-
tion of cellular interactions, tissue heterogeneity,
and biologic responses to therapy. This technology
is actively being developed for interrogation of
canine tumor tissues and will likely become an
important tool in understanding response to ther-
apy. Features of the tumor itself may also be predic-
tive of responses to immunotherapy, including MSI
(determined by sequencing of PCR-amplified
microsatellite sequences) and TMB determined by
WES or targeted next-generation sequencing (NGS)
panels, or baseline immune infiltrates (i.e., “hot” or
“cold” tumors) determined by immune transcrip-
tomic profiling with NanoString technology and
bulk or single-cell RNA sequencing. Tumor and
TIIC expression of co-inhibitory checkpoint mole-
cules such as PD-L1 and PD-1 that correlate with
response to checkpoint inhibitors in human cancer
patients will now be more routinely assessed in
canine patients as diagnostic and therapeutic canine
checkpoint antibodies become available.
Veterinary Immuno-oncology:
The Next 5 Years
The field of cancer immunotherapy has rapidly
advanced over the past decade, and veterinary
immuno-oncology is following that lead. Using key
milestones in the development of human immuno-
oncology as a guide to predict the future of canine
and feline immuno-oncology, we can expect major
breakthroughs in the use of therapeutic antibodies
and the use of ACTs, which are anticipated to
significantly improve the prognosis for several
major cancers of dogs, and within the next few
years.
Therapeutic antibodies in
immuno-oncology
Therapeutic monoclonal antibodies such as rituxi-
mab (anti-CD20), bevacizumab (anti-VEGF), pem-
brolizumab (anti-PD-1), and bi-specific antibodies
such as blinatumomab (anti-CD3-anti-CD19) have
revolutionized the treatment of human cancers
over the last quarter of a century. Importantly, anti-
bodies targeting these and other tractable target
molecules are now in advanced stages of develop-
ment for veterinary immuno-oncology, and their
introduction to the field will usher in major
changes in the management of cancer in dogs (and
eventually cats). Therapeutic antibodies engage a
number of different immunological mechanisms to
eliminate tumor cells or alter the function of
immune cells. Antibodies designed to eliminate
cancer cells directly (e.g., anti-CD19 or anti-CD20
antibodies) bind to the surface expressed target
antigen, and the Fc portion of the immunoglobin G
(IgG) molecule recruits and activates complement
leading to target cell death via complement’s mem-
brane attack complex, and engages with Fc recep-
tors expressed on macrophages and NK cells,
which triggers antibody-dependent cell-mediated
cytotoxicity (ADCC) and tumor cell destruction.
Newer antibodies such as those targeting check-
point molecules act via a different mechanism and
are specifically designed to avoid complement acti-
vation and triggering ADCC. For example, anti-
bodies targeting co-inhibitory checkpoint molecules
142 	N. Mason and S. Dow

-- 158 of 258 --

143	Cancer Immunotherapy
such as PD-1 are designed to block the interaction
between PD-1 and PD-L1 which regulates T-cell
exhaustion. Anti-PD1 and anti-PD-L1 antibodies
can rescue T cells from progressive immune
exhaustion and restore their antitumor function-
ality. By contrast, therapeutic antibodies targeting
co-stimulatory checkpoint molecules such as CD28
and OX40 are designed as activating antibodies
that bind and trigger T-cell activation and promote
T-cell responses against TAAs. Furthermore, agon-
istic antibodies against co-stimulatory molecules
expressed by APCs such as CD40 have been shown
to license APCs to both promote antitumor T-cell
activation and reeducate macrophages to eliminate
tumor stroma.
Therapeutic antibodies can also be designed to
bind and neutralize cytokines in tumor tissues or in
circulation (e.g., antibodies to neutralize immune-
suppressive cytokines such as IL-10 or TGF-β) or
neutralize secreted effector molecules (e.g., argin-
ase) that downmodulate cancer immune responses.
In other iterations of antibody-mediated immuno-
therapy, therapeutic monoclonal antibodies can
also be “armed” by covalently linking biologic or
chemical toxins to their Fc domain, such that the
cytotoxic moiety can be delivered specifically to the
target 	cell 	(antibody–drug 	conjugates). 	This
approach reduces off-target side effects and enables
the targeted delivery of higher doses of cytotoxic
agents safely in vivo.
The use of therapeutic antibodies in veterinary
oncology has been delayed in part due to the lack
of available cross-reactive antibodies (Jubala et al.,
2005). An 	earlier 	impediment, 	now 	largely
addressed, was the necessity to create fully canine,
or nearly fully canine, antibodies to avoid the
development of neutralizing anti-drug antibodies
that can significantly reduce the half-life of the
therapeutic antibody and render it ineffective. With
the advent of technologies such as scFv phage dis-
play libraries, antibody caninization, in silico
design, and the genetic engineering of mice that
harbor canine immunoglobulin loci, the generation
of specific therapeutic antibodies with reduced or
absent immunogenicity against canine (and feline)
target antigens is now a possibility (Braganza et al.,
2011; Lascelles et al., 2015). One clear example of
the feasibility of generating cost-effective monoclo-
nal antibodies for companion animals is the canine
anti-IL-31 antibody (CytoPoint), which has quickly
become a mainstay in the management of atopic
skin disease and pruritis.
Based on the CytoPoint precedent, new antibod-
ies are likely to be introduced into the oncology
armamentarium in the near future. Indeed, prelimi-
nary work both in vitro and in vivo in mice and
dogs with antibodies or antibody fragments
directed against the B-cell marker CD20 (Ito et al.,
2015; Rue et al., 2015; Jain et al., 2016; Weiskopf
et al., 2016), the checkpoint molecules PD-1 (Coy
et al., 2017; Nemoto et al., 2018; Choi et al., 2020;
Igase et al., 2020), PD-L1 (Maekawa et al., 2017),
CTLA-4 (Mason et al., 2021), c-KIT expressed
(London et al., 2017), VEGF (Michishita et al.,
2013; Adelfinger et al., 2015; Michishita et al.,
2016), and epidermal growth factor receptor
(EGFR) (Singer et al., 2014) have been published
and it is anticipated that these antibodies or deriva-
tives thereof will be the first to enter the veterinary
oncology market.
Adoptive cell therapy in veterinary oncology
The field of ACT for canine cancer immunotherapy
is rapidly expanding both in the number of differ-
ent cellular platforms being used and in the com-
plexity of genetic engineering to target tumor
antigens and to provide allogeneic, off-the-shelf
products that will be more cost-effective, more
readily available, and have improved cellular fit-
ness in comparison with current autologous prod-
ucts. Results of several small pilot studies in dogs
are starting to show early signs of clinical activity
of ACT approaches, although optimization of
manufacturing protocols and preconditioning regi-
mens will likely be necessary to further improve
outcomes. For a glimpse into the near future of
ACT in canine cancers, a Phase I trial using mul-
tiple doses of allogeneic TGF-β imprinted (resistant)
NK cells administered intravenously in combina-
tion with carboplatin in dogs with appendicular
OSA has recently been initiated (Foltz et al., 2018).
Furthermore, additional CAR constructs including
those that target HER2/neu, GD2, B7-H3, and
IL-13Rα2 are also under investigation for CAR-T
cell therapy of solid cancers including OSA and
high-grade glioma in dogs. Creative new strategies
including CRISPR/Cas9 technology are under
investigation to enable the development of allogen-
eic, off-the-shelf CAR-T cell products for use in
dogs and the use of xenogenic (human) edited
CD20-targeting CAR-T cells in dogs with relapsed
BCL is already being evaluated in two separate
clinical trials at academic institutions. Thus, significant

-- 159 of 258 --

advances in the field of veterinary immuno-
oncology are anticipated in the next 5–10 years that
aim to induce lasting antitumor immunity and bring
complete and durable remissions to veterinary
patients with solid and hematologic malignancies.

Fig. 9. 	Gene Editing: No Longer Science Fiction.

9 	Gene Editing and Gene Therapy in
Oncology
WESLEY A. WIERSON1*, ALEX M. A BEL1, ELIZABETH L.
S IEGLER2, STEPHEN C. EKKER1,3, CHAD M. JOHANNES1,4,
SAAD S. KENDERIAN1,2, AND JONATHAN P. MOCHEL1,4,5*
1LifEngine Animal Health Laboratories, Rochester, Minnesota, USA; 2Mayo Clinic,
Rochester, Minnesota, USA; 3Mayo Clinic Cancer Center, Rochester, Minnesota, USA;
4Iowa State University,Ames, Iowa, USA; 5University of Georgia,Athens, Georgia, USA
Introduction
With rapid advances in gene editing and gene ther-
apy technologies, the development of genetic-, cell-,
or protein-based cures to disease is no longer the
realm of science fiction but that of today’s practice.
The impact of these technologies is rapidly bringing
them to the veterinary market both as enhanced
therapeutics and toward modeling their outcomes
for translational application. Simply put, gene edit-
ing enables scientists to modify an organism’s DNA
a priori through the use of site-specific DNA-
targeting tools like clustered regularly interspaced
short palindromic repeats and CRISPR-associated
protein 9 (CRISPR/Cas9) (Fig. 9). Gene therapy is a
broader definition that encompasses the addition of
exogenous genetic materials into specific cells to
correct a genetic defect. More precisely, the US Food
and Drug Administration (FDA) defines gene ther-
apy as “a technique that modifies a person’s
genes to treat or cure disease” by: (i) replacing a
disease-causing gene with a healthy copy of the gene;
(ii) inactivating a disease-causing gene that was not
functioning properly; or (iii) introducing a new or
modified gene into the body to help treat a disease.
In some instances, this can be accomplished through
direct transfer of DNA or RNA into target cells of
interest or more broadly through gene editing.
While gene therapy is possible through the simple
addition of genetic information into cells of interest,
gene editing allows the genome to be reprogrammed
intentionally through the deletion of diseased alleles,
reconstitution of wild-type (WT) sequence, or tar-
geted integration of exogenous DNA to impart new
function. Cells can be removed from the body,
altered, and reinfused, or edited in vivo. Indeed,
manufacturing and production efficiencies in gene
editing and gene therapy in the 21st century have
brought the therapeutic potential of in vitro and
in vivo reprogrammed cells to the front lines of
therapeutic intervention (Brooks et al., 2016). For
example, chimeric antigen receptor (CAR)-T cell
therapy is revolutionizing hematologic cancer care
in humans and is being translated to canines by us
and others, and gene therapy trials are ongoing for
mitral valve disease in dogs.
Gene editing and gene therapy are increasingly
used in the human clinic today and their applica-
tion in companion animals is beginning to emerge.
About 700 monogenic diseases have been reported
in various dog breeds, with at least 200 of these
diseases harboring known causative mutations
(Switonski, 2020). About 400 of these spontaneous
diseases in dogs are considered potential models for
human disorders (https://omia.org/home, accessed
22 February 2023). This makes the dog a particu-
larly attractive animal model for accelerated com-
mercial deployment of gene editing and gene
therapy candidates with applications in cancer,
hemophilia, lysosomal storage diseases, ophthalmol-
ogy, immune-mediated disorders, muscular dystrophy,

and others (Acland et al., 2001, 2005). These indi-
cations may share genetic drivers, physiology, and
presentation with their human counterparts. This
creates bidirectional value where, on one hand,
human experience and research may de-risk similar
innovations in veterinary patients and, on the other,
accelerated application of the underlying therapeu-
tic in veterinary medicine can answer translational
questions not effectively answered in preclinical
studies or even human trials. Ultimately, regulatory
incentives to develop parallel (veterinary and
human) drug development programs would present
an opportunity to streamline, accelerate, and
improve pharmaceutical research and development
in veterinary and human oncology.
In cancer research, gene editing and gene therapy
applications in canines have garnered considerable
interest since, in contrast to mice, cancers develop
spontaneously in dogs (i.e., without genetic manip-
ulation) and in the context of an intact immune
system with a syngeneic host and tumor microenvir-
onment (Gordon et al., 2009). As more information
on the dog genome is being released, multiple stud-
ies have demonstrated significant homologies
between canine and human cancer-associated
genes, including those encoding MET, mTOR, KIT,
and TRAF3 (Paoloni and Khanna, 2008). As such,
biologic and genomic similarities between canine
and human cancer provide an impetus for parallel
development of novel drug candidates (including
gene therapy and gene editing) in canine and
human clinical trials (Schneider et al., 2018).
Specifically, ample literature has established simi-
larities between the pathologic, biologic, immuno-
phenotypic, and genetic components of diffuse
large B-cell lymphoma (DLBCL) in dogs and
humans (Richards et al., 2013; Mochel et al.,
2019). Based on these similarities, preliminary
proof-of-concept studies from Dr Nicola Mason’s
group are the first public reports of CAR-T cell
therapy being used in companion animals (Panjwani
et al., 2016).
Besides applications in companion dogs, descrip-
tions of gene editing in veterinary medicine have
been reported in various species, including horses
and cats. In horses, CRISPR/Cas9 was used to cor-
rect a deleterious point mutation associated with
glycogen branching enzyme deficiency in primary
fibroblasts (Pinzon-Arteaga et al., 2020). Likewise,
lentivirus (LV)-delivered CRISPR/Cas9-directed
gene editing was used in a series of in vitro experi-
ments to modulate the proviral load and production
of virions of the feline immunodeficiency virus
(FIV) (Murphy et al., 2020). In that proof-of-
concept study, the authors reported a reduction of
cell-free viral RNA in gene-edited cells relative to
control. The reduced infectious potential of this new
construct was later confirmed by infecting feline
naïve T cells with cell-free FIV harvested from FIV-
infected and CRISPR/Cas9 LV-treated cells.
Our knowledge on the role of genetic variation
in disease continues to evolve and developments in
the Dog Genome Annotation Project (DoGA) are
rapidly aiding in comparative medicine efforts.
Advances in DoGA combined with faster, cheaper,
and more efficient gene editing and gene therapy
methods will lead to even greater emphasis on
translational modeling and parallel drug develop-
ment efforts using spontaneous dog diseases. In this
chapter, through a translational lens based on suc-
cesses and failures in human medicine, we will
present imminent application of gene therapy and
gene editing in companion animals; how we got to
the use of gene editing and gene therapy in com-
panion animals; how these technologies may bring
curative outcomes to canines with cancer and other
diseases; and how the future of companion animal
medicine as a whole will undoubtedly include
genetic cures to disease.
How We Got Here: A Journey
from Past to Present
In considering how gene therapy and gene editing
are now mentioned alongside routine veterinary
medicine applications, one must understand how
abrupt and revolutionary the advances in these
enabling technologies have been. Advances in the
design, safety, and transduction efficiencies of gam-
maretroviral- and lentiviral-based gene delivery in
the mid-1990s and early 2000s were paramount to
the pioneering study of CD19-targeting CAR-T
cells in Phase I human trials in 2009 (Hucks and
Rheingold, 2019) and the plethora of ongoing gene
and cell therapy FDA approvals and trials using
viral vectors (Shahryari et al., 2019). Moreover,
recent analyses demonstrated that the cost for a
single pair of the first readily reengineered, modu-
lar gene editor, zinc-finger nucleases (ZFNs), was
US$25,000 as recently as 2012 (WareJoncas et al.,
2018). Today, generating gene editing reagents like
CRISPR/Cas9 in academic labs costs well under
US$100 per experiment. This substantial reduction
in operating cost, democratizing access to enabling
156 	W.A. Wierson et al.

-- 172 of 258 --

157	Gene Editing and Gene Therapy in Oncology
technologies and enhancing the efficiency of desired
outcomes, has led to over 22,000 peer-reviewed
publications mentioning CRISPR/Cas9 and over
29,000 peer-reviewed publications mentioning
gene therapy in the last decade (PubMed search,
January 2021). Here, we summarize seminal stud-
ies that have led to modern-day gene therapy and
gene editing, and their current applications in basic
research and translational science, emphasizing dog
models and/or applications where appropriate.
Modern gene therapy
Gene therapy was introduced in biomedical sciences
as early as 1972 by Theodore Friedmann and
Richard Roblin after Stanfield Rogers came up with
the idea to replace defective DNA for the treatment
of inherited diseases (Friedmann and Roblin, 1972).
While eukaryotic viral vectors were developed from
DNA viruses in animals, none of these viruses pro-
vide solutions to recombine the viral genome into
the host genome. Thus, the idea for gene therapy
was not realized for decades due to limiting tech-
nologies for the introduction of foreign DNA into
cells. In 1981, Shimotohno and Temin reported the
first viral recombination of foreign DNA into mam-
malian cells using a retrovirus (RV); however, the
production of these RVs was inefficient, limiting
wide adoption of the technology (Shimotohno and
Temin, 1981). A pioneering study in 1984 demon-
strated the first efficient technology for production
of infectious virions and subsequent transfer of
foreign DNA into mammalian cells using engi-
neered RV vector systems (Cepko et al., 1984),
although the cost and scale of this approach did not
allow broader use of the technology.
As research into using viruses as DNA delivery
vectors continued to progress, warranted apprehen-
sion arose regarding the use of these infectious
agents in the clinic. Therefore, modern gene therapy
approaches that rely on viral vectors for DNA deliv-
ery utilize highly engineered viral particles wherein
only a minimal amount of viral genome is retained.
Nonreplicative and tissue-specific viruses have been
developed using such genetic engineering approaches,
which continue to drive innovations in safety, qual-
ity control, and efficacy of modern gene therapy.
Within the past 50 years, technological innova-
tions in recombinant DNA technology have rapidly
propelled advancements in gene therapy. Along
with continuous gains in our understanding of
molecular genetics and gene regulation brought
about by the genetic revolution, methods to safely
and efficiently deliver foreign genes into cells
remains an active area of research. In particular, the
development of viral vectors as gene delivery sys-
tems capable of stably integrating genetic cargo
into the genome has shown clinical efficacy as years
of incremental advances in the production and
efficiency of retroviral recombination led to the
first National Institutes of Health (NIH)-sanctioned
gene therapy clinical research study in 1991 (Ferrari
et al., 1991). In this pioneering study, two children
afflicted with adenosine deaminase (ADA) defi-
ciency were given retroviral transduced T cells
containing a functional copy of the ADA gene to
rescue a severe combined immunodeficiency (SCID)
phenotype.
Gene therapy-based interventions utilizing both
viral and nonviral vectors in humans have contin-
ued to progress over the past 30 years with impor-
tant implications for veterinary medicine. Here we
will discuss the foundational biology of RVs, LVs,
adenoviruses (AdVs), and adeno-associated viruses
(AAVs) with special emphasis on the technological
innovations and genetic interventions that have
allowed these infectious agents to become some of
the most widely utilized gene delivery systems for
gene therapy. Examples of nonviral methods of
gene delivery will be briefly discussed in the latter
portion of this section.
Viral gene delivery
RNA VIRUS VECTORS: RETROVIRUSES AND LENTIVIRUSES
RNA virus vectors derived from RVs were one of
the first viral delivery systems used for gene ther-
apy and remain among the most used today. They
are represented by a large family of enveloped
viruses encompassing 7–12 kb plus-sense RNA
genomes. LVs, including human immunodeficiency
virus (HIV), represent a class of RV often used for
biomedical research and require the same basic
components as other RVs for successful cellular
entry and viral genome integration (Verma and
Weitzman, 2005).
To employ the natural ability of RVs to facilitate
gene transfer for either ex vivo or in vivo gene
therapy applications, notable modifications to the
viral genome were required to maximize safety and
ensure efficacy before clinical benefit could be
evaluated. RVs bring natural tissue tropism, like
HIV’s propensity to infect T cells, and are replicative
in nature. Accordingly, first-generation lentiviral

-- 173 of 258 --

vectors were modified to include the envelope pro-
tein of vesicular stomatitis virus, VSV-G, which
functions to broaden cellular tropism by targeting
the low-density lipoprotein (LDL) receptor that is
ubiquitously expressed (Finkelshtein et al., 2013).
However, these first-generation vectors retained
much of the original HIV genome and warranted
broad safety concerns. Thus, known virulence fac-
tors were removed from the viral genome to pro-
duce second-generation lentiviral vectors (Vannucci
et al., 2013). Third-generation lentiviral vectors
were then developed to further improve safety
wherein multiple modifications were incorporated
to eliminate the possibility of producing replication-
competent LVs (Dull et al., 1998).
DNA VIRUS VECTORS : ADENOVIRUSES AND ADENO-
ASSOCIATED VIRUS 	AdVs and AAVs are the most
prominent DNA viruses used for modern gene
therapy applications. Although both viruses encap-
sulate a DNA genome within a nonenveloped ico-
sahedral protein capsid, the AdV genome consists
of ~36 kb double-strand DNA (dsDNA) while
AAV possesses a much smaller genome, ~4.7 kb,
and comprises single-strand DNA (ssDNA). Similar
to RVs and LVs, plasmids encoding essential viral
components can be introduced into packaging
cell lines to generate AdV and AAV vectors for
transgene delivery; however, critical differences in
virus replicative cycles necessitate unique modifica-
tions for their production and implementation as
gene therapy agents (Verma and Weitzman, 2005).
The human AdV family contains over 50 unique
serotypes with a wide tissue tropism. The majority
of these viruses utilize the Coxsackie-adenovirus
receptor for cellular attachment (Philipson and
Pettersson, 2004) and internalization is facilitated
through an interaction with cellular integrin αv
receptors (Wickham et al., 1993). AdV DNA is not
normally integrated into the host genome (Pombo
et al., 1994), so in terms of gene therapy applica-
tions, only transient transgene expression can be
achieved with AdV vector systems. To ensure safety,
essential viral replication genes were deleted in the
first-generation AdV vectors that could incorporate
transgenes ranging from 4.7 to 4.9 kb (Bett et al.,
1993), and transgenes up to 8.3 kb were later
cloned into second-generation AdV vectors wherein
additional viral genes had been deleted. Although it
is noteworthy that recent developments towards
third-generation AdV vectors have further enhanced
the potential for efficient gene delivery and long-term
transgene expression, high immunogenicity remains
a hurdle that must be overcome before AdV vectors
are to be widely used for gene therapy in vivo
(Crystal, 2014).
AAV serotype 2, a nonpathogenic human parvo-
virus, is the best characterized AAV vector to date.
AAV2 utilizes ubiquitously expressed heparan sul-
fate proteoglycan for cell attachment (Summerford
and Samulski, 1998) and membrane internalization
is facilitated by either the fibroblast growth factor
receptor or integrin αvβ5 (Qing et al., 1999;
Summerford et al., 1999).
In gene therapy studies, AAV vectors have dem-
onstrated transduction in the muscle, retina, brain,
liver, and lungs where a slow rise in transgene
expression plateaued after a few weeks in vivo
(Xiao et al., 1996). Although AAV vectors have
been successfully used for gene therapy applica-
tions in vivo in animal models, a relatively small
transgene capacity of ~4 kb and a high prevalence
of neutralizing antibodies directed against the viral
capsid proteins represent significant limitations
(Verma and Weitzman, 2005).
Nonviral methods of gene delivery
It is important to note that nonviral methods
indeed exist for delivery of proteins and nucleic
acids into cells, however they are not typically con-
sidered part of the “gene therapy” class, as they are
all currently utilized ex vivo for cell programming.
Although viral vectors are currently the most effi-
cient approach used to deliver DNA cargo into
host cells in vivo, nonviral approaches are becom-
ing much more common due to a better potential
safety profile and technical advantages in use and
production. From a biosafety perspective, viral
vectors can be highly immunogenic and lead to
adverse inflammatory reactions in patients such
that, in 1999, the first gene therapy-related fatality
was reported in a clinical trial due to an inflamma-
tory reaction in response to an AdV vector
(Lehrman, 1999). A phenomenon known as “inser-
tional mutagenesis”, wherein the chromosomal
insertion of viral DNA unintentionally results in
cellular transformation by either disrupting the
expression of a tumor suppressor gene or activating
an oncogene, represents another potential safety
concern regarding the use of viral vectors in gene
therapy. Additionally, as viral vector-mediated inte-
gration into the genome can occur at random
loci, each individual engineered cell is theoretically
158 	W.A. 	Wierson 	et al.

159	Gene Editing and Gene Therapy in Oncology
different. Ultimately, this leads to heterogeneity of
the resulting therapy with potential consequences
resulting from differential expression of the cargo
gene. For these reasons, nonviral vectors are widely
considered to be a safer alternative (Ramamoorth
and Narvekar, 2015) and, due to advances in nano-
technology, in vivo applications for nonviral deliv-
ery systems have recently been realized in the context
of gene therapy (El-Sayed and Kamel, 2020).
The flexibility of nonviral delivery systems is a
notable advantage as they can be used to introduce
various types of nucleic acids into cells including
chemically synthesized small DNA molecules (oli-
godeoxynucleotides), large DNA molecules (plas-
mid DNA), various RNA molecules such as
ribozymes, small interfering RNAs (siRNAs), and
mRNAs, and even proteins directly into cells.
Although many nucleic acids can be passively deliv-
ered to cells via endocytosis, physical methods of
gene delivery can help facilitate the introduction of
genetic material into cells by temporarily disrupt-
ing the cell membrane using physical forces.
Common physical methods of gene delivery include
microinjection, electroporation, sonoporation,
particle 	bombardment, 	and 	magnetofection
(Ramamoorth and Narvekar, 2015). Chemical car-
riers can also be used to deliver nucleic acids into
cells. These delivery systems are most commonly
made of a nucleic acid complexed with either cati-
onic lipids (lipoplexes), cationic polymers (poly-
plexes), or a combination of cationic lipids and
polymers (lipopolyplexes) (Midoux et al., 2009).
These chemical complexes function to protect
encapsulated nucleic acids from degradation and
enhance their intracellular uptake via electrostatic
interactions with glycoproteins and proteoglycans
on the cell membrane. Nucleic acid complexes may
also influence intracellular trafficking of nucleic
acids. For instance, the cationic polymer polyethyl-
enimine (PEI) disrupts endosomal membranes
resulting in the translocation of the complexed
nucleic acid into the cytosol and cationic peptides
comprised of basic residues, such as lysine and/or
arginine, can be employed to target specific cell
surface receptors or provide nuclear localization
signals to facilitate the nuclear entry of cargo DNA
(Al-Dosari and Gao, 2009).
Modern gene editing
Gene editing allows the mutation or alteration of
DNA at specific locations in the genome a priori
(Yeh et al., 2019). Gene editing can be used as a
basic scientific tool to heighten understanding of
disease pathophysiology using cell systems and
animal models, including complex disease like can-
cer, as well as monogeneic disorders such as cystic
fibrosis, hemophilia, sickle cell disease, heart dis-
ease, and HIV infection (Doudna, 2020). Multiple
approaches to gene editing have been developed in
the 21st century, but the crux of the technology
requires the ability to direct enzymatic activity to a
chosen locus in the genome. To achieve this, scien-
tists use “programmable nucleases” that induce
DNA damage in the form of a double-strand break
or nick at specific loci in the genome. Whereas gene
editing is the broader concept, programmable
nucleases are the critical tool for the modern devel-
opment of cell-based therapies and gene therapies.
Programmable nuclease-induced DNA double-
strand breaks can result in random mutations
around the break, specific alterations of endogen-
ous base pairs using homology templates, or the
targeted integration of exogenous DNA via an
engineered donor template.
What makes programmable nucleases so power-
ful is their ability to induce DNA repair at their
target sites, allowing scientists to rewrite the genetic
code at these genomic loci. Although oversimplified,
an effective analogy converts the genome to a word
document, the nucleases to a mouse cursor, and
donor DNA templates to a keyboard. Scientists can
“click” the genome, and “delete” or “rewrite” the
paragraph surrounding the cursor. Sometimes
referred to as “genome writing”, this technology
gives scientists endless possibility toward inducing
targeted mutations, correcting genetic defects, or
giving cells an ability to perform functions that
nature did not evolve (Doudna, 2020).
Brief history of gene editing tools
Modern gene editing ideals can be traced back
to seminal works by Dr Mario Capecchi and
Dr Maria Jasin. Dr Capecchi, who later won the
2007 Nobel Prize in Physiology and Medicine for
his work, pioneered strategies using the DNA repair
pathway of homologous recombination (HR) to
specifically engineer mouse embryonic stem cells
and mouse models using targeted DNA integration
(Thomas and Capecchi, 1987). Dr Jasin’s pioneer-
ing discovery demonstrated that targeted DNA
integration, i.e., the addition of exogenous DNA to
a locus of interest through homology-directed

-- 175 of 258 --

repair (HDR), can be stimulated 100–1000 times
over Capecchi’s work by causing a DNA double-
strand break at the locus of interest in the presence
of a repair template (Rouet et al., 1994). This find-
ing has served as a seminal discovery in the field of
gene editing. However, the nuclease used in this
case, I-SceI, is a large restriction enzyme whose
endogenous DNA-binding activity cannot be repro-
grammed to target DNA outside of its restriction
site, as is possible with modern programmable
nucleases like transcription activator-like effector
nucleases (TALENs) (Joung and Sander, 2013) and
CRISPR systems (Jinek et al., 2012). ZFNs, as well
as some homing endonucleases like I-CreI (MacLeod
et al., 2017), predate TALENs and are used today in
clinical trials (Tebas et al., 2014), but limitations in
their genomic targeting range and expense to engin-
eer generally relegate them to use in industry set-
tings and they will not be discussed here.
TALENs were invented in 2010 by Bogdanove,
Voytas, and colleagues (Christian et al., 2010),
after fusing the FokI nuclease to a bacterial tran-
scription factor, called a TAL effector. In nature,
TAL effectors evolved to bind to promoters and
activate host genes in plant–pathogen interactions
(Moscou and Bogdanove, 2009). TAL effectors rely
on highly conserved, modular repeats containing
34–35 amino acid loops repeated 12–20 times,
with two amino acid residues in each loop specify-
ing near 1:1 nucleotide binding. Thus, through the
addition of the FokI nuclease, individual TALENs
can be engineered to bind short stretches of DNA
to induce a DNA double-strand break. The FokI
used is an obligate heterodimer that requires
another TALEN to be supplied to the target site
spaced 12–20 bp opposite of the first. TALENs
require relatively complex, multi-day cloning reac-
tions to engineer a single TALEN pair for gene
editing. Even still, TALENs have been used to tar-
get DNA breaks, inducing mutations, or used for
exogenous gene integration in basic research, trans-
lational science, plant biotechnology, and clinical
settings for a decade.
The most widely adopted programmable DNA-
binding agent, and 2020 Nobel Prize of Biochemistry
winning technology, is called CRISPR/Cas9, short
for clustered regularly interspaced short palindro-
mic repeats and CRISPR-associated protein 9.
Evolved as a bacterial immune system to catalog
and resist bacteriophage, CRISPR systems are now
utilized to target DNA double-strand breaks, DNA
nicks, targeted nucleotide edits, or exogenous gene
integrations to precise loci in genes of interest on a
routine basis. While TALENs and ZFNs require the
engineering of entirely new proteins to target differ-
ent genes, the power of CRISPR systems is that the
genomic target site is specified by a short, ~20 bp
RNA molecule (called a “guide RNA” or gRNA)
that, with the help of Cas enzyme DNA melting, is
able to bind 1:1 to a homologous match through
simple RNA–DNA base pairing. Engineering
CRISPR to bind new genomic target sites is thus as
simple as in vitro transcription of gRNAs specifying
a new target site or ordering an RNA primer from
a nucleic acid synthesis company. While CRISPR/
Cas9 technology specifically won a 2020 Nobel
Prize, studies have shown that up to 40% of bacte-
ria and 90% of archaea contain at least one func-
tional CRISPR system (Westra and Levin, 2020).
These systems differ in their CRISPR-associated
proteins, guide RNAs, nucleic acid binding kinetics,
and nucleolytic activities, but all accomplish the
same feat: targeting enzymatic activity to a genomic
locus of interest to induce gene editing.
Outcomes of gene editing
For simplicity, we will narrow our focus of gene
editing to the use of CRISPR tools, but the ideas
that follow generally hold true for other program-
mable nucleases. In most applications, these tools
are combined with gene delivery as discussed above.
After CRISPR induces a DNA double-strand
break, cells work to repair it using one of two
major pathways generally called “non-templated
repair” and “templated repair”. These pathways
differ in their outcome pending the availability of a
repair template, supplied by either a sister chroma-
tid for endogenous repair or a donor DNA tem-
plate for genome writing applications. Two specific
pathways for non-templated repair are nonhomolo-
gous end joining (NHEJ), which results in random
insertions or deletions (indels), and microhomology-
mediated end joining (MMEJ), which results in
short deletions but can be predicted (Bae et al.,
2014; Ata et al., 2018). While viral gene therapy
brings the ability to randomly supply diseased cells
with donor DNA carrying a corrected version of
defective proteins to treat diseases, CRISPR muta-
tions are rarely therapeutic in and of themselves
and require templated repair. Indeed, gene editing
technologies rely on precision control of the DNA
repair outcomes after CRISPR targeting to alter a
single or a few nucleotide(s) surrounding the target
160 	W.A. Wierson et al.

-- 176 of 258 --

161	Gene Editing and Gene Therapy in Oncology
site or to integrate a cargo DNA for reverse genet-
ics and functional genomic applications and for
therapeutic benefit in the clinic.
When programmable nucleases cut their target
DNA site, enzymes specific to sub-pathways of
DNA repair compete to heal the DNA double-
strand break. These pathways hinge upon the ini-
tial recognition of the DNA double-strand break
and subsequent processing of the DNA ends for no,
short-range, or long-range end resection.
NON - HOMOLOGOUS END JOINING 	The most com-
mon non-templated DNA repair outcome is called
NHEJ, which results in short insertions/deletions
(indels) at the target site. In research settings,
CRISPR is most often used in reverse genetics
applications to generate indel mutations in the
genome in order to abrogate gene function and
study resulting phenotypes, although CRISPR is
also particularly powerful for forward genetic
screens. Indeed, CRISPR gene knockouts have
been used in canine reverse genetics to study car-
diovascular disease (Feng et al., 2018), Duchenne’s
muscular dystrophy (Mata Lopez et al., 2020), and
even to generate germline edits of the myostatin
gene (Zou et al., 2015). NHEJ activity requires
KU70/80 to stabilize the DNA ends, preventing
end resection, and DNA-PKcs (Chang et al., 2017).
These proteins recruit other components, impor-
tantly DNA ligase IV that seals the broken DNA
ends. Competition with end resection enzymes
and more complicated DNA break structures (like
5′ and 3′ overhangs) results in the random indels
associated with NHEJ.
MICROHOMOLOGY - MEDIATED END JOINING 	MMEJ
is another non-templated outcome of CRISPR-
induced DNA breaks and competes directly with
NHEJ (Black et al., 2019). The core difference
between them is that MMEJ requires end resec-
tion to reveal short 3′ overhangs. Short stretches
(commonly two to five nucleotides) of homology
are found by polymerase theta and LigIII is used
to seal the DNA break, thus resulting in small dele-
tions of the intervening sequence and one copy of
the microhomology. Interestingly, CRISPR target
sites can be chosen a priori to induce MMEJ, thus
resulting in predictable DNA repair outcomes,
increasing the likelihood of an outcome of interest
(Martinez-Galvez et al., 2021). The ability to select
CRISPR target sites that will result in predict-
able outcomes is invaluable in research settings to
ensure that a resulting mutant will carry an out-of-
frame deletion and early translational stop codon
to abrogate gene function. More importantly, in
therapeutic settings, the ability to select MMEJ
sites in somatic tissue editing brings predictable
outcomes to clinical applications. For example,
one in ~1000 cases of human limb-girdle muscular
dystrophy 2G (LGMD2G) contain an 8 bp dupli-
cation in exon 1 of TCAP (Nigro and Savarese,
2014). Using CRISPR/Cas9, this mutation has been
successfully reprogrammed to WT in up to 57%
of alleles in patient-derived inducible pluripotent
stem cells (iPSCs) using MMEJ repair (Iyer et al.,
2019). Not all diseases, however, carry such defined
genomic signatures to be exploited for reversion to
WT. In these instances, scientists could use diseased
cell- and tissue-based genomics to identify MMEJ-
prone CRISPR target sites that may abrogate gene
circuits involved in pathologies.
HOMOLOGY-DIRECTED REPAIR 	HDR, as the name
suggests, is the general set of pathways that uses
homologous templates to direct DNA break repair
(Jasin and Rothstein, 2013). After endogenous
DNA breaks, e.g., from DNA replication stress
or radiation, the cell uses a sister chromatid as
template. However, in gene editing applications,
scientists supply an exogenous repair template
embedding the changes desired. Pending the desired
edit, multiple sub-pathways of HDR are utilized.
● Templated repair to induce single nucleotide
polymorphism (SNP) changes:
 Most often, templates for SNP changes are
<100 bp single-stranded oligonucleotides
(ssODNs) containing 50 bp homology arms
flanking the desired SNP. The first demon-
strated use of ssODNs in vivo was developed
using TALENs (Bedell et al., 2012), and sub-
sequent deployment with CRISPR systems
has shown this is a universal HDR strategy to
achieve single or few nucleotide changes
desirable to rescue a mutant phenotype, like
the A→T SNP in sickle-cell anemia (Frangoul
et al., 2021). The molecular mechanisms of
this type of targeted DNA repair change are
currently the subject of debate, but most
likely involve combinations of the Fanconi
anemia pathway important to stabilization of
stalled replication forks, and the synthesis-
dependent strand annealing (SDSA) pathway
(Yeh et al., 2019). In this model, it is speculated

-- 177 of 258 --

that the homology supplied in the ssODN
anneals with a matched, resected 3′ DNA
end, and subsequent DNA polymerase activ-
ity incorporates the desired changes before
the template dissociates. Whether or not the
template itself is incorporated into the chro-
mosome is currently unknown.
 It is also possible to utilize longer homology
templates to incorporate single or multiple
nucleotide changes into genes of interest. In
general, the mechanisms governing this type
of templated gene editing fall under HR. HR
is well known for its role in meiosis but can
also be induced by supplying donors with
>500 bp homology arms flanking an insert of
interest (Jasin and Rothstein, 2013; Yeh
et al., 2019). HR proceeds after MRN/CtIP
complex-induced long-range end resection
involving many components, importantly the
5′–3′ exonuclease ExoI. After DNA ends are
resected, the RAD family controls the preci-
sion of repair through RAD51 DNA end sta-
bilization, homologous template search and
sampling, RAD52-mediated strand invasion,
annealing, and subsequent template poly-
merization and end capture (Yeh et al., 2019).
Many types of donors have been used to
induce this type of repair, including adeno-
associated viral templates, ssDNA, linear
dsDNA, and plasmid DNA. The use of these
types of donors and the requirement for HR
is arguably less efficient than the use of
ssODN for SNP incorporation.
● Templated repair to incorporate new genes:
 For many gene-edited cell therapy applica-
tions, scientists do not wish to fix SNPs but
need to add exogenous DNA to educate cells
with new functions that nature did not
evolve. In research applications, this could be
the addition of DNA encoding fluorescent
proteins to tag spatiotemporal gene expres-
sion patterns in model organisms and cell
lines (Wierson et al., 2020). In the clinic, the
best example is the addition of DNA encod-
ing CARs to impart tumor killing activity to
T cells. Whatever the application, the incor-
poration of multi-kilobase gene cassettes into
CRISPR-induced DNA double-strand breaks
generally requires a repair template carrying
homology arms that flank the DNA break.
Just like in templated SNP alterations, the
HR pathway of DNA repair is a commonly
employed mechanism for these alterations.
There are publications demonstrating the
efficacy of many types of templates to accom-
plish this feat: single-stranded or double-
stranded linear DNAs (Shin et al., 2014;
Roth et al., 2018), plasmid DNA (Wierson
et al., 2020), or recombinant adeno-associated
virus (rAAV) donors (MacLeod et al., 2017)
to mediate site-specific integration of this
DNA. More recently, scientists have discov-
ered that delivering a donor template with
CRISPR sites flanking homology arms and
cargo DNA is an efficient way of inducing a
sub-pathway of HDR, dubbed “homology-
mediated end joining”, to create engineered
model organisms and cell lines (Hisano et al.,
2015; Yao et al., 2017; Wierson et al., 2019,
2020).
BASE EDITING FOR SINGLE NUCLEOTIDE CHANGES 	An
alternative form of CRISPR-based single-nucleotide
alterations is accomplished through the fusion of
“base editors” to Cas enzymes. Base editors can be
used to alter single nucleotides in DNA or RNA.
The first base editor, engineered by David Liu’s lab
in 2016, is a fusion of a Cas9 nickase enzyme (so
that only a DNA single-strand break is induced) to
the cytidine deaminase enzyme APOBEC1 (Komor
et al., 2016). Nicking the non-base edited DNA
strand using a Cas9-nickase induces a mismatch
repair pathway that effectively “tricks” the cell to
use the uracil as a template for DNA replication,
thus converting the target cytosine/guanine base pair
to a thymine/adenine base pair. Similarly, the Liu lab
used directed evolution to engineer an ADA that can
effectively target adenine/tyrosine base pairs for con-
version to guanine/cytosine (Gaudelli et al., 2017).
With these two tools and their enhanced versions,
63% of known pathogenic single-nucleotide vari-
ants could theoretically be corrected. Additionally,
an advantage of base editing is that no DNA
double-strand break has to be generated, as emerg-
ing concerns with DNA breaks have been noted
(Ihry et al., 2018; Kosicki et al., 2018; Cullot et al.,
2019). An elegant review was recently published on
the advances and opportunities for furthering base
editing technology (Porto et al., 2020).
Armed with the toolboxes of viral integration,
gene editing, and nonviral gene delivery, scientists
now have control over the genome at a scale and
resolution never before imagined, to engineer living
therapies.
