Human clinical gene therapy
Numerous experimental gene therapy trials have
been initiated with varying degrees of success, lead-
ing to the first FDA-approved gene therapy in
humans in 1998, fomivirsen (Vitravene®) (Stein
and Castanotto, 2017). This antisense oligodeoxy-
nucleotide was indicated for the local treatment of
cytomegalovirus (CMV) retinitis in immunocom-
promised patients but was later removed from the
market in 2002 and 2006 in the EU and USA,
respectively (Stein and Castanotto, 2017). In
Europe, the very first gene therapy ever approved
was based on an rAAV vector to treat familial lipo-
protein lipase deficiency (alipogene tiparvovec,
marketed under the trade name Glybera®) (Yla-
Herttuala, 2012). Since 1998, 22 gene therapy
products, including naked nucleic acids, nonviral
and viral vectors, as well as cell-mediated therapies
have been approved for commercialization and are
elegantly described in a 2020 review by Ma and
colleagues (Ma et al., 2020). An additional five
gene and cell therapy products have been approved
by the FDA since Ma et al.’s review in 2020 (https://
www.fda.gov/vaccines-blood-biologics/cellular-
gene-therapy-products/approved-cellular-and-gene-
therapy-products, accessed 13 March 2023).
Advantages of canine models
for gene therapy
Animal models serve a critical role in biomedical
research both as basic science tools for elucidating
molecular mechanisms as well as for the preclinical
evaluation of novel therapies. Dogs play an integral
role in modern society and enhance the lives of
countless individuals by providing both mental and
physical assistance, security, and companionship.
The domestic dog has also been recognized as a
valuable model of monogenic diseases in humans
and possesses key advantages over inbred rodent
models classically used for preclinical studies
regarding gene therapy. Not only do causative
mutations spontaneously occur in dogs as they do
in humans, detailed pedigrees and the opportunity
to evaluate treatments over a long term, often
years, provide crucial advantages in a preclinical
setting (Switonski, 2020).
Specifically, immunotherapies present unique
opportunities to be tested in vivo in dogs before
formal evaluation into human clinical trials, since
an intact immune system and tumor microenviron-
ment can be adequately modeled in the dog (as
opposed to mice). This is particularly relevant for
future accelerated development of many novel
treatment 	options, 	including, 	among 	others,
immune checkpoint inhibitors, CAR-T cells, and
adoptive T-cell transfer therapies in both veterinary
and human oncology.
Also, it has been well established that spontane-
ous tumorigenesis occurs in dogs through similar
mechanisms to what is known to occur in humans.
Although preclinical studies in dogs have contrib-
uted to the development of cancer therapeutics for
human medicine, approaches utilizing gene ther-
apy remain limited in this regard, as gene therapy
is not an explicit class of therapeutic options for
oncology.
One could ponder how spontaneous disease in
dogs could again be of use to test novel hypotheses
for gene therapy-based solutions in oncology that
correct genomic risks in somatic tissues. One such
hypothesis involves hijacking a cancer cell’s reli-
ance on MMEJ. As MMEJ is inherently mutagenic,
cancers carry many genomic hallmarks of MMEJ-
based rearrangements (Alexandrov et al., 2020), as
well as overexpression of protein components
involved in MMEJ repair (Lemee et al., 2010).
Drugs are currently under development that can
induce lethality, synthetic or otherwise, at the pro-
tein level. Theoretically, as tissue-specific in vivo
gene delivery continues to advance, one could
imagine a scenario where gene therapy is combined
with gene editing to exploit MMEJ to correct
driver mutations or to induce synthetic lethality in
cancer cell populations. As discussed at length in
the cell therapy section below, we are most inter-
ested in the use of gene-edited cell therapies (not
explicitly “gene therapies”) in oncology. However,
we are interested in testing these hypotheses in
spontaneous cancers via collaboration with in vivo
gene delivery and gene therapy experts. Given the
few formal descriptions of gene therapy that have
been forwarded in veterinary oncology (Thamm,
2019), examples of translational medicine regard-
ing gene therapy outlined herein apply specifically
to monogenic diseases.
A special issue of Human Genetics published in
2019 highlights many recent discoveries regarding
monogenic diseases in dogs that have significant
implications for human health (Shaffer, 2019). For
instance, variants in the TTN gene are known to

-- 179 of 258 --

contribute to cardiomyopathies in humans and a
missense mutation in TTN was discovered in
Doberman Pinscher dogs with diagnosed dilated
cardiomyopathy (Meurs et al., 2019). Another group
studying amelogenesis imperfecta (AI) in Parson
Russell Terriers and Akita dogs identified variants in
the ENAM and ACP4 genes that are implicated in
the pathophysiology of human AI, further highlight-
ing relevant physiological similarities between
humans and dogs (Hytonen et al., 2019).
There have been numerous successful proof-of-
concept gene therapy studies in dogs, both as a
model for human translational application and to
solve pressing needs in canine health. As of 2017,
hundreds of gene therapy trials have been under-
taken to deal with monogenic diseases and research-
ers have recently been able to shed light on the
molecular mechanisms underpinning many disor-
ders to pave the way for novel interventions utiliz-
ing gene therapy. Beginning in 1993, the First
International DogMap Meeting in Oslo, Norway
sought to gain a more in-depth understanding of
the genetics driving approximately 700 monogenic
diseases known to afflict dog breeds (Switonski,
2020). Although analysis of genome sequence vari-
ations between different dog breeds is currently
underway (Ostrander et al., 2019), known causa-
tive mutations are continuously being identified
and approximately 430 monogenic diseases in dogs
have the potential to serve as preclinical models for
homologous human diseases (Switonski, 2020). In
fact, gene therapy has shown efficacy in treating
many monogenic diseases that afflict both canines
and humans and positive results in preclinical
canine studies have resulted in the initiation of
multiphase clinical trials. These diseases are repre-
sented among multiple organ systems and include
ocular diseases, muscular dystrophy, hemophilia,
severe combined immunodeficiencies, leukocyte
adhesion deficiencies, and lysosomal storage dis-
eases (Table 9.1).
Engineering living cells ex vivo
for therapeutic use
Mainstream application of viral transduction, gene
editing technologies, and most recently nonviral
gene delivery into cells ex vivo has led to a massive
shift in the way scientists think about disease treat-
ment. It is now routine to “educate” cells ex vivo
with genetic information to impart therapeutic
benefits with the intention of transplanting them
back into diseased patients. However, only a hand-
ful of research groups are developing these strate-
gies for dogs, with only two clinical reports to date
(Panjwani et al., 2016, 2020). Here, we will focus
on the enabling technologies and their use in
humans, knowing that translation of this technol-
ogy to canines is sure to follow.
In the context of oncology, the most engineered
cell is the T lymphocyte (see Mason and Dow,
Chapter 8, this volume, 2023). Although there are
many subtypes of T cells, CD8+ “cytotoxic” T-cells
are naturally equipped to rid the body of virally
infected cells and even some malignant cells
through major histocompatibility complex (MHC)
class I peptide recognition with the T-cell receptor
(TCR) (Kumar et al., 2018). Armed with this
knowledge, scientists long sought to reprogram the
TCR to engineer T-cell specificity and killing.
Indeed, the idea to use genetically reprogrammed
T cells as therapy began in 1992 with a pioneering
study by Michel Sadelain reporting the use of ret-
roviral transduction to engineer T cells with exog-
enous DNA. Later, in 1993, Zelig Eshhar generated
the first CAR (chimeric antigen receptor) by fusing
an antibody domain to the CD3ζ domain of a TCR
in what has become known as a “first-generation
CAR”. Studies in the late 1990s and early 2000s set
the field ablaze by generating “second-generation
CAR-T cells” containing a co-stimulatory domain
in addition to the antibody and CD3ζ signaling
domain (Maher et al., 2002), which culminated in
the first report of in vivo efficacy of CAR-T cells by
targeting CD19 on leukemic B cells in a mouse
model (Brentjens et al., 2003).
Numerous subsequent reports and clinical trials
utilized CD19-targeting, autologous CAR-T cells
generated from T cells isolated from the patient’s
peripheral blood mononuclear cells (PBMCs)
(Hollyman et al., 2009). These efforts have culmi-
nated in six FDA approvals from 2017 to 2022
(https://www.fda.gov/drugs/resources-information-
approved-drugs/fda-approves-axicabtagene-ciloleucel-
large-b-cell-lymphoma, https://www.fda.gov/drugs/
resources-information-approved-drugs/fda-
approves-tisagenlecleucel-adults-relapsed-or-refractory-
large-b-cell-lymphoma, https://www.fda.gov/drugs/
resources-information-approved-drugs/fda-
approves-idecabtagene-vicleucel-multiple-myeloma,
https://www.fda.gov/drugs/resources-information-
approved-drugs/fda-approves-brexucabtagene-
autoleucel-relapsed-or-refractory-mantle-cell-
lymphoma, https://www.fda.gov/drugs/resources-

Proof-of-concept CAR therapies in dogs
As noted in this chapter and described in Mason
and Dow (Chapter 8, this volume, 2023), the only
peer-reviewed literature for CAR-T cell therapy in
canines is via work from the University of
Pennsylvania with two publications by Panjwani
and co-workers (Panjwani et al., 2016, 2020). In
these seminal studies, the authors used either
mRNA or retroviral transduction of canine T cells
to generate doses of autologous CAR-T cell therapy
designed to target CD20 on B-cell lymphomas. The
first proof-of-concept experiment showed limited

-- 181 of 258 --

effect, and while the CAR-T cells did traffic to the
lymph nodes and reduce tumor burden, this effect
was only transient, potentially due to the nature of
mRNA-based CAR expression, which is not stably
integrated.
In the second publication by Panjwani et al. in
2020, five dogs were treated with stably transduced
autologous CAR-T cells, although the doses of
CAR-T cells varied in every dog and were all far
lower than the target of 1 × 106 to 3 × 106 CAR-T
cells/kg used in humans. Canine anti-mouse anti-
bodies were detected, likely in response to the
murine-derived CAR itself, which the authors pos-
tulated triggered rejection of the CAR-T cells and
subsequently limited clinical benefit. In any case,
the authors concluded that CAR-T cells were
detectable in dogs, had modest antitumor activity,
and, in some instances, selectively forced CD20
antigen loss on malignant B cells, indicating that
the dog as a model can faithfully recapitulate pit-
falls previously described in human CAR-T cell
therapy studies (Maus et al., 2013; Enblad et al.,
2015; Majzner and Mackall, 2018). More recently
from the Mason group, Atherton et al. published a
case report with evidence of cytokine release syn-
drome (CRS) in a patient dog, revealing increased
levels of multiple key cytokines known to be
involved in human CRS (Atherton et al., 2022).
In addition to canine CAR-T cell therapy being
developed for B-cell lymphoma, there are reports of
CAR therapies being applied to the treatment of
glioma (Yin et al., 2018), sarcoma (Zhang et al.,
2022), and melanoma (Forsberg et al., 2023). In
the Yin et al. (2018) study, scientists aimed to
develop a novel antigen-binding protein to develop
CAR-T cells that target interleukin-13 receptor
subunit α2 (IL-13Rα2), commonly found on both
human and canine gliomas, but not on healthy tis-
sues. Solid tumors like glioma are historically
harder to treat with CAR-T cell therapy than liquid
cancers, such as leukemia and lymphoma (O’Rourke
et al., 2017). Yin et al. engineered human cells
expressing a cross-reactive CAR for both human
and canine IL-13Rα2 and showed it effectively
targeted IL-13Rα2 in both species in vitro and was
effective in vivo towards an orthotopic mouse
model of canine glioma. Interestingly, the authors
engineered both canine and human cells with
IL-13Rα2 CARs and showed that both elicit killing
of IL-13Rα2-positive cells, indicating that human
T cells can kill canine cells when armed with a
CAR specific for a canine antigen. The authors
concluded that they are moving forward to enroll a
pilot trial to use this technology toward fighting
canine gliomas as a preclinical model of the
approach in humans (Herranz et al., 2016).
It is notable to discuss here that there are cur-
rently multiple industry groups in the USA offering
autologous tumor vaccinations or “adoptive T-cell
transfer” to fight differing cancers, which is quite
different than CAR-T cell therapy. Respectively,
dogs are either vaccinated with their own tumors to
induce a cellular immunity response to the cancer,
or T cells are isolated from dogs, grown in the pres-
ence of tumor neoantigens, and reinfused in the
hope that the cells naturally acquire tumor antigen-
specific killing properties (O’Connor et al., 2012;
O’Connor and Wilson-Robles, 2014). Data on
these approaches in dogs is currently scant with
various stages of regulatory approvals ongoing;
however, it is well established in humans that
genetically reprogramming cells with anticancer
properties (i.e., CAR-T) is absolutely a more effec-
tive approach to induce durable disease remissions
than more simple adoptive transfer strategies.
Gene-edited cell therapies in dogs
With Dr Mason’s pioneering work, the translation
of CAR-T cell therapy from humans to companion
dogs is emerging. While the work in the Mason lab
is so far the only peer-reviewed literature for in vivo
trials of CAR-T in dogs, publicly available know-
ledge for awarded federal and foundation grants
gives us a glimpse of what is to come in this area.
These include federal grant awards to Dr Nicola
Mason (3U24CA224122-02S1), Dr Carl June, and
Dr Gerald Linette (1U54CA244711-01) and other
colleagues at the University of Pennsylvania
(5R01AR075337-03); 	foundation 	awards 	to
Dr Heather Wilson-Robles and colleagues at Texas
A&M University (AKC-CHF #1418); and a Small
Business Innovation Research award to the bio-
technology company LifEngine Animal Health
Laboratories (LEAH Labs, NSF #2006130). In all
instances, the scientists note the need for better
canine therapies and seek to use the high-impact
potential of spontaneously occurring disease in a
large animal model system to study the effects of
novel cell therapies. As mentioned above, the
opportunity to support parallel development of
novel drug candidates in veterinary and human
oncology through a One Health approach could
increase availability of revolutionary treatment
166 	W.A. 	Wierson 	et al.

167	Gene Editing and Gene Therapy in Oncology
options in animal health, while reducing attrition
rates in Phase II clinical programs. The public sum-
mary statements of these grants indicate that gene
editing is being used in the development of novel
cell-based therapies; however, to date, there are no
peer-reviewed reports of gene-edited cell therapies
for dogs.
One of the biggest challenges to overcome
regarding successful translation of CAR-T cell
therapy into canines is the cost to deliver the ther-
apy to patients. Notably, the current cost of FDA-
approved CAR-T cells in human medicine ranges
from US$373,000 to US$475,000 and represents a
large barrier to effective translation of this technol-
ogy to canines. This cost is largely due to the need
for individualized manufacturing, lentiviral prepar-
ations, FDA regulation, and Good Manufacturing
Practice standards. In considering autologous cell
therapy in dogs, apheresis to obtain PBMC popula-
tions from which to generate cell therapies costs
>US$2000. This feature, coupled with the labor-
intensive processes of isolating, culturing, engineer-
ing, and expanding canine T cells, will likely result
in a therapy that costs well over US$10,000, vastly
limiting adoption of this breakthrough therapy to
the broader veterinary community. Gene editing
could alleviate much of this cost burden by allow-
ing the engineering of allogeneic CAR-T cell ther-
apy, such that one manufacturing run would
essentially generate enough material to dose multi-
ple, if not ten or 100 dogs with a single batch.
Fortunately, research and clinical trials for human
CAR-T cell therapy are paving the way for allogen-
eic cell therapy to be possible in dogs (Jung and
Lee, 2018).
As these challenges are overcome and as ongoing
cell therapy trials in humans for a litany of onco-
logic disorders progress (Table 9.2), one can envi-
sion how the use of gene editing technology will
surely allow the translation of these technologies to
companion dogs for the same types of cancers.
Strategies for allogeneic cell therapy
One of the biggest hurdles in allogeneic CAR-T cell
therapy 	is 	graft-versus-host 	disease 	(GVHD)
(Gajewski et al., 2009; Poirot et al., 2015). GVHD
is mediated by the TCR recognizing non-self
through MHC–human leukocyte antigen (HLA)
interactions. Thus, GVHD is dependent on the
TCR. To avoid GVHD, scientists use gene editing-
based knockouts of the T-cell receptor α chain
(TRAC), which disrupts the TCR (Qasim et al.,
2017). In the first cohort of patients with ALL who
were dosed with TALEN-mediated allogeneic
CAR-T cell therapy containing TCR knockouts, no
GVHD was observed, and clinical remission was
induced from one dose of these CAR-T cells

(Qasim et al., 2017). In fact, publications have
shown that disruption of the endogenous TCR via
targeted integration of the CAR at the TRAC locus
actually enhances CAR-T cell activity in vitro and
in vivo (MacLeod et al., 2017). Additional benefits
of targeted integration of the CAR module are bet-
ter control of transgene expression (versus using an
exogenous promotor) and the ability to make a
theoretically homogeneous therapy where every
cell contains the same edit, both of which are limi-
tations in the random integration of CAR via LVs
(Xu et al., 2018).
Indeed, multiple gene editing approaches have
been developed towards engineering allogeneic
CAR-T cells for human blood malignancies, using
viral and nonviral approaches to CAR delivery.
Nuclease-based knockout of the TCR is often com-
bined with lentiviral-based CAR delivery and has
been the method used to manufacture allogeneic
CAR-T cells in multiple FDA trials. Moreover, AAV
cassettes are relatively efficient vectors to induce
homology-directed integration of cargo cassettes at
CRISPR cut sites (MacLeod et al., 2017). DNA
molecules, either plasmids, dsDNA, or ssDNA, are
also used as HDR templates to generate nonviral
CAR-T cells (Eyquem et al., 2017; MacLeod et al.,
2017; Jung and Lee, 2018; Roth et al., 2018;
Sachdeva et al., 2019). Based on these studies and
unpublished work at numerous biotechnology
companies and academic centers, there are multiple
human clinical trials ongoing for allogeneic CAR-T
cell therapy in cancer (https://clinicaltrials.gov,
accessed 22 February 2023).
Dogs as a unique model for cell therapy
development
Many advances have been made in improving effi-
cacy through the inclusion of additional synthetic
biology strategies into the CAR construct (Kloss
et al., 2013; Diaconu et al., 2017), or by combining
CAR-T cells with monoclonal antibodies (Gargett
et al., 2016; Sterner et al., 2019) or small-molecule
inhibitors (Ruella et al., 2016; Giavridis et al.,
2018). However, equally important as fine-tuning
the CAR-T cells themselves is testing the therapy in
an appropriate animal model. Different mouse
models – syngeneic, xenograft, transgenic, and
humanized – have been implemented in CAR-T
research, and some of these models have exposed
CAR-T limitations or risks that were not adequately
detected in other models (Siegler et al., 2017).
Even though CAR-T cells have been especially
successful in treating hematological malignancies,
an estimated 30–50% of patients will relapse
within 1 year of treatment (Maude et al., 2018;
Park et al., 2018), arguing for the need to better
evaluate preclinical assets before investing in Phase
I trials and beyond. The vast majority of preclinical
CAR-T studies have been performed in mouse
models, which are convenient but do not faithfully
reproduce or predict clinical outcomes. Importantly,
the incredible outcomes of CAR-T cell therapy in
human oncology comes with significant adverse
reactions in the form of neurotoxicity (NT) and
CRS. Thus, there is a disconnect between preclini-
cal models, which display robust antitumor effects
and minimal toxicities, and clinical trials, which
yield more limited durable responses and often
demonstrate serious toxicities such as CRS and NT.
Currently, three different mouse models are being
utilized to study CAR-T cell toxicities. These include:
(i) xenograft humanized models (Sterner et al.,
2019); (ii) humanized mouse models (Giavridis
et al., 2018); and (iii) syngeneic models (Kueberuwa
et al., 2018). These models are limited by the lack
of spontaneous tumor development, no relevant
tumor microenvironment, absence of immune cells
in the case of immunocompromised mice, and use
of murine T cells in the case of syngeneic models.
Briefly, syngeneic models are immunocompetent
and thus reflect a more realistic tumor microenvi-
ronment, but require all components – engineered
T cells, tumors, and target antigens – to be of murine
origin. Thus, syngeneic models do not provide
insight into the functions of human CAR-T cells.
Xenograft models are immunocompromised and
permit the engraftment of human tumors and T cells,
but do not give information into off-tumor toxicities
or interactions between tumor and host immune
cells. Immunocompetent transgenic mice express a
human antigen to better determine off-tumor effects
but have limited availability (Pegram et al., 2012;
Chmielewski et al., 2013). Humanized mice recreate
components of the human immune system in immu-
nocompromised mice to allow the study of human
cells and targets within the context of the human
immune system. However, these models are often
primitive, with frequent defects in the myeloid com-
partment, limiting the full recapitulation of human
immune interactions with CAR-T cell therapy
(Holzapfel et al., 2015; Zhen et al., 2015).
No less, there have been advances in the under-
standing of CAR-T cell biology and host responses
168 	W.A. 	Wierson 	et al.

-- 184 of 258 --

169	Gene Editing and Gene Therapy in Oncology
and methods to abrogate toxicities like CRS and
NT. One study used gene editing to make CAR-T
cells containing knockouts of granulocyte mac-
rophage colony-stimulating factor (GM-CSF), a
protein suggested to be responsible for bridging
CAR-T cells with NT and CRS. Indeed, either with
a GM-CSF neutralizing antibody (lenzilumab) or
CRISPR/Cas9-based GM-CSF knockouts, NT and
CRS were abrogated and CAR-T cell function was
not impacted (Sterner et al., 2019).
Historically, CAR-T cell therapy has been most
successful in hematologic malignancies, with few
complete responses induced in solid tumor trials.
Solid tumors present a number of hurdles for cell
therapy activity that are less prevalent in liquid
tumors. One issue to effectively deploying CAR-T
for solid tumors is what is known as the “antigen
dilemma”; this is essentially because cell types in
solid tumors are more heterogeneous, displaying
different tumor antigens throughout the tumor.
Therefore, if CAR-T cells are designed to target a
single antigen, cells without that antigen cannot
be targeted by the therapy, a hurdle that can be
alleviated by the use of bi-specific CARs (Dai
et al., 2020).
Another challenge in CAR-T cell therapy for
solid tumors lies in the immunosuppressive nature
of the tumor microenvironment. One approach to
counteracting this for enhanced CAR-T cell activ-
ity at solid tumor sites is to use CRISPR to disrupt
the PD-1/PD-L1 (programmed cell death protein 1
and its primary ligand) immune checkpoint block-
ade that inhibits T-cell function (Zhao et al., 2018;
McGowan et al., 2020). And last, on-target but
off-tumor effects can result in the CAR-T cells
attacking healthy tissues. In the context of a
xenotransplant, 	immunocompromised 	mouse
model, it is nearly impossible to determine how a
CAR-T cell’s antigen receptor may react to these
off-tumor antigens.
Another challenge to overcome for solid tumor
targeting is the need to improve CAR-T cell fitness.
Even in blood malignancies where targeting single
antigens can induce clinical remission, the repeated
activation of CAR-T cells via the chimeric TCR
can induce T-cell exhaustion and lower efficacy in
some cases (Blank et al., 2019). An interesting
approach to enhance the fitness of CAR-T cells
was described by Sachdeva et al., where they gen-
erated multiplexed CAR-T cells that can selectively
induce secretion of interleukin-12 (IL-12) upon
antigen stimulation to enhance T-cell activity
(Sachdeva et al., 2019). Again, testing CAR-T cell
therapy in spontaneous disease models like the dog
versus immunocompromised, xenotransplant mice
may help scientists understand the gene networks,
gene edits, or other strategies to enhance CAR-T
cell fitness.
While xenotransplants of cancer into immuno-
compromised mouse models have been the gold
standard for preclinical testing of human CAR-T
cells for blood malignancies, they cannot faithfully
recapitulate these hurdles in bringing cell therapies
to human application. The use of spontaneous
disease in dog models with an intact immune sys-
tem could be a game-changing new paradigm of
testing novel cell therapy strategies, designs, and
treatment regimens to increase the confidence of
the safety and efficacy of novel cell therapy strate-
gies during the preclinical evaluation phase of drug
development.
Advanced gene-edited cell therapy
technologies
Indeed, as the gene editing toolbox continues to
grow and more cell types are engineered and
shown to work as cancer and other disease therapy,
we will continue to see the growth and application
of gene-edited therapies in dogs.
While third-generation, autologous CAR-T cell
therapy is leading the field for reprogrammed
immune cells, there is considerable attention given
to other types of modalities and engineered cells
(Yu et al., 2020). T cells can also be engineered
with programmed TCRs themselves versus the chi-
meric approach used in CAR-T cell therapy. Indeed,
the first clinical application of CRISPR/Cas9 to
engineer living cell therapy was a Phase I trial of
TCR-engineered T cells with endogenous TCR and
PD-1 disruption (NCT03399448). Natural killer
cells are also under evaluation in clinical trials after
being engineered with CARs to mediate tumor
antigen-specific killing and may bring several
advantages over engineered T cells, including an
abrogated risk of GVHD, reduced rates of NT and
CRS due to differential cytokine profiles, and the
innate ability to kill tumors in a CAR-independent
manner, overcoming limitations in tumor antigen
heterogeneity (Xie et al., 2020). Finally, CAR-
macrophages are currently under investigation as a
potential advance in the ability to penetrate solid
tumors and overcome the immunosuppressive
tumor microenvironment (Mukhopadhyay, 2020).

A xenogeneic approach to cell
therapy in dogs?
In the late 1990s, a group of scientists demon-
strated the efficacy of a transformed human T-cell
line, TALL-104, as a therapeutic option for canine
cancer in a series of studies (Cesano et al., 1995,
1996; Visonneau et al., 1997, 1999). Interestingly,
the use of this cell line in dogs did not result in any
toxicity like GVHD and even provided clinical
benefit in many cases. This, combined with the sup-
porting evidence of the ability to engineer allogen-
eic CAR-T cells in research and clinical settings for
humans that do not cause GVHD, has generated
interest in the use of canine antigen-targeting,
human CAR-T cells in dogs (Yin et al., 2018).
The use of xenogeneic CAR-T cells for canine
therapy would alleviate the burden of isolating,
expanding, and engineering canine T cells (methods
that have not been broadly studied), and would
create a more straightforward strategy to using
canine modeling of CAR-T cell therapeutic efficacy.
Indeed, the University of Pennsylvania is currently
recruiting dogs to participate in a trial with human
CAR-T cells engineered to fight canine B-cell lym-
phoma. In industry, LEAH Labs is developing a
similar approach using CRISPR to knock out the
TCR while simultaneously integrating CAR DNA
using their nonviral GeneWeld platform (Wierson
et al., 2019, 2020). Of note, a combination
approach using an LV to introduce the CAR
transgene and gene editing to knock out the TCR
to generate xenogeneic CAR-T cells for canine use
may be an effective strategy toward the application
of this therapy.
Future Applications of Gene Editing and
Gene Therapy in Our Canine Companions
Improving the cell and gene therapy discovery
and validation pipeline
As discussed above, large animal models may better
serve preclinical testing of CAR-T cell therapy, as
mouse models have the tendency to overstate effi-
cacy and understate toxicity. To date, a few nonhu-
man primate models have tested CAR-T safety.
However, these studies are expensive and ethically
fraught, and no tumors were implanted or spontane-
ously developed prior to CAR-T administration
(Berger et al., 2015; Kunkele et al., 2017). Canine
models of CAR-T cell therapy may circumvent many
issues seen in murine and primate modeling
(Migliorini et al., 2018). Unlike laboratory mice,
dogs are more genetically diverse and develop spon-
taneous cancers that share similar histology, muta-
tions, microenvironments, and metastases to their
corresponding human cancers (Kirkness et al., 2003;
Breen and Modiano, 2008; Richards et al., 2013).
Humans share a more similar environment and
microbiome to pet dogs than they do to laboratory
mice, which likely affects tumor development and
therapeutic 	response 	(Coelho 	et 	al., 	2018;
Gopalakrishnan et al., 2018). Finally, spontaneous
disease in dog models has the potential to serve as
relevant models to investigate toxicities after
CAR-T cells and other cell therapies. The develop-
ment of CRS and NT following CAR-T cell therapy
is caused by the interactions between CAR-T cells,
tumor cells, and the tumor microenvironment (such
as myeloid cells). Canine models were instrumental
in developing methods for hematopoietic stem cell
transplant (Panse et al., 2003; Graves et al., 2007),
and it logically follows that dogs can also be key to
bridging the gap between bench and bedside in
CAR-T cell therapy.
Interestingly, provisions in federal regulatory
code 9 CFR 107.1 allow veterinarians to treat their
patients with any therapeutic provided it is manu-
factured in-house and administered within an exist-
ing veterinarian–client–patient relationship. This
code was originally intended to allow for friction-
less vaccination of herd animals in case of pandem-
ics, but it may also allow for the use of client-owned
dogs as unique spontaneous disease models for
biomedical research. One could envision a compan-
ion animal biotechnology company of the future
that develops novel cell and gene therapy strategies
that, once validated in vitro or in mouse models,
could be quickly ported to patient dogs with con-
senting pet owners as a mechanism for compas-
sionate use. In this way, scientists could glean
clinical data in spontaneous disease models that is
important for future regulatory submissions with
little friction. Additionally, with the One Health
model in mind, these data may prove invaluable to
human pharmaceutical companies as they seek bet-
ter models to test their novel cell and gene therapy
hypotheses.
Two-clinical-stage gene therapy examples
As the companion animal market continues to rise,
so has funding for university spinouts of high-risk,
high-reward intellectual property into companion

animal biotechnology companies. Two companies,
in particular, are currently in the clinic with their
gene therapy products: Rejuvenate Bio and Scout
Bio, spun out of the notorious labs of Dr George
Church and Dr Jim Wilson, respectively. Academic
work out of the Church lab showed that delivery of
a combination of AAV payloads containing two
genes was successful at treating four diseases in a
single mouse: obesity, type II diabetes, heart failure,
and renal failure (Davidsohn et al., 2019). As a
proof of concept for this therapy working outside
of lab models, Rejuvenate Bio is focused first on
using this cocktail gene therapy to treat mitral
valve disease in Cavalier King Charles Spaniels. As
of this writing, they are currently recruiting
patients. Scout Bio is using gene therapy to deliver
feline erythropoietin (EPO) in vivo to treat anemia
associated with chronic kidney disease in cats. In
another study, they are using AAV to deliver gluca-
gon-like peptide 1 (GLP-1) to cats as a treatment
for diabetes. Without a doubt, both companies are
garnering interest from human pharma for their
work, and each has aspirations to translate its tech-
nology to the human clinic.
Fixing diseased alleles for generations
through germline editing
Gene editing is not only useful for engineering
somatic cells or stem cells to be used as therapy, but
also opens the possibility to actually correct alleles
that can be passed through the germline. With gene
editing, it is theoretically possible to correct the
over 700 described monogenetic diseases in dogs
and establish new, disease-free dog lines. A review
by Pepin and co-workers (Pepin et al., 2014) exam-
ining 36 breed-associated canine monogenetic dis-
eases reports that single genetic defects are
responsible for the vast majority of these disorders,
with 91% of the mutations involving coding
regions resulting in amino acid substitutions or
truncations in the encoded protein. Similar to
humans, about half of these diseases involve the
nervous and visual system – e.g., cataract in the
Australian Shepherd (Mellersh, 2014), glaucoma in
the Beagle (Kuchtey et al., 2013), or spinocerebellar
ataxia in the Parson Russell (Forman et al., 2013).
Additionally, naturally occurring MDR1 deletion
mutations are common in certain dog herding
breeds, such as Collies (Firdova et al., 2016), mak-
ing them vulnerable to severe side effects (which
can be fatal) from parasiticides such as macrocyclic
lactones (Geyer and Janko, 2012). The MDR1 gene
codes for P-glycoprotein (P-gp), a drug efflux trans-
porter that plays an important role in cell detoxifi-
cation 	and 	resistance 	to 	antimicrobial 	and
chemotherapeutic drugs. Using adult intestinal
stem cell-derived enteroids, ongoing work by Dr Jon
Mochel and colleagues focuses on mimicking the
WT, 4 bp deletion mutation of the MDR1 gene.
Additionally, by creating the exact WT deletion,
these studies lay the framework to rescue this geno-
type by simply replacing the HDR template with a
template containing the four missing base pairs in
the MDR1 gene in the affected canine’s germline.
Using our companions as an exploration
into gene editing ethics
The long history of canines and others as compan-
ion animals showcases their cultural significance
well beyond their study as natural models of
human disease. Consequently, all work beyond
somatic gene editing will undoubtedly bring its
own array of important ethical discussions that will
have cultural contexts as diverse as the rainbow of
human–canine relations around the globe, conver-
sations that will undoubtedly presage parallel work
in human gene editing.
People have been working to change the germ-
line of dogs since our first domestication from
wolves over 10,000 years ago. Selective breeding
has developed a rich array of different shapes,
colors, and dispositions – while causing clustering
of 	genetic-based 	diseases 	in 	certain 	breeds.
Maintaining the unique features of a classic dog
breed while removing these negative and unin-
tended consequences of human intervention is chal-
lenging and time-consuming when it is possible at
all. This genetic complexity also exists in food ani-
mals such as cows, represented by the naturally
occurring hornless cow trait that is found natively
in only a few breeds. Approaches to accelerate
genetic exchange to bring in highly valued genetic
loci while maintaining other key aspects (such as
milk production) have been demonstrated with the
polled allele (Carlson et al., 2016). Germline gene
editing in dogs offers the opportunity to similarly
maintain the distinction many people value in our
different breeds of canine companions while reduc-
ing the negative impact of specific disease alleles.
Finally, the controversial use of gene editing for
enhancing specific non-disease traits in dogs is also
a proven reality using CRISPR (Zou et al., 2015).

-- 187 of 258 --

As with nearly all other aspects of gene editing, our
“best friend” will share this complex journey
towards our new genetic heritage.

JACOB CAWLEY1,2*
1Case Western Reserve University, Cleveland, Ohio, USA; 2Ethos Discovery, San

Introduction to Cancer Epigenetics
Epigenetics is the study of heritable changes that
influence gene expression without affecting the DNA
sequence. These nongenomic changes relate to chem-
ical modifications on proteins and DNA fostering
transcription through conformational changes to the
three-dimensional (3D) genomic structure. The sum
of epigenetic modifications within a cell is called the
“epigenome”. The epigenome determines cellular
lineage, controls differentiation, and enables tran-
scriptional response to external stimuli. Countless
epigenomes exist for every single genome, creating
diversity in cellular phenotype (Fig. 10).
Cancer is a plastic disease. Characteristics of cancer
cells include avoiding immune destruction, disrupting
normal tissue environments, and surviving exposure
to exogenous stress. Traditional tenets sought to
explain these adaptive capabilities through sequential
genomic alterations. However, recent advancements in
sequencing technology have made it evident that can-
cer is a disease of both genetic and epigenetic conse-
quences. Cancer epigenetics is a rapidly evolving field
that is helping explain cancer biology and reveal novel
approaches for treatment. This chapter will focus on
defining basic principles of cancer epigenetics and cel-
lular plasticity to explain mechanisms underpinning
epigenetic therapeutics. An understanding of this field
is essential as “epidrugs” are becoming mainstays in
the treatment of human cancers and inevitably will
become commonplace for veterinarians as well.
Gene Expression is Regulated by
Epigenetic Modifers and 3D Genome
Architecture
Epigenetic regulation is carried out by effector proteins
that alter chromatin structure, DNA accessibility,
and enable or disable transcription of genes. In this
section we will discuss how DNA is packaged into
chromatin – complexes of DNA, protein, and RNA
that form the structure of chromosomes – and how
certain families of proteins alter chromatin struc-
ture. We will also discuss the effects of DNA methyla-
tion on gene expression and the proteins responsible
for writing and maintaining DNA methylation. These
concepts are fundamental to understanding how
current epigenetic therapies work against cancer.
Chromatin is composed of
nucleosome building blocks
Chromatin is composed of individual building
blocks, or nucleosomes, which consist of 147 bp of
DNA wrapped around an octamer protein core
composed of two copies each of the histone pro-
teins H2A, H2B, H3, and H4. Expression of a gene
requires a concert of modifications made by effec-
tor proteins on histone proteins to allow transcrip-
tion factors to bind and transcribe a gene.
Chromatin comes in two basic forms: euchroma-
tin, which is chromatin accessible for transcription;
and heterochromatin, which is inaccessible for
transcription. The pattern of euchromatin and het-
erochromatin within a given cell help define cell-
type-specific gene expression patterns that maintain
differentiation state.
The role of histone modifcations
in gene regulation
An octamer of histone proteins forms the nucleo-
some core around which DNA is wrapped. Histones
H2A, H2B, H3, and H4 compose the nucleosome
core, while histone H1 binds to the nucleosome and
181
*Email: jcawley@ethosvet.com
© CAB International 2023. Therapeutic Strategies in Veterinary Oncology (C. Khanna ed.)
DOI: 10.1079/9781789245820.0010

-- 197 of 258 --

stabilizes linker DNA extending from one nucleo-
some to the next. Posttranslational modifications of the
core histones (histone marks) are deposited by a
class of proteins called “writers”. Histone marks
are recognized by proteins called “readers” that act
as coactivators of transcription (Musselman et al.,
2012; Winter et al., 2017; Sabari et al., 2018;
Crump et al., 2021). “Erasers” are proteins that
remove specific histone marks, providing flexibility
and adaptive mechanisms for depositing and
removing marks in response to internal or external
stimuli. The concert of histone marks throughout
the genome dictates the 3D structure of the genome
and provides a template for cell-type-specific and
context-specific gene expression (Carrozza et al.,
2005; Valencia-Sánchez et al., 2019; Worden et al.,
2019; Feng and Pauklin, 2020).
Histone marks are reversible chemical changes
made on the N-terminal tail and include acetyla-
tion, methylation, phosphorylation, ubiquitylation,
SUMOylation, citrullination, and more. The pat-
tern of histone marks within a cell makes up the
epigenetic code, similar to nucleotide sequence for
the genetic code. Histone marks are named by the
histone protein (H2A, H2B, H3, H4), the amino
acid residue in the N-terminal tail that is modified,
and the covalent modification (acetylation, mono-,
di-, or trimethylation, etc.). For instance, H3K4me3
denotes trimethylation of the fourth residue (a
lysine, or “K”) of the N-terminal tail of H3. Amino
acids can be mono-, di-, and trimethylated and each
has a different significance. For instance, H3K4me3
is generally placed at active gene promoter sites but
H3K4me1 marks are typically placed at enhancers
(Balasubramanian et al., 2012; Local et al., 2018;
Bae and Lesch, 2020; Lismer et al., 2021). Different
writers are responsible for mono- versus di- or tri-
methylation of given histones, while specific read-
ers recognize the different histone marks. The
complexity of epigenetic regulation lends to con-
text-specific gene expression, whereby a mark and
its associated set of effector proteins are the context
that lend to vast differences in cellular phenotype
within an organism. It is easy to imagine why these
effector proteins are commonly mutated or altered
in cancer, making them promising drug targets for
cancer therapy (Geutjes et al., 2012; Jones et al.,
2016; Kelly and Issa, 2017; Nebbioso et al., 2018;
Miranda Furtado et al., 2019; Montalvo-Casimiro
et al., 2020). Histone marks localize to regions of
the genome that act as anchor sites for epigenetic
effector proteins that regulate gene expression.
These noncoding DNA sequences are referred to as
cis-regulatory elements (CREs). Like the effector
proteins that modify, recognize, or erase histone
marks, CREs play a role in activating, enhancing,
or repressing gene expression. CREs are an exam-
ple of the intimate connection between genetics and
epigenetics. Mutation to the DNA sequence of a
CRE may alter the ability of effector proteins to
recognize the site or could lead to inappropriate
binding of a different effector protein. Both scen-
arios could have dramatic consequences on gene
expression and result in neoplastic transformation
(Pant et al., 2004; Katainen et al., 2015; Sur and
Taipale, 2016). This helps explain why previously
disregarded noncoding mutations are being shown
to be critical driver mutations in cancer and why
targeted epigenetic therapeutics are becoming so
relevant as an approach to cancer treatment.
CREs are noncoding regions of the genome
where epigenetic effector proteins bind to regulate
gene expression. Promoters are located just
upstream of the transcription start site (TSS) of a
gene. RNApolII localizes to promoter sites to carry
out transcription of the associated gene. Enhancers,
unlike promoters, can be upstream or downstream
of a gene, and may be located kilobases away from
the affected gene (Banerji et al., 1981; Plon and
Wang, 1986; Fukaya et al., 2016). Despite the separ-
ation between gene and enhancer, enhancers tend
to have nonrandom partnerships with genes. Active
enhancers are typically marked by acetylated his-
tones, such as the H3K27ac mark. The unique
properties of enhancers raise several important
questions about the impact of enhancers on gene
expression: (i) how do noncoding sequences of the
genome located kilobases away from a gene impact
gene expression; and (ii) what prevents enhancers
from randomly interacting with genes across the
genome? It turns out the 3D structure of chroma-
tin, which can be thought of as a series of loops and
folds stacked on top of one another, enables region-
and gene-specific activity of enhancers. These folds
create contact points between regions of the
genome that would normally be large distances
apart and are mediated by insulators. Bromodomain
and extraterminal (BET) family proteins recognize
the acetylated histones of enhancers and mediate
interaction with gene promoters by forming a pro-
tein bridge that links the two sites and coordinates
transcriptional machinery docking on the gene
(Bradner et al., 2017; Winter et al., 2017; Shu et al.,
2020; Crump et al., 2021; Kim et al., 2021). As
182 	J. Cawley

-- 198 of 258 --

183	Epigenetic Targeting of Cancer
mentioned above, insulators help to facilitate chro-
matin looping. Like other regulatory elements,
insulators are noncoding regions of the DNA but
create binding sites for ring-shaped proteins, such
as CCCTC-binding factor (CTCF), which form
barriers across the genome to prevent inappropriate
interactions between enhancers and genes. Chromatin
strands are extruded through these ring-shaped
proteins to form regulatory neighborhoods, also
called “topologically associating domains” (TADs),
which allow for distant enhancers to contact pro-
moters. Translocations, inversions, viral DNA
insertions, copy number alterations, and mutations
of insulator DNA-binding sites can disrupt TAD
boundaries and result in aberrant enhancer–
promoter interactions (Plon and Wang, 1986;
Flavahan et al., 2019; He et al., 2019; Morton
et al., 2019; Wu et al., 2019; Asakawa et al., 2020;
Fang, 2020; Feng and Pauklin, 2020; Leong and
Lung, 2021). Oncogene expression is commonly
driven by cancer-specific enhancer networks, mak-
ing enhancers and chromatin structure interesting
targets for cancer therapy. Targeting specific
enhancers is not yet possible in patients as it
requires gene editing techniques. However, various
classes of drugs exist that target effector proteins
binding or modifying cis-regulatory sites and will
be covered in the coming sections.
Mutations in genes encoding for histones
can drive cancer progression
Recent work has uncovered mutations in histone
coding genes that seem to be especially common in
human pediatric cancers such as chondroblastoma
and diffuse intrinsic pontine glioma (Qiu et al.,
2018; Nacev et al., 2019). Oncohistones have
altered conformation and cannot be regulated simi-
larly to normal histones. H3K27M and H3K36M
oncohistones have a lysine–methionine substitution
of the N-terminal tail (at position 27 or 36) block-
ing normal function of histone methyltransferases
that modify those lysine residues. This alters nor-
mal distribution of histone marks, disrupting gene
expression patterns and inducing genomic instabil-
ity (Qiu et al., 2018; Nacev et al., 2019; Amatori
et al., 2021). Oncohistone mutations are likely
more common than previously understood in
human cancer. The prevalence and importance in
veterinary species have not been studied but given
the increased awareness will likely be discovered as
drivers in animal cancers. How these mutations can
be exploited therapeutically has not been well elu-
cidated, although several preclinical studies have
shown promise in using various different epidrugs
(Qiu et al., 2018; Nacev et al., 2019; Zhang and
Zhang, 2019; Amatori et al., 2021).
DNA methylation
DNA methylation is a critically important process
during embryonic development, cellular differenti-
ation, and for maintaining genome stability in
mature cells (Jones, 2012; Greenberg and Bourc’his,
2019). The impacts of DNA methylation vary by
genomic region and context. Traditionally thought
of as a silencing mark, it is now understood that
DNA methylation contributes to transcriptional
activation and repression. Cell-type-specific DNA
methylation patterns are rigorously maintained
during cellular differentiation and repressive DNA
methylation marks are placed on germline-specific
(stem-cell-specific) genes in mature cells (Kafri
et al., 1992; Razin, 1998; Herman, 1999; Esteller,
2002; Jones, 2012; Greenberg and Bourc’his,
2019). DNA methylation even contributes to
X-chromosome inactivation (Avner and Heard,
2001). The widespread importance of appropriate
and timely DNA methylation makes it a great tar-
get for disruption during cancer development.
Drugs that modulate DNA methylation were the
first epidrugs developed and have continued to
expand in use for treating cancer.
DNA methylation refers to methylation of the
fifth carbon on cytosines (5-methylcytosine (5mC)).
5mC is deposited by DNA N-methyltransferases
(DNMTs). 5mC can also be removed by demethyl-
ase proteins, such as TET2. There are three DNMTs
known in humans: DNMT1, DNMT3A, and
DNMT3B. DNMT3A and DNMT3B catalyze de
novo DNA methylation (Ambrosi et al., 2017).
DNMT1 preferentially methylates hemimethylated
DNA and thus serves more of a maintenance role
in preserving methylation patterns during cell divi-
sion (Bashtrykov et al., 2012; Ambrosi et al.,
2017). DNMT and TET2 alterations are known
drivers of cancer development and result in signifi-
cant alterations to DNA methylation patterns and
gene expression (Gaidzik et al., 2012; Dhawan
et al., 2013; Li, X.D. et al., 2016; Wong et al., 2019;
Xu et al., 2019; Jiang, 2020).
Dinucleotide repeats of cytosine and guanine
(CpG) are enriched for in transcriptional start sites
of gene promoters. These “CpG islands” are the

-- 199 of 258 --

most common sites for DNA methylation to occur.
Hypermethylation of promoter CpG islands inhib-
its binding of transcriptional machinery and
represses gene expression. Promoter hypermethyla-
tion is commonly found at tumor suppressor genes
in cancer (Herman, 1999; Esteller, 2002; Tian et al.,
2013; Lucia et al., 2021). Contrary to the role of
DNA methylation at promoters, hypermethylation
of CpG islands in gene bodies is typical of actively
transcribed genes (Carrozza et al., 2005; Maunakea
et al., 2010; Yang et al., 2014). The exact role that
DNA methylation plays in this context is not well
understood, but global DNA hypomethylation is a
common occurrence in cancer. One sequela to this
is loss of protective methylation over transposable
elements that are typically inactive in mature
cells (Burns, 2017; Ponomaryova et al., 2020).
Transposable elements, such as LINE-1, are numer-
ous throughout mammalian genomes and can
contribute to genomic instability when active as
these are mobile DNA elements. Other roles for
gene body methylation are currently being investi-
gated but will not be covered in this text. It is likely
that gene body methylation has diverse functions
that are context dependent, as is true for DNA
methylation in general, and better understanding
of these functions will improve the understanding of
DNA methylation-targeting agents in cancer.
Nutrition and cancer metabolism can alter
DNA methylation patterns and epigenetic
regulation of gene expression
Nutri-epigenetics is a vast and growing field.
Nutrition seems to play a large role in modulating
epigenetic regulation systemically. In one study,
nutrition was even found to alter heritable traits
passed down through the sperm of mice (Lismer
et al., 2021). This brings new meaning to the say-
ing, “You are what you eat.” Nutrition is a hot
topic for cancer prevention and treatment but is a
challenging field to study as controlling diet can be
quite difficult. This is likely something that would
be more easily studied in dogs, once databases are
widely available containing epigenetic profiles of
normal canine cell types. On a smaller scale, cancer
metabolism has already been shown to cause sig-
nificant changes to epigenetic regulation of gene
expression. By-products and intermediate metabo-
lites from the tricarboxylic acid (TCA) cycle can
have inhibitory effects on epigenetic regulatory
proteins and are thus called “oncometabolites”.
The most studied oncometabolite is 2-hydroxyglu-
tarate (2-HG). 2-HG accumulates due to mutations
in the isocitrate genes, IDH1 or IDH2. Gain-of-
function mutations of IDH1 or IDH2 are relatively
common in acute myeloid leukemias (AMLs) and
adult glioblastomas. 2-HG is a competitive inhibi-
tor of α-ketoglutarate-dependent dioxygenases that
are essential for DNA demethylase proteins, such
as TET2. Loss of TET2 function shifts the balance
of methylation and demethylation activity across
the genome and induces a hypermethylated DNA
state that alters gene expression globally. Mutually
exclusive loss-of-function mutations of TET2 are
seen in the same cancer types with similar outcome
on gene expression. This highlights the significance
of alterations in DNA methylation as a driver in
cancer and has resulted in the US Food and Drug
Administration 	(FDA) 	approving 	two 	drugs,
ivosidenib and enasidenib, for the treatment of
IDH-mutant AMLs in people.
Targeting Epigenetic Effector Proteins
Epigenetic regulators modify DNA and histones
and have a crucial role in transcription, DNA
repair, and replication (Reik, 2007; Fukaya et al.,
2016; Peng and Zhang, 2018; Yokoshi and Fukaya,
2019; Crump et al., 2021). Targeted agents against
the different classes of epigenetic regulators are
available for use against various human cancer
types, with nine drugs currently approved by the
FDA.
Targeting epigenetic readers
Readers are proteins that recognize particular his-
tone marks and facilitate gene expression. The two
major classes of readers are bromodomain and
chromodomain proteins, which bind acetylated
histones and methylated histones, respectively.
Drugs targeting bromodomain proteins are a popu-
lar focus for drug development, with clinical trials
for various disease states including cancer and
cardiovascular disease. A subfamily of bromodo-
main proteins, called BET proteins, have received a
significant amount of interest. JQ1 was the first-in-
class BET inhibitor and is a small molecule that
binds all four BET proteins: BRD2, BRD3, BRD4,
and BRDT. BET proteins are known to be overex-
pressed in human cancer (Stathis and Bertoni,
2018) and BRD4 (and less commonly BRD3) forms
a fusion protein with NUT leading to characteristic
184 	J. Cawley

-- 200 of 258 --

185	Epigenetic Targeting of Cancer
“megadomains” of acetylated histones and aber-
rant gene expression of oncogenes, such as MYC
(Filippakopoulos et al., 2010; Filippakopoulos and
Knapp, 2014; Grayson et al., 2014). After JQ1
demonstrated preclinical activity against models
for human NUT carcinoma (Filippakopoulos et al.,
2010), several BET inhibitors have reached clinical
evaluation (Berthon et al., 2016; Stathis and
Bertoni, 2018; Ameratunga et al., 2020). This class
of epidrugs holds promise based on preclinical
findings but has yet to break through clinically in
people. Preclinical studies in dogs have demon-
strated efficacy of BET inhibitors against models of
canine B-cell lymphoma and canine mammary
carcinoma (Xavier et al., 2019; Kong et al., 2020).
Chromodomain inhibitors are not as well stud-
ied as their acetyl-recognizing counterparts but are
known to play a role in cancer development and
progression. Polycomb group proteins (PcG) form
repressive complexes (PRC1/2) that modify his-
tones to silence genes (Sauvageau and Sauvageau,
2010). PRC1/2 are critical in lineage specification
and maintaining differentiation state of somatic
and stem cells (Sauvageau and Sauvageau, 2010;
Abdouh et al., 2016; Connelly et al., 2019).
Chromodomain proteins recognize methyl histone
marks and help localize PRC1/2 to particular
regions of the genome (Sauvageau and Sauvageau,
2010; Connelly et al., 2019; Tatavosian et al.,
2019; Wang et al., 2021). Several chromodomain
proteins have been shown to be upregulated in
various cancers and are prognostic markers in pan-
creatic and gastric carcinomas (Sauvageau and
Sauvageau, 2010; Chen et al., 2021; He et al.,
2021). Furthermore, various other PcGs are known
oncogenic drivers and will be discussed further in
other sections of this chapter. The varied role of
PRC1/2 in cancer makes these complexes interest-
ing targets for cancer therapy, with chromodomain
inhibitors being an exciting method for reducing
PRC1/2 activity (Mills, 2010; Koppens and van
Lohuizen, 2016; Liu et al., 2018; Wang et al., 2020;
Wang et al., 2021).
Targeting epigenetic writers
Writers are proteins that add modifications to his-
tones or DNA and include DNMTs, histone lysine
methyltransferases (KMTs), and histone acetyl-
transferases (HATs). Writers are commonly mutated
in human cancers (Kanai et al., 2003; Jones et al.,
2016; Wong et al., 2019; Bates, 2020; Yang et al.,
2020), implicating a role for this group of epigen-
etic effector proteins in cancer development. Of the
three types of writers, DNMTs have been studied
the most and currently two DNMT inhibitors are
commercially available. Many cancers have altera-
tions in methylation status driving cancer-specific
gene expression and phenotype (di Croce et al.,
2002; McCabe et al., 2010; Pronina et al., 2017; de
Souza et al., 2018; Beetch et al., 2020). This is
important to note because it suggests that DNMT
inhibitors may have a broad use in treating cancer
and should not only be thought of in the context of
specific DNMT mutations. Maintaining appropri-
ate methylation status is a critical step in preserving
the epigenetic program of a cell and DNMT inhibi-
tors offer a potential for restoring “order” to can-
cer gene expression (Gnyszka et al., 2013). These
agents have been studied within preclinical and
clinical studies for canine cancers (Momparler
et al., 1989; Klecker et al., 2006; Hahn et al., 2012;
Thayanithy et al., 2012; Dhawan et al., 2013;
Flesner et al., 2014; Fulkerson et al., 2017) and
offer a novel therapeutic approach for veterinary
oncologists; however, much work is still needed to
find appropriate contexts for their use in veterinary
cancer patients.
DNA methyltransferase inhibitors
DNMT inhibitors fall into the “antimetabolite”
class of chemotherapeutic drugs. These drugs com-
petitively inhibit the addition of cytidine into DNA
and RNA and possess a nitrogen at position 5 of
the pyrimidine ring that rends DNMTs incapable
of placing a methyl group (Gnyszka et al., 2013;
Yang et al., 2020). DNMT inhibitors are hypo-
methylating agents and act by reestablishing gene
expression of hypermethylated tumor suppressors
(Bates, 2020). Azacitidine and decitabine are
approved by the FDA as single-agent therapies for
AML. Early-phase clinical trials of single-agent
azacitidine or decitabine have not demonstrated
the same profound responses as in hematologic
cancers. Still, preclinical studies suggest a role for
DNMT 	inhibitors 	in 	treating 	solid 	tumors
(Newman et al., 2015; Yu et al., 2019; Idrissou
et al., 2020). It is likely that combinations of
DNMT inhibitors and other epidrugs or cytotoxic
chemotherapy will help overcome some of the
obstacles in treating solid tumors.
Azanucleoside drugs appear to have clinical use
for dogs with cancer. Azacitidine treatment of

-- 201 of 258 --

canine mammary tumor cell lines resulted in re-
expression of DAPK1 and MGMT associated with
decreased proliferation of cells (Harman et al.,
2016). Azacitidine has also been studied as a treat-
ment for dogs with urinary bladder carcinoma. In
a preclinical study of 19 dogs with urothelial carci-
noma, daily subcutaneous injections of azacitidine
resulted in clinical benefit for 72.2% of dogs, with
four dogs achieving a partial remission (Hahn et al.,
2012). Global hypomethylation was assessed in
peripheral blood mononuclear cells and from
tumors samples pre and post treatment for some of
the dogs on study. Global hypomethylation was not
correlated with responses in that study. Activity
of DNMT inhibitors may not be confined to hypomethy-
lation and re-expression of tumor suppressors.
Recent evidence suggests that response to DNMT
inhibitors may be linked to hypomethylation of
transposable elements ((TSEs), also known as endog-
enous retrotransposons) (Ohtani et al., 2020). TSEs
are mobile sequences of DNA that remain dormant
in somatic cells due to methylation. Active TSEs
can stimulate innate immunity through upregula-
tion of interferons leading to immune targeting of
cancer cells (Chiappinelli et al., 2015; Koonin and
Krupovic, 2015; Ohtani et al., 2020).
A potential major challenge of implementing
azacitidine and decitabine in veterinary medicine is
the fact that both drugs are parenteral but require
frequent administration for activity. This makes
having an orally bioavailable DNMT inhibitor
attractive for treating veterinary cancer patients.
Zebularine is an oral cytidine analog that has dem-
onstrated favorable pharmacokinetics in dogs
(Fulkerson et al., 2017). This drug also has activity
against canine malignant lymphoid and osteosar-
coma cell lines (Thayanithy et al., 2012; Flesner
et al., 2014). Further studies are necessary to
understand the appropriate use cases for zebularine
and other DNMT inhibitors in veterinary medicine,
but preliminary evidence suggests that this drug
class holds promise for veterinary cancers.
Non-nucleoside analogs have also demonstrated
direct or off-target DNMT-inhibiting effects. The
antiarrhythmic procainamide has demonstrated
specific DNMT1 inhibitory effects and in vitro
activity against various human cancer cell lines
(Lee et al., 2005). Hydralazine, an antihypertensive
drug, has been shown to modulate ERK signaling,
which 	reduces 	expression 	of 	DNMT1 	and
DNMT3a (Deng et al., 2003; Candelaria et al.,
2017). Additionally, curcumin has hypomethylat-
ing activity and appears to directly inhibit catalytic
activity of DNMT1 (Al-Yousef et al., 2020). Many
drugs initially are intended for one indication
before having additional uses discovered. Epidrug
repurposing offers an alternative path toward
delivering novel agents for treatment of veterinary
cancers and can avoid costly and time-consuming
pharmacokinetic and toxicity studies (Montalvo-
Casimiro et al., 2020).
Histone lysine methyltransferase inhibitors
KMTs catalyze a broad range of methylation events
on histones that regulate genomic structure and gene
expression. Mutations, translocations, and altered
expression of KMTs are frequently observed in can-
cer (Jones et al., 2016). Of the many KMTs that exist
in mammalian cells, EZH2, NSD2, DOT1L, and
SETD2 are the most studied and an EZH2 inhibitor,
tazemetostat, recently received accelerated approval
for the treatment of human follicular lymphoma.
The various KMTs catalyze specific histone methyla-
tion marks and thus play a role in cell-type-specific
gene expression. In this section we will explore some
of the drugs in late developmental stages and evidence
for use of KMT inhibitors in dogs.
EZH2 AS A DRUG TARGET 	EZH2 is a component of
the polycomb repressive complex 2 (PRC2), and is
responsible for depositing mono-, di- and trimeth-
ylation marks on H3K27. Acetylation of H3K27
loosens chromatin and allows for gene transcrip-
tion while also serving as a dock for bromodomain
family proteins, such as BRD4 (Bradner et al.,
2017; Gaub et al., 2020). EZH2, as part of PRC2,
trimethylates H3K27 resulting in regional gene
repression and is considered a critical component
in stem cell fate determination (McGrath and
Trojer, 2015; Duan et al., 2020). Both gain- and
loss-of-function mutations of EZH2 have been
discovered in human cancers (Jones et al., 2016),
and increased expression is associated with canine
mammary carcinoma (Choi et al., 2016). Gain-of-
function mutations in human follicular lymphoma
have been the basis of developing EZH2-inhibiting
drugs. Hot-spot mutations of Y641 in EZH2
increase methylation capability on H3K27me1/2
while decreasing de novo activity on H3K27.
Tazemetostat has demonstrated significant activity
in heavily pretreated human patients with relapsed
or refractory follicular lymphomas (Morschhauser
et al., 2020). Of note, patients with hot-spot
186 	J. Cawley

-- 202 of 258 --

187	Epigenetic Targeting of Cancer
mutations of EZH2 were more likely to respond
(objective response rate: 69%) to tazemetostat;
however, 35% of patients with wild-type EZH2
responded and had similar response durations to
cases with mutant EZH2. This suggests activity
beyond its use as a targeted therapy for gain-of-
function EZH2 mutations and recent evidence
has validated other contexts for EZH2 inhibitors.
The SMARC family protein complex SWI/SNF has
chromatin remodeling activity and associates with
H3K27ac at enhancers to modulate gene expres-
sion (Alver et al., 2017; Mashtalir et al., 2018). It is
estimated the SWI/SNF genes are mutated in 20%
of all human cancers, suggesting activity in main-
taining lineage-specific gene expression for many
different cell types (Alver et al., 2017). Loss-of-
function mutations in SWI/SNF are associated with
increased H3K27me3 repressive marks and silenc-
ing of genes (Jones et al., 2016). This effect seems
to be mediated in part by EZH2, with inhibition
resulting in cell death for malignant cells harboring
mutations in genes encoding a variety of SMARC
family proteins, including SMARCA2/SMARCA4,
ARID1A, and PBRM1 (Jones et al., 2016; Januario
et al., 2017). Tazemetostat proved to be active in
epithelioid sarcomas possessing SMARCB1/INI1
mutations as well as synovial cell sarcomas with
SS18–SSX fusions and loss of SMARCB1 (Jones
et al., 2016; Hale et al., 2019). This emphasizes the
importance of therapeutic biomarkers as determi-
nants of precision medicine context and not just
mutations in genes.
SETD2 INSTILLS CANCER DEPENDENCIES 	SETD2, a
KMT, trimethylates H3K36, is integral for main-
taining genome stability, and participates in gene
transcription (Li, J. et al., 2016). SETD2 is mutated
in 21–42% of canine osteosarcomas (Sakthikumar
et al., 2018; Gardner et al., 2019). SETD2 has
tumor-suppressive activity making direct targets of
this protein challenging; however, loss of SETD2
can provide opportunities for synthetic lethality.
SETD2 is required for maintenance of H3K79
dimethylation, a histone mark that is catalyzed
by the histone methyltransferase DOT1L (Skucha
et al., 2018). Inhibition of DOT1L in the setting
of SETD2 loss in AML cells has profound effects
(Skucha et al., 2018), implicating DOT1L inhibitors
as potential treatment options for SETD2-mutant
canine osteosarcoma. Furthermore, inhibition of
the phosphatidylinositol 3-kinase (PI3K)–protein
kinase B (AKT) axis has demonstrated synthetic
lethality in SETD2-deficient kidney cancer cells.
PI3K pathway mutations occur in 37% of canine
osteosarcoma tumors (Gardner et al., 2019), which
further emphasizes a potential role for PI3K/AKT
inhibitors for this disease.
Targeting epigenetic erasers
Erasers are proteins that remove epigenetic modifi-
cations from DNA or histones. Erasers that remove
methyl marks from DNA or histones are called
demethylases, whereas erasers that remove acetyl
groups are called deacetylases. Erasers play a vital
role in maintaining appropriate gene expression by
counterbalancing methyl- and acetyltransferases
that deposit epigenetic marks on DNA and his-
tones. In this section we will discuss the various
types of erasers, there impact in cancer, and tar-
geted therapeutics against these proteins.
Genomic and metabolic inhibition
of TET2 can be exploited through
epigenetic targeting agents
DNA demethylation is catalyzed by ten-eleven
translocation methylcytosine dioxygenases (TETs).
Initially, TET oxidizes 5mC (5-methylcytosine) to
5-hydroxymethylcytosine (5hmC). This first oxida-
tive step is then followed by hydroxylating steps
that produce 5-formylcytosine (5fC) and 5-car-
boxylcytosine (5-caC). 5fC and 5caC are recog-
nized as intermediate bases, excised, and repaired
as cytosine (Jiang, 2020). It is important to note
that methylated cytosine (5mC) is an unstable base
and can spontaneously deaminate to thymidine,
which, if not appropriately repaired, can lead to
mutations in methylated DNA regions. TET2 has
tumor-suppressor activity and is commonly altered
in human hematopoietic cancers. Loss-of-function
mutations in TET2 result in decreased levels of
5hmC (the oxidized form of 5mC) and specific
hypermethylation 	of 	hematopoietic-specific
enhancers (Itzykson et al., 2011; Gaidzik et al.,
2012; Xu et al., 2019; Jiang, 2020). The combina-
tion of these events results in altered gene expres-
sion programs and leukemic progression (Jiang,
2020). DNMT inhibitors, such as azacitidine, have
been used with success in human patients with
TET2-mutant acute leukemias, suggesting that
DNA methylation writers are important in the
altered epigenetic programs of TET2-mutant cells
(Itzykson et al., 2011).

-- 203 of 258 --

TET2 function can also be inhibited in cancer
through mutations of the TCA cycle enzyme isoci-
trate dehydrogenase (IDH1 and IDH2). Normally,
IDH catalyzes the decarboxylation of isocitrate to
α-ketoglutarate. Mutant IDH1 and IDH2 gene
products have neoenzymatic activity, catalyzing
α-ketoglutarate to the oncometabolite 2-HG (Dang
et al., 2009). TET2 is part of a large family of
α-ketoglutarate-dependent 	dioxygenases 	that
include DNA and histone demethylases. 2-HG
competitively inhibits α-ketoglutarate-dependent
dioxygenases resulting in altered epigenetic pro-
grams. 2-HG also decreases hypoxia-inducible fac-
tor (HIF) levels and disrupts NADP+/NAPDH
balance resulting in increased levels of reactive
oxygen species (Dang et al., 2009; Miller et al.,
2017). Mutations of IDH1 and IDH2 are fre-
quently detected in various cancers including gli-
oma (80%), AML (20%), cholangiocarcinoma
(20%), and chondrosarcoma (80%). Targeted thera-
peutics have demonstrated single-agent efficacy for
IDH-mutant AMLs: ivosidenib and enasidenib.
These drugs target mutant IDH1 and IDH2,
respectively (Stein et al., 2017; Roboz et al., 2020).
The experience with mutant IDH inhibitors has
not been as fruitful for the treatment of low-grade
adult gliomas (Miller et al., 2017). This may be due
to context-specific differences between gliomas and
AMLs. For instance, elevated levels of 2-HG are a
negative prognostic indicator for IDH-mutant
AML (DiNardo et al., 2013; Miller et al., 2017);
however, the picture is not as clear in IDH-mutant
gliomas. This suggests that 2-HG has differential
effects based on the cancer cell type of origin.
TET2 mutations appear to be present, albeit
rare, in canine mast cell tumors and peripheral
T-cell lymphomas (McDonald et al., 2018; Xavier
et al., 2020). Several studies have evaluated expres-
sion of IDH mutants in canine gliomas with mixed
findings (Reitman et al., 2010; Kawakami et al.,
2020). A large comparative genomic analysis of
human and canine gliomas did definitively show
shared hot-spot mutations affecting IDH1 R132
codon. However, whereas 80% of low-grade adult
human gliomas harbor this mutation, it was seen in
only 3.7% of canine gliomas (Amin et al., 2020).
Histone deacetylase inhibitors
Proteins that erase acetyl marks from histones and
cytoplasmic proteins are called histone deacetylases
(HDACs). There are 11 HDAC proteins grouped
into four major classes of HDACs: I, IIa, IIb, and
IV. The various HDACs have different roles in
deacetylating histones and other proteins, while
also acting as bromodomains that bind acetylated
substrates (McClure et al., 2018). Four HDAC
inhibitors are approved by the FDA for treatment
of human cancers. These agents include vorinostat,
romidepsin, belinostat, and panobinostat. Each
HDAC inhibitor has variable activity against the 11
different HDAC proteins, providing context-spe-
cific activity (Jones et al., 2016). In general, HDAC
inhibitors act by preventing deacetylation of his-
tones, and therefore increase acetylation of his-
tones. This results in increased gene expression at
acetylated sites. Cytotoxic effects of HDAC inhibi-
tors are complex and mirror the diverse roles that
HDAC proteins play. Proposed mechanisms of
action for HDAC inhibitors include re-expression
of tumor suppressors, DNA and mitochondrial
damage, and increased acetylation of cytoplasmic
proteins (McClure et al., 2018; Bates, 2020).
Acetylation of cytoplasmic proteins is modulated
by class II HDACs. Inhibition of this process can
lead to aggregation of misfolded proteins that is
cytotoxic to cancer cells (Kulka et al., 2020).
HDAC inhibitors are well studied in human can-
cers and several translational canine studies have
been performed as well. These drugs, similar to
other epidrugs, have demonstrated profound sin-
gle-agent 	activity 	in 	hematopoietic 	cancers.
Vorinostat and romidepsin are FDA approved for
treatment of human cutaneous T-cell lymphomas.
Romidepsin has also demonstrated efficacy in
treating human peripheral T-cell lymphomas and
has received FDA approval, along with belinostat,
in this setting. Panobinostat is FDA approved in
combination with dexamethasone for treatment of
human multiple myeloma. Vorinostat, belinostat,
and panobinostat are HDAC class I and II inhibi-
tors, while romidepsin is a class I-specific inhibitor
(Hui and Chiang, 2014). Valproic acid, an antiepi-
leptic drug with HDAC-inhibiting activity, is well
tolerated at doses up to 240 mg/kg/day concurrent
with doxorubicin treatment in dogs with cancer
(Wittenburg et al., 2010). Valproate induced H3
hyperacetylation at the reported dose both in
peripheral blood mononuclear cells and in tumors.
It is important to note that global hyperacetylation
is not likely the best predictor of response to
HDAC inhibitors given the broad activity of these
drugs. Importantly, this treatment protocol was
well tolerated, suggesting that valproate alone or in

189	Epigenetic Targeting of Cancer
combination with cytotoxic therapeutics can be
further studied to evaluate clinical benefit for spe-
cific disease contexts in dogs. Preclinical in vitro
studies of various canine cancer cell lines, including
transitional cell carcinoma (TCC) (Eto et al., 2019),
osteosarcoma, T-cell lymphoma, mast cell tumor,
and histiocytic sarcoma, have demonstrated sensi-
tivity to HDAC inhibitors (Kisseberth et al., 2008;
Lin et al., 2010; Murahari et al., 2017). These col-
lective studies suggest that HDAC inhibitors hold
promise in veterinary oncology. Appropriately
designed clinical trials are warranted to identify
biomarkers of response and expand their use in
treating animal cancers.
Targeting super-enhancers and
transcriptional machinery
Super-enhancers are collections of enhancers in a
shared genomic region that drive lineage-specific
gene expression (Peng and Zhang, 2018). Super-
enhancers become rearranged in cancer to drive
new transcriptional programs that contribute to
cancer-specific phenotypes and metastatic pheno-
types (Sengupta and George, 2017; Morrow et al.,
2018; Jia et al., 2019). Cancer becomes addicted to
transcription and demonstrates expression levels
far exceeding normal cells, making drugs that tar-
get super-enhancers an interesting approach to
cancer therapy with the possibility of lower risk for
side effects (Bradner et al., 2017). There are cur-
rently several different approaches now in develop-
ment that target super-enhancer-related proteins or
subunits of the major transcription complex, RNA
polymerase II. Anti-transcriptional agents include
cyclin-dependent kinases 7 and 9 (CDK7 and
CDK9) and BET inhibitors. This is a new and excit-
ing field of drug development for human and vet-
erinary oncology that is growing rapidly and
gaining novel insights for clinical applications but
remains mostly preclinical at this current point
(Ema et al., 2016; Pawlak et al., 2017; Xavier et al.,
2019), aside from the use of BET inhibitors for
human NUT midline carcinoma (Bates, 2020).
Combination Therapies and the Future
of Targeting Cancer Epigenetics
Many different combinations involving epidrugs
have been studied preclinically and show promising
effects. For instance, DNMT inhibitors can demethy-
late transposable elements that induce an innate
immune response. Combinations with immuno-
modulatory drugs hold promise for treating a vari-
ety of cancer types (Gomez et al., 2020; Moufarrij
et al., 2020). Currently, there is only one FDA-
approved combination therapy with panobinostat,
bortezomib, and dexamethasone for previously
treated human myeloma (Hansen et al., 2018). One
of the challenges of combination therapy is
sequence and timing of drugs. Combination proto-
cols of immune therapeutics for cancer have
revealed the importance of this concept. Anti-PD-1
and OX40 therapy can either have little combined
effect, a synergistic effect, or inhibit one another
depending on the order and timing of administra-
tion (Messenheimer et al., 2017). Consider a com-
bination therapy with a BET inhibitor and cytotoxic
chemotherapy. If the BET inhibitor induces cell
cycle arrest but the cytotoxic drug requires cells to
undergo cell division for activity, then giving the
BET inhibitor concurrently or just before cytotoxic
chemotherapy could induce resistance to the cyto-
toxic drug. Careful consideration and appropriate
preclinical studies are necessary to help define
sequence and timing of combination protocols.
Single-agent activity of epidrugs has remained dis-
appointing outside of specific uses in human
hematopoietic cancers. It is likely that combination
therapies are necessary in order to obtain robust
responses in the broader field of oncology. Future
studies will help to reveal disease-specific contexts
and guide appropriate drug selection for both
human and veterinary cancer patients.
