11Precision Medicine
JOELLE FENGER1,2*
1Ethos Veterinary Health, Woburn, Massachusetts, USA; 2Ethos Discovery,
San Diego, California, USA
Introduction
The care of most cancer patients begins with a
pathologic diagnosis of the cancer. This diagnosis
presumes that the cell or organ of origin for a can-
cer can guide patient care from prognosis through
to therapy. This use of a pathologic diagnosis has
been a convention in oncology for over 150 years,
beginning at the time when active debate surrounded
the question of whether cancers were created by
abnormal cells and whether cells were a basic unit
of a living organism. Since this time, the characteri-
zation of cancers has continued to depend on the
light microscope despite the unequivocal under-
standing that altered chromosomes and DNA in
these cells was responsible for the altered behavior
of these cells. Recent advances in genomic techniques
(so-called “next-generation sequencing” (NGS))
have created the opportunity to deliver a genomic
characterization of cancer in a clinically relevant
timespan and within a clinically useful timeline.
The result is the possible shift from the light micro-
scope to a genomic characterization of cancer. It is
intuitively obvious to imagine how this genomic
analysis could complement, augment, or replace
the light microscope to deliver patient value. Use
cases for this genomic characterization will reason-
ably address many of the known challenges associated
with a light microscopic pathologic characteriza-
tion, including diagnosis, subgroup identification,
prognosis, and therapeutic selection (i.e., Precision
Medicine). The horizons for the delivery of evi-
dence in support of this genomic characterization
will likely be distinct. Indeed, it is likely that some
evidence and use cases will be resolved sooner than
others. Further adoption of these technologies in all
use cases should not be necessary for recognition of
value from a single use case. Nonetheless, it is very
likely that such genomic characterization of cancer
will be a growing part of the future of oncology
and veterinary oncology. At this time, the body of
published evidence on genomic medicine applied to
veterinary oncology is limited and as such, we will
reflect on the progresses and challenges in the
human delivery of genomic medicine for this
chapter.
Cancer Precision Medicine, Genomic-Directed
Medicine, or Personalized Medicine (herein, PMED)
has been introduced to human cancer patients over
the last 20 years. Despite the ongoing and instinc-
tive appeal and traction among cancer patient fami-
lies, the challenges of the field have been realized
and by many accounts, the field is receding from the
heightened promise at its introduction into human
oncology. The premise, promise, and reality for
PMED in humans (Fig. 11) will be discussed in this
chapter and is summarized below:
● cancer is a disease of dysregulated genes;
● however, cancer biology is highly complex, and
the best evidence suggests that understanding
the dysregulated genes in a specific patient’s
tumor has been surprisingly difficult to translate
into meaningful therapeutic improvements in
that patient;
● important gaps in knowledge and the applica-
tion of PMED remain and must be addressed
before this approach will add value to most
newly presenting cancer patients;
● the challenges and missteps in delivering PMED
to human cancer patients provides a guide to
deliver this future of genomic medicine more
effectively to veterinary oncology patients; and
● interestingly, an immediate value related to
genomic medicine that will simultaneously
address some of the gaps in PMED will involve
199

DOI: 10.1079/9781789245820.0011

the use of these genomic tools to define molecu-
lar subgroups for specific cancers such that care-
fully designed clinical trials can determine if/
which drugs are best aligned with each molecu-
lar subgroup.
Fundamental Hypothesis: Cancer
as a “Disease of the Genome”
Cancer has historically been defined by its gross
organ or tissue of origin, or by its microscopic cel-
lular characteristics. The widened availability NGS
has led to a significant increase in cancer molecular
profiling, allowing for the characterization of DNA
sequence variants in tumor tissues (Vogelstein
et al., 2013; Berger and Mardis, 2018). These
advances have revealed that the pathogenesis of
cancer involves a multistep dynamic process that
includes genetic diversification/evolution, epigen-
etic modifications, and clonal pressure/selection
within tumor cells that creates cancer lesions in
patients that will interact closely with noncancer-
ous cells in the tumor microenvironment, ulti-
mately creating the clinical problem for patients
(Gerlinger et al., 2012; Meacham and Morrison,
2013). Tumor progression is further accelerated by
the accumulation of successive genomic alterations
resulting in the acquisition of phenotypic proper-
ties of increased cell replication, inhibition of the
processes that keep cell division in check, invasion
into surrounding tissues, travel to distant organs by
lymphatic and vascular routes, and evasion of the
immune system’s surveillance and control mecha-
nisms (Gerlinger et al., 2012).
Cancer-predisposing alterations that confer an
uncontrolled growth advantage to a population of
cells may be heritable and present in every cell at
birth (i.e., germline alterations) or they may be
acquired in a subset of cells in the body after birth
(i.e., somatic alterations). Genetic alterations in
cancer include the abnormal activation of onco-
genes (gain-of-function) or inactivation of tumor
suppressor genes (loss-of-function). Whereas gain-
of-function oncogene alterations act in a dominant
fashion where alteration of only one of the two
alleles is sufficient for activation and potential can-
cer induction, loss-of-function of tumor suppressor
genes follows a recessive mode of action in which
both alleles need to be inactivated to contribute to
tumorigenesis. Additionally, certain tumor suppres-
sor genes exhibit “haplo-insufficiency”, meaning
that a single-copy mutation or loss of one copy of
the gene is insufficient for proper function and may
contribute to tumorigenesis and cancer progres-
sion. Activating mutations in oncogenes tend to
occur in specific genomic locations (known as “hot
spots”) and contribute to all parts of the cancer
phenotype. In contrast, loss-of-function or inacti-
vating mutations found in tumor suppressor genes
may occur across the full length of a gene and
result in impaired regulation of intrinsic protective
mechanisms that control the development and
growth of tumors.
Several distinct classes of genomic alterations
exist that may variably drive cancer initiation and
progression, including smaller genomic aberrations
such as single nucleotide variants (SNVs) that
involve a change in just one nucleotide in the
genome or indels (nucleotide insertions and dele-
tions) in which one to several nucleotides are
inserted into, or removed from, the normal DNA
sequence (Vogelstein et al., 2013; Bailey et al.,
2018). Larger classes of genomic disruption affect-
ing thousands to millions of nucleotides are referred
to as “structural alterations”. These commonly
include copy number variants (CNVs), in which
large segments of DNA (up to an entire chromo-
some) are abnormally amplified or completely
absent, and chromosomal translocations whereby
DNA strands from unrelated parts of the genome
are joined together and result in “fusion genes”.
The actual contribution to the cancer phenotype
requires the transcription of these altered cancer
genes into mRNA species, regulated through the
epigenome.
It is important to note that a large proportion of
the genetic aberrations found in cancer genomes do
not result in a deleterious effect, do not confer a
discernible growth advantage to the cell, and are
considered “passenger” alterations (Hess et al.,
2019). Genomic alterations that provide a selective
growth advantage to affected cells are termed
“driver” mutations; however, it is not trivial to
decipher the “driver” alterations in genomically
complex tumors or to determine the functional
impact of these cancer-related genes on cellular
processes such as cell survival, cell fate, and
genome maintenance (Zehir et al., 2017; Bailey
et al., 2018). An additional layer of complexity lies
in the observation that a primary “gatekeeping”
alteration provides an initial growth advantage and
may allow the affected cell to replicate more
quickly than the surrounding cells, becoming a
microscopic clone; in time, a cell within this clone
200 	J. Fenger

-- 216 of 258 --

201	Precision Medicine
will randomly acquire secondary alterations, typi-
cally in other genes, and initiate subsequent rounds
of clonal expansion with enhanced selective growth
advantage for the cells containing multiple aberra-
tions (Gerlinger et al., 2012). This process of novel
mutation acquisition beyond the original clone fol-
lowed by clonal expansion continues, leading to
the evolution of malignant subpopulations of
tumor cells (i.e., subclones). This phenomenon,
known as “spatial heterogeneity”, can manifest
clinically as intratumoral heterogeneity and/or as
intrapatient heterogeneity whereby discrete meta-
static deposits within the same individual can sub-
sequently accumulate additional, new alterations
(i.e., private mutations) distinct from those present
in the primary tumor.
Accordingly, while there should be no debate
about the presence of genomic alterations in cancer
and their foundational impact on the cancer pheno-
type, it is clear that knowledge of the presence of
these genes does not convey significant clinical
value to a presenting patient without a deeper
understanding of the biologic role of these altera-
tions in that patient’s cancer type (Macconaill and
Garraway, 2010; Garraway, 2013). Greater knowl-
edge about the role of altered genes in each cancer
type is necessary to convey clinical value to patients
in all species. Furthermore, knowledge of the
impact of targeting an alteration in that tumor with
a specific drug is needed before therapeutic value
from a drug-matching hypothesis as part of PMED
can be delivered to presenting patients. Indeed, the
totality of evidence regarding drug matching as
part of PMED (in human patients) reveals impor-
tant gaps in knowledge and allows a reasonable
conclusion that although cancer is a disease associ-
ated with altered genes, these altered genes repre-
sent the “tip of the iceberg” in aspirations to deliver
clinical value to patients. What remains in the
understanding of the “iceberg” includes the com-
plexities of genomic heterogeneity, genomic evolu-
tion, and the poorly understood aspects of cancer
biology that result in altered genes in one patient
impacting that patient differently than an identical
genomic alteration in a distinct cancer, irrespective
of other observed genomic alterations (often
described as “biologic context”). Accordingly,
while interrogating genomics has become easier,
medicine remains difficult, and it should not be
surprising that careful studies that address the gaps
in PMED and inform its application to veterinary
patients are still needed.
Origins and Evidence Surrounding the
Use of PMED in Human Oncology
The promise of the above future in PMED is most
strongly supported by genomic and matched thera-
peutic advances in specific cancers, validated one
cancer at a time. There are several examples of suc-
cessful therapies for which demonstrated clinical
benefit has been shown in appropriately powered,
prospective clinical trials. These include imatinib in
BCR-ABL1-fusion-positive chronic myeloid leuke-
mia patients (Ottmann et al., 2002; Sawyers et al.,
2002; O’Brien et al., 2003); trastuzumab in HER2-
positive breast cancers (Perez et al., 2011, 2014);
vemurafenib and dabrafenib in patients with
advanced-stage melanoma harboring BRAF V600E
mutations (Chapman et al., 2011; Hauschild et al.,
2012; Long et al., 2015); and erlotinib and gefitinib
in non-small-cell lung cancer harboring sensitizing
EGFR mutations (Fukuoka et al., 2011; Rosell
et al., 2012). Notably, these successful examples of
PMED implementation did not conflict with the
required standards of evidence-based medicine for
several reasons. First, a large proportion of the
population harbored the genomic alteration tar-
geted by select agents allowing for large-scale clini-
cal trials to be conducted. Second, prospective trials
were able to demonstrate the clinical utility of
diagnostic markers and companion diagnostic tests
in addition to clinical benefit derived from these
targeted therapeutics in a disease-specific manner
that could ignore the “pan-cancer” perspectives of
many PMED offerings (Moscow et al., 2018).
Although it is unclear if human lung cancer rep-
resents a success of PMED, it represents a clear
example of the value of the use of genomic tools in
human oncology. This perceived value has many
possible explanations that should be collectively
recognized as necessary for successful implementa-
tion and launch of PMED in veterinary oncology:
● the presence of discrete subsets of human lung
cancer that can be defined using genomics; and
● molecular drivers that characterize the identified
subsets; and
● availability of drugs that effectively target these
drivers; and
● substantial knowledge and experience with
these same drugs in lung cancer patients.
The success in human lung cancer may be more
appropriately recognized as a success of using
genomic tools to identify molecular subsets of lung

-- 217 of 258 --

cancer patients (often referred to as “selectivized
medicine”), prior to the launch of prospective stud-
ies in those disease subsets. Finding additional
human cancers beyond those described above that
achieve the elements of successful PMED imple-
mentation has been challenging. Despite enthusi-
asm fueled by reports of rare exceptional or
super-responders, the most comprehensive human
PMED studies to date have not demonstrated clini-
cally important benefits from PMED compared to
the clinical intuition of the oncologist unless
applied outside of a pan-cancer approach where
small lists of matchable drugs are considered as
part of drug matching (Prasad, 2016; Kimmelman
and Tannock, 2018; Moscow et al., 2018). In fact,
most trials – including the SHIVA trial, the
TARGET trial, both IMPACT-I and IMPACT-II,
and ongoing prospective trials such as the US
National Cancer Institute (NCI) Molecular Analysis
for Therapy Choice (MATCH) – suggest that the
majority of human cancer patients do not benefit
from PMED (Le Tourneau et al., 2015; Belin et al.,
2017; Tsimberidou et al., 2017; Middleton et al.,
2022). The realization of these challenges has been
appropriately aligned with an expansion of existing
academic efforts in the human PMED field.
Unfortunately, such academic innovation designed
to address the gaps in PMED have not yet emerged
in veterinary oncology. It has become increasingly
apparent that the success of PMED in all species
will be defined in narrow subsets of patients and
will not be delivered from an approach that pre-
sumes that the simple matching of drugs to genes
will be effective in all cancer histologies.
The Paradox of PMED Implementation
in Veterinary Oncology
A major conundrum surrounding PMED is that as
increasingly complex targeted therapeutic regimens
are tailored to the treatment of ever smaller subsets
of patients (thus achieving the goal of precision
medicine in oncology), the clinical evidence that
forms the basis of our understanding of the benefits
and risks of these therapeutic strategies will erode
evidence standards that have historically supported
clinical practice. This will require the conduct of
prospective clinical trials in rare patient popula-
tions and will require an equipoise that recognizes
that PMED outcomes for patients may be superior
or inferior to the best advice of a clinician. To this
end, while cancer treatments are becoming more
precisely targeted, the evidence upon which clinical
decisions will be made is becoming much less pre-
cise. This paradox was also challenged during the
launch of human PMED and was characterized by
a retreat from evidence that initially presumed that
genomic characterization of a presenting patient
must deliver clinical value and therefore it may be
unethical to conduct such clinical trials. Fortunately
after some delay, the human PMED field realized
that such high-evidence randomized prospective
studies in PMED were necessary (Moscow et al.,
2018; Flaherty et al., 2020; Brown et al., 2022).
These studies provide a roadmap for the know-
ledge gaps that exist in PMED. Collectively, experi-
ence in human PMED can now be described as an
initial 	retreat 	from 	evidence 	(Prasad, 2016;
Kimmelman and Tannock, 2018; Pollard et al.,
2019, 2022; Weymann et al., 2021). In veterinary
oncology, recognizing the challenges that exist
below the tip of the iceberg, and addressing the
gaps in PMED through prospective, correlative
clinical trials, will deliver the desired value of
PMED to patients and create a sustainable model
for the delivery of genomic medicine to patients.
Not surprisingly, the enthusiasm around PMED
has found its way to veterinary medicine where the
absence of regulatory oversight permits immediate
commercialization to a “needing” market eager to
adopt innovations in pet cancer care. Further con-
tributing to the allure of delivering PMED in veteri-
nary oncology is the commercial resiliency of the
veterinary market during the global COVID-19
pandemic and worldwide financial crisis, and a
healthcare market without as many third-party
payors. Beyond the scientific allure of PMED there
is a strong commercial rationale to pursue PMED
in veterinary oncology. It is too early to know if a
retreat from evidence will plague PMED in veteri-
nary oncology or if commercial and academic
partnerships can emerge to address these recog-
nized gaps in the PMED field and effectively deliver
the promise of genomic oncology.
Are There Lessons from the Challenges
in PMED in Humans?
In general, the experience derived from most
human PMED studies is that a minority of genomi-
cally screened patients are ultimately matched with
and receive a targeted agent. Within this select
group harboring a putative genomic target, only a
minority of treated patients experience clinical
202 	J. Fenger

-- 218 of 258 --

203	Precision Medicine
benefit and that clinical benefit, if achieved, is typi-
cally short in duration (Prasad, 2016). There are
lessons from this human PMED experience that
can be used to better deliver this future of cancer
care to pet animals and better realize the promise
and potential of PMED in the veterinary market, as
described below.
Failure to understand molecular “drivers”
The ideal prescription of effective therapies should
be reliant upon the assignment of clinically vali-
dated active agents to tumors that harbor specific,
clinically validated genomic alterations that have
been shown to promote the cancer phenotype in
that cancer. The concept of separating the “wheat
from the chaff” – or discerning the important
therapeutic targets among a number of other irrel-
evant passenger events – requires a thorough
understanding of cancer biology and confirmation
of the clinical relevance of the target in a specific
cancer (Moscow et al., 2018). Furthermore, PMED
requires that agents demonstrate clinical activity
not broadly against a target gene but against the
specific genomic abnormality detected in the target
gene in the specific molecular and clinical context
in which the aberration is detected. For example,
chronic myeloid leukemia is a homogeneous malig-
nancy primarily driven by pathogenic BCR-ABL1
gene fusions, for which the development of the
small-molecule inhibitor imatinib ushered in an era
of highly effective targeted therapies (Frantz et al.,
2013). Clear benefit of imatinib in this context was
quickly demonstrated in several prospective, rand-
omized clinical trials. In contrast, acute myeloid
leukemia (AML) comprises a group of heterogene-
ous disorders characterized by high levels of
genomic complexity. One study involving 1540
patients with AML demonstrated a total of 5234
putative driver mutations across 76 genes, produc-
ing 1080 distinct genotypes (Papaemmanuil et al.,
2016). In spite of the plethora of genomic altera-
tions identified in AML patients, only those associ-
ated with the FLT3 and IDH1/2 genes have, to
date, led to the development of a novel targeted
therapy (Levis, 2017; DiNardo et al., 2018).
Genomic profling and cancer evolution
It is clear today that a single biopsy from a treat-
ment-naïve primary tumor may not accurately
recapitulate the complex biology underpinning
recurrent or metastatic lesions. As tumors evolve
over time, shaped by the selective pressures created
by treatments, the challenge of repeating or obtain-
ing multiple samples for genomic interrogation
whenever a change in treatment is contemplated is
often deemed unacceptable in terms of patients’
safety and multiplication of the molecular analyses
costs (Lipinski et al., 2016; McGranahan and
Swanton, 2017). However, knowledge of the spec-
trum of acquired resistance mutations associated
with individual targeted therapies is critical to the
development of therapy combinations that can
delay the onset of acquired or innate resistance in
patients. Longitudinal assessment of circulating
tumor DNA (ctDNA) (i.e., liquid biopsy) remains a
possible alternative and/or replacement to costly,
and potentially harmful, repeat tissue biopsy proce-
dures and may provide insight into different stages
of tumor evolution, including premalignant and
malignant progression and response to therapy
(Heitzer et al., 2019). While several challenges
associated with employing this methodology exist,
the utility of ctDNA sampling for genomic profil-
ing irrespective of cancer type and metastatic site
remains promising and will be discussed in more
detail below.
Biologic context of genomic variants:
avoiding the pan-cancer approach despite
the commercial allure
Although cancer is a disease of altered genes, can-
cer biology describes the fact that these altered
genes function within cancer cells, which interact
with other cancer cells and the tumor stroma,
within organs and within patients. This biology
that occurs in cells is very cell-specific and not pre-
dicted by altered genes alone. This heterogeneity of
cellular phenotypes is not predicted by the hypoth-
esis that cancer is primarily a disease of altered
genes. The complexity of cancer biology obscures
clarity from cancer genomics and suggests that
cancer is, in fact, a disease of altered cell biology/
phenotype. Evidence of this gap between cancer
genotype and cancer phenotype, especially in the
setting of drug-to-gene variant matching (PMED),
has been described as biologic context. Biologic
context is best exemplified by the observation that
an altered cancer gene variant in one cancer type
does not necessarily predict the response of the
targeted inhibition of that variant in all cancers.
For example, the V600E mutation in BRAF in

-- 219 of 258 --

human melanoma provides a strong genomic
rationale for the use of RAF inhibitors in these
patients (Chapman et al., 2011; Hauschild et al.,
2012; Long et al., 2015). Indeed, these agents
deliver valuable therapeutic benefit to melanoma
patients with V600E-mutant BRAF. Intriguingly,
the identical V600E mutation in BRAF in human
colon cancer, when treated with the same RAF
inhibitor, does not deliver similar benefit (Prahallad
et al., 2012). A concurrent amplification of epider-
mal growth factor receptor (EGFR) in human
colon cancer is believed to provide an explanation
for the failure of RAF inhibitors in colon cancer,
despite harboring a presumedly pathogenic gene
variant. The genomic knowledge about the impact
of concurrent EGFR amplification represents a
relatively rare instance where further genomic
knowledge predicts the failure of a targeted therapy
to deliver therapeutic value to a patient whose can-
cer expresses a relevant altered disease target.
Importantly, the role of EGFR alteration in this
assessment of therapeutic failure is not possible
without the clinical annotation of “responder” or
“nonresponder”, highlighting the need for correla-
tive PMED trials that seek to answer questions
surrounding the complexities of genomic heterogen-
eity, genomic evolution (i.e., biologic context), that
challenge our understanding of the PMED iceberg
(Hierro et al., 2019). Our knowledge of biologic
context predicts that if a gene variant must be
understood within each human cancer, such knowl-
edge of a gene variant in the biologic context in
each veterinary cancer will be required before
PMED can deliver important value to veterinary
oncology. We simply cannot expect knowledge of
potentially pathogenic variants in humans to be
necessarily 	translated 	to 	veterinary 	patients.
Nonetheless, knowledge of human pathogenic vari-
ants represents an important starting point for new
knowledge in veterinary oncology and may help
prioritize hypotheses that must be resolved in the
delivery of PMED to veterinary patients.
Geographic heterogeneity
Tumor diversity, not only among tumors from dif-
ferent patients (intertumoral heterogeneity) but
also within various portions of a tumor within the
same patient (intratumoral heterogeneity), adds
another layer of complexity to the successful imple-
mentation of PMED (Lipinski et al., 2016). The
spatial and temporal heterogeneity that exists
within tumors is thought to be the result of a
branching evolution of a cancer’s molecular char-
acteristics, with the clonal “trunk” containing com-
mon mutations and the numerous “branches”
representing areas of the tumor containing geneti-
cally divergent subclones, each carrying successive
and potentially clinically relevant genomic aberra-
tions (Gerlinger et al., 2012; Meacham and
Morrison, 2013). While comparative studies dem-
onstrate that the molecular alterations found in
metastatic samples are reflective of the patterns of
subclones that already exist within the primary
tumor, a portion of these subclones may also
acquire additional mutations that may correlate
with organ-specific metastasis (Meric-Bernstam
et al., 2014). To this end, subclonal evolution may
result in metastatic lesions that harbor resistance/
sensitivity markers that are initially observed in
very low frequencies within the primary tumor.
This challenges the concept that a single biopsy
sample can fully inform upon the genomic charac-
teristics of an entire tumor – or multiple tumor sites
in those patients with metastatic disease.
Failure to adapt PMED to nonmutated variants
(i.e., copy number alterations)
At this time, treatment selection is relatively straight-
forward when a patient’s tumor has an actionable
genomic alteration and an approved therapeutic
targeting that alteration is available for that tumor
type (e.g., V600E BRAF mutation in metastatic
melanoma). However, clinical data is largely absent
or insufficient to support routine clinical imple-
mentation of biomarker–drug matched therapies in
the setting of these genomic alterations in other
cancer histologies and for other genomic altera-
tions (Hierro et al., 2019). For nonmutated vari-
ants, substantial work is needed to determine the
actionability and clinical relevance of gene copy
number changes and to identify appropriate thresh-
olds for delineating clinically relevant amplifica-
tions. For example, defining the number of copies
of a specific oncogene that reflects its potential
amplification relies upon the tumor cellularity and
ploidy and may require further confirmation or
correlation with protein expression using immuno-
histochemistry techniques to validate whether the
amplitude of the gain is considered relevant (Le
Tourneau et al., 2016). Likewise, tumor suppressor
gene inactivation implies that two alleles that code
for a particular protein are altered. While loss-of-
204 	J. Fenger

-- 220 of 258 --

205	Precision Medicine
function tumor suppressor gene deletions may be
considered relevant, additional mechanisms of
inactivation such as DNA hypermethylation and
the clinical significance of various additional alter-
ations revealed by these more comprehensive
approaches 	are 	unclear 	and 	require 	further
elucidation.
Failure to use liquid biopsy technology
Unsurprisingly, rapid progress in the field of
genomics has prompted the use of clinical genomics
in cancer care and is gaining traction with cancer
patients and oncologists eager to derive clinical
benefit from genome-driven oncology. Access to
tumor material for genomic profiling usually
requires invasive procedures that are not always
feasible and do not lend themselves to dynamic
surveillance in PMED. Now, attention is turning to
minimally invasive sampling methods, including
highly sensitive “liquid biopsy” assays (Berger and
Mardis, 2018; Heitzer et al., 2019). Liquid biopsy
sampling leverages the fact that cell death in
actively growing tumor cells leads to the release of
cell-free tumor DNA (cftDNA) into the circulation
and other body fluids that are in direct contact
with organs (Diehl et al., 2008). The detection of
cancer-specific genomic alterations in the blood
offers an alternative approach to interrogate the
mutational status of a tumor, monitor response to
therapy, and assess the extent of tumor heterogene-
ity and clonal progression beyond a single tissue
biopsy sample. Nevertheless, considerable chal-
lenges exist and must be overcome before their
optimal clinical validity and utility are realized. The
low portion of cftDNA that can be reliably detected
in the circulation is substantially lower than that
present in tumor tissue; therefore, modified sample
preparation methods and deeper sequencing cover-
age approaches are necessary to achieve sufficient
sensitivity, particularly for low-frequency subclonal
mutations. While liquid biopsy techniques hold
considerable appeal with respect to more accu-
rately capturing the extent of intratumoral hetero-
geneity, this is largely reliant upon the sensitivity of
the assay and the extent of cftDNA shedding
(Berger and Mardis, 2018). This issue becomes
particularly relevant when considering the clinical
utility of liquid biopsy assays in the setting of early
disease detection and minimal disease monitoring
as studies have previously shown that both tissue
site and tumor stage lead to differential levels of
cftDNA in the circulation (Bettegowda et al.,
2014). Ultimately, validation of cftDNA as a
marker against the presumed gold standard analy-
sis of tumor tissue biopsy and conventional imag-
ing-based modalities will be necessary to advance
precision cancer surveillance and establish mean-
ingful clinical benefit by showing improved out-
comes of medical decision-making based on the use
of these assays.
Failure to understand “matched”
drug in the disease of interest
A major hurdle in the human PMED field has been
a sufficient and necessary understanding of the
biologic underpinnings of drug–target matches in a
specific cancer type. As genomic mutations occur
within cells that are present within organs, the bio-
logic context of these alterations has a greater
impact on the influence of a specific genomic
alteration on the responsiveness of that cancer to a
matched therapeutic agent compared to the altered
gene alone. Furthermore, mechanisms of drug
resistance ultimately emerge in response to molecu-
lar therapeutics and in many cases, these resistant
tumor subclones (i.e., drug persister cells) may exist
prior to the introduction of a drug. The conven-
tional PMED approach presumes that a histology-
agnostic genomic analysis of any tumor provides
the answer as to what therapy is best for a tumor
in which the gene or potentially actionable muta-
tion or presumed “matched” drug may have never
been previously investigated. It is therefore crucial
to recognize that until the effectiveness of molecu-
lar therapies is formally evaluated within the con-
text of individual cancer types (i.e., histologic or
molecular subgroups of cancer), the clinical imple-
mentation of PMED will involve a trade-off
between a lower standard of evidence to adopt
these new therapies (as is the case in patients with
orphan diseases), in exchange for more precise
treatment assignment (Moscow et al., 2018).
Failure to model optimal combination
therapies
In many cancers, the single-agent use of a molecu-
lar therapy for cancer is unlikely to deliver an
optimal therapeutic outcome; therefore, it is increas-
ingly recognized that combination approaches are
needed in nearly all instances. It is suggested that
the lack of more complete and durable responses

-- 221 of 258 --

within many PMED trials can be attributed to both
tumor heterogeneity and the rapid development of
acquired or evasive drug resistance that can be
expected with the administration of a single tar-
geted agent (Garraway and Jänne, 2012). As
molecular therapies are often the recommendation
of PMED strategies, a more comprehensive under-
standing of the effectiveness of molecular-targeted
therapies when administered in combination with
cytotoxic chemotherapeutics, other targeted inhibi-
tors, or other treatment modalities such as radio-
therapy is necessary before the paradigm of PMED
can be implemented to its fullest extent. Indeed, the
observed poor performance of PMED compared to
oncologist intuition likely represents an unfair
comparison since most PMED treatment assign-
ments are single-agent recommendations and most
oncologist recommendations include drug combi-
nations. Algorithmic models for PMED must evolve
to deliver rational drug combinations. Recognition
of this gap in PMED in humans has been recog-
nized and now seeks an answer to questions sur-
rounding the clinical benefit of drug combination
strategies through a further iteration of the US
NCI’s MATCH trial, NCI ComboMATCH (Chen
et al., 2019). Determination of how matched drugs
can be used, either alone or in combination, in
order to overcome both tumor heterogeneity and
drug resistance and to provide maximal benefit for
as many patients as possible is fraught with
increasing complexities; however, achieving a
vision of PMED that moves beyond a single-agent
regimen will require the demonstration of mean-
ingful levels of clinical benefit and establishment of
safety, tolerability, and drug–drug interactions that
occur in specific drug combinations.
Selectivized Medicine versus
Personalized Medicine
As discussed above, PMED refers to the use of
genomic or other orthologous “omic” approaches
to define disease targets in an individual cancer
patient taken from a population of patients with
any form of cancer and attempts to identify one or
more drugs for use in that single patient. Despite
the allure of such an individualized and genomi-
cally directed approach to cancer care, the most
comprehensive studies of this form of PMED have
failed to demonstrate an advantage compared to
the convention of an oncologist’s best guess.
Although prospective studies are underway, the
evidence currently available fails to demonstrate an
advantage to PMED for most cancer patients when
used in the above approach (Prasad, 2016; Moscow
et al., 2018). Furthermore, no evidence exists to
assess the value of PMED in veterinary oncology,
beyond early reports of its feasibility (i.e., it can be
done). Nonetheless, a nuanced and slightly distinct
approach to genomic medicine has demonstrated
important therapeutic value to patients. “Selec-
tivization” or genomic subclassification of cancers
refers to the use of a PMED strategy to identify
molecular subclassifications of cancer and then
conduct clinical trials in those subsets of disease
(i.e., umbrella study designs), rather than the entire
population of patients with that cancer (Brown
et al., 2022). The narrowed or selected subpopula-
tion allows the clinical trial to resolve the complex-
ity of biologic context and determine which drugs
(alone or in combination) are best used in the nar-
rowed population (Polley and Cheung, 2019;
Tsimberidou et al., 2020). This approach to sub-
classification has been successfully deployed in
leukemia patients and may, in part, explain the
success of PMED seen in human lung cancer. The
success of this approach to refine genomic subsets
within heterogeneous cancers and test a small set of
rationally selected drugs in these subsets is consist-
ent with the clinical instincts of oncologists and
does work. Importantly, this selectivized approach
is distinct from a conventional PMED approach
that presumes that a genomic analysis of any tumor
provides the answer about what therapy is best for
a tumor in which the gene or the presumed
“matched” drug may have never been previously
studied.
Compared to PMED, why are the “guesses” of
oncologists so good? Because:
● the drugs being used have multiple targets; and
● oncologists sit at the intersection of cancer biol-
ogy, cancer genomics, and cancer therapy; and
● biologic context is answered in clinical trials;
and
● knowledge of how to recommend therapeutic
combination strategies.
Retreat from Evidence and Remaining
Gaps in PMED
During the 20-year delivery of PMED to human
oncology there has been the expected tension
between innovators who are able to conduct
206 	J. Fenger

-- 222 of 258 --

207	Precision Medicine
genomic analysis of a tumor and physicians and
patients expecting evidence in support of this
approach. This expected tension has been pro-
tracted in the human PMED field largely resulting
from the instinct and belief that genomics would be
a simple answer to the problem of cancer and the
resultant sporadic retreats from conventions of
evidence in medicine. As stated above, this retreat
from evidence in the PMED field can be initially
traced to the presumed certainty that a genomic
understanding of cancer would deliver a major
advance in patient management and the perception
that evidence in support of this hypothesis was
both unnecessary and largely impossible to obtain
from the recognized pinnacles of clinical evidence
(including prospective and randomized studies).
The frustration by innovators and aligned groups
to conduct necessary, high-level evidentiary studies
delayed their launch and completion and resulted
in efforts to claim that lesser forms of evidence
(including clinical anecdotes and retrospective
studies) were sufficient to demonstrate clinical bene-
fit from the PMED strategy (Kimmelman and
Tannock, 2018). This also delayed the recognition
of gaps in knowledge and delayed advancing
needed solutions to the field. The recent completion
of high-standard evidence studies in PMED has
been enlightening and clarified the need for new
knowledge to advance the field and overcome the
causes of failure of current PMED strategies
(Flaherty et al., 2020; Brown et al., 2022). Indeed,
these studies have elucidated new questions that
should have been asked years ago and the human
oncology field has largely recognized the cost and
consequences of these unanswered gaps. Namely,
why some cancers are not “responders” and what
gaps in knowledge must be addressed to bring
PMED to other cancers. These gaps are the subject
of intense work by several academic groups that
continue to dominate the human PMED field. A
number of these academic groups have overcome
perceived challenges and have now launched sev-
eral rigorous prospective studies to address the
remaining scientific and translational gaps in the
delivery of PMED. As this data matures, it is likely
that the human commercial PMED market can
finally flourish and become sustainable beyond
alluring the interests of vulnerable patient families.
Similarly, the allure of a robust veterinary market
in the absence of regulatory oversight and third-
party payor systems predicts the ongoing entry of
innovators in PMED to veterinary oncology, often
in the absence of knowledge and/or evidence neces-
sary to justify this strategy in veterinary patients.
Veterinary academic and research groups should
recognize opportunities to address these gaps in
knowledge and lead efforts with rigorous studies.
Importantly, veterinary oncologists should seek
training to recognize gaps and demand answers to
appropriately meet their expectations.
In the near future, key issues that take into
account the aforementioned challenges in the
PMED strategy need to be examined in order to
resolve these remaining gaps in knowledge. Progress
in the following areas will be critical to ensuring
that the implementation of PMED fulfills the
needed evidence to support its clinical application
and ensure it delivers clinical benefit for veterinary
cancer patients.
Need for evidence
Despite the rapid uptick in the pace of PMED
advancements, the majority of human PMED uses
emerge from patient requests of physicians and
academic clinical studies. A minority of uses emerge
from gold standards in human medical practice.
This retreat from evidence can explain the majority
of this distribution of uses. In the context of imple-
menting PMED in the nonregulated veterinary
marketplace, the risk of repeating this outcome is
especially worrisome and may undermine the value
and rigor of the veterinary drug approval process.
In the absence of regulatory oversight, veterinary
oncologists 	are 	additionally 	challenged 	with
demanding evidence and rigor from innovators
who can commercialize. Without these demands
for high-level evidence surrounding PMED strate-
gies and implementation, it is likely that the future
of PMED will not deliver value to veterinary
patients.
Need for oncologist education
While rapid improvements in NGS techniques and
emerging novel therapeutics have created enthusi-
asm and opportunities to deliver genomically
informed personalized cancer therapy, it has been
acknowledged that opportunities for the over-
whelming majority of practicing oncologists to
receive the basic level of training required to inter-
pret and disseminate the results of increasingly
sophisticated genomic analyses to cancer patients
are generally lacking (Gray et al., 2014). Ongoing

-- 223 of 258 --

and parallel support mechanisms to provide oncol-
ogists with the technical understanding needed to
interpret this data is critical to facilitate rational,
value-centered decision-making by pet owners. In
the earliest days of PMED deployment in humans
there was a presumption that the complexity of
clinical decision-making by oncologists could be
replaced with curation of the literature and machine
learning, within a concise PMED report. This early
implementation of PMED was met with frustration
from clinicians who described profound lack of
knowledge about direct-to-consumer genetic test-
ing reports and challenges surrounding how to
support patients in this area. This approach has
been replaced with the deliberate input of physi-
cians and scientists (e.g., molecular tumor boards)
who convene to consider clinical and genomic data
in order to recommend optimal treatments for
patients (Harada et al., 2017; van der Velden et al.,
2017; Rolfo et al., 2018). Additionally, several
large institutions have created easily accessible
online genomic knowledge navigators and tools to
help physicians manage profiling results and pro-
vide clinical decision-making support (Meric-
Bernstam et al., 2015; Moorcraft et al., 2015; Li
et al., 2017). Veterinary oncologists are uniquely
poised to serve as “honest brokers” to pet owners
and are experts in the interpretation of the nuances
of a pathology report as they deliver the best
options for treatment to their patients. As genomic
data is included in this decision-making process,
veterinary oncologists will require training in the
fundamentals of clinical cancer genomics so that
they can actively and effectively contribute to
teams involved in genomic analyses and therapeu-
tic matching, and robust clinical decision support
will be necessary at the point of care to help guide
clinical decision-making as PMED tools enter the
clinical and diagnostic space.
Need for standardized technical
aspects of PMED delivery
The adoption of comprehensive “pan-cancer” ver-
sus a more cancer-specific targeted approach to
genomically profiling tumors is a key consideration
regarding the use of NGS-based diagnostic cancer
assays. While an array of genomic assays and
decision-support tools is already commercially
available, these tools lack standardized vocabulary
for the naming of variants and lack standardized
approaches for annotating the pathogenicity of
specific variants or their susceptibility to treatment.
For example, the term “actionability” is not uni-
formly defined and according to some reports from
human PMED trials, actionable alterations can be
documented in up to 91% of tumors, whereas
other prospective trials, such as the US NCI’s
MATCH trial, identified far fewer actionable alter-
ations (Hakenberg et al., 2016; Uzilov et al., 2016;
Flaherty et al., 2020). Indeed, the definition of
actionability used to assess the clinical utility of
molecular profiling varies across different trials
and among institutions, thereby providing limited
evidence for clinicians to determine whether a vari-
ant has functional relevance in cancer biology or
carries clinical significance. In essence, comparing
studies that match drugs and drug combinations to
specific genomic alterations using distinct PMED
assays or sequencing platforms that interrogate and
filter data from tumor biopsy samples through a
particular data-analysis algorithm may yield wildly
different outcomes, irrespective of the underlying
biology of the tumor or the activity of the agents
investigated (Le Tourneau et al., 2017). Addressing
this need for evidence of the diagnostic accuracy,
reproducibility, and concordance among diagnostic
tests would help oncologists to better understand
genomic test results and their limitations. In addi-
tion to providing a more uniform consensus regard-
ing standards of genomic data annotation and
reporting, the following key issues must be
addressed in order to establish reliable diagnostic
platforms that provide appropriate levels of evi-
dence for the implementation of PMED in veteri-
nary oncology:
● determination of whether an alteration is
“actionable”;
● assessing the effect of a genomic alteration on
cancer biology and therapeutic implications;
● prioritization of multiple molecular alterations
in cancer;
● technical considerations for proposed NGS cov-
erage depth, tumor cellularity, allelic frequency
of a mutation, gene copy number threshold, and
proposed interpretation depending on gene type
analyzed;
● data integration and bioinformatics pipeline
validation;
● classifying 	and 	reporting 	actionability 	of
genomic alterations;
● interpretation of results and clinical implica-
tions of alteration; and
208 	J. Fenger

-- 224 of 258 --

209	Precision Medicine
● establishment of veterinary molecular tumor
boards with the deliberate input of clinicians
and scientists as a means to provide clinical deci-
sion-making support.
Bridging the gap between biologic context
and molecular therapeutics
A challenge for the human PMED field has been
the necessary knowledge regarding the biology of
the drug target for cancer. Genomic mutations
occur within cells that exist within organs; the
influence of a specific mutation on the biology of
these cell and organs (i.e. biologic context) has a
greater impact on the responsiveness of a cancer to
a therapy than the presence of the altered gene
alone. Resistance mechanisms will emerge to
molecular therapeutics and in many cases may exist
prior to the introduction of a drug as these resistant
subclones are often present in the primary tumor,
albeit at low frequency. The single-agent use of a
molecular therapy for cancer is unlikely to deliver
an optimal therapeutic outcome; therefore, combi-
nation approaches are needed in nearly all instances.
Since molecular therapies are often the recommen-
dation of a PMED approach, addressing gaps in
our knowledge regarding the effectiveness of
molecular therapies within the context of individ-
ual cancer types is necessary. Veterinary oncologists
must seek knowledge surrounding therapeutic
strategies that may be integrated into the care of
patients. It is unlikely that any single therapeutic
innovation will solve the problems of cancer
patients, and the complex intuition and knowledge
of forward-thinking clinicians will always be
needed.
Clinical trial design considerations
for veterinary oncology PMED studies
Prospective, randomized, and other study designs
that deliver high-evidence data are fully feasible in
the context of PMED and should be the focus of
the field. In the setting of this need in both human
and veterinary oncology, it is unclear why lesser
standards of evidence would be pursued. As the
PMED strategy in oncology remains a hypothesis
in need of verification, lesser evidentiary studies
will create delays in adoption and successful imple-
mentation in practice. Furthermore, these delays
will slow the innovations needed to address the
increasingly recognized scientific gaps in the field.
Addressing these gaps quickly creates the opportu-
nity that innovators can deliver PMED platforms
that can be successful and may be better integrated
into the future of veterinary cancer care. One
requirement is the design and conduct of prospec-
tive (patient-forward or correlative) clinical trials
in veterinary patients that will identify novel
genomic subgroups within a known cancer and
then examine the benefit of specific “matched”
therapeutic approaches in these novel patient sub-
groups 	(so-called 	selectivized 	medicine)
(Tsimberidou et al., 2020). Furthermore, careful,
prospective studies are needed to better define the
features of veterinary patients that are considered
“exceptional responders” or “nonresponders”
when drug–biomarker trial designs are employed
(Pilling et al., 2021). This will optimally include
prospective studies within cancer histologies using
a relatively small but well-understood list of drugs
that may be considered as potentially matched
therapies. An integrated vision for the future of
PMED in veterinary oncology includes comprehen-
sive multi-omic tumor characterization, dynamic
monitoring of liquid biopsy samples, annotation
that is automated through advancements in bioin-
formatic pipelines but guided by experts’ clinical
input, and the development of innovative clinical
trials that not only test drug–biomarker matching
but also longitudinally investigate genomic evolu-
tion and meaningfully inform the efficacy and
activity of therapies in single cancers.
Conclusions
If the missteps in PMED delivery in humans are
recognized and addressed with rigorous, prospec-
tive, and correlative trials, future human and veteri-
nary oncologists will integrate PMED into the care
of all cancer patients, validated one cancer at a
time, using narrow molecular features (including
gene alterations) that have been defined as drivers
of the disease in that cancer. This knowledge will
lead to prospective correlative studies that will
demonstrate the value of the combination of tar-
geted inhibitor(s), immuno-oncology, or conven-
tional cancer therapy approaches for that disease
subset. This needed data will then allow future
presenting patients to receive molecular analysis of
tumor or cell-free tumor DNA to assign the
patient’s presentation by genomic subgroup so as to
recommend a validated treatment for that subgroup.

-- 225 of 258 --

Follow-up analysis of cftDNA signatures will opti-
mally guide ongoing clinical decision-making.
Unfortunately, it is challenging to imagine that
patient outcomes will improve from PMED with-
out such new knowledge being available.
The veterinary market, led by veterinary oncolo-
gists, should be familiar with the failures and suc-
cesses of PMED in humans and apply these lessons
effectively as this important future in veterinary
oncology is delivered to pet patients. At this time,
more evidence is needed from carefully designed
prospective studies to provide proof of benefit from
this precision strategy. Pet owners may be easily
misinformed to believe: (i) that the human PMED
experience has been successfully delivered to all
patients; (ii) that all questions related to PMED
and its implementation in human medicine have
been fully resolved; and (iii) that it is currently a
standard of care in humans. As many pet owners
are eager to undergo tumor sequencing, they may
be easily influenced to believe that commercial
products that are available will deliver value to
their pet. Indeed, the same misperceptions exist
among many human cancer patients, emphasizing
the need for healthcare providers to communicate
the potential benefits of PMED as well as its risks
and limitations to patients. Identifying and deliver-
ing knowledge to gaps in the field of PMED will
allow the important advances in cancer genomics
to be useful to patients.

12Glucocorticoid Therapy in Oncology
ANDI FLORY *
PetDx, San Diego, California, USA
Introduction
Synthetic glucocorticoids (GCs), such as prednisone,
prednisolone, and dexamethasone, are used to
manage many parts of the continuum of care
needed by veterinary oncology patients, from direct
treatment of neoplastic conditions to management
of cancer treatment toxicity, to palliation of clinical
signs from cancer. GC effects can be separated into
effects on tumor cells, effects on the tumor micro-
environment, and effects on the patient. In this
chapter we provide foundational knowledge to
guide an assessment of the risk/benefit balance for
this class of drugs, very commonly prescribed to
veterinary cancer patients (Fig. 12).
The term “corticosteroid” is used to describe the
steroid hormones that are secreted by the adrenal
cortex 	(Behrend 	and 	Kemppainen, 	1997).
Corticosteroids include both: (i) mineralocorti-
coids, which help to retain salt; and (ii) glucocorti-
coids (Behrend and Kemppainen, 1997), which are
named after their role in maintaining glucose
homeostasis (Lin and Wang, 2016). These sub-
stances are released by cells in the adrenal cortex,
as part of the hypothalamic–pituitary–adrenal
(HPA) axis (Behrend and Kemppainen, 1997).
Natural GCs have roles in immune responses,
metabolism, cell growth, development, and repro-
duction (Lin and Wang, 2016). They act on nearly
all cells in the immune system to suppress inflam-
mation by decreasing leukocyte recruitment, induc-
ing immune cell apoptosis, changing immune cell
differentiation, inhibiting cytokine release, and
inhibiting immune cell migration (Perretti and
Ahluwalia, 2000; Baschant and Tuckermann, 2010).
Their use as an anti-inflammatory is achieved using
lower dosages than those required to mediate
immunosuppressive effects (Yamanaka et al.,
2019). Beyond this conventional perspective, we
now recognize this drug class to have genomic and
nongenomic effects.
Genomic and Nongenomic Effects
of Glucocorticoids
Genomic effects of glucocorticoids
GCs primarily function by activation of an intracel-
lular GC receptor (GR), which is present in the
cytoplasm of nearly all cells (Panettieri et al.,
2018). GCs exert their anti-inflammatory and
immunosuppressive effects using genomic and non-
genomic mechanisms (Zen et al., 2011). GCs are
lipophilic and can pass freely through cell mem-
branes (Jeffery, 2014); once bound to the GR, the
GC–GR complex dimerizes and then translocates
to the nucleus, where it can exert its actions (Zen
et al., 2011). In the nucleus, the activated GR (the
GC–GR complex) can have direct involvement
with DNA to activate or inactivate genes, or can
alter gene expression by indirect genomic mecha-
nisms, such as binding to and inactivating tran-
scription factors or their co-factors (Zen et al.,
2011). The genomic effects typically take hours to
days 	to 	manifest 	(Panettieri 	et 	al., 	2018).
Nongenomic effects (meaning those that modulate
the expression of genes) occur more immediately
(Panettieri et al., 2018), typically within minutes to
hours (Maurice-Dror et al., 2018). The GC–GR
complex can also mediate epigenetic effects through
the modification of inflammatory gene expression,
via activation of a group of proteins with histone-
deacetylase activity or by binding to coactivators of
histone acetyltransferase (Zen et al., 2011).
The GR is a member of the nuclear receptor
superfamily of transcription factors (Schoneveld
et al., 2004). The GR gene in humans is located on
the fifth chromosome (5p31q region) and has nine
215
