DOI: 10.1079/9781789245820.0012

-- 231 of 258 --

exons (Mitre-Aguilar et al., 2015). There are five
known isoforms of the GR gene in humans (Mitre-
Aguilar et al., 2015), however the primary isoform
is the GRα. The nucleotide sequence of the canine
GR gene (obtained by PCR amplification of GR
cDNA derived from one liver sample and two sam-
ples of peripheral blood mononuclear cells) from
three healthy Beagle dogs was 91% identical to the
human GRα (Yamanaka et al., 2019). Another
study showed that GR expression levels were lower
in GC-resistant mast cell tumor (MCT) tissues than
in GC-sensitive MCT tissues (Matsuda et al.,
2011). It has been reported that, relative to humans
and dogs, cats have a reduced number of GRs (van
den Broek and Stafford, 1992).
In general, the anti-inflammatory and immuno-
suppressive effects of GCs are due to transrepres-
sion (reducing the expression of pro-inflammatory
genes), whereas side effects occur due to transacti-
vation (activation of target genes involved in the
metabolism of sugar, protein, fat, muscle, and
bone) 	(Schäcke 	et 	al., 2002; 	Bosscher 	and
Haegeman, 2009). The negative regulation of gene
expression by interaction with other transcription
factors is called “tethering” and is thought to be the
basis of the immunosuppressive effects of GCs (Lin
and Wang, 2016).
Nongenomic effects of glucocorticoids
GCs also induce almost immediate nongenomic
effects, such as nonspecific interactions with the
cell membrane, direct and indirect interaction with
cytoplasmic proteins, and direct effects on neuronal
function (Haller et al., 2008; Zen et al., 2011;
Panettieri et al., 2018). These effects are typically
mediated by intracellular Ca2+ as a second messen-
ger (Mitre-Aguilar et al., 2015). Examples include
rapid effects of GCs on airway smooth muscle
reactivity and tone, rapid effect on reactive oxygen
species generation, acute inhibition of inflamma-
tion via mechanisms such as inhibition of epider-
mal growth factor-induced release of arachidonic
acid, and inhibition of neutrophil degranulation
(Panettieri et al., 2018). These rapid nongenomic
effects are thought to be mediated at least in part
by a mitochondrial GR (Panettieri et al., 2018).
GCs promote acute mitochondrial apoptotic path-
ways, which lead to the release of proapoptotic
factors; it is through this mechanism that GCs can
mediate rapid apoptosis of immune cells (Panettieri
et al., 2018).
Known Effects of Glucocorticoids
on Cancer Growth
Effects on tumor cells
Lymphoid malignancies were the first and remain
the most common cancer to benefit from the
chemotherapeutic effect of GCs (Pufall, 2015). GCs
have been shown to cause apoptosis in human leu-
kemia, lymphoma, and myeloma cells (Greenstein
et al., 2002; Frankfurt and Rosen, 2004), as well as
canine and feline lymphoma and leukemia cells
(Sano et al., 2005; Ammersbach et al., 2006;
Pawlak et al., 2014) and neoplastic canine mast
cells (Takahashi et al., 1997). Continuous adminis-
tration of GCs is required to cause death of cancer
cells, as there is an initial growth arrest lasting
about 24 hours, and if GCs are continuously
administered, subsequent cell death occurs 2–3 days
later (Ploner et al., 2005; Pufall, 2015). Tipping the
balance toward apoptosis by modulating the
expression of BCL-2 family members is the main
mechanism of GC-induced cell death in lymphoma/
lymphoid leukemia, and also in myeloma (Pufall,
2015).
GC therapy has been reported to cause responses
in about 20% of late-stage, hormone therapy-
resistant prostate carcinoma in men, where sup-
pression of the production of testosterone by the
adrenal gland is thought to at least partially medi-
ate this effect (Pufall, 2015); the same benefit has
not been demonstrated in dogs or cats. Conversely,
GC therapy has been suspected to promote tumor
progression in resistant prostate cancer in men
whose tumors express GR (Arora et al., 2013) and
in metastatic human breast carcinoma (Mitre-
Aguilar et al., 2015). Accordingly, the clinical con-
text for which GC is chosen has distinct risk/
benefit features to consider. Canine mammary car-
cinoma cells have also been shown to express GR
(Martin et al., 1984), however the impact of GC
therapy has not been investigated in this species.
Effects on tumor microenvironment
Tumors exist in a microenvironment that includes
vascular cells, cancer-associated fibroblasts, and
infiltrating immune cells (Maurice-Dror et al., 2018).
GCs have been shown to inhibit angiogenesis in a
variety of ways, including inhibition of tube forma-
tion by vascular endothelial cells and decreasing
expression of vascular endothelial growth factor
(VEGF) by tumor cells (Arisawa et al., 1995; Heiss
216 	A. Flory

-- 232 of 258 --

217	Glucocorticoid Therapy in Oncology
et al., 1996; Logie et al., 2010). The anti-inflammatory
functions of GCs can reduce immune cells in the
tumor microenvironment, inhibit connective tissue
fibroblasts, and control macrophage sensitivity to
antigens (Ramalingam et al., 1997; Shimba and
Ikuta, 2020). GCs also reduce the production of
stem cell factor (the ligand for the KIT receptor on
mast cells that causes their growth, differentiation,
and chemotaxis, and allows for their survival and
adhesion to the extracellular matrix) (Silva et al.,
2006) by fibroblasts and epithelial cells.
Anti-inflammatory activity of GCs occurs due to
reduction of pro-inflammatory molecules, such as
interleukin (IL)-1β, IL-2, IL-4, IL-5, IL-6, IL-8,
IL-12, IL-18, cyclooxygenase-2, E-selectin, induci-
ble nitric oxide synthase, interferon-γ, tumor necrosis
factor-α (TNF-α), intercellular adhesion molecule,
monocyte chemoattractant protein-1, and vascular
cell adhesion molecule (Bosscher and Haegeman,
2009). GC side effects occur due to activation of
genes involved in amino acid and muscle catabo-
lism and gluconeogenesis, including tyrosine
aminotransferase, glutamine synthetase, glucose
6-phosphatase, and phosphoenolpyruvate carbox-
ykinase (Bosscher and Haegeman, 2009).
Effects on patients
Biologic effects of glucocorticoids
The biologic effects of GCs essentially result from
their function of protecting glucose-dependent cere-
bral functions (Platt et al., 2005) by preserving
normoglycemia (Behrend and Kemppainen, 1997).
Normoglycemia is maintained by increasing lipoly-
sis and gluconeogenesis and decreasing the periph-
eral utilization of glucose (Behrend and Kemppainen,
1997). Because GRs are present in nearly all tissues,
the effects of GCs in the body are diverse (Behrend
and Kemppainen, 1997).
The metabolic effects of GCs are related to the
maintenance of glucose balance. GCs cause insulin
resistance and decrease insulin secretion by pancre-
atic β cells (Gilor et al., 2016). GC administration
has been reported to cause hyperglycemia in dogs
(Masters et al., 2018; Tinklenberg et al., 2020) and
severe hyperglycemia in cats (Ployngam et al.,
2006). This can cause clinical problems, particu-
larly in cats. Iatrogenic hyperadrenocorticism
(HAC) due to chronic or excessive administration
of GCs has been described in cats (Schaer and
Ginn, 1999; Lien et al., 2006; Smith et al., 2014).
In one such report of iatrogenic HAC due to
chronic GC administration, six of 12 cats had
hyperglycemia, and transient diabetes mellitus
occurred in four of these cats (Lien et al., 2006).
Prednisolone-induced diabetes occurred in 10% of
cats receiving prednisolone at 2 mg/kg daily for
longer than 3 weeks, and the majority of those
diagnoses occurred within the first 3 months of
prednisolone therapy (Nerhagen et al., 2020).
GC-induced diabetes mellitus may be reversible by
discontinuation of GC therapy and administration
of exogenous insulin therapy (Rozanski, 2010).
In order to maintain glucose balance and provide
precursors for gluconeogenesis (Platt et al., 2005),
GCs are catabolic to connective tissue, muscle, and
bone (Behrend and Kemppainen, 1997). They also
inhibit 	fibroblast 	proliferation 	and 	function
(Behrend and Kemppainen, 1997) and suppress
insulin-like growth factor I activity, which reduces
the synthesis of type I collagen (Trikudanathan and
McMahon, 2008). The catabolic effects of GCs
occur by activation of the ubiquitin–proteosome
pathway (Freeman, 2012). The clinical result of this
increased breakdown of proteins is muscle wasting,
muscle weakness/myopathy, delayed wound heal-
ing, and thin skin (Behrend and Kemppainen,
1997; Platt et al., 2005; Trikudanathan and
McMahon, 2008). Osteoporosis, or a loss of bone
density, can also result from GC therapy, due to
adverse effects on calcium balance, decreased osteo-
blast formation and activity, promotion of osteoblast
apoptosis, and increased osteoclast maturation,
activity, and survival (van Staa, 2006). Reduction
of bone mineral density has been proven for dogs
receiving corticosteroids, at both high (Costa
et al., 2010) and low (Park et al., 2015) doses.
Osteoporosis is commonly seen in people on
chronic GCs, causing an increased risk of fracture
in the hip and spine, especially in the elderly popu-
lation; rapid bone loss and increased risk of frac-
ture are seen within the first few months of GC
therapy in people (Berris et al., 2008). When osteo-
porosis occurs naturally or is induced, dogs and
cats do not experience fracture at a rate compara-
ble to that seen in humans, which is thought to be
due to the difference in the loading ensemble of
their vertebral bodies (Egermann et al., 2005).
Treatments to prevent GC-induced osteoporosis in
people include oral supplementation with vitamin
D and calcium, and bisphosphonates (Berris et al.,
2008), none of which have been evaluated in dogs
and cats with chronic GC-induced osteoporosis.

-- 233 of 258 --

However, bisphosphonates have been reported to
be effective for management of malignant osteo-
lysis in dogs and cats, by reducing the rate of bone
resorption (Fan, 2009).
GCs function to maintain blood pressure and
volume, as well as water balance (Behrend and
Kemppainen, 1997). A deficit of GCs, as is seen in
Addison’s disease, can lead to volume depletion
and shock (Behrend and Kemppainen, 1997). Dogs
have a high sensitivity to the water balance func-
tion of GCs, seen clinically as polyuria and poly-
dipsia, which occur in the majority of individuals in
this species, whereas these signs are uncommon in
people and cats on GCs (Behrend and Kemppainen,
1997). The effects of GCs may be of concern for
patients with coincident heart disease, as even
short-term GC administration has been reported to
cause an increase in blood pressure and thus
increased afterload, increased glomerular filtration
rate, and hyperglycemia in dogs (Masters et al.,
2018; Tinklenberg et al., 2020), and moderate to
severe hyperglycemia, increased plasma volume,
increased heart size, and suspected plasma volume
expansion in cats (Ployngam et al., 2006; Block
and Oyama, 2020) – all of which can contribute to
the development of congestive heart failure in these
patients. Consideration of GC avoidance or reduced
dosing and careful monitoring should be under-
taken for patients with preexisting heart disease.
In people receiving GC therapy, psychiatric and
mood disorders can be seen, as well as decreases in
cognition, memory, and learning (Brown, 2009;
Leppert and Buss, 2012). These conditions occur due
to the inhibition and excitation of neurons, decreased
dendritic branch points, and atrophy of the hippocam-
pus, a structure that is involved in memory (Dubovsky
et al., 2012). Dogs receiving GCs have been reported to
show behavioral changes, including nervousness/rest-
lessness, fear/decreased confidence, food aggression,
excessive barking, as well as being prone to startling,
aggressive reaction when disturbed, and social avoid-
ance (Notari et al., 2015). In addition, dogs in that
study were also reported to have reduced amount of
play behavior (Notari et al., 2015). In one study, three
dogs receiving chronic prednisone for lymphoma
developed unspecified psychoses, which resulted in
discontinuation of the drug (Zemann et al., 1998).
Negative impacts of glucocorticoid therapy
In the short term, orally administered GCs can
cause a variety of unwanted clinical signs; however,
communication with the family is important for
tolerance for side effects by the pet owner
(Rozanski, 2010). Common acute side effects noted
in dogs include polyuria/polydipsia and polypha-
gia, which occur in virtually all dogs on short-term
treatment (Kovalik et al., 2012), as well as panting
and changes in the sleep–wake cycle. In a short
course, these signs typically improve as the GC
medication is tapered. Clinical sign improvement
typically lags reductions in dose.
Chronically high levels of GCs in the body from
GC administration can lead to iatrogenic HAC and
adverse effects in many organs/tissues, such as
hypertension, thromboembolism, hepatomegaly,
urinary tract infections or other infections such as
superficial and deep pyoderma or pyometra in
intact female dogs, abdominal distension, diabetes
and diabetic ketoacidosis, gastric or intestinal per-
foration, and dermatologic signs including bilater-
ally symmetric endocrine alopecia, thin skin,
pyoderma, and calcinosis cutis (Toombs et al.,
1986; Rozanski, 2010; Bruyette, 2020).
There are few studies on the outcome of chronic
GC administration to veterinary patients. Healthy
Beagle dogs administered oral prednisolone at a
dose of 2 mg/kg twice daily for 84 days developed
thickening of the left ventricular free wall and
interventricular septum, decreased left ventricular
diastolic function, and increased systolic blood
pressure (Tanaka et al., 2020). This thickening was
primarily due to fibrosis, which was confirmed
histologically at necropsy in these patients, along
with a decrease in GR levels at these sites (Tanaka
et al., 2020). Subclinical bacterial cystitis occurred
in 18% of dogs receiving chronic GCs, whereas no
cases of bacterial cystitis were seen in dogs not
receiving GCs (Torres et al., 2005). It is reasonable
to wonder if bacterial cystitis may be confused for
sterile hemorrhagic cystitis in dogs receiving cyclo-
phosphamide and prednisone. Prednisone was dis-
continued in six of 57 (17%) dogs receiving
long-term prednisone for lymphoma in a multi-
agent chemotherapy protocol for unspecified psy-
choses, polyphagia, diarrhea, or hind-limb weakness
(Zemann et al., 1998). In another study, one dog
experienced restlessness, circling, and hyperactivity
on chronic prednisone for lymphoma, which
resolved when dexamethasone was substituted
(Myers et al., 1997).
Hematologic and biochemical changes are com-
mon with patients on chronic GC therapy, includ-
ing “stress” leukogram (in dogs: mature neutrophilia,
218 	A. Flory

-- 234 of 258 --

219	Glucocorticoid Therapy in Oncology
lymphopenia, and eosinopenia), which occurs due
to the ability of GCs to modify leukocyte traffick-
ing (Reusch, 2015). Other changes include mild
thrombocytosis 	and 	erythrocytosis, 	increased
serum alkaline phosphatase (ALP) and milder
increase in alanine aminotransferase (ALT), hyper-
cholesterolemia, hypertriglyceridemia, hyperglyce-
mia, and decreased urine specific gravity (<1.018)
(Lowe et al., 2008; Bruyette, 2020). Although the
association between thromboembolic risk and GC
administration has not been proven, there is a pos-
sible risk of thrombocytosis (Winkle and Bruce,
1993; Laurenson et al., 2010; Respess et al., 2012)
and decreased anticoagulant factors have been
noted in patients receiving GC therapy (Romão
et al., 2013). Monitoring for signs of a hypercoagul-
able state and treatment with antithrombotic ther-
apy has been suggested for dogs with risk factors
receiving GC therapy (deLaforcade et al., 2019).
GC use has been linked with vacuolar hepatopa-
thy and hepatomegaly in dogs (Sepesy et al., 2006).
Patients with vacuolar hepatopathy may have ele-
vations in ALP, γ-glutamyltransferase (GGT), and
cholesterol (Sepesy et al., 2006), and typically ALP
will be higher than ALT. Dogs receiving lomustine
are at risk for lomustine-induced hepatotoxicity,
which also causes liver enzyme elevation, with ALT
typically being greater than ALP. One study found
that dogs that were started on prednisone at the
time of initiation of lomustine were at 1.5 times
greater risk for a greater than fivefold elevation of
ALT compared to dogs that did not receive pred-
nisone or were already receiving it prior to lomus-
tine initiation (Hosoya et al., 2009). Another study
of dogs receiving concurrent lomustine and pred-
nisone showed that discontinuation of prednisone
resulted in ALT normalization in nine of 13 (69%),
which suggests that hepatotoxicity in some patients
may be due to the combination of lomustine and
GC rather than lomustine alone (Lien et al., 2006;
Rassnick et al., 2010).
Induction of chemotherapy resistance
GCs have been shown to induce cancer cell resist-
ance to chemotherapy (Maurice-Dror et al., 2018).
The exact cause for this is not clear; however,
possible mechanisms include upregulation of multi-
drug resistance proteins (see below), GC-mediated
cell cycle arrest, GC-mediated antiapoptotic sig-
naling, and GC effects on the immune system
(Maurice-Dror et al., 2018). GCs cause G1 cell
cycle arrest, which can render tumor cells relatively
chemotherapy insensitive (Maurice-Dror et al.,
2018). This was demonstrated when decreased
efficacy was seen when GCs were given concomi-
tantly with chemotherapy, however GCs given 24
hours prior to chemotherapy resulted in enhanced
effect (Mattern et al., 2007). GCs have been shown
to produce antiapoptotic effects on cell lines of
solid tumors by inhibiting death ligands, death
adapter molecules, and caspases (Herr et al., 2003).
Molecular mechanisms for development of resist-
ance have been postulated, with the upstream
mechanism of failure to induce GR expression
being identified in one study (Ploner et al., 2005).
Although pretreatment with GCs prior to treat-
ment with chemotherapy has been associated with a
poorer prognosis in canine lymphoma (Price et al.,
1991; Piek et al., 1999; Gavazza et al., 2008;
Marconato et al., 2011), the mechanism by which
this occurs is unclear (Zandvliet et al., 2015). Steroid
hormones including cortisol, dexamethasone, and
methylprednisolone are substrates of P-glycoprotein
(P-gp), a drug efflux pump of the ATP-binding cas-
sette superfamily (Martinez et al., 2008). Expression
of P-gp has been shown to cause resistance to many
chemotherapy drugs (Mealey et al., 1998; Zandvliet
et al., 2014, 2015) and can be induced in human
cells by exposure to dexamethasone (Martin et al.,
2008; Manceau et al., 2013). Expression of P-gp has
been shown to correlate with a poorer response to
chemotherapy and shorter survival in canine lym-
phoma (Bergman et al., 1996; Lee et al., 1996; Page
et al., 2000), so the assumption was that GCs could
also induce P-gp in canine lymphoma (Zandvliet
et al., 2015). However, prednisolone was not found
to induce P-gp expression or have an effect on treat-
ment outcome in a more recent study (Zandvliet
et al., 2015).
Specifc Indications for Glucocorticoids
in Cancer Patients
Tumor-directed effects
Oral glucocorticoid therapy
GCs are used as a single agent or as part of multi-
agent chemotherapy protocol for a wide variety of
cancers in both dogs and cats, including canine and
feline lymphoma and leukemia, MCT, plasma cell
disorders, and histiocytic sarcoma.

-- 235 of 258 --

The primary use of GCs in oncology is in lym-
phomas and leukemia, where they can cause apop-
tosis of cancer cells and thereby cause tumor
response. Prednisone is commonly used to treat
lymphoma in dogs and cats (Vail et al., 2020). A
survey of veterinarians demonstrated that 79% of
the 110 respondents recommended prednisone
when dog owners declined chemotherapy (Regan
et al., 2013). Single-agent treatment of canine lym-
phoma with GCs has been reported in the veteri-
nary literature: older studies indicate response rates
of 40–48% for dogs treated with prednisone (Squire
et al., 1973; Bell et al., 1984), while more recent
studies found median response duration of 50–68
days (Hanot et al., 2020; Rassnick et al., 2021).
It is unclear what role GC has in multi-agent
CHOP (cyclophosphamide, doxorubicin (hydroxydau-
nomycin), vincristine (Oncovin), prednisolone)
therapy for canine lymphoma. The inclusion of pred-
nisolone in a CHOP protocol did not affect remission
rate or duration in dogs with lymphoma, and there
was no statistical difference in the frequency or sever-
ity of toxicity for dogs receiving prednisolone versus
those that did not (Zandvliet et al., 2013). The
authors of the study suggested that prednisolone
should be omitted from first-line multidrug protocols
for lymphoma (Zandvliet et al., 2013).
Response of MCTs to single-agent GC therapy
has been documented after both oral (McCaw
et al., 1994; Dobson et al., 2004; Stanclift and
Gilson, 2008; Matsuda et al., 2011; dos Santos
Horta et al., 2018; Linde et al., 2021) and intra-
lesional (Case and Burgess, 2018) administration.
Responses are likely due to tumor cell apoptosis
(Takahashi et al., 1997) as well as reduction in
peritumoral edema and inflammation (London and
Thamm, 2020). Response 	rates 	of 	70–75%
(Dobson et al., 2004; Stanclift and Gilson, 2008;
Matsuda et al., 2011) have been reported with
neoadjuvant single-agent prednisone therapy of
MCTs in dogs. Clinical factors that have been
reported to correlate with MCT clinical response to
GC therapy include well-differentiated tumors,
being a recurrent tumor, advanced clinical stage,
and mitotic index of greater than 7 (Takahashi
et al., 1997; dos Santos Horta et al., 2018). In
another study, dose of prednisone used (1 or 2.2
mg/kg daily for a median of 9 days) was not shown
to affect response rate (Stanclift and Gilson, 2008).
In solid tumor therapy, GCs may cause tumor
responses due to reduction of peritumoral inflam-
mation and edema, rather than antitumor activity
(Rutz, 2002; Mitre-Aguilar et al., 2015). The effect
of GCs in this tumor setting is primarily on pallia-
tion of clinical signs caused by the tumor, rather
than effects on the tumor cells (Rutz, 2002). In
solid tumors, GC therapy can be particularly useful
in cancer pain management if there is a significant
inflammatory component or significant peritu-
moral edema (Lascelles, 2013).
GCs are a standard part of therapy for patients
with brain tumors, as they help to reduce intracra-
nial pressure, cerebrospinal fluid (CSF)-acquired
hydrocephalus, and peritumoral edema (Platt et al.,
2005; Jeffery, 2014). Peritumor edema occurs due
to tumor-derived VEGF, which causes proliferation
of blood vessels and increased permeability of the
blood–brain barrier (Jeffery, 2014). The reduction
in vasogenic edema may occur both due to the anti-
inflammatory effects of GCs and the endothelial
cell protein modification by GCs, namely the tight
junction proteins occludin, claudin-5, and ZO-1,
along with matrix metalloproteinases and VEGF
(Murayi and Chittiboina, 2016). GC therapy can
start to improve clinical signs within 24 hours of
commencing administration (Jeffery, 2014).
A recent systematic review of published veteri-
nary literature of palliative care of brain tumors
with GCs revealed an overall median survival time
of 65 days in 22 studies (Hu et al., 2015). Definitive
treatment of brain tumors is typically accomplished
with radiation therapy in addition to GCs. An over-
all median survival time of 351 days was found in
13 studies in the abovementioned systematic review
(Hu et al., 2015). Tumor location may be predictive
of outcome: median survival time has been reported
to be longer for supratentorial brain tumors (fore-
brain tumors) treated palliatively than for patients
with infratentorial brain tumors (intracranial
tumors originating in the regions of the brain
located in the caudal cranial fossa: the cerebellum,
fourth ventricle, cerebellopontine angle, brainstem,
and related structures). In one study, patients with
supratentorial tumors treated with GC therapy
alone had a median survival time of 178 days,
while those with infratentorial tumors had a
median survival of only 28 days with GC therapy
(Rossmeisl et al., 2013). However, in another study,
patients with infratentorial tumors treated with
GC therapy alone had a median survival time of
89 days; survival with GC therapy alone was statis-
tically different than those treated with GC plus
radiation therapy, which had a survival time of
756 days (Treggiari et al., 2017). In addition with
220 	A. Flory

-- 236 of 258 --

221	Glucocorticoid Therapy in Oncology
GCs, chemotherapy has limited efficacy for treatment
of brain tumors (Rossmeisl and Pancotto, 2020). One
retrospective study showed no survival benefit for
patients receiving lomustine and GC versus GC alone
(93 versus 60 days) (Van Meervenne et al., 2014).
There is less information available for GC ther-
apy to treat spinal tumors; GC therapy is indicated
in these patients to treat nerve root compression
and pain; starting at a high anti-inflammatory dose
and tapering to effect is advised (Platt et al., 2005).
Intralesional glucocorticoid therapy
Intralesional GC injection has been reported to
cause responses in canine lipomas and MCTs: vol-
umes of injection of triamcinolone acetonide were
based on tumor size, with 0.5 ml being used for
lipomas < 3 cm in diameter, 1 ml for lipomas > 3 cm
in diameter, and 1 mg per centimeter of longest
tumor dimension being reported for treatment of
MCTs (Lamagna et al., 2012; Case and Burgess,
2018). Intralesional injection of subcutaneous and
subfascial lipomas with triamcinolone acetonide
under ultrasound guidance caused complete regres-
sion in nine of 15 dogs, and reduction in tumor size
and alleviation of discomfort and/or lameness in the
remaining dogs; six of the 15 dogs had polyuria/
polydipsia for about 2 weeks. (Lamagna et al.,
2012). A retrospective case series of 23 dogs with
MCTs reported complete or partial responses in four
out of five treatment-naïve tumors with intralesional
injection of triamcinolone acetonide alone, and an
overall response rate of 67% for dogs treated with
intralesional triamcinolone acetonide in addition to
oral glucocorticoid and/or chemotherapy, with a
median time to progression of 161 days (Case and
Burgess, 2018). Only one dog treated with intra-
lesional triamcinolone acetonide had evidence of local
mast cell degranulation causing hemorrhage, while
two dogs had gastrointestinal signs suspected to be
related to gastrointestinal ulceration. It was not
stated in the report whether dogs were premedicated
with histamine antagonists; however, given the pro-
pensity for mechanical manipulation to cause mast
cell degranulation (London and Thamm, 2020), it
seems prudent to administer histamine antagonists
prior to attempting intralesional injection of MCTs.
Treatment of paraneoplastic syndromes
GCs can be used to treat paraneoplastic conditions;
however, this should not be started until a diagnosis
regarding the cause of the paraneoplastic syndrome
has been achieved (Behrend and Kemppainen,
1997). In general, the underlying cause of the para-
neoplastic syndrome should be treated, and clinical
signs are likely to improve as a tumor response is
achieved. In some paraneoplastic syndromes, GC
therapy can help to speed response and alleviate
clinical signs.
Patients with hypercalcemia will typically show
signs such as polyuria, polydipsia, and anorexia.
The goals of supportive therapy for patients with
hypercalcemia of malignancy include enhancement
of renal excretion of calcium and prevention of
calcium absorption/reabsorption (Feldman, 2015).
Saline fluid diuresis is the mainstay of therapy;
however, GCs can also help to reduce paraneoplas-
tic hypercalcemia by reducing bone resorption,
reducing intestinal absorption, and increasing renal
excretion of calcium (Feldman, 2015).
The most common cause of paraneoplastic hypo-
glycemia in dogs is an insulin-producing β islet cell
tumor of the pancreas. This can cause neuroglyco-
penia, resulting in weakness, ataxia, collapse, dis-
orientation, behavioral changes, and seizures
(Nelson, 2015). The best treatment for insulinoma
is surgical excision of the tumor and, if metastasis
is found at the time of surgery, all abnormal-
appearing tissue as well, if possible (Nelson, 2015).
If surgical resection is not possible, hypoglycemia
persists, or when metastatic disease results in recur-
rent hypoglycemia, then medical therapy is advised
to avoid an acute hypoglycemic crisis (Nelson,
2015).
Treatment-directed effects
In addition to managing cancer and paraneoplastic
syndromes, GCs can also be used to manage the
effects of cancer therapy such as chemotherapy and
radiotherapy. Common uses of GCs in veterinary
oncology therapy effect management include pre-
vention or treatment of hypersensitivity reactions
due to chemotherapy drugs or solvents used in
chemotherapy formulations, prevention or treat-
ment of cutaneous manifestations of chemotherapy,
and prevention or treatment of acute radiation
toxicity.
Hypersensitivity reactions to l-asparaginase
have been reported in dogs; however, only a single
case of hypersensitivity in a cat, which received
l-asparaginase by the intraperitoneal route, has
been published (Jeglum et al., 1987). The native

-- 237 of 258 --

form of the drug, which is the form used in veteri-
nary medicine, is derived from Escherichia coli
(Blake et al., 2016). Hypersensitivity reactions to
asparaginase occur due to immune responses elicited
by this large protein of bacterial origin (Burke,
2014). Anti-asparaginase antibodies have been
shown to bind to the asparaginase molecule, pre-
venting its activity, and have been associated with
the development of clinical allergy in people (Burke,
2014). Anti-asparaginase immunoglobin (Ig)G and
IgM antibodies have been detected in the plasma of
30% of dogs that have received one dose of l-aspar-
aginase (Kidd et al., 2015). Hypersensitivity reac-
tions were reported in six out of 142 (4.2%) dogs
receiving a single intramuscular dose of l-asparagi-
nase with diphenhydramine pretreatment, and in
five out of 88 (5.7%) dogs receiving multiple doses
(Blake et al., 2016). In another study in which
patients received subcutaneous l-asparaginase with
both diphenhydramine and dexamethasone as a
premedication, no signs of clinical hypersensitivity
were seen, despite 30% of these patients having
demonstrable anti-asparaginase antibodies. The
authors state that either dexamethasone masked
the signs, or these patients may represent the silent
or subclinical hypersensitivity seen in humans
(Burke, 2014; Kidd et al., 2015).
Clinical signs of hypersensitivity after doses of
l-asparaginase, including urticaria, skin rash, ery-
thema, pruritus, lethargy, gastrointestinal signs
(anorexia, vomiting, and/or diarrhea), hypotension,
tachycardia, 	fever, 	hyperesthesia, 	restlessness,
hyperactivity, collapse, anaphylactic shock, and
facial or limb edema, have been reported in dogs
(MacEwen et al., 1992; Myers et al., 1997; Moore
et al., 2001; Saba et al., 2009; Blake et al., 2016;
Thiman et al., 2016). Patients that experience clini-
cal hypersensitivity reactions to l-asparaginase will
usually show signs within 30 minutes to 4 hours
(Gustafson and Bailey, 2020). Diphenhydramine
with dexamethasone has been recommended to
treat clinical hypersensitivity to l-asparaginase
(Gustafson and Bailey, 2020). Dexamethasone has
also been recommended as a pretreatment prior to
l-asparaginase: pretreatment with dexamethasone
and diphenhydramine allowed continued l-aspara-
ginase treatment of a patient that developed clinical
hypersensitivity after multiple l-asparaginase treat-
ments (Moore et al., 2001), and dexamethasone
pretreatment along with diphenhydramine pre-
vented clinical hypersensitivity in a small group of
dogs receiving l-asparaginase (Kidd et al., 2015).
Hypersensitivity reactions to chemotherapy
drugs made with the solvents Cremophor and
Polysorbate 80 have been noted in dogs and cats.
Cremophor-associated reactions have been noted
in the majority of canine and feline patients receiv-
ing intravenous paclitaxel, despite premedication
with GCs and antihistamines (Poirier et al., 2004;
Kim et al., 2015). Replacement of Cremophor with
a more tolerative excipient XR-17 significantly
decreased hypersensitivity reactions in dogs, with-
out the need for GC premedication (Vail et al.,
2012). Hypersensitivity reactions were also noted
in dogs receiving intravenous etoposide (Ogilvie
et al., 1988; Flory et al., 2008); despite low bio-
availability, oral administration avoids this toxicity
(Flory et al., 2008) and a formulation of etoposide
phosphate caused no hypersensitivity when given
intravenously (Boyé et al., 2017).
The 	chemotherapy 	drug 	rabacfosadine
(Tanovea®), which preferentially targets lymphoid
cells, has been reported to have efficacy for canine
lymphoma, cutaneous lymphoma, and multiple
myeloma. Toxicity unique to this chemotherapy
agent includes dermatopathy and pulmonary fibro-
sis. Dermatopathy and otitis have been noted in
25–44% of patients receiving rabacfosadine with-
out GC therapy (Vail et al., 2009; Thamm et al.,
2014, 2017; Saba et al., 2018, 2020; Cawley et al.,
2020). In particular, the dermatopathy and otitis
seen with rabacfosadine treatment can be bother-
some, to patient, dog owner, and managing veteri-
narian, and most often presents as pruritic otitis
externa and/or erythemic skin lesions on the dor-
sum and in inguinal areas (Saba et al., 2020). The
best management of this seems to be prevention
with a concurrent ongoing anti-inflammatory dose
of prednisone, symptomatic therapies (such as
analgesics, antibiotics, and pentoxifylline), and
drug holidays, with drug discontinuation not being
advocated by some authors (Vail et al., 2009; Saba
et al., 2018). Prednisone has been prescribed at an
anti-inflammatory dose (0.5 mg/kg daily) in an
effort to prevent or delay dose-limiting cutaneous
or pulmonary toxicity from rabacfosadine (Morges
et al., 2014). Pulmonary fibrosis has been reported
in approximately 4% of dogs and was fatal in
seven reported dogs (Vail et al., 2009; Thamm
et al., 2017; Saba et al., 2018, 2020). The mecha-
nism by which this potentially fatal toxicity occurs
is unknown, but is thought to be idiosyncratic
(Saba et al., 2020). Careful monitoring of thoracic
radiographs for the development of pulmonary

223	Glucocorticoid Therapy in Oncology
fibrosis is advised during and after therapy with
rabacfosadine (Saba et al., 2020), as at least two
reported cases had subjective improvement of
appearance on radiographs after discontinuation of
rabacfosadine and the addition of prednisone and,
in one case, a bronchodilator (Thamm et al., 2017;
Saba et al., 2018).
Immunotherapy is becoming more and more
commonplace in veterinary oncology. GCs typically
are not used concurrently with immunotherapy
approaches so as not to dampen immune responses,
but in some cases must be used in cases of severe
toxicity. One example is in CAR T therapy, which
has been investigated in dogs (Mata et al., 2014;
Panjwani et al., 2016); prednisone has been shown
to ablate CAR T cells (Davila et al., 2014) so GC
use is avoided, when possible, if not needed for
treatment of severe toxicity.
Acute radiation dermatitis happens to the majority
of patients receiving fractionated radiotherapy and
occurs due to epithelial cell death, eicosanoid-medi-
ated vasodilation, and release of pro-inflammatory
mediators such as prostaglandins, leukotrienes, IL-1
and IL-6, TNF-α, and reactive oxygen species (Flynn
et al., 2007; Hegedus et al., 2017). GC therapy is
advocated to treat radiation dermatitis and is used by
the majority of veterinarians as a preventive for radia-
tion dermatitis (Flynn and Lurie, 2007); however, an
anti-inflammatory dose of prednisone (0.5 mg/kg
daily) did not cause a significant decrease in dermati-
tis severity, clinically or histopathologically, versus
patients receiving placebo in a study of 22 dogs
(Flynn et al., 2007). In the latter study, there was no
difference in the incidence of localized bacterial infec-
tions between the two groups (Flynn et al., 2007).
Patient-directed effects
Quality of life (QOL) is a major factor that deter-
mines whether pet owners will choose to pursue
cancer therapy for their pet, whether they will
continue therapy once started, and whether they
are happy that they elected cancer therapy (Slater
et al., 1996; Mellanby et al., 2003; Tzannes et al.,
2007; Iliopoulou et al., 2013; Giuffrida and
Kerrigan, 2014; Vøls et al., 2017; Williams et al.,
2017; Fan et al., 2018; Thornton et al., 2018). GCs
can help to improve QOL by palliation of clinical
signs of cancer, including anorexia, fatigue, and
pain. Many owners of terminally ill pets value
QOL of their pet over extended survival times
(Oyama et al., 2008; Giuffrida and Kerrigan,
2014), so focusing on patient-centered outcomes
such as QOL is of paramount importance. However,
it is extremely important to note that the use of
GCs should be avoided until a cancer diagnosis has
been achieved (Jeffery, 2014).
Appetite is a primary determinant of a pet own-
er’s interpretation of their pet’s QOL (Williams
et al., 2017). The act of feeding is itself an act of
caring, and pet owners enjoy the positive interac-
tions that come with feeding (Johannes and Musser,
2019). Thus, loss of appetite is one of the most
common clinical signs listed by clients when con-
sidering humane euthanasia for their pets (Gates
et al., 2017). Anorexia, hyporexia, and dysrexia are
common clinical signs observed in canine and feline
cancer patients (Johannes and Musser, 2019) and
anorexia and weight loss have been reported to be
negative prognostic factors for survival in dogs and
cats with cancer (Baez et al., 2007; van Stee et al.,
2015; Barber and Weishaar, 2016; Romano et al.,
2016; Sogame et al., 2018) Polyphagia is a well-
recognized side effect of GC therapy (Kovalik
et al., 2012) and in the short term may improve
appetite. The improvement in appetite seen with
GC used may be due to the “euphoric effect” of
steroids (Moertel et al., 1974).
Fatigue or lethargy is also commonly reported at
the time of diagnosis of cancer, or during cancer
therapy. Studies in humans with cancer have dem-
onstrated improvements in patient-reported fatigue
with GC treatment (Begley et al., 2016). While pet
owners may note benefits such as increased energy
level with GC therapy, these benefits may be illu-
sory as the boost in energy is gained through cata-
bolic effects (Jeffery, 2014). However if cancer
diagnosis has been achieved, and GCs are used as a
short-term palliative effect in patients with cancer,
the benefit likely outweighs the risk.
It has been estimated that 30% of canine and
feline oncology patients have significant pain at the
time of diagnosis (Lascelles, 2013). GCs can sup-
press inflammation and can also induce a state of
euphoria, so they may be used to palliate cancer
pain in dogs and cats (Behrend and Kemppainen,
1997; Lascelles, 2013). GCs are considered to be
the most effective treatment against inflammatory
pain in people (Leppert and Buss, 2012), and are
used commonly by veterinarians to manage pain
(Jeffery, 2014). They reduce cancer-associated pain
intensity by inhibiting prostaglandin synthesis and
reducing vascular permeability (Leppert and Buss,
2012). They also reduce peritumoral edema, which

-- 239 of 258 --

can reduce pain in brain tumors and tumors caus-
ing spinal cord compression (Jeffery, 2014). In the
treatment of cancer, the use of GCs to treat pain is
cautioned since their use may lead to delayed or
incorrect diagnosis if diagnosis has not yet been
achieved, may alter lab parameters and thyroid
function testing, and could potentially increase risk
of infection (Jeffery, 2014).
In humans, GCs are also used as prophylaxis to
reduce the secondary effects of chemotherapy such
as chemotherapy-induced nausea and vomiting
(Rutz, 2002). Although the mechanisms by which
this occurs are poorly understood, hypotheses
include the anti-inflammatory actions of GCs; the
reduction in 5-hydroxytryptamine (5-HT) that may
block serotonin receptors in the vagal nerve com-
plexes that transmit the vomiting response; inhibi-
tion of prostaglandins and substance P, reducing
pain; direct effects on brain centers; and maintain-
ing physiologic levels of GCs, as low levels have
been linked to nausea and vomiting (Hursti et al.,
1993; Mantovani et al., 1997; Rhen and Cidlowski,
2005; Pufall, 2015). While GCs have not been
shown to prevent chemotherapy-induced nausea or
vomiting in veterinary patients, this remains an
area in which further investigation is warranted,
given the widespread use in humans.
GCs have also been used prior to myelosuppres-
sive chemotherapy in people to prevent chemother-
apy-induced hematologic toxicity (Rinehart et al.,
2003; Leggas et al., 2009). GC therapy decreases
the proportion of marrow colony-forming units of
granulocytic/monocytic lineage, which is thought
to reduce the number of hematopoietic progenitors
at risk for damage by chemotherapy (Kriegler
et al., 1994).
A study was undertaken to evaluate pretreat-
ment dexamethasone as a preventive for chemo-
therapy-induced neutropenia in dogs receiving
lomustine, a cell cycle nonspecific alkylating agent.
The study failed to find a decrease in frequency of
severe neutropenia (Intile et al., 2009). Cell cycle
specific drugs may be better suited to this type of
protective therapy and should be investigated.

CABI – who we are and what we do
This book is published by CABI, an international not-for-proft organisation that improves
people’s lives worldwide by providing information and applying scientifc expertise to solve
problems in agriculture and the environment.
CABI is also a global publisher producing key scientifc publications, including world
renowned databases, as well as compendia, books, ebooks and full text electronic
resources. We publish content in a wide range of subject areas including: agriculture and
crop science / animal and veterinary sciences / ecology and conservation / environmental
science / horticulture and plant sciences / human health, food science and nutrition /
international development / leisure and tourism.
The profts from CABI’s publishing activities enable us to work with farming communities
around the world, supporting them as they battle with poor soil, invasive species and pests and
diseases, to improve their livelihoods and help provide food for an ever growing population.
CABI is an international intergovernmental organisation, and we gratefully acknowledge the
core fnancial support from our member countries (and lead agencies) including:
Ministry of Agriculture
People’s Republic of China
Discover more
To read more about CABI’s work, please visit: www.cabi.org
Browse our books at: www.cabi.org/bookshop,
or explore our online products at: www.cabi.org/publishing-products
Interested in writing for CABI? Find our author guidelines here:
www.cabi.org/publishing-products/information-for-authors/
